has had a tunnel cut through to allow for more convenient passage into Italy from one side to the other. And truly, although the French—since they found a way to open a much shorter and easier path through Mount Genèvre—have never used this narrow passage again; it nevertheless remains intact today and will undoubtedly remain until the end of the world, because it is carved almost entirely into the living rock. It takes approximately two hours to pass through it completely. Loaded pack-mules can be driven through it with ease. The only thing that makes it somewhat inconvenient is that without burning torches, one cannot see a hand in front of one's face. In the attached map, you can see that mountain with its long passage depicted from life. The second of those strong rivers that water Piedmont is the *Tanaro*, the third is the *Stura*—which generously shares its name with a large valley called the *Val de Stura* <note>Valley of the Stura</note>—and the last is the *Doria*. Meanwhile, besides all these, there are more than twenty-eight significant streams which bedew the land from all sides in competition with one another, causing such unbelievable fertility that, although Italy has always been praised as the richest and most abundant land in the entire world, people are still accustomed to hearing this common and ancient proverb about these two:

->If Italy were ever a delicious lamb,<-
->I would take rich Piedmont for its choice kidneys.<-

Various beautiful valleys, such as the aforementioned *Stura*, *Susa*, and others, form the outermost borders of Piedmont on its northern side. To the west, you have all the regions of which we generally speak in this work under the name of the *Piedmontese Valleys*, *Valleys of Angrogna*, and often simply as the *Valleys*; these include the Valleys of *Lucerna*, *Perouse*, and *St. Martin*. To these must be added the Alpine Valley of *Cluson* or *Pragela* on this side, which belongs to Piedmont in terms of location, but is part of the princely fiefdom of France in terms of ownership.

<margin>The ancient coat of arms and motto of the Valley of Lucerna.</margin>
The *Valleys of Lucerna*, to begin with those, have from time immemorial carried as their coat of arms a lighted torch in the midst of thick darkness, along with this motto: *Lux lucet in tenebris* <note>original Latin: "Lux lucet in tenebris"</note>, "The light shines in the darkness." From this, they undoubtedly obtained their name *Lucerna*—that is, "Lamp" or "Candle" (O, what a wonderful omen for those whom God would cause to shine in those places without ever being extinguished!). The name does not come from the watercourse *Lucerna*, which flows gently down to it from the commune of *Roras*. The valley is fifteen hours, or Piedmontese miles, in length. Its width, like that of all the others, is not uniform throughout. It contains within its bosom the communes of *Garcillane*, *Campiglon*, *Fenil*, *Bubbiana*, *Lucerna*, *Roras*, *St. John*, *Angrogna*, *La Tour*, *Villar*, and *Bobbio*. To the west, it has the mountain *Col-de-la-croix* ("Cross-Pass"), from which the river *Pelice*—which waters nearly the entire valley—comes rushing down, serving as a partition from the *Queyras* Valley. The first five mentioned communes are located mostly on a plain toward the side of *Turin* and *Saluzzo*; from these, as well as from the land of *Bricherasio* (situated between *Fenil*, *San Secondo*, *St. John*, and *Angrogna*), the persecution of the year 1655 finally drove out every last one of the poor Evangelical believers.

<margin>The commune of Roras.</margin>
The commune of *Roras* is the smallest of all and lies to the south of *Lucerna*, extending toward Mount *Viso* and ending against the Alps of *Frioland* and *Sella Bianca*. It is enclosed in a glen that is only just wide enough for the Lucerna stream to flow through from the Alps. It is remarkably mountainous and filled with cliffs; however, in all the ground between them that the plow...

# General Memorial

and furthers agriculture, is abundant in everything and very fruitful. For in the lowlands grow many vines and all kinds of other fruits; from about the middle to very high (it is four French leagues long, or to speak more accurately, high) a great multitude of chestnuts, much grain-work and other fodder; and the remaining heights provide for about eight or ten weeks a very suitable pasture, where they diligently drive the cattle as soon as the land begins to be stripped of its long-lasting snow by the warmth.

<margin>The Community of St. John</margin>
That of *St. John* <note>San Giovanni</note> would be a small earthly paradise, were it not that it was occupied nearby by Turin and so to the South and East by Roman Catholics <note>original: "Algemeeniſten", meaning "Universalists," a term used by Dutch Protestants to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note> and various monasteries, which always keep the door open for all those who seek to fall upon or surprise them, and who never stop causing them much trouble. It has a wonderfully beautiful plain, surrounded to the South by pleasant meadows, which all stretch out equally toward the Pelice <note>The Pellice River</note>, which flows and plays against them. The rest of it is an excellent field; but at the same time field, arable land, vineyard, and pleasure garden. Namely, the grapevine, or rather, fine branches are laid very high across the trees or tied so neatly over vineyard-slats that they, two by two or three by three, interwoven from one tree to another, or for lack thereof along the said rafters over cords stretched on both sides, hold fast to one another and thus create a very pleasant trellis-work, or leafy cradles. Under which they then also, in their own manner with oxen, practice their farming and subsequently are accustomed to gather the most beautiful wheat in the world in great abundance at the proper time. All the roads, pathways, and boundary markers of each person's property are very pleasantly lined, as if edged, with all kinds of fruit and especially with a great number of mulberry trees, with which the inhabitants raise their silkworms—the most certain of all their income; from which they inevitably make the most money, with which they pay their taxes. This same plain is accompanied and honored on the East and North by a very pleasant "Side-walk" (as they call it), that is, with the most excellent little hills one can imagine; there is nothing else but continuous vineyard paths, in whose shadow they likewise win much corn and all kinds of garden crops <note>original: "Hant-vrugten", literally "hand-fruits," referring to produce grown by manual labor or in gardens</note> in abundance. It is interspersed on all sides with a sufficient supply of very excellent fruit and watered everywhere from the Angrogna brook by an ingenious water-pipe as the situation requires.

<margin>The Community of Angrogna</margin>
The Community of *Angrogna* begins exactly at that place where the mentioned "Side-walk" of *St. John* ends and goes ever further and further upwards to the North, until it finally borders against the Alps *la Vakera, Seyan, la Cella, la Cella Veglia* and *Infernet*. It seems to have clearly received its name from a certain small water, or winter brook of that name, which runs down from the aforementioned Alps. It has an uncommon space; and being mountainous throughout, it divides itself into several small valleys, like a tree into its branches. It bears no wine, except only a little in the neighborhood of the "Side-walk" of *St. John*; but it fills that lack with beautiful chestnuts, all kinds of other good fruits and especially animal fodder which consistently grow there in abundance to an incredible height.

<margin>The Natural Strength of Angrogna</margin>
The Lord our God, who had specifically ordained this region to be a theater for His wondrous deeds and a city of refuge for the Ark of His Covenant <note>A metaphor common in Reformed literature for the true Church and its preservation</note>, has also shared an uncommon strength in its nature for that purpose. Namely, this community can be approached from below in only two places: one on the South side and that of Lucerna, the other on the West and that of Bricherasio. Additionally, from all ages past, it has had just as many gates in these two approaches, which one could very easily secure and garrison with only two or three men.

### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

...hold. And even if the violence, betrayal, or craftiness of the enemies had managed to seize these paths from them, these poor people would only have to retreat about half an hour higher to a place called the *Barricade*, or *Street-fort*, to find safety. For there the valley narrows like a neck and is at once very cramped and filled with large cliffs. Indeed, where these cliffs do not seem sufficient to cut off all access, a thick wall has been built across the gap, constructed quite wondrously of large cobblestones without lime or sand, which rain can never cause to collapse. Thus, since these walls serve the fugitives as well-fortified strongholds, there is not the slightest opening to approach them there. What is more, if the enemy were too quick for them even here and prevented them from fleeing to this spot, they found a shelter on Mount *La Vachera*, which is the exact center of those three valleys, as wondrous as it is safe. They sheltered in that stronghold, from which all the cunning and rage of such great and mighty enemies could never drive them or conquer them—as this work shall later confirm—following the massacre of the year 1655. On the contrary, with the aid of the Fear of the God of Jacob <note>A biblical reference to divine protection</note>, they have so often and so successfully launched sorties against the enemy that they regained and subsequently held all the valley positions they had completely lost through the treachery of the Marquis of Pianezza <note>Andrea Gastaldo, Marquis of Pianezza, led the 1655 massacre known as the Piedmontese Easter</note>. And finally, to provide those poor sheep with housing even in the utmost need, it seems as if Nature itself <note>original: "d'Algemeen-aart", the "General Nature" or the Creator of nature</note> has used all diligence to build and strengthen a certain place for them called *Pré du Tour* (Meadow of the Tower) as a final refuge; just as it did in fact serve as a sufficient protection for them in the years 1560 and 1561 against that terrible Spanish and Papal army, which had eagerly joined that of their Prince *Emanuel Philibert* to utterly root them out under the leadership of the Count de *la Trinité*. Specifically, it is a hollow, surrounded by nearly inaccessible mountains, situated west of La Vachera, which can only be reached with great difficulty along a single path, which in several places is even carved into the rock. And though it is located on the banks of the Angrogna, it can nevertheless, in times of trouble, accommodate a large number of people within its gaping expanse. It is for this reason, among others, that the old *Barbes* <note>The "Barbes" (Occitan for "uncles") were the traditional itinerant pastors of the Waldensians</note>, or shepherds of souls in the Valleys, always taught freely there and held their assemblies even during the thickest darkness and the heaviest persecutions. In these meetings, they instructed all those who dedicated and prepared themselves for the Holy Ministry. From their ranks, until the time of the Reformation, they drew most of the church ministers, whom they usually dispatched to far-off lands to preach the Gospel and to establish and maintain new churches. From here also, the clever youth were sent to the Valleys for their studies, as we shall see proven in the following chapter and elsewhere, if God wills.

While the community of Angrogna possesses such excellent qualities alone, it is no wonder that various historians and geographers, unaware of this division of the Valleys, have made of it not only a distinct valley but even the most prominent of all, causing the others to be subsumed under its name, or that of the *Angrogna Valleys*; as can be commonly noted by everyone in the histories of the Lord Chairman Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian</note> and others.

<meta>This page continues the geographic and strategic description of the Waldensian valleys, moving from the area around the "Barricade" in Angrogna toward the communities of Villar and Bobbio, and then shifting to the Perosa Valley.</meta>

# General Memoir

not far from the mutual confluence of the aforementioned Pellice and Angrogna <note>The Pellice and Angrogna are the two primary rivers of these Alpine valleys.</note> had been erected and was razed to the ground by King Francis I. In its place, the Duke of Savoy, following the massacre of the year 1655, established a firm fortress or castle, by which means he might subdue those miserable people <note>original: "bek af mogte spelen," an idiom meaning to exhaust or render someone powerless</note> whenever it pleased him; as happened in the years 1663 and 1664, when things came very close to that. This community, as well as that of *Villar*, which is situated just behind it along the same stream, has few plains; yet it produces much wine and all kinds of fruits. For just as on its southern sides nothing but chestnuts and cattle-fodder can grow, because the mountain that borders it is very high and overhanging, taking away almost all the sunshine with its long shadow; so on its northern hills, though they are quite harsh, there grows a great abundance of wine even at high altitudes, and where that stops, wheat and fodder.

<margin>The Community of Bobbio.</margin>
Bobbio is the highest community of the Luserna Valley toward the side of the Dauphiné <note>The Dauphiné was then a province of France; this area was a frequent crossing point for refugees and soldiers.</note>, which splits and divides itself into several beautiful branches and noteworthy valleys toward the south, west, and north. In the lowlands it yields an abundance of wine; and where the land becomes so high and cold that no vineyard can be maintained, it yields no less corn and hay, provided only that a channel <note>An irrigation ditch or "bief" used to divert mountain water to the fields.</note> can be made to carry the water from the mountain peaks for the necessary moistening of the fields. But to depart from this valley, look here at all the Alpine mountains which surround the aforementioned communities on all sides, except toward the east, or downward, and especially that of Bobbio, like so many boundary stones: namely those of *Jane*, *Liozze*, *Pis* (bordering this is the valley called *Val Guicchard* and *la Combe des Charboniers*), the beautiful mountain range of *Pra*, through which the frequently mentioned path *Col de la Croix* <note>The "Pass of the Cross," a vital mountain pass between Italy and France.</note> runs, forming the divide between the Valleys of Queyras and Luserna; and further south those of *Pis*, *Crosenne*, *Blanchet*, and *Julian*.

<margin>The Valley of Perosa.</margin>
The Valley of Perosa takes its name from a hamlet extended upon its heights, or rather from a fortress of the same name, very well situated on a small hill at the upper end of the said village, so as to conveniently command the confluence of the Chisone and Germanasca and the approaches to the Valleys of St. Martin and Chisone. It is ten Piedmontese miles in length and has very few flat fields. The aforementioned Chisone flows through it sideways; into which the Germanasca discharges and loses its water along with its name. The southern and flood-prone part of this valley is entirely covered by the barren shadow of the mountains, which completely prevents the sun from reaching it. For this reason, it yields little wine; but in its stead, much fruit and beautiful meadows for cattle. This part belongs entirely to the Duke of Savoy. But the most pleasant and best part, being on this side of the water and having the most favorable sun—and consequently being incomparably more abundant in wine—has remained the property of His Majesty of France <note>Louis XIV</note>, along with the city of Pinerolo, by the treaty of the year 1633. And while this part, with its heights, borders the Valley of Chisone (belonging to the Dauphiné), and since the King no longer possesses the path of Susa or that of the Marquisate of Saluzzo; His Majesty uses it as a route to the mentioned Pinerolo, in order to always be able to enter Italy through it. This valley includes the communities of *Portes*, *St. Germain*, *Pramol*, *Villars*, *Pinache*, and *Perosa*, almost all of the same quality as the aforementioned Torre and Villar of the Luserna Valley. Only the small community of Pramol, enclosed between the mountains of St. Martin and Angrogna above that of St. Germain, has this distinction: that it is very difficult to access and, producing very little wine only in the low areas, is otherwise found to be very suitable for grain-work and meadows.

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.
G 2
<meta>catchword: the.</meta>

<margin>The partition between the two mentioned Valleys.</margin>
Between the Valleys of Luserna and Perosa, situated slightly toward Pinerolo and San Secondo, lie the small communities of Prarustin, Saint Bartholomew, and Roche-platte. The first of these, along with a portion of the second—though both are quite steep and overhanging—are essentially nothing more than a single vineyard-covered mountain; the remainder of the latter and the third community produce only fodder, chestnuts, and very little grain.

<margin>The Valley of Saint Martin.</margin>
The Valley of Saint Martin is so named after a desolate place of that name, where the fallen stone heaps of an old church, formerly dedicated to that supposed saint, can still be seen. It is about fifteen miles long and borders at its foot, or eastward, on the Valley of Perosa; westward on that of Queyras in the Dauphiné <note>The Dauphiné was a province in southeastern France.</note>; northward on that of Chisone; and southward partly on that of Luserna and partly on Pramollo. It has almost no width beyond what the Germanasca river occupies as it washes through it. Regarding its fertility, it is much like the community of Bobbio, though slightly more difficult; the lower parts provide good wine and other fruits; the middle is well-supplied with beautiful chestnuts, and the peaks with nutritious fodder. It also branches out into several larger and more beautiful arms, which are like so many little valleys, each making up a particular community; such as those at the highest elevations: Prali, Rodoretto, Macel, and Salza; somewhat lower on the northern side: Maniglia, Perrero, Saint Martin, and Bovile; and finally toward the south: Faetto and Riclaretto. Moreover, it is the strongest <note>Meaning the most easily defended or naturally fortified.</note> of all the other valleys. For, except from above along the high mountains that bound it on all sides—which for eight or ten months of the year become almost entirely impassable due to an unspeakable multitude of eternal snows—one can enter nowhere except through a narrow gap called <term>the Tower Bridge</term> <note>original: "le Pont de la Tour"</note>, which is carved out of a stone rock. This gap is only just wide enough for the aforementioned Germanasca river to barely press through with its roaring current. Over this gap there actually lies a bridge of unbelievable height, fixed on both sides to terrifying cliffs upon which the border-mountains of the valley lean; and through which, with great labor, a path has been made that is only wide enough for a single mule to pass, or for a horse to be led by hand. Thus, it is entirely unthinkable and impossible to attempt to attack it in any way if the said bridge (which can be done very easily) is broken down and prevented from being replaced by another. Even the women—however excellent a work it may be—could very easily accomplish this alone, if they simply rolled moderate-sized cobblestones down from those rocky heights to cast down anyone who might recklessly attempt to approach. The Alps, which embrace it on all sides except for its eastern lowland, are <italic>the Sea, Bianca, la Calancia, la Balma, Giuliano, Bodelcol,</italic> and <italic>le Pies</italic>. But what is most wonderful is that seven pleasant water pools shine atop the highest peaks of those mountains which are thrust between the Valley of Luserna and this one like a partition wall.

In all the valleys, and most especially in that of Saint Martin, very wild and high-reaching forests generally cover the largest mountains and the most inaccessible rocks. The ground there is also so thickly covered with hawthorn that it has never been cleared by anyone. From these forests they gather much turpentine, pitch, and resin from fir trees, called by the Italians <term>fir-tree tears</term> <note>original: "Lagrima Sapino"</note>, and in the apothecary shops very incorrectly named, in my opinion, <term>Venetian Turpentine</term>. This substance has been found to have wonderful powers for the discharging of gravel, the breaking of stones <note>Referring to kidney or bladder stones, a common medical preoccupation of the era.</note>, the cleansing of the kidneys, and the removal of all evil sores, both internal and external.

# General Memorial Script

...side. It swarms everywhere with an unusual number of white hares, which never, as in other countries, turn grey again in the summer; but they are even somewhat smaller and less flavorful than the common ones. The area teems everywhere with an unusual abundance of **white hares**, which, unlike those in other countries, never turn gray-brown in the summer; however, they are somewhat smaller and have a poorer taste than the common variety. Many foxes, very large pheasants, as well as white and other field-hens are also found there. <margin>Of the damage caused by bears.</margin>

# General Memoir

They keep themselves atop the peaks of the inaccessible mountains, where the snow can never completely thaw; and they usually sleep on the ice, which likewise never fully melts. They far exceed the Chamois <note>original: "Sjamois"</note> in speed. The peasants themselves, who commonly eat their meat, derive from it—I know not what—a wondrous nimbleness of body and thereby become especially swift-footed. What is more, when they find themselves somewhat unwell, they take but a few drops of Ibex <note>original: "Boeketijns," referring to the Alpine Ibex or Steinbock</note> blood in meat broth or wine and immediately go to lie down warmly; by which they quickly begin to sweat and subsequently regain their previous health. Wondering greatly at this, I also once took a little of that congealed blood (for it can be kept good as long as one wishes) and broke it into a little wine; and having poured it onto a full basin of other clotted or curdled blood, I found that it returned to its original liquid state in an instant and became such as if it had only just been drawn fresh from its veins. After which experience, both I and anyone else can now easily guess how it must come to work within the human body.

<margin>And of the Jumarts.</margin>
So much then for the wild game that is produced nowhere else. Among all the tame animals, I find only the *Jumarts* <note>A legendary hybrid animal long believed to be the offspring of a bull and a horse or donkey; modern biology recognizes such a cross as impossible.</note> to be entirely unknown in these northern regions. They are bred from a Bull and a Mare, or from a Bull and a She-Ass; of which the former are somewhat stouter and are called *Bas*, while the latter are somewhat more slender and are called *Bis*. The former also have, almost like pigs, the lower jaw slightly more recessed than the upper, and such that the lower row of front teeth sits fully a thumb- or two-finger-breadth deeper than the upper teeth; these [the *Bis*], by contrast, have lower jaws much longer, like hares or rabbits, and their teeth project much further out. So that neither of them can ever graze comfortably in any meadows, except those in which the grass has shot up so high that they can cut it off with their tongues: which, however, with respect to the length of their jaws, can be done sooner by one than by the other. <margin>Curiosities of the Mountains.</margin>
People also come from very far away, from Italy as well as France, to pick many and various medicinal herbs and flowers on these mountains, which can hardly be obtained in other places with the same or appropriate potency. Indeed, it is held there that, among others, the excellent *Moonwort* <note>original: "Maan-ruyten"; a type of fern traditionally associated with alchemy and medicine</note> is found there in abundance. The mountains are also quite high and densely covered with tasty strawberries and black *bilberries* <note>original: "Herefes," likely a local name for the Alpine blueberry or bilberry</note> (a small fruit so named) which are round, the size of peas, and grow abundantly year in and year out on small, low shrubs that resemble the Boxwood <note>original: "Palm"</note> very closely in every respect. They are exceptionally good to the taste and at the same time possess a powerful ability to treat the slow dysentery <note>original: "bloet-loop," literally "blood-run"</note>.

<margin>Wonders of the Small Carline Thistle.</margin>
But what I have often marveled at most is actually a kind of artichoke called *White Carline Thistle* <note>original: "Witten Ever-wortel"; Carlina acaulis</note> or *Sjardouffe*; which, with its unstemmed head, about as thick as a large turnip, always remains crouched against the earth and has its surrounding leaves serrated and armed everywhere with sharp-stinging thorns. It is a delicious food and a precious sugar-preserve <note>original: "Infuykerfel"; likely a medicinal syrup or candied root</note>, also serving as a powerful antidote against the poisonous Plague. The peasants also have this additional benefit from it—which is quite marvelous—that they have in it a reliable weather-indicator <note>original: "Weer-beduyder"</note> at all times. This is not only while the plant still stands in the ground and draws its nourishment from it, but even after it has been picked, brought into their houses, and, according to their old custom, fixed entirely flat against a wall. For let it be as dry as it will, even for several [years]...

# General Memorial-Chronicle

...years old; it is certain (I have found it myself more than a thousand times) that the leaves, which grow thickly around the said bud, will close over it like a purse, or embrace and cover it like a hand, two or three days before the rain; and again, about just as long beforehand, they will bloom, open wide, and completely expose the bud when the weather is about to clear and become more beautiful.

All these Valleys, Hills, and Mountains are also consistently sown with beautiful and living water-springs; their streams are rich only in Trout <note>original: "Vooren"</note> and some Perch, which can by no means be considered the poorest of fish.

But so that the Reader does not incautiously conclude from all the aforementioned that the Tower-meadow (*Pré du Tour*) or the Community of *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angronje"; a central stronghold for the Waldensian resistance</note> have at all times been the only hiding places of the Divine Ark of the Covenant <note>A metaphor for the true Church or the presence of God's word</note>, nor unknowingly rob several places in all the other Valleys of the rightful honor that God has bestowed upon them in this regard; he should please take note here that in the Valley of *Luserna* <note>original: "Lucerna"</note> the entire Dale, or the Community of *Rora*, which currently still shelters one of the Valley Congregations alongside that of la Tour, the whole land from *St. Margaret’s* Bridge upwards and especially the Valleys *li Tailjaret*, *li Bonnet*, and *li Cabrol*, have always shared this same advantage. For in the said Community, one still sees today very wondrous footprints and remains of this on a certain peak of Mount *Vandelin*, which the Father of the Universe <note>original: "Vader des Algemeyn-aarts"; referring to God as the creator of all</note> had prepared for His children as a strong fortress against all the raging and madness of their enemies; and of which they also made use with all bravery in their greatest need. Namely, there <margin>A wondrous Cave.</margin> is, in a hollow between the ridges of the mentioned mountain, or rather of the Rock *Vandelin*, a wide subterranean cavern, as much by nature as by art entirely hollowed out of a rock, being nearly round and vaulted exactly like an oven, so spacious that between three and four hundred people may comfortably fit inside together. There are even some crevices in the rock that can serve both as windows and as quarters for sentinels. It also has several rooms, a large water-spring, some trees, and an oven to bake bread. One still finds there, among other things, some ancient and decayed pieces of both a kneading trough and a supply chest. This place can be entered in no other way than through a single hole from above, through which one can only be lowered one at a time; who then must slide down uncomfortably along many rocky little steps. So that a single man inside could defend himself with a bare spear or halberd against an entire army.

Now, while in those Valleys other similar beautiful and deep caves also appear everywhere, which very often served those poor people as a refuge—where they, like *the Dove of the Song of Songs* <note>Reference to Song of Solomon 2:14: "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock..."</note> in the crevices of the stone rocks, fled with especially their women and children during the heaviest persecutions, and where the *Barbes* <note>The traditional term for Waldensian pastors or "uncles"</note>, or spiritual caregivers, usually visited them, and even not seldom taught and distributed the Holy signs of Faith <note>The sacraments, likely the Eucharist</note> among them all, just as they often had to do in the forests and other remote places—so it must be noted here once and for all in passing that their evil persecutors took occasion from this alone to accuse them as if they committed all manner of filthiness there together.

To proceed, in the Community of *Villar*, the places *Val Guichard* <note>original: "Giksjard"</note> and *la Combe*; in that of *Bobbio* <note>original: "Boby"</note> all the Valleys and especially *la Comba di Corbonniers*, *Julian*, and *Villeneuve* <note>original: "Ville-neuve"</note> with the hills *la Sarcena*, *le Poy*, *le Pontet*, and some others; in that of *Perosa* <note>original: "Peyrouse"</note> the great *Diblon*, or *Talucco* <note>original: "Taluc"</note>, *Balmats*, *Costabella*, and *le Pevi*, shared the mentioned fortune and honor with the aforementioned.

Among which also in that of *St. Martin* all its branches and Valleys, upwards toward

# Regarding the History of the Waldensian Churches.

H

...extending to the *Rabioes* bridge, especially *Macel*, *Salse*, *Rodoret*, and *Prals*, in which—just as in *Duckira* and other places of the *Comba* or *Faët Valley*—several monuments of such antiquity are still in existence, must rightly be included. This has always been so well known and acknowledged by the Court of Turin that Duke *Emmanuel Philibert* <note>Duke of Savoy (r. 1553–1580), who initially persecuted the Waldensians but later granted them limited tolerance.</note> (of blessed memory), through the same Edict by which—following the bloody wars he waged against the Waldensians in the years 1560 and 1561—he again granted them the right to live peacefully throughout all of *Piedmont* without any public exercise of their religion; nevertheless, he fully and freely granted it to them in the aforementioned places, as well as in the territory covered by the communities of *Angrogna*, *Bobbio*, *Villar*, and *Torre Pellice* <note>original: "Angronje, Boby, Villar en la Tour"</note>, excluding the plain between the two aforementioned villages. Furthermore, among the above-mentioned communities and valleys, he included those of *Saint Martin* and *Perosa*, and finally in that of *Rocheplatte* <note>original: "Rosje-platte"</note> between *Luserna* and *Perosa*, where the boundaries of the Godijns <note>A local term likely referring to the borders of the Waldensian ancestral lands or a specific family/district name.</note> extend. This was granted solely because these places had been used since time immemorial, as that Proclamation states: "usual places for holding sermons, congregations, and other ministries of their religion" <note>original Italian: "luoghi soliti da farnisi Prediche, Congregationi & altri ministeri della loro Religione"</note>; that is, such places where they were accustomed to practice and attend their church teachings, gatherings (this name has been given to our church assemblies since olden times), and other services of their faith.

I can even testify that before the Murder and Burning of the year 1655 <note>Refers to the "Piedmontese Easter," a notorious massacre of Waldensians by the troops of the Duke of Savoy.</note>, I had in my library several writings from old church assemblies, from which it clearly appeared that at that time there was a much larger number of church ministers in those Valleys than there are today. They made mention of the teachers of *Rodoret*, *Macel*, and *Faët* in the Valley of *Saint Martin*; *Taluc*, or great *Diblon*, *Saint Germain*, or *Balmats*, in those of *Perosa* and *Revansjie*, *Tailjaret*, or *Bonnet*, *Bezze*, *Val Giksjard*, and *the Comba di Carbonniers* in *Val Luserna*: all of which places are now attached to others and incorporated into those to be named hereafter. This, to touch upon it in passing, I consider to have occurred primarily because the people, having fallen into dismal poverty, could not bear or endure the burden of taxes and the cost of maintaining so many Ministers of the Word at once.

I do not describe here the beautiful and large Valley of *Cluson* <note>The Chisone Valley</note>, situated adjacent to those of *Saint Martin* and *Perosa*, where likewise by God's grace the Evangelical Truth has been preserved through all ages and still is today. It remains without the slightest mixture of any Roman Catholics <note>original: "Roomse Algemeynisten," a term for Catholics referencing their "Universal" church.</note>, except for one priest living at *Mantoules* who may perform Mass only for his spiritual company or for some travelers (unless one counts that the Council for the extirpation of heretics <note>original Latin: "extirpandis Hæreticis"</note> has recently caused some Jesuits to nestle at *Fenestrelle*). It still nurtures six large and flourishing congregations in its bosom because, sheltering under the wings of the protection of God and Her Great Majesty of France, it has not suffered the terrible persecutions that have so often blown over the heads of its neighbors. Truly, God has preserved them in deep rest, just like the *Queyras* Valley on the side of *Val Luserna*, so that they might serve as a safe sanctuary for the scattered Savoyards of the Ducal Valleys.

<margin>The fourteen remaining Churches of the Valleys.</margin>

That of the community of *San Giovanni* <note>original: "St. Jan"</note>, which until the aforementioned Massacre of the year 1655 also covered those of *Bubbiane*, *Fenil*, *Luserna*, *Campiglione*, *Glon*, and *Garcillane* with its border. 2. That of *Angrogna*. 3. That of *Torre Pellice*. 4. That of *Villar*. 5. That of *Bobbio*. 6. That of *Rora* and finally 7. That of *Rocheplatte*, to which the communities of *Saint Bartholomew* and *Prarostino* equally belong. These seven congregations also [form] a <term>Classis</term> <note>A regional governing body of pastors and elders in the Reformed tradition, similar to a presbytery.</note>, or

# General Historical Record

...or <term>Church Colloquy<note>A regional gathering of church elders and ministers, similar to a presbytery.</note></term>, which together they constitute, and which is usually named after the Valley of *Luserna*. Furthermore, in the Valley of *Perosa* <note>original: "Peyrouſe"</note>, besides the church of *Villar*, there is 8. that of *San Germano*, 9. that of *Pramollo*, 10. that of *Pinache*, and finally 11. that of *La Cappella*, which encompasses only the communities of *Pomaretto* and *Meana* in its jurisdiction. Regarding this, it must be precisely noted that the <term>Overseers<note>The Dutch "Opſienders" here refers to the ministers or pastors of these congregations.</note></term> of these last three have their residence on Royal soil <note>Refers to territory then under the control of the French Crown.</note>, even though they are situated for a large part on the Savoyard ground of the Duke; and consequently, they do not cease to be members of the Valleys' assemblies. Indeed, they cannot be part of the <term>Dauphiné Church Assembly<note>A provincial synod in neighboring France.</note></term>, which belongs under France, because by the Treaty entered into between this Prince and the French Crown in the year 1633—alongside the granted half of the mentioned Valley for free access to their city of *Pinerolo*—it was also understood that regarding church matters, not the slightest thing should be renewed or changed.

Finally, in the Valley of *San Martino*, there are 12. the church of *Villasecca* <note>original: "Ville-ſasje"</note>, composed of the communities of *Faët*, *Ricclaretto*, *San Martino*, *Bovile*, and *Traverse*; 13. that of *Maniglia*, consisting of the communities of *Macello*, *Salse*, and *Cabrant*; and lastly 14. that of *Prali*, of which the community of *Rodoret* also forms a part. Now, these other seven—namely the four from the Valley of *Perosa* and these three from that of *San Martino*—likewise form the "Church Colloquy of the Valleys of *San Martino* and *Perosa*," as they call it. From all of these together arises their <term>Church Assembly<note>The "Kerken-vergadering," or Synod, the highest governing body of the Waldensian Church.</note></term> or "General Meeting," to use their terms, which must be regarded in all respects as a national church gathering or Chief Consistory; as it is not subordinate to any other, it acknowledges no other authority above it.

From ancient times, the congregations of the <term>Cisalpine<note>Meaning "on this side of the Alps," referring to the Italian side.</note></term> Valley of *Chisone* <note>original: "Cluſon"</note>, or *Pragela*, and those of the <term>Transalpine<note>Meaning "across the Alps," referring to the French side.</note></term> *Queyras*, were always of one and the same Faith, and were likewise fellow members of one and the same *Piedmontese* Church Assembly. (The supreme Bishopric of *Turin*, under which the said Valleys of *Piedmont* lie, still extends today far beyond the Valley of *Cesana* to the Mountain of *Genevre*). This continued even during all the time that they simultaneously acknowledged French rule. But finally, with the beginning of the conquest and dominion of the House of Savoy, this mutual communion came to an end.

Here, a description would still be lacking of the *Marquisate of Saluzzo* and especially of its dales and hills, which for a long time were for the Believers like a narrow *Goshen* in Egypt <note>A biblical reference to the fertile land where the Israelites were protected during the plagues; used here to describe a place of refuge.</note>; as well as the Valley of *Susa* alongside its dales of *Meana* and *Mattie*. In these places, within human memory, a small Gospel light always continued to burn most miraculously, until about the year 1603. At that time, through the Edicts of the namesake grandfather of the Prince *Charles Emmanuel* <note>Charles Emmanuel II (r. 1638–1675) was the ruling Duke at the time of this writing; his grandfather was Charles Emmanuel I (r. 1580–1630).</note>—who by God's grace is currently ruling—the light was completely extinguished by the total expulsion of all non-Catholics, as will be mentioned more broadly in this writing. This is all the more significant as both these dales, lying under ancient Lombardy (that is, Cisalpine France, or *Piedmont*), will necessarily be counted and understood by everyone under the name and number of its Valleys. But since that <term>Lampstand<note>A metaphor for a local church, derived from the Book of Revelation.</note></term> has now been entirely removed from there, I shall only add here that the congregations gathered there were always considered merely as branches of those in the aforementioned Valleys of *Luserna*, *Perosa*, *San Martino*, and *Pragela*, as they were almost constantly provided for by their pastors. It would furthermore be unnecessary to speak of them at length, since in the map of the Valleys included at the beginning, they all—or at least the aforementioned *Meana* and *Mattie*—because they are situated too far away...

### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
#### CHAPTER II.

...and are separated by too great a distance from the others, they could not be easily reviewed by the reader. However, we shall abundantly add a word or two about them in the final part of this work, when we bring to light the deadly Persecutions that have so cruelly plagued them. These persecutions finally banished, exterminated, scattered, and drove out all the <term>Right-believing<note>The author uses "Regt-gelovige" (Right-believing) and "Regt-finnige" (Right-minded) to refer to the Waldensian Protestants, whom he considers the keepers of the true, orthodox faith.</note></term> from those places—as well as from Sicily, Calabria, Puglia, the Kingdom of Naples, and other parts of Italy—where they had already remained wonderfully established for many centuries.

<margin>Number of Inhabitants.</margin>
Regarding the number of inhabitants of the aforementioned *Piedmontese Valleys*, I will only add here that there is no truth to what a certain *Giovanni Botero Benese* <note>Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617) was an Italian thinker and priest; his "Universal Relations" was a famous geographical and statistical work of the era.</note> dared to assert in his book, titled *Universal Relations* <note>original: "Relationi Vniversali"</note>, printed in Venice in the year 1639. He claimed *that the Valley of Luserna alone could count twenty-five thousand souls; of which only five thousand would profess the Roman religion and the remaining twenty thousand would be heretics*, as it pleases him to call them. For the place mentioned is not nearly so populous as he pretends, and the non-Romans <note>The Protestants.</note> hardly reach half of the number that he has so clearly stated. He even adds further that he believes they have grown disproportionately in multitude since the conquest of the Valleys by the High Commander *Lesdiguières* <note>François de Bonne, Duke of Lesdiguières, a French military leader who campaigned in the region.</note>, because *soldiers (he says) at that time seized the Most Holy Sacrament with unconsecrated hands and carried it around everywhere, crying out loudly: who wants to buy their God?* These are trifles and shameless lies, which in their land <note>Refers to Catholic territories.</note> are regarded as nothing but "holy and highly meritorious deceptions," and therefore they will frequently be exposed and uncovered in this writing. 

In the Valleys of *St. Martin* and *Perosa* <note>original: "Peyrouſe"</note>, the number of the Right-minded is also no greater than that of the Valley of Luserna, being only between seven and eight thousand people. I myself had to have very accurate census lists made for the purpose of the <term>Collection of Money<note>This refers to the international aid raised for the Waldensians after the "Piedmontese Easter" massacres of 1655.</note></term> following the horrible murders committed against them, as the funds had to be distributed and shared with each of them, person by person. Furthermore, in all those aforementioned Valleys of *Piedmont*, one could not conveniently bring more than four or five thousand men to arms at most. What is more, in all the strangest battles, of which we shall speak hereafter in the final part, their bands—or "flying army," as we call it—were never stronger than fifteen hundred souls, and even then only once or twice at most. For the most part, they were a good half weaker than that, because the remaining people had to serve as necessary garrisons for each of their own Valleys and communities. Thus, we shall be able to see hereafter that they very often enjoyed the promise found in **Leviticus 26**: *five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred of you shall chase ten thousand, and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword*; and even at times that of **Deuteronomy 32**: *one shall chase a thousand, and two shall chase ten thousand*, in actual fact and according to the very letter of the text.

<margin>*Number of Inhabitants.*</margin>
Concerning the number of inhabitants of the said *Piedmontese Valleys*, I will only add here that there is no truth in what a certain *Giovanni Botero Benese* <note>Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617) was an influential Italian diplomat and priest; his *Relationi Universali* was a famous geographical survey.</note> dared to assert in his book titled *Universal Relations* <note>original: "Relationi Universali"</note> and printed in Venice in the year 1639: namely, that the *Lucerna Valley* alone could count twenty-five thousand souls, of which only five thousand allegedly profess the *Roman Religion* and the remaining twenty thousand were *Heretics*, as he chooses to call them. For the place mentioned is by no means as populous as he claims, and the *non-Romans* hardly reach half of the number he has clearly stated, even though he adds that he believes *that they have increased incomparably in multitude since the conquest of the Valleys by the Commander-in-Chief Lesdiguières <note>The Duke of Lesdiguières was a French military leader who led troops through the Piedmont; he eventually converted from Protestantism to Catholicism.</note>, because the soldier (he says) at that time seized the most Holy Sacrament with unholy hands and carried it about everywhere and showed it, crying aloud: "Who wants to buy their God?"* These are nonsense and shameless lies, which in their land are regarded as nothing but "holy and meritorious deceptions," and for that reason, they will often be exposed and refuted in this writing. In the Valleys of St. Martin and Perouse, the number of the Right-minded <note>The author's term for the Waldensian/Protestant population.</note> is also no greater than that of the Lucerna Valley, being only between seven and eight thousand people; of which I myself had to have very accurate name-tables made for the purpose of the Collection of Funds <note>This refers to the massive international relief effort, notably supported by Oliver Cromwell, following the 1655 massacres known as the "Piedmontese Easter."</note> conducted for them after the gruesome murders, as these funds had to be distributed and shared with each person, head by head. Nevertheless, in all those aforementioned Valleys of *Piedmont*, one could not conveniently bring more than four or five thousand men to arms at the most. Furthermore, in all the most remarkable Battles that we shall speak of hereafter in the final Part, their bands—or "flying army," as we call it—were never stronger than fifteen hundred souls, and even that only once or twice at most; for the most part, they were a good half weaker, because the remaining people had to stay in their own Valleys and Communities for necessary garrison duty. Thus, we shall be able to see hereafter that they have not only frequently enjoyed the promise found in *Leviticus chapter 26*: *five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred shall put ten thousand to flight, and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword*; but even at times that of *Deuteronomy 32*: *one shall chase a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight*, which they have experienced in deed and according to the very letter.

-># General Memorial Script<-

## CHAPTER II.

### On the true origin of the name Waldensian, and why we generally take "Inhabitants of the Valleys" and "Waldensians," or "Communities of the Valleys" and "Waldensian Communities," for one and the same in our work.

At first glance, even to people very well-versed in Church History, it might seem like a redundant task—nothing more than reheating a hundred-times cooked soup or serving up chewed and even digested food—to once again raise the question of the true *Origin of the Waldensians* after so many distinguished chroniclers of various faiths. The majority of them derive their descent from a certain *Waldo* of Lyons, who is said to have lived there in high esteem in the year 1173, or according to most, in the year 1180, though a few others even wish to speak of the year 1160. I cannot deny that if one accepts as fact that his name was not *Baldo* or *Baldon* (as many maintain), but truly *Waldo* or, as others prefer, *Waldensis*, then all the non-Romans of his time were quite rightly called *Waldensians* after him. In various places and times, both before and after the said *Waldo*, these people were commonly accustomed to bearing the names of their most prominent Teachers. For example, in Languedoc, Provence, and the Dauphiné, the *Petrobrusians* <note>original: "Pieter-Bruyfiers"</note> took the name of their excellent Shepherd *Peter Bruys*, whom we shall mention in his proper place. In the Valleys of Piedmont and their neighborhood, the *Henricians*, *Josephists*, and *Esperonists* took the names of their leaders *Henry*, *Arnold*, *Joseph*, and *Esperon*. And in England, the *Lollards* <note>original: "Lollardiften"</note> took the name of their leader *Walter Lollard* <note>original: "N. Lollard"</note>, a man of singular learning and knowledge.

To this must be added that, in honor of Him who is called both a *Father of the Harvest* and a *Father of Lights*, one must frankly admit that among all the church ministers the Waldensians ever had—after *Claudius*, Archbishop of Turin and the Valleys, who at the end of the eighth century (as we shall accurately note hereafter in the 20th Chapter) first began to break away from Rome—none has ever been seen to be his equal, nor was anyone as glorious as this Waldo, regarding his Calling, his Doctrine, and his Life, as well as the wonderful progress of the fruits of his faithful Service.

<margin>
*How Waldo was the most excellent Waldensian Teacher of his time: 1. regarding his Calling.*
</margin>

For first, concerning his Calling, it is held that as he was enjoying himself one evening after a meal with a fine company of his acquaintances, one of them, in the midst of the joy and after his ungodly cursing and swearing, fell down dead to the earth from a heart attack. This sad and sudden event caused the aforementioned Waldo to concern himself with nothing other than the salvation of his soul from then on. To this end, he made a holy and firm resolution to thoroughly uproot all his affections from the earth in order to replant them in Heaven. What time he had left to live here, he would spend continually as a true fellow-citizen of the Saints, a faithful member of God’s household, and a sincere follower of the lives of the Holy Apostles. Moreover, to reach this good goal more conveniently, he devoted himself entirely to the study of the Holy Scriptures, and either being linguistically gifted himself (as several describe him) or at least through others...

<margin>
*2. Regarding his Doctrine.*
</margin>

...others had their most prominent books translated and confirmed with a long chain of testimonies from the Church Fathers; undoubtedly being helped and enlightened in this Holy Work not a little by the learned writings of the Albigensians of Provence, who had sprouted from *Piedmont* and had already been a significant Congregation long before, while their doctrine—as we shall prove even more extensively hereafter—had already spread far and wide in various other places in France, and especially even in Lyon. In such a way, being shone upon by a very great light of knowledge of the Divine Word and the sentiments of the Church Fathers of the first-born and purest antiquity, he immediately began to establish his dwelling place as a true *Bethel* <note>original: "Beith-êl"</note> and a true *Bethlehem* <note>original: "Beith-léhhem"</note>, that is, a House of God and a House of Bread; there he began to distribute the heavenly Bread of God to an innumerable multitude of poor souls, who were primarily hungry and thirsty for the nourishing food of righteousness. This group ultimately increased so incredibly that he was obliged and forced to teach without distinction in all public and suitable places; these were then reformed into houses of God and were commonly more crowded with listeners than the most famous churches of the entire city. In these, he declared openly and unafraid, and asserted according to the Scriptures, *that the Roman Church had disastrously lost and abandoned the Faith of Jesus Christ, that she was the great Babylonian Whore of the Revelation, the withered fig tree that our Savior had cursed. That, on the other hand, the Pope was nothing less than the Head of the Church, his monasticism nothing but a stinking carcass, and the solemn vows of service of them both a certain Mark of the Beast; and finally that Purgatory, the Masses, the Invocation of the Saints, and the Prayers for the Deceased were only inventions of the Devil, devised and forged through the greed of the Clergy.*

<margin>3. Regarding his Life.</margin>
But, what is most important, his whole life was also so consistent with that fine and holy Doctrine, that almost all his detractors at the same time give him the praise of such love and godliness, which in such a corrupt century was found to be entirely without equal; since he gave all his means (he was exceedingly rich) for the comfort of the poor and the assistance of the oppressed—in short, he led an entirely blameless life in everything. This confession of the Church's enemies was cited with as much wonder as faithfulness by a certain *Boxhornius* <note>Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a Dutch scholar and historian.</note>, a famous man, in his general Chronicle <note>original: "Geboorteboek"</note> on the year 1159, in this sense: *though (it says) that Waldo had dared to rebuke and condemn before all men the public failures of the clergy, which had as much corrupted the truth of the Doctrine as they themselves were corrupted from the holiness of life; they themselves nevertheless did not fail to give a good testimony to the holiness of his Morals and to his virtue.* And it is from this that God so richly blessed his Service, that neither the raging of the Lyonnese Papacy, nor the violence of *Jean de Belle-maison* <note>John of Canterbury, also known as Jean Bellesmains, Archbishop of Lyon from 1182 to 1193.</note>, their Archbishop and Governor of the city, could ever stop his rapid progress. Indeed, even when he was finally forced by the Vatican thunderbolts <note>A metaphor for papal excommunication or decrees.</note> to change locations, that holy Seed could never be smothered in that great City to the point that it would not always flourish and bring forth magnificent fruits—even such that today in St. Romain, a place granted to the residents of Lyon by decree for the practice of the Reformed Service, a significant and numerous Church thereof stands in full growth. But also, God's all-wise and compassionate Providence used the expulsion of the aforementioned *Waldo* from Lyon and the majority of his faithful disciples—who underwent the loss of their goods and lonely exile from their Fatherland with joy in order to follow the Lamb wherever he might turn—

<margin>Fruits of the Dispersal of the Lyonnese Waldensians.</margin>

# General Memorial

...selecting, namely, the reproach of Christ over the profit of the world; just as in former times the dispersion of the Church, which followed the deadly martyrdom of Saint Stephen, was wisely used to sow and advance the Gospel throughout nearly the entire Christian world. And truly, just as the rejection of the Jews was once the wealth of the Gentile world, so too was the banishment of that **Waldo**, and of those **Poor of Lyon** <note>original: "Armen van Lions"</note>, as they were commonly called, in fact the wealth of Picardy, Lower and Upper Germany, England, Poland, Moravia, and Bohemia. (Waldo himself traveled to this last place to die, after having stayed in Lower and Upper Germany for a considerable time). This exile also greatly increased the already established congregations of Languedoc and Provence, and especially those of the Valleys—both in Dauphiné and Piedmont—bringing about such abundance that no small remnant of believers could be sent out from there to Apulia, Calabria, and other regions of Italy to found new churches.

<margin>
Why it has been thought that the Waldensians descended from Waldo and were named after him.
</margin>
I freely admit once more, I say, that it is no wonder that—since it pleased God to accomplish such great things through him and his disciples—they **not only became known by the honorable name of Waldensians, along with all those who voluntarily embraced their teaching**; but even most historians of that time, without any further investigation into the true cause, left the matter as it was. This is especially understandable since even today it remains customary that those who left the Roman Church communion upon the arrival of the abominable false beliefs <note>original: "afgrijffelik Waan-geloof"</note> are no longer named after their earlier founders—such as **Hussites, Zwinglians**, or the like—but are always named only after **Luther** and **Calvin**. It is as if those two great lights, as soon as they had risen above the horizons of the world’s darkness, had extinguished all the illuminating radiance of all their predecessors, even though those predecessors had so gloriously and abundantly shone upon so many dark places long before. Nevertheless, I cannot refrain, in my own plain Zeeland way <note>The author refers to his regional Dutch identity from the province of Zeeland.</note> or rather as the Waldensian that I am, from setting forth what I know of the origin of this people's name, so that the reader may then pass judgment on it as he pleases. ...to Parents also for all Men remember <note>This likely refers to the transmission of faith through generations.</note> giving its origin to the time of the Apostles, one of her letters to *Oecolampadius*, who maintains the same, and a Petition-script to the Duke of *Savoy*, their Prince, in which they presented the same matter to him so extensively that Rome had nothing at all to come upon it immediately, though they never ceased in all their Princely Petitions to come upon it immediately. as which never fought for anything else, but that they might remain in the possession of that Religion, in which they had been raised from Generation to Generation long before the Dukes of *Savoy* swayed their Princely Scepter over *Piedmont* *from time immemorial* <note>original Italian: "E da tempo immemoriale"</note>, and from times beyond memory.

<margin>Of Waldo, who was contemporary with Berengarius and according to the opinion of many the cause of the name of the Waldensians.</margin>If then those Waldensians necessarily had to boast with the name of one of their famous Teachers, it would nonetheless not be with that of *Waldo* of *Lyon*, who first appeared in the year 1180, but with far more clarity with that of this other, who already in the time of *Berengarius* <note>Berengarius of Tours (c. 999–1088) was a theologian who disagreed with the Roman Church's view of the Eucharist.</note> at the beginning of the ninth Century <note>The author attributes Berengarius to the 9th century, though he lived in the 11th century; this reflects the chronological challenges of early historiography.</note> had climbed to such great authority and prestige, that they [the Waldensians] esteemed his instruction and advice higher than that of all Men of the world, as who *dissuaded by Waldo, from whom the Waldensians* <note>original Latin: "diffuasus à Valdo, à quo Valdenses"</note>, being advised against it, as can be read more extensively below in the 23rd Chapter from *Illyricus'* <term>Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth: A work by Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1556) documenting those who opposed the Roman Catholic Church before the Reformation.</term> Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth regarding *Berengarius*, having always refused to appear in the Chief Church Council gathered at *Vercelli*, in *Piedmont*. For anyone who is even slightly in his right mind will never believe that in the cited passage that first Waldo is meant, who was only born 130 years later, because in the year 1049, when the mentioned Church Council was called, he would have had to be a very aged Man himself, if he had to share and transfer his name to the same. Of that opinion are the *Magdeburg Centuriators* <term>Magdeburg Centuriators: Authors of the 'Magdeburg Centuries', the first comprehensive history of the Christian Church from a Protestant perspective.</term> in the 9th Chapter of the 11th Century, page 455, and the aforementioned *Nicolas Vignier* concerning the year 1050 of his Church Chronology; who unanimously establish the above-mentioned contemporary of *Berengarius* as the cause of the name of the *Waldensians*. Which can then also be not a little strengthened and confirmed by the consistent and constant account of his name and the fickle and varying accounts of the whole naming of that other one. Namely, some, as *Beza* relates in his *Portraits of Famous Men* page 185, give him the first name of *John*, others of *Peter*, who follow the most common opinion. No less a difference is there over his surname, while one swears it was *Valdo*, or *Waldo*; the other, like the aforementioned *Petrus Vallis Sernensis* in the 2nd Chapter of his account of the *Albigensian Histories*, that it was *Valdio*; a third, like *Marcus Zuerius Boxhornius* regarding the year 1159 of his World Chronology, a certain *Petrus Wesembecius*, cited by him there on page 711, *Joachimus Camerarius* at the beginning of his *Bohemian and Moravian Occurrences* and yet more of the like, that it must be not *Valdo*, *Waldo*, nor *Valdio*, but only *Baldon*, or *Baldo*. Indeed, there are finally many who, with *Wernerius Laërius* in the sixth World Age of his Chronology, call him most aptly, in my judgment, *Petrus Waldensis*.

<margin>Various names of Waldo of Lyon.</margin>But on the occasion of this clash of opinions, the great and shrewd *Beza* knew how to perceive the sparks of Truth so well, that in the above-mentioned Portraits page 985, he dared to assure outright that it is so far from the truth that the *Waldensians* of the Valleys would have had their name from *Waldo of Lyon*; that on the contrary he himself was first called *Waldo*, because he had adopted their Doctrine: *some*, these are his own words, *have held that they had for a leader a merchant of Lyon, named John and surnamed Valdo. In which they are mistaken, seeing that on the contrary this John was thus sur-* <note>original French: "quelques uns ont tenu, qu'ils avoient eu pour Chef un marchand de Lion, nommé Jean & surnommé Valdo. En quoy ils s'abusent, veu qu'au contraire ce Jean a été ainsi sur-"</note>

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.
I 2

*surnamed so, because he was among the first among the Waldensians* <note>original French: "surnommé, parcequ'il etoit des premiers entre les Vaudois"</note>; as if he were saying, some have held that they had as a leader a certain merchant from Lyon, whose proper name was *Johannes* and surname was *Waldo*. But they are somewhat mistaken in this, for on the contrary, that *Johannes* was so surnamed because he was one of the principal Waldensians. And this was undoubtedly also intended by those who ascribed and attributed to him that same surname of *Waldensis*.

<margin>From whence the same name originally comes. Testimonies of Messrs. Beza and Conjard.</margin>
But if anyone is further curious to know from whence they themselves inherited that name, let them refer to the previously cited passage by Mr. *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note>, who shall answer for us there, that all the Waldensians *all drew their first denomination from the Valleys* <note>original French: "ont tous tiré leur premiere denomination des Vallées"</note>, that is, they equally received their first naming from the Valleys. This opinion of Mr. *Conjard* <note>Pierre Conjard, a 17th-century legal advocate and author.</note>, legal advocate for the High Court of Normandy, in his writing on the female Pope *Joan*, page 8, is not only presented as his particular discovery in these words: *the Vaudois received this name because of the Valleys where they dwell* <note>original French: "les Vaudois ont eu ce nom a cause des Vallées, ou ils habitent"</note>, the Waldensians carry this their name of honor because of their dwelling place in the Valleys; but it is also considered so well-founded and firm that he dares to compare it with all opposing views, and indeed considers it better than all of them. And truly, if the reader has already observed all that we have presented here before, both in the declarations of so many writers—Roman and non-Roman alike—and in the writings of the Valley Waldensians themselves, who unanimously report this naming of theirs long before that *Waldo* of Lyon, as well as before that other one who lived in the ninth century with *Berengarius* <note>As noted on the previous page, the author places Berengarius in the 9th century, though he lived in the 11th.</note>, as we have previously proven; if, I say, it pleases him to pay proper attention to the following observation, he will be able to most perfectly discover the firmness of the foundation upon which the said gentlemen lean, and subsequently see their reasons clearly.

<margin>That the name Vaudois comes first from the word "Vau" in their own language, and that of "Valdensis" from the Latin "Vallis" or Italian "Valli".</margin>
That which is called *Vallées* in French—that is, Valleys—is generally still called *VAUS* by all those people in their own Waldensian language (which has always been preserved there and is still spoken), and has always been so called from of old. Indeed, even the oldest of the French writers strictly followed the people of the Valleys in this, calling the dales (*Vallées*) or the plains between the mountains by the same name as they did, as can still be seen today in the elegant rhymes of *Marot* <note>Clément Marot (1496–1544), a famous French poet who translated the Psalms.</note> and *Beza*, the pride of eloquence in their century, and in other writings as well. Others, on the contrary, whose speech had more of Latin or Italian than of that simple antiquity, used in this instance the word *Valli*, and even commonly the short form *Val*, to distinguish between a *Val* (a dale) and a *Val* meaning a valley, always accompanied by its inseparable *di*, saying namely *Val di San Martin*, *Val di Peirouze*, *Val di Lucerne*—the Valley of St. Martin, Perosa, and Luserna. Now, to be able to grasp that the *Waldensians* have borrowed their name solely from this their land, it must be noted with particular care that those who called the valleys *Vaus* also called their inhabitants *Vaudois* (Waldensians in Dutch); just as, conversely, others in their language called them *Valdenses* or *Valdesi*, having their eye on the aforementioned word *Val*, or even, if you will, on the Latin and Italian *Vallis* or *Valle*. And just as one has generally been able to see until now that they were called *Vaudés* in their own way, and *Vaudois* by those who made more of a point of speaking pure French; so too one commonly finds among the Latin writers of their time the name *Vallenses* (Valley-dwellers) and *Convallenses* (dwellers of the joined valleys)—so the excellent *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian and statesman.</note> among others calls them—repeatedly used in respect to the joining together of the Valleys. For which distinct difference no other reason can well be devised, than...

But all this is primarily confirmed by common usage, by which even to this day the subjects of a part of the subordinate states of the Illustrious Commonwealth of Bern—otherwise called the French Land <note>The Pays de Vaud, a French-speaking region in Switzerland then under the control of the Canton of Bern.</note>, which extends from the Jura Mountains to the lands of Gex <note>original: "Jes," referring to the Pays de Gex near Geneva.</note>—are commonly surnamed *Vaudois* after their dwelling place, the Land of *Vaus*. What is more, that very region bears its said name for no other reason than that it is nothing else but a woven chain of hills and valleys; among which, however, in the lowlands of the Burgundy Mountains <note>The Jura range.</note> that run toward the Genevan Pool <note>original: "Geneeffen Poel," referring to Lake Geneva.</note>, very remarkable plains are found in several places.

Even if all the Valley-dwellers were still currently adhering to Paganism itself or Papal superstitions, they would nonetheless be called Waldenses in respect to their place (for their faith can have no part in this name); exactly like those among them who moved from there to the Episcopal city of Albi to live, immediately exchanged their first name for that of *Albigensians* as its citizens: and those who went to Picardy, for that of *Picardians*. This can seem strange to no one, as nothing is more common than to name all peoples after their regions: the *Italian* after *Italy*, the *German* after *Germany*, the *Piedmontese*, *Dauphinese*, and *Norman* after *Piedmont*, the *Dauphiné*, and *Normandy*. And why then should the Waldenses (called *Vaudés* and *Vaudois* by them, as we have seen) not just as well be named after their VAUS, or Valleys, as the *Mountaineers* after their *Mountains*, the *Alp-dwellers* after their *Alps*—and these again according to the location of their dwellings as *Cis-Alpines*, *Trans-Alpines*, and *Sub-Alpines* <note>original: "Herwaarts-alpeners, Over-alpeners en Binnen-alpeners."</note>, as the well-noted Mr. Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a prominent French historian.</note> and others speak?

<margin>How the same name was thereafter transferred to religion, or a schism.</margin>

That is to say, if *Turks* are spoken of, one immediately understands them to be *Mohammedans*; if of *Chinese* or *Japanese*, that they are *Heathens*; if of *Romans* or *Neapolitans*, that they are *Papists*; because the residents of those lands sharing those names openly make a practice of such beliefs. It is exactly the same, conversely, when one begins to mention a *Genevan* in Italy or Spain. In the same way, it also happened regarding the city-word *Albigensians*; which, after Albi (the cathedral city of Languedoc) was incredibly filled with those Valley Waldenses—who there openly practiced the Gospel service and courageously fought against Papal superstition—it was never again used as before for the *citizens of Albi*, but only for those who were of that faith. Which is still so much the case today that out of hundreds, not one who writes or speaks of the *Albigensians* has the slightest thought of the place itself, as if...

### General Memorial

<margin>Spread throughout all of Europe according to Æneas Sylvius.</margin> For firstly, almost no one has ever denied or contradicted that the Holy Doctrine, which was thereafter continued in so many other places in Europe, took its first origin from those God-fearing Waldensians. *Æneas Sylvius* <note>Æneas Silvius Piccolomini, 1405–1464, who later became Pope Pius II</note>, later Pope Pius II, explicitly states in his *History of the Taborites* <note>original: *Taborytesse Geschiedenissen*, likely referring to his *Historia Bohemica*</note> that a certain *Pieter van Deyt* and *Jacob van Misna*, both born Waldensians, came over to **Bohemia** during the time of **Jan Hus** <note>A Czech priest and reformer burned at the stake in 1415</note> and
<margin>Concerning the Bohemian Waldensians.</margin> thoroughly instructed him in their Faith. The Bohemians themselves openly confess and acknowledge that **Wycliffe** <note>John Wycliffe, 1320–1384, an English precursor to the Reformation</note> also received his doctrine from them; the reason for which is stated in the book *Concerning the Origin and Confession of the Bohemian Church* <note>original Latin: *Orig. & Confess. Eccles. Bohem.*</note> as follows: *We do not doubt that what we have that is good and true in our Churches, we have borrowed from the Waldensians. For which they are also singularly obliged and owe all gratitude; especially while Wycliffe himself is said to have been helped by them and since then our Jan Hus was both awakened and encouraged by them.* The excellent
<margin>Concerning Comenius, etc.</margin> **Comenius** <note>John Amos Comenius, 1592–1670, a famous Moravian philosopher and pedagogue</note> also agrees with this in his *Exhortation of the Bohemian Persecutions*, which we cite elsewhere; those churches, he says, have never denied that they had their calling from the Waldensians. And finally, the Hirsau Chronological Table <note>likely the *Annales Hirsaugienses* by Johannes Trithemius</note> also sets that whole matter with all its circumstances quite clearly before one's eyes.

Regarding the Waldensians of Poland, Calabria, Provence, Languedoc and 
<margin>Concerning Perrin.</margin> the like, **Perrin** <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a 17th-century historian of the Waldensians</note> confirms the same of them with an extensive account in the 7th and 8th chapters of his *History of the Pious Waldensians*. Indeed, 
<margin>Concerning Thuanus.</margin> that never-sufficiently-praised and credible **Thuanus** <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou, 1553–1617, a French historian and statesman</note> declares in his 6th Book, page 168 and 169, that Peter Waldo of Lyons wandered through Picardy, Lower and Upper Germany, the Vandal cities, and finally through Bohemia itself, so as to sow and spread the Waldensian doctrine more effectively everywhere.

<margin>And concerning d’Aubigné.</margin> A certain **d’Aubigné** <note>Théodore Agrippa d'Aubigné, 1552–1630, a French poet and soldier</note>, in the 6th Chapter of the 2nd Book of his *General Memorial*, speaking of the Waldensians of Lyons, Languedoc, and Provence, relates this: that though they were being rooted out, they nonetheless cast the seed throughout all Europe among those into whose hands the Reformation <note>original: *Geloof-herstelling*, meaning "Restoration of the Faith"</note> can and must now be very openly applied. And again somewhat lower: that all Eastern Europe embraced and cherished the Waldensian worship <note>original: *Walssen Gots-dienst*</note> with such fiery zeal—even though it was publicly cursed by Pope Alexander—that in Passau a congregation of nearly eighty thousand heads was gathered, despite the fact that they were cruelly burned on all sides under the names of 
<margin>Various names of the Waldensians.</margin> **Waldensians, Albigenses, Tramontanes, Josephists, Lollardists, Frairots or Fraticelli, Picards, Lyonners, Gazarians, Patarenes, and Apostolics.** In passing, it should be noted that they were nicknamed *Tramontanes, Fraticelli, Frairots* and so forth only because they themselves, or at least their doctrine, originated from the Alpine Mountains (that is, from the Valleys); where they were commonly called *Fraticelli* <note>Little brothers</note> by the Italians in their language, and *Frairots* in the Vaudois dialect, as well as *Gazari, Apostolici* and *Patarini*, as even the Great Cloister-Provost **Rorenco** <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo, a prior who wrote against the Waldensians in the 1630s</note>, being a nobleman of the Valleys, clearly notes in his Chronological Records. Where then all those newly-made Waldensians first began to be called after his name, as he has left his memory and that of his followers so indelibly upon the marble of that famous Tower <note>referring to the "Lollards' Tower" in London, where many were imprisoned</note>...
