<margin>The Waldensians deny that they are descended from the Poor of Lyon.</margin> In this, it may also be noted in passing that the *Waldensians* trace their descent much higher than from *Waldo* of Lyon, who, through the generous distribution of all his goods to his disciples, caused them to commonly acquire the nickname *Poor of Lyon*. Meanwhile, they themselves here openly reject the aforementioned naming *as unjust and false*, and instead acknowledge and claim for themselves the name *little Flock of Christians* as the truth. <margin>A notable testimony regarding this from Pilichdorf and Johannes Soranus.</margin> This is also why *Pilichdorf* <note>Peter of Pilichdorf, a 14th-century writer and fierce opponent of the Waldensians</note>, their sworn enemy, and *Johannes Soranus*, Canon of the Church of Krakow, in his book *On the Elucidation of the Errors of the Ruthenian Rite*, explicitly record that the *Waldensians* would never tolerate any name other than that of *Apostolics* (*Apostolici*); *namely*, these are his own words, *those who asserted that they alone were the true successors of the Apostles and of the Primitive Church* <note>original Latin: "utpote... qui se duntaxat veros Apostolorum & Ecclesiæ Primitivæ Successores astruerent"</note>, as they proved themselves to be the true descendants of the Apostles and the first Founding-church.

<margin>Concerning Peter of Waldis.</margin> Above all, it must not be overlooked on this occasion that those among them who still somewhat allowed themselves to be called *Waldensians* after one of their Teachers, considered themselves to be much older than either of the two previously mentioned *Waldos*. They appropriately placed their origin with a certain *Peter of Waldis*, whom they rightly claimed lived about three centuries after *Constantine the Great*, which is to say, exactly at the beginning of the seventh century. Namely, the aforementioned *Pilichdorf* relates this himself as their own common opinion in his *Treatise against the Poor of Lyon*, page 283 of the large-print edition: *three hundred years*, he says in so many words, *after Constantine there arose a certain man from the region of Waldis, named Peter, who taught the way of poverty; from whom the Waldensian sect was propagated* <note>original Latin: "per annos trecentos... à Constantino surrexit quidam è regione Waldis, Petrus nominatus, qui viam paupertatis docuit; à quo Valdensis secta propagata est"</note>. This is as if he said: about three hundred years after the time of *Constantine*, there arose a certain man named Peter, hailing from the land of *Waldis*, who taught that man must live in poverty, and subsequently from such people the *Waldensian* succession of teachings was established. Thus far then concerning the naming and descent of the Waldensians, which we trust will fully suffice for the whole world.

I do not doubt, however, that the majority of readers would now wish me to plunge so suddenly into the narrative of the persecutions they suffered, and especially to the portrayal of the horrific massacre of the year 1655 <note>The "Piedmontese Easter" of 1655 was a notorious massacre of Waldensians by the troops of the Duke of Savoy, which sparked international outrage.</note>, whose pitiable groans still ring in their ears today, and whose unjustly shed blood cries out to Heaven for vengeance; or that I should at least from now on begin to unfold and lay open the antiquity of their **True Apostolic Doctrine**, and at the same time how the same has been so miraculously preserved among that wretched people from the time they were happily drawn out of the darkness of **Heathenism** until now. Let us then first see what that Waldensian Doctrine has been from of old, before which **Rome** has always so greatly trembled and feared, against which she has instituted such manifold coercion of conscience, has shot so many lightning bolts and bans from her Vatican, has incited so many Powers to the simultaneous rooting out of their memory, erected so many gallows, and lit so many fires; a Doctrine, nevertheless, which alone on the whole earth carries away the honor of having seen over eight hundred thousand <term>Martyrs</term> <note>original: "Bloet-getuygen," literally "blood-witnesses."</note> in less than two hundred years, who unanimously and joyfully wrote the confirmation of the same with their own *life-fluid* <note>original: "leven-vogt," a poetic reference to their blood.</note>. I do not doubt, however, that the majority of readers would now wish me to fall suddenly into the account of the persecutions they suffered, and especially into the portrayal of the horrific massacre of the year 1655—the piteous groaning of which still rings in our ears today, and whose unjustly shed blood still cries out to Heaven for vengeance. But while satisfying this curiosity would be somewhat detrimental to the natural order of history and the concise knowledge of these matters—indeed, it would turn them completely upside down—and since, on the other hand, anyone who wishes is perfectly free to skip this first Book and step immediately into the following one (where, in my judgment, they will find their satisfaction and likely not a little beyond their expectations): I have nevertheless, after explaining the name and origin of the Waldensians, had to show above all what their Doctrine and Customs have been at all times. To this end, I shall draw proofs from the people themselves, as is proper, and from the writings of the Right-believers <note>The author uses "Right-believers" to refer to those he considers orthodox Christians, likely meaning fellow Protestants.</note>, and finally from the confirmed declarations of their adversaries themselves; as I shall do at great length in the course of this first Part, by God's grace.

### CHAPTER III.

*Concerning a list of names of the written books and other writings of the Barbes <note>The term 'Barba' (meaning 'uncle' in the local dialect) was a title of respect used for the Waldensian pastors.</note>, or Teachers of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys, the majority of which, and especially the most principal and essential, are original manuscripts or highly authenticated copies, from which we shall draw and present some samples of the Doctrine of the ancient Waldensians.*

All the pieces delivered into the hands of Mr. *Morland*, Extraordinary Envoy of My Lord *Oliver Cromwell*, Protector of Great Britain, by the Messrs. *Antoine* and *Jean Legér*, original ministers of the Valleys; and subsequently by him in the month of August of the year 1658 placed in the custody of the famous chief seat of learning at Canterbury <note>While the text says Canterbury, these manuscripts were famously deposited by Morland at the University of Cambridge.</note>, so that they might always serve for the edification and instruction of late descendants and the conviction of opponents, are the following; namely:

I. A bundle of books, marked with the letter A, containing these following writings:

1. The account of the Creation and the Flood, written in the Waldensian language <note>The Waldensian language, or Vaudois, is a variety of Occitan spoken in the Alpine valleys.</note>, which has been in use within human memory and is still present in the Valleys.
2. An excellent writing concerning various necessary teachings, which man must fittingly draw from the nature of various animals.
3. *The Treatise on Sins* <note>original: "Lo tratta de li pecca"</note>, a writing on Sin; which is nothing else but a mystical and moral explanation of the Beast described in the 13th Chapter of Revelation.
4. A writing on the Word of God and its power, how one must receive and put it into practice, written in the year 1230.
5. Various Latin works concerning the priests and the monks.
6. A writing against *the Traditions* <note>original: "li Tramettament"</note>, that is, human traditions that do not agree with Holy Scripture.
7. An admonition to Hermon, to turn to the Creator and not to the creatures.
8. A writing regarding the Pharisaic growth, which the Father has not planted; that is, the church laws and doctrinal systems of the Franciscans, Dominicans, and other such monks, never commanded or instituted by God.
9. A Latin writing regarding the duty of husband and wife.
10. Another similar one on the Apostles' Creed.
11. Another similar one on the birth and growth of Idolatry and its destruction by the Gospel.
12. Yet another Latin writing regarding the manner of the production of sin.

# General Memorial History

...parchment in octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves.</note>, containing various writings of the **Doctrine of the ancient Waldensians** in their own language; and 2. another volume of various other very weighty manuscripts, regarding the affairs of the said Valleys, composed partly in **Italian** and partly in **French**: all of which I keep in the library of our City for safekeeping, to the end that they might always be conveniently used in case of need. In witness whereof, and so forth. In Geneva, the 10th of November 1662. *Signed:*

->Gerardus, Head Pastor and Librarian.<-

But above all, one must not forget here another catalog of Waldensian books, which were first scraped together from time to time primarily in that Valley of **Pragela** (which is the King’s territory), because the Romish firebrands <note>original: "stoke-branden"; a derogatory term for those inciting religious persecution.</note> and arsonists had considerably less power there than in those other Valleys subject to the **Savoyard** lord; and which were later also sent, by order of the Waldensian Synod, to Master *Perrin*, formerly a pastor in Dauphiné, to serve as suitable resources for his **History of the Waldensians and Albigenses**. We shall insert them here in full sequence from his aforementioned work, printed in Geneva in the year 1619, even though they contain the majority of the most important pieces we have already found in the others; for they simultaneously show, alongside them, a considerable number of others of no less importance which are mentioned nowhere else.

I. In the first place, then, says the aforementioned Gentleman in the 7th Chapter of that book, page 57 (where one also finds his acknowledgment that he did indeed receive these writings) *we still have among us a **New Testament**, written on parchment in a hand as elegant as it is old, in ancient Waldensian.*

II. *Another book from the year one thousand, one hundred and twenty, called* **l’Antichrist**, *the Anti- or False-Christ, which begins with these words:* <note>original: "Qual cosa sia l'Anti-Christ ens."</note> **"What sort of thing the Antichrist is,"** *and so forth.*

4. *An exposition or expansion upon the **Ten Commandments** of the Divine Law.*

5. *A similar one upon the **Lord’s Prayer**.*

6. *A book on **Fasting**.*

VII. We also preserve a significant writing, graced with the name **Garden of Consolation**, containing many beautiful teachings, fully confirmed both by Holy Scripture and by various proverbs of the Ancients.

VIII. Another old parchment book *de l'Egliſe*, **of the Church**.

IX. A similar one called *Threſor & Lumiere de la Foy*, that is, **The Treasure and Light of Faith**.

X. Yet another with the title *Almanach Spirituel*, the **Spiritual Almanac**.

XI. Again, a parchment concerning the means to properly distinguish the precious from the base and despised, that is, the **Virtues from the Vices**.

XII. And finally also the work of **Barbe George Morel**, containing all the questions which he, alongside one **Pierre Masson**, formerly posed to **Oecolampadius** and **Bucer** <note>Johannes Oecolampadius and Martin Bucer were leading Protestant Reformers whom the Waldensians consulted in the 1530s to align their doctrines.</note> regarding religion and faith; as well as the answers to each of them in particular, brought forward by those aforementioned men at that time.

All of which books, being written partly in **Provençal** and partly in **Piedmontese-Waldensian**, are entirely sufficient to fully instruct their people on how they must both live well and believe well; which is also precisely such a doctrine that in all parts corresponds very closely with that of the modern-day **Orthodox** <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the Reformed or Protestant churches.</note> Churches and is found to be in agreement.

Thus far our cited author: who, regarding his last statement, draws no little strength from the self-authorized testimony of Master **Theodore Tronchin**, Minister and Head Professor of Holy Theology in **Geneva**, which he gave concerning this on the 17th of **November** <note>original: "Slagtmaant", literally "Slaughter-month", the traditional Dutch name for November.</note> in the year 1656, after he had undertaken a very careful examination of all those mentioned pieces, which had long since been delivered to him for that purpose by the same Master **Perrin**.

So that from this alone it would now be easy to conclude that the doctrine, which

we have always maintained against human inventions until the present day, is not new except to those who have tried with all diligence to bury it, or at least whose ancestors alone had an aversion to it because they never recognized its excellence.

Meanwhile, the Lord of Saint-Aldegonde <note>Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde (1540–1598), a Dutch statesman and theologian.</note> mentions those stirred-up writings on page 153 of his first *Table of Religious Differences*, even going so far as to assure that a good many others of just as old a character would be found in the precious library of Lord Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous French religious scholar and professor at Leiden University.</note>; it seems to me to have come from there, that the Lord of Saint-Ferriol, Minister of the Church of Orange, driven by a holy curiosity, collected the most part of them and subsequently showed them to the well-mentioned Lord.

Regarding the old Waldensian Bible, of which I shall have to speak later in this work, I currently have it in hand, after I luckily recovered it in the mountains of the Valley of Cluson <note>One of the Alpine "Waldensian Valleys" in the Piedmont region.</note>.

I likewise still have several small papers, with which those who dared to be used for the executions were usually armed at the time of the massacres. Namely, they were made to believe that by virtue of these printed papers they had nothing to fear, or rather that by leaving the earth with all its troubles through this holy war, they would go straight to Heaven—as several prisoners often assured me themselves—in order to extort from God, by virtue of that "debt-note" <note>A cynical reference to a sort of indulgence or protective charm.</note>, excessive crowns of eternal glory. The absurdity of which will shine forth enough of its own accord if we only pay a little attention to the fact that almost all of them were of this or similar content:

The Power of God † the Father, the Wisdom of God † the Son, and the Strength of the Holy † Spirit, be with you through the intercession of the most holy Virgin, Mother of God, Mary, Saint Francis, Anthony, and the Blessed Didacus and Salvator. May the Lord deliver you from every fever, plague, and sudden death; Amen. <note>original: "Potentia Dei † Patris, Sapientia Dei † Filii & Virtus Spiritus † Sancti per interceſſionem Sanctiſſimæ Virginis, Dei Genetricis, Mariæ, Sancti Franciſci, Antonii & Beatorum Didaci & Salvatoris. Liberet te Dominus ab omni febre, peſte & improviſâ morte; Amen:"</note>

But let us now finally come to the teaching itself of our old Waldensians, seeking it first in their own writings, thereafter in those of their friends, and lastly even in those of their fiercest enemies and most shameless detractors.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### *Of the first sample of their said teaching, taken from their Noble Leiçon, Excellent Lesson-task, from the year 1100.*

From the various proofs that we consistently cite and bring forward in the continuation of this book regarding the antiquity and right-apostolic timeframe of the Waldensian Churches—taken from the very writings of the Roman Catholic <note>original: "Roomſ-geſinde"</note> lords—the reader will be able to notice more and more easily what their teaching has continuously been at all times; especially since Claudius <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827), an Archbishop famous for opposing the use of images in worship.</note>, that excellent and courageous Archbishop, who at the end of the eighth century chose to give a bill of divorce to Rome, along with their adulterous image-worship and other thousandfold superstitions, which they

# Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

L
<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

which at that time were brewing, to some extent to tolerate or follow. However, in my judgment, it is highly appropriate that we first hear those Waldensians speak for themselves, as no one can better know what they believe than they themselves, nor consequently be more credible therein. For this reason, I shall frequently place in this my Work no small samples of their ancient Faith, all faithfully drawn from the original scripts themselves; just as these may be inspected by anyone in the famous book-treasures of Cambridge <note>The Dutch text says "Kantelburrie" (Canterbury), but the famous collection of Waldensian manuscripts brought to England by Samuel Morland was deposited in the University of Cambridge.</note> and Geneva, where we have placed them in safekeeping according to the lists cited in the preceding chapter. I also do not doubt that I do the reader a much greater service by all this, as these pieces are rarer than any others and have been miraculously preserved and kept against all the cunning, diligence, and expense employed by their enemies to erase their memory, both in times of silence and in the harshest storms of murder and persecution. 

And truly, it has cost me an incredible amount of effort to gather these remains of writings (for everything that I had very diligently scraped together of the Waldensian Antiquities far and wide in the year 1640—which was all that could be obtained of them—was so thoroughly stolen from me by the destroyers of my Fatherland <note>Refers to the 1655 "Piedmontese Easter" massacres and the subsequent displacement of the Waldensians.</note> along with all my books in the year 1655, and carried off to Turin—as I heard from them myself then—and to Saluzzo at the same time, such that I did not keep the smallest leaf of them). These same things, I say, I had to gather together and bring to light from the neighboring Valleys, which belong entirely to French territory and have not so often been reduced to ashes by the fire of the Vatican. Whatever the case may be, one shall be able to hear the most important of them here without the slightest change, each in its own language, both to satisfy the laudable curiosity of many and to convict the ill-will of no smaller number, who might prematurely try to accuse our translation (which we shall add alongside everywhere) of being unfaithful. See here then, as a beginning, that ancient rhymed script which has always been so well known under the name of *La Noble Leiçon*, the Excellent Lesson, that it was inserted in the aforementioned list of the Valley manuscripts by the well-noted Mr. Johannes-Paulus Perrijn <note>Jean-Paul Perrin, a 17th-century historian of the Waldensians.</note> in his chronological work; and has long been more explicitly mentioned in the history book of Mr. De Serres <note>Jean de Serres (1540–1598), a French humanist and historian.</note> and finally in the first book of the *History of the Martyrs* and others.

***

A fragmentary copy of a certain Poem, called *La Noble Leiçon*, the Excellent Lesson, written in an old Gothic letter in the year 1100; which still exists in its entirety in a handwritten book of parchment in Cambridge, just as another is preserved and kept in safety in Geneva.

That no man who lives can know his end,

The honor of God the Father must be at the beginning;

These three are the Holy Trinity,
Who as one God, must be worshipped,

That He gives us strength against the Enemies,

Which are the world, the devil, and the flesh—

That we may know the way of truth
And keep pure the soul that God has given us,
The soul and the body in the way of charity.
In this way, we may love the Holy Trinity
And our neighbor; for God has commanded it to us.

This sample of the aforementioned rhymed-scripture will suffice for this time, as it is already too long to be inserted here in its entirety. Specifically, it contains a very beautiful, brief summary of the account of Creation and the state of the world until the Great Flood, as well as subsequently until the times of *Abraham* and *Moses*; also setting forth on that occasion all the Moral, Civil, and Ecclesiastical Laws in brief! After that, it gives us a vivid description on one hand of the sins of the descendants of Jacob, and on the other, of the strict judgments of God, which they had brought upon their own necks as criminals, so that everyone might draw a lesson from them. Along with this, it moves past that "Man after God’s heart" <note>A reference to King David.</note> and many such godly Kings and Church-foretellers, or *Prophets*, to a presentation of the Babylonian Captivity and the joyful return from the same. It also mentions the blessed coming of our heavenly Savior on earth in such a way that it briefly encompasses all the Books of the New-Covenant-writers, or *Evangelists*, showing—alongside an excellent comparison of the Law and the Gospel—the sending of the Apostles, the state of the Foundation-Church <note>The early or primitive Church.</note> and the abundant pouring out of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost day. Finally, it also contains an indispensable antidote to the grossest errors of the ignorant Papacy, arranged in the same manner as the passage we cited concerning the *intrigue and simony of the Priests, auricular confession, the miserable Masses, and dead* <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "Doot-" suggests the next page begins with "doot-wercken" (dead works).</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the "Noble Lesson" (a rhymed summary of faith) to a prose example of Waldensian preaching. # Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

*Death-bed prayers, the deceptive and punishable absolution of sins, and the abuse of the Keys of the False-Christ <note>original: "Leuge-Christus," a term used by the Waldensians to refer to the Pope as a counterfeit of Christ.</note> have generally followed.* To such an extent that this Holy Work is nothing other than a concise summary of both the history and the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments, regarding both systematic theology <note>original: "self-stellige Got-geleertheyt"</note>—that which must be believed—and that which must be lived and followed. Now, those wise *Barbes* <note>term: "Barbes" (literally "uncles") was the name given to Waldensian pastors or elders to distinguish them from the "Fathers" of the Catholic Church.</note> wished to place this divine treasure into the hands of their people in their own language, in the form of rhyme or poetry, partly to make the reading of it more pleasant, and partly to more conveniently impress it upon the memory of the youth so it might remain there.

But just as we have seen until now what they knew of Rhyme, let us now cross over to the unrhymed—though by no means absurd <note>A play on words in the original Dutch between "Rijm-loose" (rhymeless/prose) and "ongerijmde" (absurd/nonsensical).</note>—nature of their Church discourses. If we are then eager to know fully in what manner they were accustomed to teaching their Churches, we can never better satisfy that curiosity than through the following Demonstration-script on the *Fear of God*; which shall clearly show the world what a deadly hatred those good people bore toward all sins and vice, and how courageously they fought the same with the sword of God’s Word and with the shield of the Holy Scriptures of the Ancient Fathers.

### CHAPTER V.

->Of the second Sample, taken from a Church-teaching on the Fear of the Lord.<-

#### On the Fear of the Lord.

<note>This column is translated from the original Occitan/Waldensian dialect.</note>

The fear of the Lord casts out sins. *Through the fear of the Lord many good things are born. Wherefore Solomon says, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. And he says again, the man is blessed who is always fearful. For through the fear of the Lord souls are delivered from the pains of Hell. And through the fear of the Lord the joys of Paradise are found. For the love of God and neighbor is charity. And he who has charity has God. And he who has God departs from worldly things; and he who loves God fears the pains of Hell and desires the joys of Paradise, in which he hopes to arrive, where there is no fear of death, nor fear of the enemy. Here is life without death. Therefore, through the love of God and neighbor, eternal life is acquired. And St. Paul says, the love of God and neighbor works no evil. And he who shall do these things shall not fall into sin. But he who inclines toward*

<column-break/>

#### On the Fear of God.

...perdition. And **Saint Augustine** <note>original: "Sant Augustin"</note> says that the greed of man cannot be satisfied, and has no measure. For [earthly] love leads to sorrow, but the love of Christ extinguishes the fire of **Hell** <note>original: "l'Enfern"</note> and casts out earthly love. <column-break/>

...is also confirmed by **Saint Augustine**, as he maintains that the desires of men are insatiable and go far beyond all bounds of moderation. In particular, what was once very truly said by someone can be applied here: *O miser* (he addresses him), *you possess no spiritual sight to behold Heaven, nor an understanding heart to know God; and consequently, through your own stubbornness, you gather for yourself the wrath of God on the day of judgment.* Let us then <margin>Seeking heavenly things.</margin> nevermore desire these worldly things, but in their place burn only for the heavenly ones and constantly set **Christ** alone as the object of our fiery love. For love for man leads only to sadness; but love for the Savior extinguishes all hellish flames and those of our earthly love. Let us then do not our own will, but only that of him who descended from Heaven, who assured us of this: *I have not come to do my will, but to do the will of him who alone sent me:* and among other things has prescribed this commandment of prayer to God; *Thy will be done.*

<column-break/>

But there are many who say: *I am still young, and I cannot break my will; but when I am old, then I will do penance.* Yet this is foolish talk. For the miserable wretch does not know if he will live until tomorrow, yet he thinks he will live many years, and thinks he will live until old age? **Josiah** <note>King Josiah of Judah, often cited as a model of early piety</note> knew that the young are forced to depart from this life, for this life is short, and that brevity is uncertain. For when we rise in the morning, we do not know if we shall reach the evening.

<column-break/>

But it seems to me I hear many here <margin>Excuses of youth.</margin> objecting: *I am still young,* they say, *and consequently cannot yet bend or break my will; but when I have reached gray old age, I will sufficiently atone for everything through humble and heartfelt repentance.* This is indeed a very foolish reason. For these poor people are not even certain that they will live until the next day, and look how they promise themselves many years, how they promise themselves late old age? That **Josiah** knew better, that all men, however much they might be newcomers in the world, are bound to depart from this life; that life itself is entirely short and this fine brevity is uncertain. And truly, when we have risen in the morning as usual, we have not the slightest assurance that we shall reach the following evening.

<column-break/>

And again, there are others who say: *Our ancestors lived and did no penance; it is enough for us to do as they did. I want to enjoy my things while I live: for it lasts...*

<column-break/>

# General Memorial-Script
### Page 48

*“It is a hard thing for me,” <note>original Occitan: "dura cosa es à my"</note> says the miser, “to distribute my things to the poor.” O foolish man, you who say these things, why do you not look around? For where are your ancestors who lived before? They are no more. And what did the riches they possessed profit them, or what benefit did the things they saved for their heirs do for their souls? And if you look at those things which you leave behind, why do you not look at those things which you lose <note>The author distinguishes between leaving material goods to others and losing one's own soul</note>? For what is more important to you: to have your soul, or to have your son, who shall be a stranger to you after death?*

<margin>
The misuse of God’s Mercy.
</margin>

*Also, he lives wickedly who turns away from the mercy of God, even though He is pious, patient, and merciful, and waits for us to amend our ways. For He does not only give pardon to those who repent; He also promises them a reward, and if they persevere, He gives them the Crown. We have an example in the thief <note>original: "leiron"</note> who was converted on the cross and earned the right to hear: “Truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in Paradise.” Therefore, blessed is he who is always prepared. For the Lord will come at an hour we do not know. Therefore, let us work while we have time and not wish to delight in this world, which is full of iniquity and in which our life is full of temptations.*

<column-break/>

...He wants to have all our goods completely, as long as we must still be citizens of this worldly dwelling; all the more so because, on the other hand, it is very hard to load one’s beloved treasures upon the poor. But O most foolish of all men, who dare to utter such things, why do you not rather note this: namely, that your ancestors, who were once in life, have now passed away and are found nowhere? What has their wealth profited them, which they possessed with such anxiety forever and ever? What benefit have those things done for their souls, which they have saved with such care only for their greedy heirs? At the least, if you want to calculate what you keep and leave behind, you must by no means overlook what you lose in exchange for it. What do you prize more highly: the mere saving and winning of your soul, or the gathering of many goods for your children and descendants, who must be completely unknown and strange to you after death?

These also make matters little better, who through their too-careless misuse turn Divine Mercy into "misery" <note>A wordplay in the original Dutch: *barm-hartigheyt* (mercy) is contrasted with *arm-hardigheyt* (literally "poor-hardness" or cruelty/misery)</note> to their own harm, whereas He otherwise takes very deep compassion on mankind and waits for their conversion with a persistent patience. Yes, He does not only grant His full forgiveness to the truly penitent; but He also promises a boundless reward and—if they persevere to the end—to honor them out of grace with that eternal Crown of Glory <note>original: "Vorst-hooft-pronk," literally "Sovereign-head-finery"</note>. We have a remarkable example of this in the thief who converted at the cross at the very last, whereupon this comforting assurance was immediately given to him by our Savior: *Verily I say unto you, today you shall be with me in Paradise.* Blessed therefore is the one who diligently prepares themselves for this at every moment of their life, especially since the Lord our God will come upon man suddenly, at such a time when one will be least expecting it. Let us then strive most earnestly, as long as we have the opportunity, to take no pleasure in this world full of unrighteousness, in which we have nothing else to promise ourselves but...

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Necessity and benefit of trials.</margin>
Many are the tribulations of the righteous. But the Lord will deliver them from all. And *Saint Paul* says: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God, and whoever will not have a part in the tribulations will not have a part in the consolations. And the Lord says in the Gospel: love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you. And *Saint Augustine* says: in as much as your enemy shall harm you, so much more should you love him. For through such love you can have eternal life. *For if the wicked man wishes to harm you, before he has done the evil to you, his own heart shall be wounded, and all the evil he wished to do to you shall return upon him. And if the scoundrel takes your property through his villainy, he loses more than you, who loses your property,*

<column-break/>

Many are the adversities of the righteous, but from all those the Lord rescues him. So says also St. Paul: through many trials we must enter into the Kingdom of God. He who then has no part in those adversities cannot also share in those corresponding consolations. In this state, our duty is prescribed to us by our Savior in the Gospel thus: *love your enemies and do good to those who bear you hatred?* Which St. Augustine comes to measure out with these words: *the more your enemy shall try to harm you, the more you are obliged to love him: for through such love you shall be able to attain eternal salvation. Namely, if the evildoer should try in any way to be a hindrance to you, he shall thereby be so sensibly wounded in his heart, even before he has come to the deed, that consequently all the evil he ever forged against you shall fall upon his own head. Furthermore, if a robber ever strips you of your goods by his violence, that unjust winner loses far more than you, because you only lose your worldly prosperity, while he loses his heavenly well-being through it.* And this can those

- **Martyrdom** (martiry): Suffering or death on behalf of a cause, here specifically following Christ.

- **Worldlings** (werreltlingen): Those preoccupied with earthly life rather than spiritual matters.

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

*...[he] quickly leaves [his good works] when he is reproached. In what manner can you keep the Commandments of God, if you have no enemy? For the Lord says in the Gospel: love your enemies. Here it can be understood that it is necessary for the evil to be mixed with the good. For as the fire proves the gold, so the evil prove the good. Good men are like gold, and evil men are like straw. If you do evil, you will be like straw in the fire, and you will make smoke. Therefore the Prophet says: fire burns the companies of the sinners. And Saint Paul says: I do not think that the passions of this time are together worthy of the glory to come which is to be revealed to us. And Saint Augustine says: what is this glory which shall be revealed to us if not that the just are Children of God, and are equal to the Angels.*

<column-break/>

...immediately lets them go, as if they lost their taste for them. But to return to the matter, how could you keep all of God's commandments if you did not have even the slightest enemies, since we have this express command in the Holy Scriptures regarding this: *love your enemies?* It is therefore necessarily required that the good are constantly mixed with the evil. Namely, just as the fire purifies and tests true gold, so the godless reveal the good; since these are gold, as the others are straw. If you then must be counted among these latter, you shall be placed like straw upon the fire and, according to the words of the Holy Prophet <note>Dutch: "H. Kerk-voorsegger", literally 'Holy Church-foreteller'</note>, vanish in smoke: *the fire*, these are the words, *shall entirely consume the gatherings of the sinners.* Finally, the words of the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>A traditional title for Saint Paul</note> are very clear on this matter: *I consider, he says, that the suffering of this present time is not to be valued against the glory that shall be revealed to us.* Which salvation is expressed a bit more closely in this sense by that Holy African Bishop <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note>: *what else shall the glory be, which must be revealed in us, but that the righteous are God's children and entirely equal to the Angels?*

<margin>Last discourse.</margin>

*Let the world rage now, let the world be frantic now, and detract with the tongue, now persecute us with the sword, now say to us all the evil that it can say by word. For all the evil that it can do to us is small in comparison to the reward <note>original: "guiardòn"</note> which God promises to us. He who kills your body cannot kill your soul, but increases your reward, and you pray for him that your reward does not fail.*

<column-break/>

Let the world then freely roar and rage, as long as it is weary, let it slander us with the tongue, persecute us with the sword, and vomit out all evil against us with full jaws to the best of its ability. The worst it can ever do to us is almost nothing in comparison to the incomprehensible reward that God’s goodness has assigned to us; because those who kill the body do not even damage the soul thereby. Expect then with patience that reward of yours, which can never-more fail you, and never fail to pray for them.

<margin>Consolation.</margin>

*We must despise for the love of God all that delights us in this age. And not only that which delights, but even that which frightens us, such as prison, bonds, poverty, hunger, cold, sword, and death. You ought to despise and hold as vile all these things...*

<column-break/>

What one must fear and not fear.

*Let us think what things we ought to fear, and what things not. He is a fool who fears the prison of this world, which passes away quickly, and does not fear the prison of Hell which shall last eternally. He is a fool who fears the Kings, and the Princes, and the Prelates of this world, and does not fear the demons of Hell. He is a fool who fears the death of this world which shall pass away quickly, and does not fear the infernal death which shall remain perpetually. For such a small path, such a long death; for such a small joy, such a long sadness; for such a small light, such great darkness; for such a small laugh, such great weeping and such bitter tears as the sinners shall suffer in the other world, of which the Lord says: Woe to you who laugh; for you shall weep and mourn: for such a small beauty, such great filth; for such a small strength, such great weakness; for such a small security, such great fear. Of which Augustine says: it is a vain fear to fear losing temporal things, and not to fear losing celestial things. It is a vain fear for one who fears losing the company of the Father, and of the*

<margin>
Wretched exchanges.
</margin>

<column-break/>

Let us then take seriously to heart both what we must do and what we must leave undone. He is a fool who is fearful of the bonds of this earth, which are broken after a short time; and instead is occupied with a drowsy care regarding those eternal ones. He is a fool who fears the Kings, Princes, and Church-prelates <note>Dutch: "Kerk-voogden," referring to high-ranking ecclesiastical authorities</note> of this world, and is unafraid of the Devils of Hell. He is a fool who is anxious about temporal death, which one can overcome in a moment; and meanwhile does not dread the spiritual dying, which with its unceasing pains can never-more pass away. For such people shall one day inevitably find a lasting death for such a fleeting life, an age of sorrow for a moment of joy, such great darkness for such a small light, so many tears for so little laughter, such bitter weeping, that our Lord Jesus himself says this regarding the coming age: *woe to you who now laugh: for you shall cry, weep, and howl:* for such small beauty such great deformity, for such slight strength such notable weakness, and finally for such an unfeeling carelessness so many moving terrors. And this also wrung these words from St. Augustine: *one is wrongly afraid of missing earthly things, instead of dreading the loss of the Heavenly. Likewise, one is wrongly afraid of missing the company of Father and Mother, instead of dreading the loss of the presence of God.*

[...your] *mother, and does not fear losing the company of God, and of the Virgin Mary. He is vainly afraid who fears losing the company of the Brothers and the Sisters, and does not fear losing the brotherhood of the Angels. Regarding which Saint John said in the Apocalypse, when he wished to worship him: See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow-servant, and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus; worship God.*

*You who fear your death, love your life; your life is the Holy Spirit. If you sin, you do not please God. The just man alone is free, and no other. The child, when he is born, cries before he laughs; the tears he sheds bear witness to him that he comes into the misery of this world; in this way the child is a prophet of his future labor. If the just man lives, he shall suffer persecution. For evil men persecute the good, not always with iron, nor with stones, nor with clubs; but with their evil life and their evil works. Therefore Saint Peter praised the life of Lot; for he had suffered tribulation among evil men. And Saint Paul says: perils among false brothers <note>original: "perilli en fals frayre"</note>. All other tribulations and persecutions may cease; but the persecution against the good shall not fail. And if you do not believe it, begin to live well, and you will see in what manner evil men persecute you.*

<column-break/>

...and the Holy Virgin Mary. One is wrongly afraid <note>Dutch: "t'onregt bevreeft," meaning a misplaced or spiritually incorrect fear</note> of missing the mutual comfort of Sisters and Brothers, instead of fearing the loss of the glorious Brotherhood of the Holy Angels; of one of whom we ourselves can hear these words through the Apostle John (who wished to worship him) in his Holy Revelation: *See, he says, that you do not do that. I am your fellow-servant and of your brothers, who have the testimony of Jesus: worship God.*

You then, who tremble so before death, cherish and love your life freely; for your true life is the Holy Spirit. If, on the contrary, you sin, you do not please God. No one is also truly free, except the righteous. Nevertheless, just as with a little child, who is born to crying before laughter, and that trickling moisture <note>Dutch: "bickelende vogt," a poetic 17th-century term for the first tears of a newborn</note> very clearly testifies to his upcoming evils—into which he is entangled here through his birth into the world—serving thus as a harbinger of his miseries; just so shall both the life and the suffering of the godly begin and end together. For evildoers will always try to oppress the good: and though they cannot always use cobblestones, sticks, and swords to the same degree, they will nonetheless seek to harm them through their scandalous life and evil works. But for that very reason, your holy life shall also be continually praised by the holy. Thus, the life of that upright Lot <note>A biblical figure who lived in Sodom; the author uses him as an example of maintaining righteousness in a corrupt society</note> is still praised by St. Peter today, *because he suffered heavy oppressions among the godless.* So also St. Paul recounts of himself, *that he found himself in danger not seldom among false brothers.* Supposing then that all other persecutions and miseries were ever to cease, yet these insults from the wicked would never be halted or come to an end. Your disciplined and holy life prevents you from doubting this in the least. You have found that even the very beginning of your so God-fearing walk immediately encountered those thorns of misery, which the malice of your haters had so abundantly sown there.

# General Memorial Record

<margin>Threefold patience.</margin>
The Wise Man <note>original: "Lo Savy"; likely referring to Solomon or the author of the Book of Sirach</note> says: the friends of God ought to have three types of patience. *The first is in all the evils that are done or said to them. The second is in their infirmities, and in all the trials that God allows to come to them in this world. The third patience is against the Devil, who strives to turn them away from their good works. But no one shall be crowned if he does not fight loyally <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:5</note>. And where there is a greater battle, there is a greater merit <note>original: "fallù"; likely meaning spiritual worth or valor in this context</note>, and a more noble crown.* Therefore says the Wise Man: *I speak to you according to the patience of God. For he who is patient under the lash, and in the persecutions of evil men, shall have a greater reward. Just as the grape, when it is most pressed, yields more wine. Just as the olive*

<margin>Fruits of Misery.</margin>
*when it is most pressed, the dregs go to one side, and the oil remains clear. Just as the wheat, when it is most threshed, the chaff goes to one side, and the grain to the other. But if you wish to be good, while you are in this life, suffer evil men near you in patience. And the Wise Man says: the truly patient one hopes to have the brotherhood of the Angels. The truly patient one does not become angry. For it is a certain thing that God loves those who shall hate the world for love of Him. The good man ought to rejoice in pain, and in his labor, and in his poverty. For God promises him eternal life. And the wicked man ought to weep for his joy, and for his delight, and for his riches. For through such joy, and such delight, and such riches, God grants him eternal punishment.*

->God supports him who bears [trials] in patience<-

<column-break/>

The Wise Man says: *all children of God have three kinds of patience to practice. And truly, the first presents itself immediately regarding the evil that is said of them, or done to them; the second after that regarding the weaknesses and calamities that God still allows to prevail in this world; and finally the last regarding the Devil himself, who exerts all his strength to turn them away from their good works. No one shall ever be crowned unless they have endured all this both courageously and faithfully; but on the contrary, where the battle has been more fierce, there shall be both a much greater salvation and a much more precious crown.* And to this applies the wise saying of someone: *I speak to you according to the forbearance <term>forbearance: the quality of being patient and providing mercy even when provoked</term> of God. For he who is patient in heavier suffering and enduring in the persecutions of the wicked, shall thereby also obtain a greater reward; nearly in the same way as after the hardest pressing of the grape follows the most wine, after the heaviest squeezing of the olive the most oil—separated from the olive-dregs—and after the most violent threshing of the ears of grain follows the most corn, easily cleansed from fine, useless straw.* If you then wish to make virtue your work, you must apply yourself above all things to this: that you must meet those evil oppressors, among whom you live, with patience in everything. The proverb of the Wise Man urges you to this, because it holds for certain that a truly forbearing person can be assured that the joyful enjoyment of the brotherhood of the Angels awaits him. Such a person is also never angered by his condition, because he knows for certain that God loves those who hate the world for His sake alone. The God-fearing man then must rejoice in his supposed sorrow, torments, and poverty, because the Lord promises him the eternally blessed life for it. On the other side, however, the godless man has reasons to constantly weep for his pleasures, joy, and wealth, since such wantonness and delights carry nothing else with them but those unceasing pains of hell.

He who considers God sufficient, can [bear] all his... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches

### N 3

patience [bears] all the evils that are done to him. And Saint Sixtus <note>Pope Sixtus II, a 3rd-century martyr often cited in Waldensian literature</note> says: Do not kill yourself, but if someone else should kill you, let it not displease you. And Saint John Golden-Mouth <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father</note> says: if Christ is with me, whom shall I fear? even if all the waves of the sea came against me, and all the Princes of this world opposed me, all these things are like sand, and more fragile than sand. I do not say this because I have confidence in myself or my own strength; but I trust in our Lord Jesus Christ and in His Commandments which I have in my heart, and in my hands, that is, in my works, which make me strong. Even if all the waves of the sea came against me, and all the Princes of this world were against me, they all cannot overcome or harm me. All those who are in the sea, and on the land, cannot harm the good man, if he does not harm himself.

The friends of God were scourged and distressed in many ways. Some were put to death by the sword, just as was Saint John the Baptist, who was beheaded in the prison of King Herod because he reproved the sin of lechery; Saint Lawrence was roasted; Saint James [son] of Zebedee lost his head in Joppa. Saint James [son] of Alpheus, while he was in Jerusalem and preaching, the son of a bishop struck him with a club <note>original: "pertia"</note> over the head, and he fell down dead. Saint Bartholomew was beaten with rods, and afterwards was flayed. Saint Peter was placed on the cross with his feet above and his head below; Saint Andrew was placed there crosswise. Saint Matthew was [pierced by] arrows.

To this are added these words of the Holy John Golden-Mouth <note>Johannes Guldemont</note>: If the Lord Jesus is with me, for whom shall I fear? though even all the wild waves of the sea rushed against me, though all the princes of this world conspired against me; that would all be but sand, and looser than sand. We do not say this, however, to ground any confidence in ourselves or in any of our own strengths; but only that we rely on Christ and His Commandments, which we carry in our hearts and hands, namely striving to put their conscientious content into practice and thereby to strengthen ourselves to the highest degree. We say then once more, that even if all those roaring waves of the sea, even if all the powers of the earth rose up against us at once, they would not be able to harm us in the least. For everything that is found either in the sea or anywhere on the earth cannot do the man any harm, so long as he does not hinder himself.

...and received the reward of their labor, and are crowned in heaven. And the Wise Man <note>likely referring to Solomon or a general biblical sage</note> says: Let us regard the life of the Holy Martyrs, of the men and of the women who allowed themselves to be killed and delivered their flesh to death and martyrdom. Therefore the lives of the Saints are written so that we may take an example from them.

<column-break/>

...[and have] been inaugurated as heavenly Kings as the reward for their manifold labor. The Wise Man says then very well: Let us always have before our eyes the lives of the holy <term>blood-witnesses: A literal translation of "bloet-getuygen," meaning martyrs</term>, both of male and female nature, who never held their lives too dear, but on the contrary, when it was necessary, submitted themselves with joy to all death-dealing mistreatment. For this shall make us certain that they would never have entered into death or any danger of life so voluntarily, if they had not been fully assured that they would surely pass from this transitory life to that eternal life. At the same time, however, we must also keep in mind these words of St. Augustine; <margin>One must not pray for the dead.</margin> on the feast days of the Saints we must by no means pray to God for them, but only for us, to the end that He may please to grant us the grace that we may also enter the same path that they once walked, and practice similar love with them, so as finally to obtain a similar right of grace to the Kingdom of God with them as well. And this is also the true reason why the lives of all Saints have been so carefully left to us in writing, namely so that they might serve as powerful examples for later descendants.

[...] familiarly with an earthly King, but it is a much greater honor to speak familiarly with the heavenly and eternal King, to whom we speak while praying; <note>original: "miliarment a lò Rey terrenàl..." – the text compares the petitioning of a human monarch to the act of prayer</note> regarding which Isidore says: "He who wishes to be frequently with God should pray and read frequently. For when we pray, we speak to God, but when we read, God speaks to us." <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages</note> Prayer is a profitable thing; for as the Lord says: "I say specifically to you, that whatever thing you ask in prayer, believe that you shall receive it and it shall be done for you." <note>A reference to Mark 11:24</note> It is also quite easy; for a man can pray in every place and at every time, and it is not necessary to seek anything outside oneself. For only to think well and to desire well is to pray; as David says: "The Lord hears the desire of the poor," that is, of the humble poor who are weak, who cannot speak nor do anything, but can only pray or desire, and God is prepared to hear the prayer of their desire, as David says: "The Lord hears the desire of the poor." Therefore, prayer is a work so honorable, so profitable, and so easy. Because of this, as is said in the Gospel, the Apostles asked Christ, as good disciples of a good Master, that he might teach them to pray; for they knew that they could not learn a better lesson, and said to him: "O Lord, teach us to pray"; to which responding he said: "when..."

<column-break/>

[...] to speak so with the heavenly and eternal King, as we always do through our prayers? This latter point is confirmed by that renowned Isidore; "the one," he says, "who wishes to have dealings with God frequently, must often apply himself to fervent prayer and holy reading." Namely, just as when we pray, we ourselves speak to God; so he speaks back to us when we read his Word. Prayer is, besides that, no less useful than it is honorable. This is shown very clearly by these words of our Savior himself: "I say to you very explicitly, that whatever it may be that you shall wish to request through prayer, it shall, if you only believe, certainly happen for you and be given to you." But finally, it is also the easiest thing that one can conceive of, because one can pour out one's prayers at all times and in all places. Add to this, that one can do nothing in this by oneself, and it should be well noted that thinking well and longing well can not infrequently be considered as praying well. We see that in these words of the royal Prophet; <note>King David</note> "the Lord," he says, "hears the longing of the poor," that is, of the humble; unless one would otherwise fittingly wish to understand by that name such weak people who can therefore neither speak nor do anything else than just pray through desire. Which can appear all the more from this, because God is said always to be ready to grant all those their wish-prayers, while the words of the Psalm, or God-song, lie thus: "the Lord hears the longing of the poor." So that from all this it is now easily to be inferred that praying must be a very honorable, very useful, and easy work. Therefore, the Holy Apostles, those good pupils of their good Teacher Christ, also requested, as we read that in the <term>Sacred Scriptures: The original Dutch "Bont-ſchriften" likely refers to the "Bond-schriften" or Covenant writings (the Bible)</term>, that it might please him to teach them to pray, as those who well knew that they could never apply themselves to a better branch of learning, and said to him: "O Lord, teach us to pray." To which request they also immediately received a desired answer. For, "when you pray," our Savior said in reply...

<margin>Explanation of the preface.</margin>
In this Prayer, he teaches us first and before all things to obtain God’s goodwill so as to be able to demand from him all that is necessary for us, when he says; *O you our Father, who art in the Heavens.* It is as if he said: you are our Father by right of Creation, just as Moses himself formerly made known in his fifth Book, Deuteronomy, with these words: is (God) not your Father, who has had you in possession, who made you, who created you? You are our Father by right of Redemption, because you have ransomed us with your own blood, giving thus the greatest proof of love that ever a Father could give to his Child. And so God is described to us in this sense in the Revelation, namely as the one who has loved us and washed us from our sins with his own blood. You are our Father in respect to nourishment, of the governance and the inheritance, with which you maintain us in being. And from this must be understood what the Lord Jesus once said to his Disciples; *and call no one here upon the earth your Father; for one is your Father, who is in the Heavens.* In all these ways then must this naming, *O you our Father*, be taken here, as by which this alone is meant: you shall, O God, or can, surely not reject our prayer, but on the contrary grant everything for which we shall pray rightly, since you are our Father, who formerly created us and once redeemed us; and who still governs us, maintains us, and promises us your inheritance.

But in that which follows, *who art in the Heavens*, we find secondly this Teaching of Christ, namely that we must strive to be such as might be worthy to be called the Heavens. And truly just as our God dwells in the tangible Heavens; so he also dwells principally with the assistance of his grace in the midst of the spiritual [heavens], that is, of his Saints. Upon this St. Isidore has looked, when he cites these [words] of King Solomon regarding these words, *which is my seat-place*; the soul

# General Memorial #

"the soul of the righteous is a throne to me." <note>original: "l'arma del juſt ès à mi ſeti." This is a common medieval citation attributed to God, reflecting the idea that God dwells within the believer.</note> *Rightly*, if we are not without spiritual sense, that is, enlightened within by true faith and without by honest conduct. Rightly is [the heart] wide, through charity toward God, through piety toward our neighbor, and through mercy toward enemies. *Rightly* is it raised from the earth by contemplation of celestial things and by disdain for earthly ones, so that we may say with the Apostle, "our conversation is in heaven": <note>Philippians 3:20. In this context, "conversation" means one's way of life or citizenship.</note> in that way the Lord recognizes the voice of our prayer when we say, *O you our Father who art in heaven*. *This* is the first part of the Lord’s Prayer, in which he teaches us first to seek the goodwill of God, and to ask of him all things necessary for us. But it is to be known that from this place until the end of the Lord’s Prayer are contained seven petitions, brief in words but deep and long in meaning. *Rightly* this prayer can hardly be fully explained by all the masters who are in the world. In these seven petitions are asked all things which are necessary for us in the present life, and in the one to come: but let us take for the present, for our edification, a simple and plain exposition.

<margin>Division and purpose of the whole Prayer.</margin>

<column-break/>

*the soul of the righteous is a throne for me*. And with justice we are considered such a Heaven, insofar as we are inwardly enlightened by honest conduct and have the bow of true godliness toward God, of true love toward our fellow man, and of compassion for our enemy always drawn. Indeed, through the contemplation and meditation on heavenly things and the despising of earthly things, we are so drawn from this earth into Heaven, that we can truly say with the Apostle; *our walk is with God in the high Heavens*. Hereby then God recognizes the voice of our prayer, namely when we say to him; *O you our Father, who art in the Heavens*. This is then the first part of the Prayer of our Lord, in which he teaches us to call upon God’s favor above all, and thereafter for our necessities. It stands meanwhile to be noted, that this entire Prayer consists of seven distinct Petitions, as rich and dignified in meaning as they are short in words; and that the same can therefore hardly be perfectly explained or interpreted by any Teacher of the world. Be that as it may, therein is always contained all that is in any way necessary for us, both for the present as well as the future life. Meanwhile, let us now endeavor for our edification to give a short and rough explanation of the same.

---

### The First Petition. ###

<margin>For chastity and against shameful unchastity.</margin>

THE first petition is, *thy name be hallowed*. In this petition we ask to be stripped of the sin of lewdness, and to be given the virtue of chastity; <note>The original term "luxuria" (Occitan) or "overdaat" (Dutch) refers specifically to lust or moral excess.</note> for we bear the name of Christ, and we are called Christians, which thing is nothing other than being a Disciple, and a servant, and a Child of Christ: but that name is defiled, and made vile, and blasphemed in us, when we live filthily and lewdly; but it is Hallowed and cleansed when we keep ourselves from all the filth of the heart, and of the mouth, and of the body.

### The First Petition. ###

THE first Petition lies in these words; *Hallowed be your name*. Through these then we request to be released from sin, but most particularly from excess, and in its place to be clothed with the virtue of a pure chastity. Namely, we bear the name of Christ and are called Christians after him, which actually signifies nothing else than that we are his Pupils, his Servants, and his Children. Now, just as this naming is defiled, despised, and slandered in us when we live in all impurity and lusts; so is it then first rightly hallowed when we keep our heart, our mouth, and body pure from all defilement, and [repent] all our previously committed misdeeds.

<term>Hallowed (Sanctifica): To make holy or to treat as holy.</term>
<term>Chastity (kuyſheyt): Moral purity, contrasted here with "luxuria" or "overdaat" (lust/excess).</term>

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches #

O 2

*bodies, and wash and purify past sins through true penitence <note>original Occitan: "vraya penedença"</note>. For just as Christians who bear the name of Christ are purified, that is, they are made Holy—for "Holy" is said to be without stain—but the sin of lust <note>original: "luxuria"</note> is called a stain. For just as a dye <note>original: "tentura"</note> takes away from the cloth its natural color, so lust takes from the soul the innocence of Baptism and all virtues. And just as the dye penetrates the cloth within and without, so lust defiles the whole man within and without. It defiles the man first in the body: by the force of impure thoughts, delights, and consent. Afterward the eyes, by unchaste looks; then the ears, by curious and inflammatory words leading to sin; then the nostrils, by the foul smells of harlots' ointments, with which devilish women paint themselves to please their lovers; then the mouth, by unchaste words, and by kissing, and by delicate and excessive eating, by which lust is nourished and inflamed; then the hands, by unchaste touching; and finally the entire body, by shameful rest, through which the Devil leads wretched sinners two by two to Hell. Therefore the meaning is, "Hallowed be thy name"—that is, O Lord, give us grace that we who have your name, and are named Christians after you, may be Holy; that is, without the stain and filth of carnal sin. O Lord, you will do these things if you give us the virtue and grace of continence, so that we may guard ourselves from the sin of lust. Of this Sanctification the Apostle says: "let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, perfecting Sanctification in the fear of the Lord." <note>2 Corinthians 7:1</note> And again the Apostle says: "this is the will of God, even your Sanctification, that you should abstain from fornication." <note>1 Thessalonians 4:3</note> But we cannot do this except through the help of God, and as*
saying

<column-break/>

wash and purify with true repentance <note>original Dutch: "boet-vaardigheyt"</note>. For those must be cleansed—that is, sanctified—who wish to be glorified by the name of Christ, because "holy" means nothing else than being without spot. Excess <note>original: "D’overdaat," referring here to both gluttony and lustful intemperance</note> is now fittingly called a smear. Namely, just as a spot deprives wool or cloth of its own naturally shiny color forever; so also the sin of gluttony strips the soul of the innocence of its Baptism and of all its further virtues. Indeed, just as dye penetrates and passes through cloth inside and out, so also excess defiles the man on all sides. It begins its filthiness first in the heart of the same through various abominable thoughts, pleasures, and secret consents to evil; from there to the eyes through lustful glances; in the ears through the hearing of many idle words that ignite the man to sin; in the nose through the smelling of the scents of harlotry, with which devilish women adorn themselves to please their lovers; in the mouth through unchaste speech and kisses and a hundred delicacies, by which excess is fanned and fed; in the hands through dishonest grasping and touching; and finally in the whole body through an unfortunate and godless laziness, which drags the sinners straight to hell. This then is the sense of these words, *Hallowed be thy name*; namely: give us, O Lord, who bear your name and are called *Christians* after you, the grace to be holy—that is, without smear or spot of fleshly sin. This you will bring about in us, O Lord, if you favor us with the virtue of chastity <note>original: "kuyfheyt"</note>, by which we may guard ourselves from the sin of immorality. Of this Sanctification the Apostle speaks: *let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, thus completing Sanctification in the fear of God*. Again, he has these words elsewhere: *this is the will of God, namely your Sanctification, and that you keep yourselves from harlotry*. # General Memorial Record #

<margin>Division and purpose of the whole Prayer.</margin> "The soul of the righteous is a throne for me" <note>This is a common medieval citation often attributed to the Church Fathers, suggesting that God dwells within a holy person as if on a throne.</note>. And rightly, if we are that spiritual Heaven, that is, enlightened within by true faith, and without by honest conduct <note>The original uses "conversation," which in the 17th century meant one's entire manner of living or behavior.</note>. Rightly it is wide, through charity toward God, through piety toward our neighbor, and through mercy toward enemies. Rightly it is raised from the earth through contemplation of celestial things and by disdain for earthly things, in such a way that we can say with the Apostle, our conduct is in heaven: in that way the Lord recognizes the voice of our prayer when we say, *O you our Father who are in heaven*. This is the first part of the Lord's Prayer, in which he teaches us to first seek the goodwill of God, and to ask of him all things necessary for us. But it is to be known that from this place until the end of the Lord's Prayer are contained seven petitions, brief in words but thick and long in meaning. Truly, this prayer can hardly be fully explained by all the masters who are in the world. In these seven petitions are asked all the things which are necessary for us in the present life, and in the one to come: but let us take for the present, for our edification, a simple and plain explanation.

### The First Petition. ###

<margin>For chastity and against shameful unchastity.</margin> **T**he first petition is, *Hallowed be thy name*. In this petition we ask to be removed from us the sin of lust <note>original Occitan: "luxuria"; Dutch: "overdaat" (excess). In this context, it refers broadly to debauchery or sexual immorality.</note>, and to be given the virtue of chastity; for we bear the name of Christ, and we are called Christian, which is nothing other than being a disciple, and a servant, and a child of Christ: but that name is soiled, and made vile, and blasphemed in us, when we live filthily and lustfully, but it is sanctified and cleansed when we restrain ourselves from all the filth of the heart, and of the mouth, and of the body,

<column-break/>

*The soul of the righteous is a throne for me*. And rightly are we considered such a Heaven, insofar as we are inwardly enlightened by honest conduct and have always kept the bow of true godliness toward God, of true love toward our fellow man, and of compassion for our enemy, drawn tight. Yes, through the contemplation and pondering of heavenly things and the despising of earthly things, we are so drawn from this earth into Heaven, that we can truly say with the Apostle; *our walk is with God in the high Heavens*. Hereby then God recognizes the voice of our prayer, namely when we say to him; *O you our Father, who are in the Heavens*. This is then the first part of our Lord's Prayer, in which he teaches us above all to call upon God's favor, and thereafter for our necessities. It should meanwhile be noted, that this whole Prayer consists of seven distinct petitions, as rich and dignified in meaning as they are short in words; and that the same can therefore hardly ever be perfectly declared or explained by any teacher of the world. Whatever the case may be, therein is always contained all that is in any way necessary for us, both for the present and the future life. Meanwhile, let us now endeavor for our edification to give a short and plain explanation of the same.

### The First Petition. ###

**T**he first petition lies in these words; *Hallowed be your name*. Through this then we request to be delivered from sin, but most especially from excess <note>original Dutch: "overdaat," referring here to the "lust" mentioned in the Occitan column.</note>, and to be clothed in its place with the virtue of a pure *chastity*. Namely, we bear the name of Christ and are called Christians after him, which actually signifies nothing else than that we are his disciples, his servants, and his children. Now just as this naming is defiled, despised, and blasphemed in us when we live in all impurity and lusts; so it is then first truly hallowed when we keep our heart, our mouth, and our body pure from all defilement, and all our past crimes

...body, and let us wash and purify past sins through true penance. For just as the Christians who bear the name of Christ are purified, that is, made Holy <note>The original Occitan text explains "Sant" (Saint/Holy) as being "without stain" (senza tentura).</note>, for "Holy" is said to be without stain; but the sin of luxury <note>The term "luxuria" in medieval and early modern theology specifically refers to the sin of lust or unchastity.</note> is called a stain. For just as a stain removes from a cloth its natural color, so the sin of luxury removes from the soul the innocence of Baptism and all the virtues: just as a dye permeates a cloth inside and out, so luxury pollutes the whole man inside and out. It pollutes the man first in the heart, through foul and unclean thoughts, delights, and consent: afterwards the eyes through unchaste looking, and afterwards the ears through curious words that inflame one to sin, afterwards the nose through the foul smelling of meretricious <note>Relating to or characteristic of a prostitute.</note> ointments, with which devilish women paint themselves to please their lovers: afterwards the mouth, through unchaste words, and by kissing, and by delicate and excessive eating, by which luxury is nourished and inflamed: then the hands through unchaste touching: and finally the whole body, through shameful rest by which the Devil leads the miserable sinners two by two to Hell. Therefore, the meaning is: "Thy name be Sanctified," that is, O Lord, give us grace that we who have Thy name, and are named Christians after Thee, may be Holy, that is, without the stain and filth of carnal sin; O Lord, Thou shalt do these things if Thou wilt give us the virtue and grace of continence, so that we may keep ourselves from the sin of luxury. Of this Sanctification the Apostle says: *Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting Sanctification in the fear of the Lord.* And again the Apostle says: *This is the will of God, even your Sanctification, that you should abstain from fornication.* But we cannot do this except by the help of God, & just as...

<column-break/>

...must wash away and purify with a true penitence. For those who wish to be glorified with the name of Christ must be cleansed in this way—that is, hallowed—since "holy" means nothing else than "without stain." Excess <note>The Dutch "overdaat" here translates the Occitan "luxuria," implying both physical excess and lust.</note> is now fittingly called a smudge. To wit: just as a spot robs wool or cloth of its own shiny color forever, so also the sin of gluttony <note>The translator uses "gulshigheyt" (gluttony/excess), linking dietary indulgence to sexual sin.</note> strips the soul of the innocence of its Baptism and of all its further virtues. Yes, just as the dyeing of cloth permeates and strikes through inside and out, so also excess defiles the man on all sides. It first begins its filthiness in his heart through various abominable thoughts, pleasures, and secret consents to evil; from there into the eyes through lecherous leers; in the ears through the hearing of many idle words which ignite a man to sin; in the nose through the smelling of the scents of whoredom, with which devilish women adorn themselves to please their lovers; in the mouth through unchaste speech and kisses and a hundred delicacies, by which excess is fanned and fed; in the hands through a dishonest grasping and touching; and finally in the whole body through an unhappy and godless laziness, which drags the sinners straight toward hell. This then is the sense of these words: *Hallowed be thy name*, to wit: give us, O Lord, who bear Thy name and are called Christians after Thee, the grace to be allowed to be holy—that is, without smudge or stain of fleshly sin. This Thou shalt, O Lord, bring about in us, if Thou favorest us with the virtue of chastity, through which we may guard ourselves from the sin of lewdness. Of this Sanctification the Apostle speaks: *let us cleanse ourselves well from all defilement of flesh and spirit, thus completing Sanctification in the fear of God.* Again he has these words elsewhere: *this is the will of God, namely your Sanctification, and that you keep yourselves from whoredom.* But while we, without God's help <margin>The assistance of Grace.</margin> can progress in nothing in this, and that according to the saying...
