### The Second Petition

<margin>Against greed and in favor of love and spiritual poverty.</margin>
Now follows the second petition: *Thy Kingdom come*. In this petition, we ask the Heavenly Father that the sin of avarice <term>avarice: the sin of greed or the excessive desire for wealth</term> be removed from us, and the virtue of spiritual poverty, and of piety and mercy, be given to us: for the Kingdom of Heaven is denied to the greedy and to the rich of this world; as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> says: the greedy shall not possess the Kingdom of God. And the Lord says in the Gospel: the rich shall enter the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty, for it is an easier thing for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And again he says: woe unto you rich, who have your consolation here; but on the contrary, the Kingdom of Heaven is given to the poor; as the Lord says: blessed are the poor in spirit, for the Kingdom of Heaven is theirs. He says "poor in spirit" well, that is, by will, not by force or necessity in life. And as a Saint says, there is poverty of three kinds, namely: slothful <note>original: "enfegnayriç"; the Dutch column clarifies this as poverty arising from laziness or "luyigheyt"</note>, necessary, and voluntary. Furthermore, we must flee from slothful poverty, of which David says: they wish to be poor in such a way that they suffer no need. We must patiently sustain necessary [poverty], and embrace the

<column-break/>

saying of King Solomon, no one can be restrained and temperate unless such is given by God Himself, and that this knowledge is a heavenly wisdom; I understand it from those whom God has enriched with such gifts; so we are always compelled to cry out to Him: *O Lord, O You, our Father, who art in the Heavens, hallowed be Your name.*

### The Second Petition

Here now follows the second Petition; *Thy Kingdom come*. Through this, we request of the Heavenly Father that He may be pleased to deliver us from the sin of greed and to put the virtue of spiritual poverty, of compassion and mercy in its place. For the Kingdom of the Heavens is denied to the money-hungry and the rich of this world. The Apostle indicates this regarding the first group in these words: *the greedy*, he says, *shall by no means possess the Kingdom of God*. Concerning the others, we have the words of our Savior in the Gospel: *the rich shall reach the Kingdom of the Heavens with difficulty. For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to come into the Kingdom of Heaven.* And therefore He also speaks elsewhere: *a woe upon you, O rich, who here below wish to create all your contentment alone.* To the poor, on the contrary, God's kingdom is given, which our Savior himself confirms in this sense; *blessed*, he says, *are the poor in spirit: for to them alone does the Heavenly Kingdom rightfully belong.* He very well uses these emphatic words *the poor in spirit*, that is, the simple folk and those who possess little goods here on earth; because, as a certain Saint very well says, there are three kinds of deficiency <note>Dutch: "gebrekelikheyt"; referring here to states of poverty</note>: one namely, *which comes from laziness*, another, *which comes from necessity*, and a third, *which has its origin in free will*. Now, just as we must flee with all diligence the first poverty of sloth—of which the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> speaks thus: *they fall into want because they will undergo no labor*—and overcome necessity with patience; so

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches. #

...voluntarily and with all one's heart, for in this way they become poor in spirit. Of this poverty Saint James says: <note>James 2:5</note> *Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in Faith, as heirs to the Kingdom, which God has promised to those who love him?* And Saint Augustine speaks in the person of Christ: *I have something to sell, I have something to sell; and what? The Kingdom of God, Heaven, the Kingdom of Heaven.* In what manner is it bought? Through poverty; rest through labor; life through death; the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to the poor. Therefore it must be acquired through poverty, as the Holy Apostles and their followers were; that is, all the truly religious who leave all temporal things and follow Christ in poverty. Yet it is necessary that it be bought from him by the poor through works of mercy given to the poor. Just as Zacchaeus did, who gave half of his goods to the poor, and if he had defrauded anyone, he restored it twofold; <note>The text says "doblès," meaning double, though the biblical account in Luke 19:8 specifies fourfold.</note> and as all the good rich do, to whom it shall be said on the day of judgment: *Come, blessed of my Father, possess the Kingdom that is prepared for you from the beginning of the world.* But no one can excuse themselves from the purchase of this kingdom; for as Gregory <note>St. Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential theologian.</note> says: The Kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess. It was worth the boat and the nets to the Holy Apostles; it was worth half his goods to Zacchaeus; it was worth two small coins to a widow, which she placed on the altar of God; and to another, it was worth a cup of cold water. As Gregory says: *Therefore, nothing is cheaper when it is being bought, nor more precious once it is possessed.* But if you say that you cannot have even a cup of cold water to give to the poor, you still cannot excuse yourself from the purchase of the heavenly Kingdom. For if you have nothing else, a good will...

<column-break/>

...we must also embrace that voluntary poverty with all our hearts. For in that way alone one becomes poor in spirit. It is also of this poverty that Saint James uses these words: *Has God not chosen the poor of this world, who are rich in faith, to be heirs of the Kingdom, which is prepared for those who love him?* Saint Augustine elsewhere introduces our Savior speaking thus about it: *I have something for sale, I have something for sale. And what then? The Kingdom of God, Heaven, and the Kingdom of the Heavens.* But how is it bought? With Poverty; since rest is obtained through effort and life through death. *The Kingdom of Heaven belongs to the Poor.* We must then and can only obtain it through such poverty, as we have clearly seen in the Holy Apostles and their followers, that is, in all true servants of the Lord, who fully and readily leave all their temporal goods to better follow Christ in poverty. So did Zacchaeus in former times, among others, who distributed half of all his riches to the needy, and if he had wronged anyone in anything, he compensated them richly twofold. So also all those rich people try to do, to whom on the Day of Judgment this will be said: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.* No one can excuse themselves from the acquisition of this Kingdom. For Saint Gregory says very well: <margin>The value of the Kingdom of God.</margin> *The Kingdom of God is worth everything that a person possesses; to the Apostles their little boat and nets, to Zacchaeus half of all his goods, to the poor widow her two pennies, which she solemnly brought to the altar of the Lord, and to another a cup of fresh water.* There is then, as he says in another place, *nothing so cheap while it is for sale, nor anything of such high value once one is in possession of it.* Yes, even if you might say that you do not even have a drink of refreshment to give to the poor, you still cannot relieve yourself from taking in this Heavenly Kingdom. For your good desire, your good will, shall then fully serve <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page "ſtrecken" completes the sentence on the next page as "verſtrecken" (to provide or serve).</note> you in all things.

### The Third Petition.

<margin>Against sloth.</margin>

**W**e now come to the third petition: *Thy will be done.* By this, we pray for this alone: that we might be delivered from the sin of <term>sloth</term><note>The original Dutch uses "vuygheyt," referring to laziness or spiritual apathy, often called "acedia" in theological texts.</note>. For sloth alone gives birth to all excess, nurtures gluttony, sows all strife and division of minds, and fosters all hatred toward those who live well. Indeed, even when we do something good, we do it so sluggishly, without zeal, and somewhat contemptuously; by that means, instead of a rich blessing, we bring a heavier curse upon our necks, since according to the saying of the Prophet Jeremiah, <note>Jeremiah 48:10</note> *all those are cursed who do the work of the Lord with sluggishness.* In this way, it is also sloth to be unwilling to bring a work once begun to its end. And what wonder is it, then, that we do not reach our reward, since it is not the beginning, but the end of the struggle that brings about the crowning? But furthermore, such lazy people also transgress the command of the Law, which holds that one *must solemnly dedicate every sacrificial beast entirely to God, with both head and tail.* <note>A symbolic interpretation of Levitical law, suggesting a good work must be completed from start to finish.</note> That is to say, all good works that we hallow to the Lord and do to His honor are our altar-cattle; the beginning of them is the head, and the end is the tail. ### Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches. ###
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

The head is the beginning of the work, but the tail is the end. Let us offer the sacrifice to God, the head with the tail, by persevering and bringing the good work to its conclusion. <note>original Occitan: "cap ès lo commançamènt de lobras: ma la coa ès la fin." A metaphor meaning that a task begun must be completed to be a worthy offering.</note> And the *slothful* <term>acidia: a state of spiritual apathy or "the sin of sloth"</term> and the *lazy* would not do anything, but would be idle at all times. This is a great danger to the body and the soul; and thus it is said in *Wisdom* <note>original: "sapiença", likely referring to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 33:27: "Send him to work, that he be not idle; for idleness teacheth much evil."</note>, *idleness teaches many evils.* For the thought of man can hardly ever be idle: for when it is not occupied with good, it is occupied with evil. And therefore it is said that idleness is the sink <note>original: "sentina", meaning a bilge-well or a sewer</note> of all evils. The bilge is the lowest place in the ship, and there serpents and reptiles are easily born. Just as it often happens that in the idle soul, evil thoughts, consents, and delights are born. And *Gregory* <note>St. Gregory the Great</note> says: Solomon's heart abandoned the wisdom of God as soon as no discipline guarded him from without. Therefore it is necessary for man to be watchful in his self-guarding, and to carefully guard the castle of the heart and soul, and to be occupied at all times in some good thought, or speech, or work; just as *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome</note> says: always do something good so that the Devil finds you occupied. Therefore we ask that this very dangerous sin of sloth be removed from us when we say *Thy will be done*, and we ask here that the virtue of devotion, true love, and good work be given to us. But devout men, inflamed with Divine love, never want to be idle: but they always study to occupy themselves in doing the will of God on earth: just as the Saints who are in Heaven did and do.

<column-break/>

...then first properly offered, when one fulfills the once-started good works with a persistent perseverance until the very last. Now the good-for-nothings and idlers never seek anything else than to do nothing and to remain lying in inner filthiness. Meanwhile, this is very dangerous both for the body and for the soul. In this way, the wise Solomon speaks thus regarding this matter: *idleness is a teacher of a hundred evils.* And truly, just as the thoughts of man can hardly, or rather never, be inactive, so they are constantly busy with either something good or something evil. Therefore it is written in another place, that idleness is the *bilge-water of all kinds of evil.* Just as in the bilge <note>Dutch: "buyk-denning", the lowest part of a ship's hold where foul water collects</note>, through neglect, snakes and all kinds of venomous vermin very easily come to grow; even so an empty soul commonly brings forth evil thoughts, and efforts, and unlawful pleasures. This is confirmed by the great Gregory, when he says: because the heart of Solomon had left the *dwelling-place of Divine wisdom, so he also followed not even the slightest discipline outwardly.* So that it is highly necessary that man be awake to be able to guard himself properly before all things, to cautiously preserve the strength of his heart and soul, and to constantly make good reflections, good reasoning, and all kinds of good works his habitual business. This is the admonition of St. Jerome: *always do,* he says, *something good, so that the Devil may never find you without work.* The objective then of our Prayer, which we often present to God in these words *Thy will be done*, is only the deliverance from this dangerous evil—I mean the shameful sin *of sloth*—and the obtaining of the opposite virtue of godliness, of true love, and all good works. For no godly people, or even those who are in any way kindled with divine love, will ever want to give themselves to idleness; but on the contrary, make it their constant work here on earth to always do God's will in all things, just as the Saints in Heaven likewise do.

# General Memorial-Script. #

<margin>The assistance of Grace.</margin>
But we cannot do this without *Divine grace* <note>original Occitan: "Divina gracia"</note>, therefore we must ask that your will be done, as it is done in Heaven, so let it be done on earth. For the will of God is done in Heaven without ceasing, without sorrow, without murmuring, and without contradiction: in this same way all good *Christians* strive to do on earth, and as *Gregory* <note>St. Gregory the Great</note> says: the proof of the work is the fulfillment of love, and the love of God is never idle, for it performs great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is not love. And Saint Bernard says; O good Jesus, your love is never idle: those who love you do not grow weary. To speak of you is perfect consolation, to speak of you is full restoration. To draw near to you is eternal life; to depart from you is perpetual death. O good Jesus, may you be honey in the mouth, a sweet song in the ear, joy in the heart. Therefore, this is the third request; your will be done, in which we ask to be delivered from the sin of <term>sloth: acidia, a state of spiritual apathy or boredom</term>, and to be given the virtue of devotion and of good works.

<column-break/>

But while we can advance not even the least bit in this without the grace of the Lord, we must desire from our God, *that His will be done on earth, as it is in Heaven*. Just as the will of God is done in Heaven without ceasing, without reluctance, without murmuring, and without contradiction; so must all Christians here on earth especially apply themselves to the same. St. *Gregory* is of this same opinion here, when he says: *the testing of the work is the perfection of love, and the love of God is never idle, because everywhere it finds itself, it works out very great things; also such that as soon as it ceases to be so active, it simultaneously ceases to be love*. With this, these words of St. Bernard agree: *O Lord, the love that one bears for you is never inactive. Those who truly love you never grow faint in it. To speak of you is a perfect comfort, to speak of you is a complete satisfaction. To approach you is eternal life and to depart from you is eternal damnation. O good Jesus, you are the honey for the mouth, the soothing song for the ears, and a complete joy for the heart*. So much then for the third Petition, through which we request to be delivered from the sin of laziness and to be favored with the virtue of godliness and fitness for good works.

---

The explanation of the following Petitions is not found in the original manuscript, of which we have added and obtained a portion above. However, since this same Prayer is explained in its entirety in a certain book of the *Waldensians*, called *The Treasure of the Faith* <note>original Occitan: "Lou Trefor de la Fe"</note>; I have seen fit to include here only the faithful translation given to us by the Lord of Perrin <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a 17th-century historian of the Waldensians</note> of that exposition in the 5th Chapter of his *History of the Waldensians and Albigensians*, page 201, the more so because one can always consult the aforementioned original manuscript in their own language in his work.

### Another Exposition, written by the Waldensians and Albigensians concerning the Lord's Prayer. ###

<margin>How one can pray much with few words.</margin>
"**S**t. Augustine, having been asked once by one of his spiritual daughters to teach her how to pray, wrote and taught there; that *a multitude of words does not make the prayer*. And truly, one prays in the opposite way no less, if one only wishes to remain in the thoughts of praying. Namely, one prays well and much only when our prayers are appropriately fervent: it is then no 'much praying' to demand one's necessities with superfluous words; it is much...

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches. ###

,, ...to pray much with a persistent disposition and inclination of the heart, entreating God for all that is necessary for us. This is also much better achieved through tears and sighs, because the Lord our God, who perfectly sees the secrets of our hearts, can be moved more by a sigh, by groaning and tears drawn from the innermost parts of our hearts, than by a thousand words. Nevertheless, there are today not a few people like the Pharisees—whom the Lord Christ did not want His disciples to resemble—who claim that through the use of many words in their prayers they will be heard much sooner. And from this it follows that such people, under the appearance of praying, often uselessly waste much time.

,, Meanwhile, the holy Job says somewhere—and it is confirmed by experience—*that man, as long as he lives, is never found in the same state, but that he is now more inclined to one thing than to another.* <note>This refers to the inherent instability of the human condition; even in prayer, the mind tends to wander.</note> And how then can anyone, without a miraculous and now unhoped-for grace of God, keep his thoughts focused on prayer for whole days and nights? Or, without this attentiveness of the heart, not lose his time and pray otherwise than in vain? For this reason, even the good God has prescribed many edifying exercises, both of soul and body, to His servants, with which they could habitually occupy themselves for their own sake and for their fellow man, and in some way lift up their heart to God and thus completely remove its emptiness. Not to mention that those who, according to God's will and the teaching of His saints, <margin>Prayer of the heart.</margin> order and arrange their lives, are considered to pray always; because every good work done by man serves before God as an invocation of His Name.

,, Whatever the case may be, he who lives much should know that all prayers of the Old and New Testament agree with this [the Lord's Prayer] in all parts. Since no prayer is heard by God or is pleasing unless it is contained within this one; therefore, all Christians are very strictly obliged to sharpen their senses and understanding so that they might thoroughly understand and learn the same, as their Savior taught it to them with His own mouth.

,, Meanwhile, it is certain that just as he who is to be heard by God must love Him, so also he who has already been heard must be thankful to Him for all the good that he has received so manifoldly from the same. For ingratitude is a wind that dries up the fountain of God's mercy and compassion. So, if you wish to ask or pray for anything from the Lord, you must first of all diligently consider within yourself what and how many benefits you have already enjoyed. And if you cannot grasp them all in your thoughts—as is certainly the case—this request at least must always play within them: that you may have the grace from Him to call Him Father.

,, For He is generally a Father to all creatures through <margin>Why and how God is called our Father.</margin> *Creation*, because He has mightily brought them forth out of nothing; through *Governance*, because He arranges and fits each of them in their place as so many good things; and through *Sustenance*, because He preserves and maintains all things—among which you yourself also belong—in such a way that they do not fall back into their <term>nothingness: wese-loose, literally "essence-less," referring to the state of non-existence before creation</term>.

,, He is a Father of the human race by right of *Redemption*, because He has kindly redeemed it with the precious blood of His Son, that lamb without blemish; of *Instruction*, because through His Prophets, through His Son, through His Apostles and Teachers, He opens again to us in various ways the path to the Heavenly Garden of Delight, which the sin of our first father Adam had thrown shut, casting us out; and finally of *Visitation*, since He chastises and teaches us in various ways in this life, so that we might return to Him and thus escape eternal damnation in the life to come.

->*May your name be sanctified*, <note>Original: "Lo teo nom fia Sanctificà." This is the Waldensian/Occitan version of the Lord's Prayer.</note> that is, Hallowed be your Name;<-

,, Your name, which to Christians is lovely, but to the Heathens, Jews, and

,, saying: *O our Lord and God, how wondrous, how glorious is your name!*
,, It is, then, as if one said: O our Father, who art in the Heavens, we
,, pray you, that your holy name may be hallowed in us as is fitting, through
,, purity of heart and the contempt of the flesh and the world; and that we
,, may be holy through a firm perseverance in your love, just as your name
,, is holy—which we unworthily bear and after which we Christians are 
,, named. Let it, to that end, always be and remain among us, so that
,, we may be wise unto holiness and righteousness.

->*May your Kingdom come*, <note>Original: "Lo teo Regne adviene."</note> that is, Your Kingdom come.<-

<margin>The second.</margin>
,, It is necessary for all those who regularly occupy themselves with reading to
,, carefully observe that God the Father has two *Kingdoms*: one of
,, *Glory* and of the *Eternal*, the other of *Virtue* and the *Christian life*. These
,, are also so joined to one another that there is nothing between them
,, but the very point of death. Meanwhile, according to the arrangement of divine 
,, Justice, the Kingdom of Virtues comes before that of Glory. 
,, Which is why it is also beyond doubt that those who live well 
,, in virtues under the First—through which we all must pass to be able 
,, to approach the Kingdom of Glory—shall likewise rule for ever in the 
,, Last, the more so because one can never reach it through any other 
,, means. And this is also the reason that moved our Savior to speak 
,, thus to His Disciples: *seek first the Kingdom of God and his righteousness*,
,, that is, the Kingdom of Virtues, such as Faith, Hope, Love, and all the 
,, further Virtues of Righteousness. But while you cannot achieve the 
,, least bit in this without Heavenly Grace, you must therefore earnestly pray and
,, beseech, saying: *O our Father, who art in the Heavens, may your Kingdom come
,, among us*, namely the love for Virtue and the hatred against the world.

->*Thy will be done, as it is done in Heaven so may it be done on earth*; <note>Original: "La ton volonta fia fayta, en ayma es fayta en Cèl ſia fayta en terra."</note> that is,
Your Will be done, just as in Heaven, so also on the 
earth.<-

,, One can never consider anything so much, nor desire anything so

,, eternal life. Now, the doing of God's will consists in this alone: that one 
,, holily denies oneself, that is, one's own will, and carefully 
,, strives to arrange and prepare all that one either carries inwardly 
,, in the heart, or must perform outside oneself in temporal things, 
,, according to God's Law and the Teaching of Christ's Gospel: 
,, in a word, that one is perfectly content with everything that God does and 
,, allows, both in trial and in consolation. But some think to excuse

,, will. Yet that they therein greatly deceive themselves can be seen 
,, from this: namely, that the will of the Lord is very clearly described, 
,, revealed, and proven in His Holy Word, which they never 
,, deign to seek out. For thus the Holy Apostle speaks of it 
,, elsewhere: *and do not compare yourselves, nor agree with those*

<margin>The fifth.</margin>
,, It must not seem strange or difficult to anyone to forgive his fellow
,, man from the heart for everything he might ever have committed
,, against him. For even if all the crimes that were ever
,, committed against any man in the world, or ever are yet to happen,

,, on a scale of justice, equal even the slightest sin committed against God
,, in their combined weight. It is true that the pride
,, of man prevents him from thinking on this and seeing such matters rightly,

,, of his own sins from God himself by forgiving

,, to our Lord God that He will give to his debtors, or to those who
,, have wronged him, the grace to know their own misdeeds through

,, can never nor will ever think of how he might repay them according
,, to their worth, or long for his revenge; but rather, on the contrary, how he

,, of divine release except the fear of eternal misery,
,, because this true saying is found in God’s Word: *a merciless*

# General Memorial-Record #

### VIII. CHAPTER.

#### Concerning the fifth part of the Waldensian Doctrine, regarding their faithful translation and Explanation of the Apostle's Creed <term>Hooft-begrip des Geloofs: literally "the main-concept of the faith," referring to the Apostles' Creed</term>, which begins among them as follows: *Nos deven croyre en Dio, Payre tot-poissant* <note>Original Waldensian: "We must believe in God, Father almighty"</note>; in which they confirm all the main articles of the same with explicit Scriptural verses throughout.

<margin>Deut. 6:4.</margin>
WE must believe in God the Father, the almighty Creator of Heaven and Earth, who is a single Trinity, just as the words in the Law state: *Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one God*. Isaiah agrees with this: *I am the Lord, it says, and there is no other, nor any other God, but I*. St. Paul says likewise: *One Lord there is, one Faith, one Baptism, one God and Father of all people*. In St. John we have these words: *there are three who bear witness in Heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one*. In the Gospel of John, we also find no small proof that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are but one, when we carefully consider these words of our Savior: *that they all may be one, even as we are one*. Besides this, it remains for us to believe that this Holy Trinity created all things and is consequently a single Lord of all that is found in heaven, on the earth, and under the same, just as St. John testifies: *all things were made through him and without him was nothing made*. So it is written in the Holy Revelation: *worship him who brought forth the Heaven and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters out of nothing*. The Prophet David sings somewhere: *it is you, Lord, who in the beginning founded the earth and the Heavens are the work of your hands*; and again in another place: *the Heavens are made by the Word of the Lord and all their powers by the breath of his mouth*. All these things and many other similar reasons and proofs of the Holy Scriptures sufficiently confirm that God created all things, whatever they may be, out of nothing and caused them to appear. We must also believe that God the Father sent His Son from heaven to the earth, and that He thus, in the sanctified womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, for us and for our salvation, took on our flesh, just as the Prophet once foretold: *Behold, he said, a virgin shall become pregnant, shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel*; which, translated, is nothing other than *God with us*. And truly, we have the fulfillment of this in the words of our blessed Savior Himself, which sound thus somewhere in the Gospel: *I have gone out from the Father and come into the world, and I now leave the world again and return to my Father*. In another place we find this: *the Word became flesh and dwelt among us*. The same is repeated in the Letter of St. John with nearly as many words: *but we know, it says, that the Son of God has come and has given us the understanding that we may know the true one, and we are in the true one, namely in his Son Jesus Christ, who is the true God and eternal life*. Again, in the Letter to the Galatians: *when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law*. That the same was also, by command of God the Father and His own free will, raised and crucified upon the altar of the cross...

### CHAPTER IX.

#### Regarding the sixth specimen, containing the true expansion of the Ten Commandments, faithfully translated from the original text, which can still be found in a certain book named *Lou libre de las Vertus*, that is, the Book of Virtues.

->Explanation of the first Commandment.<-

> *The first Commandment of the Divine Law is this: You shall have no foreign God before me:* <note>original: "Lou premier Comendament de la Ley de Dio es aqueſt; Tu non aurés Dio eſtrang devant mi"</note> that is, The first Commandment of the Divine Law is this; You shall have no foreign God before my face.

<margin>In what way and how one is a transgressor of this Commandment.</margin>
,, All those who love the creature above the Creator always fail 
,, to fulfill this Commandment. Everything that someone honors 
,, and serves more than God himself becomes a God to them for that very reason. In 
,, this sense, St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was an influential early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> says in his explanations of the Gospel 
,, of Matthew, *the evil to which man is a slave, is to him a God.* <note>original: "het quaat daar de mens een ſlave van is, is hem een Got"</note> Now, if someone 
,, should say: how shall I be able to know that I love God more than that thing 
,, which I must not love because of his prohibition; it should be noted that 
,, one generally loves less that which one can more easily and willingly 
,, do without and lose in times of need, and that, on the contrary, one loves 
,, above all else that which one wishes to keep and preserve with all diligence. 
,, So it is with the rich merchant, who, running the danger of shipwreck 
,, and out of fear of death, attempts to negotiate the preservation of his life 
,, through a voluntary loss of his most precious goods, thereby 
,, demonstrating that he values his life far higher than all his merchandise. 
,, Now, go into yourself and weigh all of this. If, in any situation, you 
,, would much rather lose all temporal things, or any of the same—such as 
,, your money, your house, your cattle, your wife and children, yes, even your 
,, own body—rather than alienating yourself from your God and losing 
,, him in any way through the slightest sin; then you can be certain that 
,, you do not value or love your Lord God poorly above all the aforementioned 
,, things. But if, on the contrary, you would rather commit all sins 
,, than endure such loss; then it is beyond doubt that you worship and 
,, serve all those things, so to speak, more than God himself, and 
,, consequently commit idolatry <term>af-goden-dienſt: the worship of idols or false gods</term> thereby. This must then also 
,, clash with this Gospel Commandment of our Savior: *if 
,, anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, his mother, his wife and 
,, children, his sisters and brothers, yes, even his own life, he can in no way 
,, be my disciple.*
,, Those also act against this first Commandment who firmly believe that 
,, the wandering stars <note>meaning the planets; from the Greek "planetes" (wanderer)</note> can in any way bend or do violence to the 
,, free will of man. For by thus attributing to the mere creature that which 
,, can only be attributed to the Creator, they sufficiently hold, as 
,, much as is in them, those lifeless stars to be so many gods. Against 
,, such people, the Prophet Jeremiah cries out these words somewhere: 
,, *and do not learn to follow the way of the nations, nor fear those things that 
,, the heathens fear.* The Apostle Paul also seems to have this in mind 
,, when he uses these words in his Letter to the Galatians in the 4th 
,, Chapter: *you observe days, times, and months and years; but I fear that I 
,, might have worked among you in vain.*

### Explanation of the Second Commandment.

->You shall not make for yourself any carved image, or likeness,<-
->and so forth.<-

<margin>The sense and purpose of this prohibition.</margin>
,, You shall not make for yourself any carved image of stone, wood, or any other 
,, material that can be carved into an image, nor any painting or 
,, whatever kind of representation it might be of any thing that 
,, is there above in Heaven, such as the Angels, the Sun, the Moon, and the 
,, Stars; nor here below on the earth, such as humans and all other 
,, animals, just as the Egyptians once did in former times; nor in the waters 
,, such as the fish, just as in former times the idol Dagon was 
,, worshiped by the Philistines, who resembled a fish at the head; 
,, nor under the earth, such as the devils, just as the Ekronites 
,, once honored and served Beelzebub: you shall not worship them, 
,, neither by the showing of an external reverence, nor by the 
,, service of an internal high-esteem: you shall never set your 
,, hand to any work that might serve toward their high-esteem and 
,, honor. Such that it is here openly forbidden for one to 
,, be allowed to make a carved image of anything in the world to serve it...

<note>This passage reflects the strict aniconism—the opposition to religious images—of the Waldensian faith, which they shared with later Protestant movements. They viewed the use of statues or icons in worship as a direct violation of the biblical prohibition against idolatry.</note>

### Explanation of the Third Commandment.

->You shall not use the Name of the Lord your God lightly,<-
->and so forth.<-

<margin>Purpose of this Commandment.</margin>
„ In this commandment it is forbidden to commit perjury with lies and to 
„ swear vainly or out of habit, just as we have in the 19th chapter 
„ of the book of Leviticus: <note>The author attributes this quote to Leviticus 19, but the phrasing "the man who swears often... punishment shall not depart from his house" is actually from the deuterocanonical book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 23:11.</note> *the man, it says, who swears often and*
„ *lightly, shall be filled with iniquity, and the punishment shall not* 
„ *depart from his house*. The oath also confesses that God knows the truth and 
„ serves at the same time to confirm a doubtful matter. And while swearing 
„ is a work of worship, all those perform iniquity who therein 
„ use any worldly elements. For this reason, the Lord 
„ Christ also clearly forbids that one should swear by any thing of the world, 
„ namely *neither by Heaven, nor by the Earth, nor by any other thing*; 
„ but says on the contrary *that our speaking must be yea, yea; nay, nay; and that which* 
„ *is beyond this, is of the evil one*. With which also the Apostle James 
„ agrees, who uses these words in the 5th chapter of his Letter: 
„ *my brothers, above all things do not swear, neither by Heaven, nor by* 
„ *the Earth, nor by any other thing, so that you do not fall into condemnation*.

### Explanation of the Fourth Commandment.

->Be mindful of the Day of Rest, and so forth.<-

<margin>Four things required for the Hallowing of Sunday.</margin>
„ All those who intend to celebrate and keep the Day of Rest of the Christians, 
„ that is, to properly hallow the Rest of Sunday, must 
„ primarily observe these four things; the first, that 
„ they entirely cease all earthly and worldly work for that purpose; the second, 
„ that they do not sin; the third, that they are not sluggish in the performing 
„ of good works; and finally the fourth, that they occupy themselves with 
„ things that are useful and beneficial for the soul.

<margin>The 1st: To cease from earthly works.</margin>
„ Concerning the first, the Law says: *Six days you shall labor* 
„ *and do all your work; but the seventh is the Day of Rest of the Lord, your God;* 
„ *you shall do no work at all upon the same*. In another place in Exodus 
„ we have this Commandment: *Keep my Day of Rest; for it is holy. Everyone who* 
„ *defiles it, shall surely die*. We also read in the Book of Numbers 
„ <note>original: "Numeri"</note> regarding this matter this remarkable history: namely, that one of the Children 
„ of Israel had found a certain man of his people who, on the Day of Rest, was busy 
„ gathering wood and had therefore brought him to Moses. Who then, 
„ having been held fast by him for a time; as they were uncertain what 
„ should be done with him, the Lord himself said to Moses: 
„ that man shall surely be put to death and the whole people shall stone him 
„ with stones until he dies. Whereupon he was immediately led outside the 
„ camp and subsequently stoned to death there. To wit, it was God's 
„ commandment and will that his Day of Rest be celebrated with such reverence 
„ that the Children of Israel did not even dare to gather that divine Manna, 
„ given to them from Heaven, upon the same.

„ to pour out godly prayers, to hear His Commandments and holy 
„ Teaching with diligence, to meet Him with gratitude for His 
„ benefits, to teach the ignorant, to set right the errant—in short, 
„ to guard oneself against all sin. And truly, only by so doing is

„ reads thus: *repent of the works of unrighteousness and learn instead to 
„ do good.* From all of which it is now easy to gather that rest 
„ is very evil and harmful if it is not accompanied by good works.

### Explanation of the Fifth Commandment.

-> **Honor your Father and your Mother, and so forth.** <-

<margin>In what this duty consists, and its reasons.</margin>
„ Behold here now subsequently all the Commandments that prescribe 
„ and command us in what manner we are bound to live at all times 
„ with our fellow man. These words *Honor your Father and your Mother* 
„ are not to be understood merely as if they only looked to the 
„ outward respect of children toward their parents; but insofar

„ namely, Being, Upbringing, and Instruction, which they will never 
„ be able to pay back perfectly or fully reward. To this the

„ are the words) and do not ever forget the sorrows of your mother. Remember

„ them.* In respect then of our own natural Being, or nourishment, 
„ which we enjoy from Father and Mother, we must meet and 
„ serve them especially in three ways with humility and reverence; 
„ and first of all with all the strength of our bodies, because we 
„ are obliged to support their bodies and even to serve them with 
„ our own hands. Upon this stand these words of the aforementioned 
„ Preacher in the 3rd chapter: *He who fears the Lord shall honor his 
„ father and mother and [serve] those who have [begotten] him*

„ cast our eyes upon the instruction we receive from father and mother, 
„ we find ourselves bound by virtue of that to obey them in everything 
„ that tends toward a good end and our salvation. So it is written in 
„ the Letter to the Ephesians in the 6th chapter: *Children, obey your parents* 
„ *in the Lord; for that is a righteous thing.* And of this obedience, the Savior 
„ himself left us a living example, which is recorded in the Gospel of Luke in 
„ the 2nd chapter with these words: *and he went down with them and was* 
„ *subject to his father and mother.* The conclusion is that one must first 
„ always show all service and honor to the Father who created us, then 
„ the father who begat us, then our mother who carried us under 
„ her heart and brought us into the world, so that our days on the 
„ earth may be lengthened and we, persevering in goodness until the end, 
„ may finally pass from this world into that eternal inheritance.

### Explanation of the Sixth Commandment.

->Thou shalt not kill.<-

<margin>The aim of this Commandment.</margin>
„ Just as murder <note>The original Dutch uses *man-slag*, literally "man-striking," referring to homicide or murder.</note> is specifically mentioned and forbidden 
„ in this Commandment, so too is generally included all injury to our 
„ fellow man, by whatever means it might be committed, such 
„ as words of backbiting or similar wrongs, which are 
„ accompanied by an actual striking of our neighbor, or something similar. 
„ This appears clearly from the nature of anger, which belongs here, 
„ about which we read these words in the 5th chapter of the Holy Evangelist 
„ Matthew: *whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable* 
„ *to judgment.* St. James also says this of it in the 1st chapter of his 
„ Epistle: *the wrath of man does not fulfill the righteousness of God.* St. Paul 
„ therefore defines it carefully when he says in the fourth chapter of his 
„ Letter to the Ephesians: *let not the sun go down upon your wrath.* It stands 
„ then, that he who is wrongly angry with his brother is worthy of 
„ punishment and condemnation, but not the one whose anger is 
„ based on good reasons. And truly, if in some circumstances one did 
„ not show anger, the Doctrine itself would be somewhat 
„ unserviceable, justice would be without discernment, and sins without 
„ their deserved punishments. Indeed, it is so far from being 
„ slanderous that a just anger is the mother of all Discipline, <note>The Dutch *Tugt* refers to church discipline or moral correction.</note> 
„ and consequently, those who do not thus become angry commit 
„ no small sin thereby. For tolerance without reason is the seed 
„ of vices and the nourishment of all negligence, which can lead 
„ not only all wicked men, but even the best, to rebellion.

,, This commandment generally forbids all unlawful desires and impurities

,, commits fornication with the body, so here also a spiritual adultery 
,, is to be understood, consisting namely in this: that a person 
,, comes to recklessly separate themselves from God.

### Explanation of the Eighth Commandment.

->You shall not steal.<-

,, By this Commandment, all theft and unlawful means are forbidden by

,, a theft is committed thereby; because one must restore 
,, that which was lost. Furthermore, those who—as some Lords <note>The text uses "Heeren," referring to rulers or nobility.</note>

,, somewhere in this sense: *the leaders, or the Lords, are companions* 
,, *of thieves and likewise love gifts.* Similarly, those are also 
,, held to commit theft who in any way withhold the wage

### Explanation of the Ninth Commandment.

->You shall not bear false witness.<-

<margin>Pestilent effects of false testimonies.</margin>
,, In this Commandment, not only is the lie forbidden, but even every kind of
,, harm that can be done to our neighbor, whether with words
,, or with feigned works. For all those who love the lie, and
,, through it steal their neighbor's honor or give false testimony before the wicked,
,, are nothing other than children of the Devil. But to speak of that last point
,, more closely, according to the saying of St. Augustine <note>original: "H. Augustinus"</note> it harms three parties
,, at once: namely God, whose presence is thereby
,, despised; then the Judge, who is deceived by the liar; and
,, finally the innocent blood, which is oppressed by the false witnesses.
,, Meanwhile, backbiters <note>slanderers</note> also sin against this Prohibition. These are
,, compared to an open grave, just as the royal Prophet <note>King David</note> sings somewhere: *their*
,, *mouth, or throat, is an open grave.* And indeed there is no grave so
,, stinking before God as the foul mouth of a bridleness slanderer. This also
,, caused St. Ambrose <note>original: "H. Ambrosius"</note> to burst out once in these words: *a thief is more*
,, *tolerable than a slanderer, because the former only takes away physical goods,*
,, *while the latter robs one even of their good name.* So that a thief of honor is worthy
,, of being hated by both God and men, the more so because the wounding of the
,, tongue completely crushes the bones.

### Explanation of the Tenth Commandment.

->You shall not covet, and so forth.<-

<margin>What covetousness is forbidden here.</margin>
,, By this Commandment all desire for property is forbidden, such as the Wife,
,, the Manservant, the Maidservant, Fields, Vineyards, Houses, and so forth. To
,, this also belongs the lust of the eyes and of the flesh. And truly the
,, desire of the flesh is like running water and that of the eyes like earth,
,, because of their earthly inclinations. Now, just as from earth and water a tangible
,, mire must be made, so also from both those desires arises that
,, spiritual mud of the soul, which makes man so hateful to God.

## CHAPTER XI.

### Regarding the eighth sample of the Waldensian Doctrine, comprising an excellent *Book of Questions*, <note>or Catechism</note> or understanding of Faith, arranged in the manner of a dialogue between a Teacher and his Pupil, compiled in the year 1100.

I have judged this ancient piece to be of such weight and regard that, for the satisfaction of those people who are driven toward all things with a commendable curiosity, I could not nor would not omit showing it to them in its original language alongside the translation. I have but one word to say: that the entire essence <note>original: "sap"; literally "juice" or "sap," meaning the core vitality</note> of religion will be found in it with a concise simplicity.

Concerning the eighth specimen of the Waldensian Doctrine, containing an excellent *Book of Questions*, or understanding of the Faith, arranged in the manner of a dialogue between a Teacher and his pupil, compiled in the year 1100.

I have judged this ancient piece to be of such weight and importance that, to satisfy those people who are driven by a commendable curiosity for everything, I could not and would not omit showing it to them in its original language <note>Original: "gront-taal"; referring here to the Waldensian dialect/Old Occitan</note> before the translation. **The Uncle <note>Heer-oom</note>, that is the Teacher.**
**Q.** If you were asked what you are, what would you then answer?
**The Child.**
**A.** That I am a rational and mortal creature of God.

**Q.** Why has God created you?
**A.** In order that I might know and serve Him and finally thus become saved through His Grace.

**Q.** In what then does your salvation consist?
**A.** In three of the prominent cardinal virtues, which are necessarily required for salvation.

**Q.** Which are these?
**A.** Faith, Hope, and Love.
**Q.** With what do you prove that?
**A.** With that which the Apostle writes to the Corinthians in his first Letter in the 13th Chapter, consisting of these words; *these three things remain: Faith, Hope and Love.*

**Q.** What is Faith?
**A.** It is a *substance of the things that are hoped for and an evidence of those which one does not see*, as St. Paul teaches in his Letter to the Hebrews in the 11th Chapter.

...to lay another foundation than that which is already laid, namely Jesus Christ.

**Q.** *By what means can man come to this foundation?*
<margin>Concerning Faith in Him.</margin>
**A.** *Through Faith: as Saint Peter says. "Behold, I will lay in Zion the sovereign cornerstone, chosen and precious; he who believes in him shall not be confounded." <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:6</note> And the Lord says: "He who believes in me has eternal life."*

**Q.** *In what way can you know that you believe?*
**A.** *In that I recognize Him as the very God and very man, born and suffered, etc. for my Redemption, Justification, etc. <note>The "etc." likely refers to the standard theological list: suffering, death, and resurrection</note> I love Him and desire to fulfill His Commandments.*

**Q.** *By what means are the essential virtues attained—that is, Faith, Hope, and Charity?*
**A.** *By the gift of the Holy Spirit.*
<margin>Concerning the Holy Spirit.</margin>
**Q.** *Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?*
**A.** *I believe in Him. For the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and from the Son, is one Person of the Trinity, and according to His Divinity, is equal to the Father and the Son.*

<margin>Concerning the Holy Trinity.</margin>
**Q.** *You believe God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are three in persons. Therefore, you have three Gods?*
**A.** *I do not have three.*
**Q.** *Nevertheless, you have named three?*
**A.** *This is by reason of the distinction of the persons: but not by reason of the Essence of the Divinity. For although He is three in persons, nonetheless, He is one in Essence.*

**Q.** *This God in whom you believe, in what way do you adore and worship Him?*
<margin>Concerning the worship that is due to Him.</margin>
**A.** *I adore Him through the worship of <term>Latria</term> <note>original: "Latria"; a theological term from Greek meaning the highest form of worship and devotion, which is reserved for God alone, as opposed to the honor given to saints</note>, both exterior and interior. Exterior by the bending of knees, the lifting of hands, by bowing, by hymns, by*

<column-break/>

*...to lay another foundation, than that which is already laid, to know the Lord Jesus Christ.*

**Q.** But in what way can man reach that?
**A.** Through Faith. Thus says the Holy Apostle Peter: *behold, I shall lay a prominent cornerstone in Zion, which shall be precious and chosen, and all those who shall build upon it shall never be deceived or shamed.* Our Savior Himself agrees with this; *all those, He says, who believe in me, have thereby alone eternal life.*

**Q.** Whereby could you now know, that you so believe?
**A.** Because I recognize Him as true God and true man, who was born, who suffered, and so forth, to Redeem me, to justify me, and to declare me Free, and so forth; that I love Him and seek to follow His Commandments.

**Q.** But by what means are those Chief Essential Virtues to be obtained—I mean Faith, Hope, and Love?
**A.** Through the gift of the Holy Spirit.
**Q.** Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?
**A.** Yes, I believe in Him; which consists in this: that I hold Him as proceeding from the Father and from the Son, as one <term>Person (Subsistence)</term> <note>original: "Self-standigheyt"; a 17th-century Dutch theological term for a 'person' of the Trinity, indicating an individual existence within the divine essence</note> of the Holy Trinity, equal to the Father and the Son according to His Divinity.

**Q.** Do you believe then that God the Father, and God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are three particular Persons? If it is so, you necessarily have three Gods.
**A.** I have nevertheless not three.
**Q.** Have you then not named three?
**A.** I have only spoken to distinguish the Persons, not at all in respect to the Essence of the Divinity. For although three Persons are found, they are nonetheless all of one and the same Essence.

**Q.** In what way do you pray to and serve the God in whom you believe?
**A.** I pray to Him inwardly and outwardly with a worship belonging to God alone (*adoration of <term>Latria</term>*); which consists outwardly in the folding of my knees, the lifting of my hands

...through spiritual songs, through fasts, through invocations, but interiorly through pious affection, through a will prepared for all things well-pleasing to Him; but I worship Him through Faith, through Hope, and through Charity in His Commandments.

And again, "As I live," says the Lord, "every knee shall bow to me." And Jesus Christ says: There shall be true adorers, who shall adore the Father in spirit and truth. And the Angel did not want to be adored by Saint John. Nor Peter by Cornelius.* <note>Refers to Revelation 22:8-9 and Acts 10:25-26, highlighting the Waldensian rejection of worshipping saints or angels.</note>

**Q.** *In what way do you pray?*
**A.** *I pray using the prayer delivered by the Son of God, saying: Our Father who art in Heaven, etc.*

**Q.** *What is the other substantial virtue of necessity pertaining to salvation?*
**A.** *It is Charity.* <note>original: "Charità", meaning Christian love or Caritas.</note>
**Q.** *What is Charity?*
**A.** *It is a gift of the Holy Spirit by which the soul is reformed in will, enlightened by Faith, through which it believes all things to be believed, and hopes for all things to be hoped for.*

**Q.** *Do you believe in the Holy Church?*
**A.** *No. For she is a creature, but I believe concerning her.* <note>The Waldensians made a sharp distinction: one believes *in* God (trust), but only believes *about* the Church as a created institution.</note>

**Q.** *What do you believe concerning the Holy Church?*

<column-break/>

...[the lifting of my] hands, the bowing of my body, the singing of divine psalms and spiritual songs and the observance of Fast and Prayer days: inwardly with a holy will and inclination, ready to carry out His pleasure; that is, I serve Him according to His will and Commandments through Hope, through Faith and sincere Love.

**Q.** *Do you pray to, or serve anything else, as a God?*
**A.** *By no means.*
**Q.** *Why then?*
<margin>And Him alone.</margin>**A.** *Because He has strictly forbidden it in His Commandments: "You shall," it is written, "properly worship the Lord your God and, to the exclusion of others, serve Him alone." Again we have this in another place: "I shall not give my honor to any other;" and likewise these words: "As truly as I live," says the Lord, "every knee shall bow before me." Which the Lord Jesus Himself thus expands somewhere: "There shall then first be true worshippers, who shall call upon the Father in spirit and truth." The examples of the Angel and St. Peter are also known, of whom the first by St. John, and the other by the Centurion Cornelius, would by no means be honored through worship.*

<margin>Of Prayer.</margin>**Q.** *But what prayers do you say for the most part?*
**A.** *The words of that which the Son of God has given us Himself, saying: "Our Father, who art in the Heavens," and so forth.*

**Q.** *Which now is the second of those fundamental virtues, which are necessarily required for salvation?*
**A.** *It is Love.*
**Q.** *What is Love?*
<margin>Of Love.</margin>**A.** *It is a gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the soul, as far as the will is concerned, is entirely recreated and itself enlightened through Faith; by which I believe everything to be believed, and hope for everything that is to be hoped.*

**Q.** *Do you also believe in the Holy Church?*
<margin>Of the Church.</margin>**A.** *No; for it is nothing other than a creature. I believe, however, that there is a Church.*

**Q.** *What do you believe then of the Holy Church?*

**A.** I ask of the soul itself that the Church is to be considered in two manners: one in terms of its substance, the other in terms of its Ministry. In terms of substance, the Holy Catholic Church consists of all the elect of God, from the beginning until the end, in the grace of God through the merit of Christ, gathered by the Holy Spirit, and foreordained to eternal life; the number and names of whom only He knows, who chose them. And finally, in this Church, no reprobate <note>The original Occitan "proscrit" and Dutch "Geloof-ban" refer to those cast out or not among the predestined elect.</note> remains. But the Church according to ministerial truth consists of the Ministers of Christ with the people subject to them, exercising the ministry through Faith, Hope, and Charity.

<margin>In her identifying marks.</margin>
**Q.** By what thing must you know the Church of Christ?
**A.** By the suitable Ministers and the people participating in truth in the ministry.

**Q.** But by what thing do you know the Ministers?
<margin>Concerning her Ministers.</margin>
**A.** By the true sense of the Faith, and by sound Doctrine, and by a life of good example, and by Evangelization <note>The preaching of the Gospel.</note>, and by the proper administration of the Sacraments.

**Q.** By what thing do you know the false Ministers?
**A.** By their fruits, by their blindness, by bad works, by perverse Doctrine, and by the improper administration of the Sacraments.

**Q.** Whereby is blindness recognized?
**A.** When they do not know the truth of necessity pertaining to salvation, and they observe human inventions as if they were the Commandments of God, of which that saying of Isaiah is verified, which Christ spoke in Matthew 15: *This people honors me with their lips: but their heart*

<column-break/>

**A.** I hold that the Church can be considered in two ways: firstly, in view of her Essence itself, and secondly, in view of her Ministry and Governance. If you wish to view the Essence of the Church, by the same is understood the Holy Universal Church, which encompasses all those together who, from the beginning of the world to its end, are chosen by God in His Divine Grace through Christ’s Merit and gathered by the Holy Spirit, having been destined long before to eternal life; whose number and names can be known only to Him who has thus set them apart. So that in this Church, no "Excommunication from Faith" <note>Dutch: "Geloof-ban". This suggests that those truly chosen by God cannot be spiritually severed from the body of the elect by human decrees.</note> can take place. But when the Church is reckoned according to the truth of her Ministry, then it is that Society of the Ministers of Christ with the People who are subject to her, putting her Governance into practice through Faith, through Hope, and through Love.

**Q.** Whereby can you now know the Congregation of Christ?
**A.** By her capable Ministers and her subordinate People, who in deed also become in some way partakers of her Ministry.

**Q.** But by what shall you know those Ministers themselves?
**A.** By the true feeling of Faith, by an edifying example of life, by the Proclamation of the Gospel, and by the proper administration of the Holy Covenant-signs <note>term: "Bond-teykenen" (Covenant-signs). A common Reformation-era term for the Sacraments, emphasizing them as signs of God's promise.</note>.

**Q.** How can you now distinguish the evil from her?
**A.** By their fruits, by their blindness, by their evil works, by their perverted Teaching, and by their improper Administration of the Seal-signs of the New Covenant.

**Q.** From what then does one notice the blindness?
**A.** Chiefly from this: that being ignorant of the truth which is necessarily required to be known for salvation, one holds certain human inventions for God's commandments; just as that is touched upon in the Gospel of Matthew in the 15th Chapter by our Savior Himself: *This people honors me with their lips, but*

### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
<page-num>91</page-num>
<meta>catchword: Lord (original: gnor, from Seignor)</meta>

...their [heart] is far from me; but in vain they worship me, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men. <note>Quoting Matthew 15:8-9.</note>

Q. **By what is the evil operation <note>Refers to "bad works" or behavior.</note> known?**

A. By the manifest sins of which the Apostle speaks in *Romans 1*: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Q. **By what is the perverse Doctrine known?**

A. When it teaches against Faith and Hope, such as Idolatry committed in many ways toward creatures—whether rational or irrational, sensible, visible, or invisible. For only the Father, with his Son and the Holy Spirit, must be worshiped, and no other creature whatsoever. But against this, they attribute [worship] to man, and to the work of his hands, or to words, or to his authority, such that men blindly believe and think themselves joined to God through false religion and through the greedy simony <term>simony|The sin of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices</term> of the priests.

Q. **By what is the improper administration of the Sacraments known?**

A. When the priests do not follow the sense of Christ, nor know his intention in the Sacraments, and say that grace and truth are enclosed only within the external ceremonies, leading men to receive these same Sacraments without the truth of Charity. And the Lord protects his own from such false priests, saying: "Beware of false Prophets." Also: "Beware of the Pharisees," that is, of their leaven, which is their Doctrine. Also: "Do not believe, do not go after them." And David hated the church of such as these, saying: "I have hated the church of the malignant." <note>Quoting Psalm 26:5.</note> And the Lord...

<column-break/>

*...their heart is removed from me. But in vain they serve me by teaching human teachings and commandments.*

Q. **By what, after that, are their evil works known?**

A. By their public sins, which the Holy Apostle in his letter to the Romans in the 1st Chapter clearly testifies, *that those who do such things shall not inherit the Kingdom of God.*

Q. **By what, again, is their perverse Doctrine known?**

A. By this: namely, that one is teaching something against Faith and Hope. Thus it is with manifold Idolatry, whether it be practiced toward rational, sensory, visible, or invisible creatures. For whereas the Father alone, along with the Son and the Holy Spirit—and no other creature of whatever kind it may be—can be honored with such service; yet they attribute it to mere man, to the work of his hands, to his words, and to his authority. Whereby blind men also go so far that they think that through their false worship and the greedy simony of the popes, money is still coming into God's hand.

Q. **By what, finally, is the improper administration of the Covenant-seals <note>The Dutch "Bond-zegelen" is a common Reformed term for the Sacraments.</note> known?**

A. From the stupidity of the Priests, by which they are quite ignorant of Christ's meaning regarding the same; they claim that grace and truth are enclosed in them by mere outward ceremonies and finally dare to draw and call men to the communion of the same without Faith, Hope, or Love. And against such false Shepherds our Savior himself commands in places that we must carefully beware: *beware*, he says, *of false Prophets.* In another place we have this exhortation: *beware of the Pharisees, that is, their leaven, or their Doctrine:* and again; *and never give them belief, nor follow them.* We also see in the Royal Prophet <note>Referring to King David.</note> that he has a hatred for the congregation of such people, when he cries out these words in a certain place; *I hate the congregation of the ungodly.*

<meta>catchword: CHAPTER XII</meta>

*...vocations, etc., trusting to acquire by them that grace, which no one but God alone in Christ can give. Thus working in vain, they lose their money and their life, and [neglect] not only the present life but the future; for which reason it is said, the hope of the wicked shall perish.* <note>original Occitan: "l'Esperança de li felon perirè." A reference to Proverbs 10:28.</note>

<margin>Of the Holy Virgin.</margin>
**Q.** *And what do you say of the Blessed Virgin Mary? For she is full of grace, as the Angel testified: "I greet you, full of grace."*

**A.** *The Blessed Virgin was, and is, full of grace regarding her own needs, but not regarding the communication [of grace] to others. For only her Son is full of grace regarding participation, as is said of him: and we all receive grace for grace from his fullness.* <note>The Waldensian view here distinguishes between Mary possessing grace for herself and Jesus being the sole source from which others can "participate" in or receive grace.</note>

**Q.** *You do not believe in the Communion of Saints.*

<margin>Of the true communion of Saints.</margin>
**R.** *I believe that there are two things in which the Saints have communion. Some are Substantial, and some are Ministerial. The communion in the Substantial is through the Holy Spirit in God, through the merit of Jesus Christ. But the communion in the Ministerial or Ecclesiastical is through the ministries duly performed, namely through the words, through the Sacraments, and through the Prayers. I believe in both of these communions of the Saints. The first is only in God, and in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit, by the spirit. The other is in the Church of Christ.*

**Q.** *In what does eternal life consist?*

**R.** *In a living and active Faith, and in perseverance in the same. The Savior says in John 17: "This is eternal life, that they might know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." And he who shall persevere until the end, he shall be saved. Amen.*

<column-break/>

...with their own gifts, with pilgrimages, with invocations, and so on and so forth, trusting thereby to acquire that grace which no one but God and our Savior can give to man. In doing so, one works in vain and loses both his money and truly not only his present, but even his eternal and future life; in which sense it is written: *the Hope of the godless shall perish.*

**Q.** But what do you say then of the Blessed Virgin Mary: for she is *full of grace* according to the testimony of the Angel; *I greet you, he says to her, you, who are full of grace?*

**A.** The Blessed Virgin has always been, and still is, full of grace for herself, but not to share it with others. That is to say, it is the privilege of her Son alone that he is full of grace to also favor others with the same; concerning which we read these words: *and we receive from his fullness grace for grace.* <note>original Dutch: "genade voor genade." Reference to John 1:16.</note>

**Q.** Do you also believe in the Communion of Saints?

**A.** I hold that there are primarily two kinds of things in which the believers have communion with one another: namely, that which belongs to the Essence itself, and that which belongs to the Ministry of the Church. In the first, they are partakers in God through the Holy Spirit and the merit of Jesus Christ; in the latter—that is, the Ecclesiastical—through the well-performed Service, namely through the Word, through the signs of the Covenant <note>original Dutch: "Bond-teykenen," a common Reformed term for the Sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper</note>, and through Prayer. I believe then in both of these two communions of the Saints, insofar as the first only occurs according to the spirit in God and in Jesus Christ and in the Holy Spirit; the other according to the body in the Church of Christ.

**Q.** In what does eternal life consist?

**A.** In a living and active Faith and a steadfast perseverance in the same. And this is what our Savior speaks of in the Gospel of John in the 17th Chapter: *This alone is eternal life, that they know you the only true God and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.* And elsewhere: *He who shall persevere courageously to the end, shall be saved; Amen.*

### CHAPTER XII.

Of the ninth example of the aforementioned Teaching, concerning primarily the *Sacraments*, or seal-signs of the New Covenant, from a certain original manuscript, called *Spiritual Almanac*, also faithfully transcribed into our language.

If anyone is further curious—after so many glorious examples of the ancient Teaching of the Waldensians, or inhabitants of the Valleys, shown by the previously mentioned pieces—to know somewhat more specifically what they believed and taught then regarding the *Holy Sacraments*; let them please, without any partiality, just look into and consider a little what we have wanted to set down here from a certain part of the above-cited work, beginning with the words *Sacrament according to the word of St. Augustine* <note>original Occitan: "Sacrament second lo dire de S. Augustin"</note> and so forth:

<margin>Distinction between the Sacrament and its substance.</margin>
> „ The Sacrament is, according to the saying of St. Augustine in his book *The City of God* <note>original Dutch: "vande Gots", referring to Augustine's "De Civitate Dei"</note>, an *invisible grace, represented and depicted by a visible sign*. One can also say otherwise, that the Sacrament is a sign of a Holy thing. Now there is a great difference between the bare Sacrament and the Substance of the *Sacrament*, which is to say, as much difference as between a sign and the signified thing itself. For the substance of the Sacrament is the Divine Grace and the Merit of our crucified Savior, who alone is the restoration of all those who had fallen. In such a way that this substance of the *Sacrament*, with regard to the power, the essence, and the authority, is in God, and in the Lord Jesus with regard to his merit; namely, insofar as he has acquired grace and righteousness for the believers through his very cruel suffering and blood-shedding. Likewise, the same is also in the soul of the believer himself through participation, as the Apostle says somewhere; *we have*, he says, *become partakers of Christ*; in the word of the Gospel through the preaching or spreading of the same, and in the *Sacraments* in a sacramental manner. The reason now, why our Lord and Savior has instituted the aids of the outward Sacraments, is this: namely, so that the Ministers of the Word might establish and increase Faith thereby, and thus, adapting to human dullness and weakness, use the preaching of the Gospel more usefully for their Teaching.
> „ There are two such Sacraments: the one being that of water, and the other that of nourishment—that is, in which the bread and wine are consumed.

#### Of Baptism.

<margin>Of Baptism.</margin>
> „ The first of these is called Baptism, which properly, to speak somewhat more clearly in our language, is a washing with stream- or spring-water, which is performed as is fitting in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; so that then through the Grace of God the Father, looking upon his Son, and through the Enjoyment of Jesus Christ, who alone has ransomed us all, and through the Renewal of the Holy Spirit, who imprints the living Faith in our hearts, the sins of the baptized might first be forgiven and they be accepted into grace. Whereby they then also, ultimately persevering, might obtain salvation in Christ Jesus.
> „ Now the Baptism, with which we are washed, is the very same, where...

<margin>
Refutation of the Ceremonies of the Roman Church regarding Baptism.

*That which is outside of the necessity regarding the administration of Baptism includes the exorcisms, the blowing <note>The ritual of "sufflation," where the priest breathes on the candidate to signify the Holy Spirit</note>, the sign of the cross on the chest and the forehead, the putting of salt in the mouth, the anointing with saliva in the ears and the nose, the anointing on the chest, the hood <note>The "chrism-cloth" or white cap placed on the head</note>, the anointing of the chrism on the crown of the head, and similar things consecrated by the Bishop, the giving of the candle into the hands, the putting on of the white garment, the blessing of the water, the three-fold dipping, and the requirement of Godparents. All these things concerning the administration of this Sacrament are without need, that is to say, they are not of necessity, nor of the substance required for the Sacrament of Baptism, from which many take occasion for greater error and superstition than for the building up of salvation, and according to some Doctors, they are without any useful virtue.* <note>original: "Fora lo necessari enterca l' administration del Baptisme, son li exorcissimi..."</note>

That which is entirely unnecessary for the administration of Baptism are the exorcisms, the blowing, the sign of the cross drawn on the forehead and the chest of the infant, the salt that is placed in its mouth, the saliva that is rubbed in its nose and ears, the anointing of the Confirmation <term>Chrism|A consecrated oil used in Catholic rituals</term> performed on the top of its head, and all other such consecrated things besides, which were instituted by the Bishop in that regard; such as the handing over of a wax candle, the putting on of a snow-white overgarment, the blessing of the water, the triple immersion into the water, and the requirement of Godparents or Baptismal witnesses. All these things, customary among them <note>the Roman Catholic Church</note> in the administration of this sign of faith, are in no way required for the same, because they belong neither to the matter itself nor to the seal-sign in any degree. Meanwhile, they serve many people as an occasion for error and superstition rather than for edification and preservation, being—according to the words of various Teachers—even without any use or power of significance.

But see here another similar sample concerning the Holy Supper of the Lord, which is to be read in the oft-mentioned Book of the False Christ <note>original: "Leuge-Christus," referring to a medieval Waldensian treatise on the Antichrist</note> as follows:

*The eating of the sacramental bread is the eating of the body of Christ in figure <note>original Old Occitan: "en figura"</note>, Christ saying: in whatever way you do this, do it in my remembrance: for if this were not eating in figure, Christ would be bound to this continually: Because the spiritual is almost necessary to be done continually: as Augustine says, He eats Christ in truth who believes in him. And Christ says, that eating him is to remain in him. Regarding the celebration of this Sacrament, prayer, love, the preaching of the Holy Scriptures in the vernacular <note>original: "en volgar"</note>, and edifying things, and whatever other things are ordained for this according to the Evangelical Law, are profitable, so that peace and charity may increase among the people. But the other things besides the Consecration of the Eucharist, like the things the Priests do in the Mass, or the Clerk sings in the choir, from the introito <note>the beginning of the Mass</note> to the end: and the ornaments of the Priests such as are used at present in the Church with those adhering to it, are not of necessity pertaining to the Holy Supper.*

<column-break/>

The eating of the Sacramental Bread is Christ’s Body (in *figure* <note>original Latin: "figurâ"</note>) eating by representation, while He Himself has indeed said; whenever and as often as you come to do this, then do it in my remembrance. And truly, if it were not to be understood as such an eating of representation, then our Savior would have obligated Himself to be eaten almost constantly, since that spiritual food is often required for the sustenance of man. Not to say, that Saint Augustine had the same sentiment regarding this; *this person,* he says somewhere, *truly eats Jesus Christ, who trusts in Him with a true faith.* Thus had our Savior even preceded him, when He once said, *that to eat Him was nothing other than to remain in Him.* 

Now for the proper administration of this Sacrament, only these following things are useful: namely prayer, love, the edifying explanation of the Holy Scriptures in the mother tongue <note>the use of the "volgar" or vernacular language was a key Waldensian tenet, opposing the use of Latin which the common people could not understand</note> and whatever other things they might be, which according to the Law of the Gospel might be arranged for that purpose, so that peace and love might grow among the people. 

But what on the contrary is practiced outside the Sanctification of the Supper, such as what is done by the Priests <note>original: "Papen," a term used by reformers for Catholic clergy</note> in the Mass—namely, that the singing-company of the Clergy sings in the Choir from the beginning to the end, and that the Ministers of the Mass go adorned with such a garment as is currently in use by the Roman Church and its followers; none of all those, I say, necessarily belong to the Holy Supper of the Lord.
