<margin>2. Reason.</margin> But moreover, the people fall into Idolatry through this glorifying and calling upon all these Saints, as they have more trust in a Saint than in the Lord Himself, serving them with more affection than the only God; and testifying to this in deed by the decking out of more costly Altars, the louder ringing of bells, the greater number of consecrated candles, and other ceremonies. Through which the simple-minded folk also firmly believe the Saints to be moved to more mercy than God Himself, since they also believe that they can still free from damnation through their prayers those whom God has already condemned. From which they are also somewhat taught that the Saints crave gifts, offerings, and songs of praise; indeed, that they serve as more diligent mediators to those who give them the most incense, gifts, praises, and honor. All of which must be fled from and loathed with great diligence, just as we have therefore intended to speak of this Invocation of the Saints, namely to make our feeling known to everyone.

<margin>What invocation is.</margin> We hold, first and foremost, this for certain: that the words *to call upon* and *invocation* signify one and the same thing, namely such a prayer that one draws from the innermost part of one's heart and soul, and which is offered through the voice to God alone. Secondly, we also take this as a firm truth: that the man Christ is the mediator <term>middelaar (mediator): a go-between who reconciles two parties, in this case, God and humanity.</term> between God and men, their *Rightful-advocate* <note>original: "Regt-voorspraak", a legal term for a defense attorney or intercessor.</note> with God the Father, the only one who makes satisfaction for our sins, approaching God through Himself and so living continually and praying for us, so that no one can come to the Father except through Him: likewise, that whatever one shall ever ask and pray for from the Father in His name, it will undoubtedly be given to the petitioner, as He who comes to reach out all things generously to everyone and never reproaches anyone for it. In such a way that He alone being the *Rightful-advocate* with the Father, as has been said, can alone also our sins only can...

The previous page established that Christ is the sole mediator and that the practice of praying to saints leads the "simple folk" into a form of idolatry where they trust in the mercy of human figures more than in God. This page provides a dual-column presentation: the left column contains the original Romance (Waldensian) dialect, and the right column provides a Dutch translation/paraphrase from the 17th century. Both columns argue that saints should be honored as examples to follow, rather than as deities to be worshipped.</meta>

# General Memorial
### Y 3

->He presents himself to us in some manner before we move. He stands at the door and knocks so that it may be opened to him; He, wishing to close the path to all idolatry, existing in Heaven at the right hand of the Father, desires that every believer have Him in mind and look to Him alone: as the care of the faithful must be toward Christ, through thought and affection, and similarly in understanding that which is above. Just as it is said: *If you then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God.* <note>original: "Si vos ensemp resuscités cum Christ querè aquellas cosas lasquals son desobre, alqual luoc Christ ès, sesènt en la dextra de Dio."</note> He is the door through which, if anyone enters, he shall be saved. No one comes to the Father except through me.<-

<margin>That one must follow the Saints, not worship them.</margin>
We submit thirdly that the Saints are not left to us for worship <note>original: "coltivament," referring to the religious "cult" or devotion</note>, but for imitation. Saint Paul says: *O brothers, be imitators of me as I am of Christ, and look to those who walk according to the pattern you have in us.* Saint Peter did not allow himself to be worshipped by Cornelius, nor the Angel by John the Evangelist. And for this reason, Augustine wrote concerning True Religion: *O religious man, let the worship of dead men not be for you; for if they lived holily, they did not do so because they sought such honor, but they want Him to be worshipped by us, through whom they were enlightened and we are comforted with them.* Therefore they are to be honored by imitation, not worshipped by religion.

These things being established above, we say that any man who has departed from the body,

<column-break/>

...can forgive. What is more, he offers himself openly to us, without us needing to move a foot for it. He himself stands at the door and knocks, so that it might be opened to him by us. Indeed, now seated at the right hand of his Father in Heaven, he desires that every believer lift up their thoughts there to him alone and keep them fixed on him alone, in order to cut off the path to all idolatry. And indeed it is proper so, namely that all diligence and longing of all believers should look to Christ alone through meditation and love, and that they be primarily desirous to hear something of heavenly things, just as it is written somewhere: *if you be risen together with Christ, so also seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God.* <note>Colossians 3:1</note> Namely, he alone is the true door, through whose mere access all men become blessed; and no one, he says himself therefore also somewhere very well, comes to the Father but through me.

We establish in the third place this also as certain, that the Saints are not presented to us to be worshipped, but only to be followed by us. So speaks of this somewhere the Holy Paul: *O Brothers, be then my followers, as I am always those of Christ, and take good note of those who walk such, as you have us for an example.* <note>1 Corinthians 11:1</note> But to speak also of examples, did the Holy Peter allow himself to be worshipped by the centurion Cornelius, or the Angel by the Holy Evangelist John? <note>Referring to Acts 10:25-26 and Revelation 22:8-9 where Peter and the Angel both refuse worship.</note> For this reason, the Holy Augustine says somewhere in a certain letter written to a friend about true worship: *O God-fearing man, banish then the longing for the dead from your bosom. For though they have lived in great holiness throughout, they have nevertheless never allowed themselves to be treated as if they earned such honor through it: but on the contrary, they have very clearly willed that He alone might be glorified through it, by whom they themselves being enlightened yet hope that we shall become like them therein.* In such a way that the same must be honored only with a mere imitation, in no way with Worship.

Everything being thus confirmed, we say roundly that no one but the Lord...

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

...no one other than Christ is to be worshiped, nor is anyone else a certain or true Advocate, nor mediator between God and men, nor intercessor for sinners before the Father. Nor is it necessary that they <note>The saints.</note> be invoked by that intercession of the living: for he <note>Christ</note>, taking an oath, received from the Father the priesthood, that which I ask, and I will pray for the human generation, which he reconciled by his death. And he is the unique and sole mediator between God and men, and Advocate, and intercessor in Heaven before the Father for sinners, being so sufficient that the Father refuses no one who asks in his name, but out of reverence for him, hears him in what he asks and prays for. For approaching God through himself, being alive, he prays always for us. For such a high priest was fitting for us, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the Heavens, the first-born Son of the Father: who alone among all men possesses the power and authority to sanctify others, and to pray and intercede for them. *Augustine wrote on the 64th Psalm concerning Christ: You are the Priest, you are the Sacrifice, you are the Offerer, and you are the Offering, etc.* <note>original: "Tu sies Preire, tu siès Sacrifici, tu siès l'offrador, e tu siès l'offerta"</note> Jesus did not enter into houses made by hands, which were patterns of the true ones, but into Heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us. *Of him Saint John says:* We have an Advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. *And Saint Paul says:* Jesus Christ who died for us is also risen, who is at the right hand of God, and who also prays for us. Therefore, he alone would be the one who requires—

<column-break/>

<margin>
Christ alone may be worshiped.
</margin>

Lord Jesus, as soon as he was separated from the body, could be worshiped, or held as a true and certain Advocate or Intercessor with the Father for sinners, or in any way as a Mediator between God and men. It is also entirely unnecessary that they <note>the deceased saints</note> be worshiped through such calling-out by the living, because our Savior fully assures us that he has obtained this privilege from the Father: that all which he shall request for the human race, he shall immediately acquire, as he has reconciled the same through his death. He alone is that unique Mediator between God and men, who in Heaven before God the Father so sufficiently pleads and speaks for the best of sinners, that he will never refuse anything to anyone, when it is merely requested properly in his name, but will hear and grant all prayers for his sake. For living always through himself, he can also pray for us without ceasing. Namely: *such a High Priest was fitting for us, who was holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners and exalted far above all Heavens, the first-born, begotten of the Father:* which unique Son, glorified above all men, has the power and authority to sanctify others, to pray for them, and to work out a mediation. Thus writes St. Augustine of our Savior in his commentary on the 64th Psalm: *You are, it is written, the priest, you are also the sacrificial beast; you are the one who offers and even the sanctified offering itself, etc.* The Holy Scripture says likewise: *The Lord Jesus has not entered into Tents <note>meaning the Tabernacle</note> made with hands, which were images pointing to the truth; but he has entered into Heaven itself, to appear presently for us before God.* St. John agrees with this, using these words of him: *we have an Advocate with the Father, namely Jesus Christ the righteous;* and St. Paul these: *the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, was also raised up and is constantly praying.* It would then be foolishness to still want to [seek] <note>The Dutch text ends on the catchword 'soucken' (seek).</note> other mediations—

*...there would be no other intercessor. For Christ is always living with the Father, and prays for us, and is very ready and willing to enter the mind of every traveler <note>The term 'viadòr' or 'wayfarer' refers to a believer on their journey through life toward heaven.</note> who loves him. Therefore, taking his word, it is not necessary to ask another Saint as a mediator, as he is more kind and more prompt to help than any other of them. Otherwise, the mind of those praying would be scattered by the multitude of Saints they might have, as their affection moves away from Christ; consequently, it is diminished as it is divided among many. And it is seen by many that when the prayer is directed singularly to one, that person acts as a mediator for spiritual help. Then the Church would profit and grow more than it does now, if the mind found fewer intercessions. Therefore it would be seen as great folly to abandon the most ready fountain and turn to the muddy and more distant stream.*

*Therefore these things are declared: 1. that nothing exists, nor can be obtained from God, except through Christ the mediator. 2. that it would be more expedient to worship Christ among men simply; for he is the best and kindest Mediator and Intercessor, reaching to both one and the other extreme. 3. That in taking his word, it is not necessary to involve other Saints: as he is more prompt to help than any other Saint, who is ordained by God for this, so that the appeal, or intercession, be through him, who is more merciful than the others: for he knows for whom it is a just thing to pray for them, of whom he never forgets, having them written in his hands, at his breast: 4. ...wish to speak. For just as Christ, always living, prays to God the Father for us, so he also stands continually ready to help those who love him. And why then not remain with this, without seeking any Saints as other Mediators, especially since he is more favorable and more ready to help than any of the others? He adds that the thoughts of those who pray so are scattered and bewildered by the multitude of Saints to be prayed to, and their affection for the Lord Jesus is removed; finding themselves divided among so many in such a way, they slacken not a little in their zeal. Many also hold it to be true that prayer offered to that one alone chooses him as the sole mediator <note>original Dutch: 'scheydf-man', literally a 'divider' or 'arbitrator'—one who steps between two parties.</note> and moves him more effectively to our spiritual help. Thereby the Church would increase and grow significantly more if it were once relieved of that heavy multitude of newly-invented Intercessions. But finally, would it not be an utter madness to leave the spring of living, welling water with a good heart, only to turn thereafter to its muddy and distant watercourses?

We see then clearly the truth of these things: 1. that outside the Mediator the Lord Christ, not the least thing is to be obtained from God. 2. that therefore it would be much more useful among all people to worship the Lord Jesus simply and purely; since he would settle and mediate our affairs with the greatest goodness and inclination, even at the highest level regarding both extremes. 3. that if one wishes to believe his word, one must in no way turn to other Saints as mediators, especially since he stands much readier to help than they, being appointed to that purpose by God himself—namely, so that through him, who is much more merciful than all others, the mediation and intercession might be accomplished; since he knows that it is right that he makes his prayers count for them, as for those for whom he has shed his own blood, and finally he will never forget them, as having written them in his hand and on his breast.

### CHAPTER XVII.

#### Concerning the Doctrine of the Waldensians in general, containing several of the confirmed Confessions of Faith.

I suspect that currently, hardly anyone remains in doubt regarding the Faith of the ancient Waldensians, both in respect to all the Head-parts of the Christian Faith, and those pieces which only began to be known as matters of faith-dispute at the time of the aforementioned writings, and were therefore crossed out by them as new inventions. Nevertheless, in order not to give the blackest wickedness the slightest foothold to find any further slanders or excuses—as if they had held other sentiments regarding these matters—I shall here, for the sake of abundance, provide the reader with the most solemn and confirmed Confessions of Faith which they ever collectively established or presented to their Sovereigns at various times. This is so that if the breath of the Devil or any other slanderer, wishing to incite people to their ruin, tried to make them believe they held very monstrous doctrines, they might be convicted of untruth and deceit. I shall then begin with such a piece that is very wonderful due to its age and subject matter, found in the aforementioned old manuscript book and mentioned by Mr. Perrin in his Histories, page 225. <note>Jean-Paul Perrin was a 17th-century historian whose work "Histoire des Vaudois" (1618) is a primary source for Waldensian history.</note> It bears the date of the year 1120, and consequently existed in the world between 60 and 80 years before Waldo of Lyon. <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205) was a leader of the Waldensians; the author argues here that the movement's doctrines predated him, asserting their ancient origin.</note> It begins as follows:

### 8. MAIN ARTICLE
->That our Savior is the only Advocate.<-

*And likewise we hold firmly that there is no other Mediator and Advocate before God the Father except Jesus Christ: but that the Virgin Mary was holy, humble and full of grace: And thus we believe of all the other Saints, that they await in Heaven the resurrection of their bodies at the Judgment.* <note>The left column contains the original Occitan (Waldensian) dialect.</note>

In like manner we also hold for certain, that outside of the Lord Jesus, we have no Mediator or Advocate with the Father; that nevertheless the Virgin Mary was holy, humble, and full of grace: just as we also believe of all other Saints, that they await the Resurrection of their bodies for Judgment in Heaven. <note>The Waldensians sought to honor Mary and the saints as historical figures of faith while rejecting the practice of praying to them for intercession.</note>

---

### 9. MAIN ARTICLE
->Against Purgatory.<-

*Item, we believe, that after this life there are only two places, one for the saved, which we call by name Paradise, and the other for the damned, which we call Hell, denying altogether that dreamed-up Purgatory of the Anti-Christ, invented against the truth.*

Furthermore, we believe for a truth that after this life there shall be only two places, namely one for the Blessed, which we call *Paradise*, or the Garden of Delight, and another for the Damned, called Hell; rejecting so entirely that dreamed-up Purgatory of the Anti-Christ, as being fabricated and invented against all truth. <note><term>Anti-Christ</term> In Waldensian and early Protestant literature, this term was frequently used to refer to the institutional Papacy rather than a single individual.</note>

---

### 10. MAIN ARTICLE
->Against human Ordinances.<-

*Item, we have always believed all things invented by men to be an abomination, not to be spoken of before God, such as are the Feasts, and the Vigils of the Saints, and the water which they call Holy, and the abstaining on certain days from meat, and from other foods, and similar things, and principally the Masses.*

So have we also always been of the opinion, that all Doctrines and inventions of men—such as all Feast-days and Saint-eves, the Holy-water as they call it, the withholding of meat on certain days, and a hundred suchlike, but especially the Mass—are an abomination, which before God must be silenced. <note>The Waldensians rejected the Catholic <term>Mass</term> as a human invention that distracted from the simplicity of the biblical Lord's Supper.</note>

---

### 11. MAIN ARTICLE
->Against Traditions.<-

*We abominate human inventions as Anti-Christian, by which we are troubled, and which prejudice the liberty of the Spirit.*

We likewise have a loathing for all human Traditions, as being the work of the Anti-Christ, by which we are daily plagued and the freedom of the Spirit is entirely restricted.

### 12. MAIN ARTICLE
->Concerning the Sacraments in General.<-

*We believe that the Sacraments are signs of the holy thing, or a visible form, holding it to be good that the faithful use these said signs or visible forms at times, if it can be done. But besides this, we believe and hold that the said faithful can be saved without receiving the said signs, when they have neither the place nor the means to be able to use the said signs.* <note>original Occitan: "Nos cresèn que li Sacramènt son fignàl de la cosa Sancta, o forma vefibla..."</note>

<column-break/>

We also believe that the Sacraments are signs, or the visible appearance of Holy things, also holding that the Believers must use these signs or visible representations from time to time, as far as possible, with all proper reverence; yet in such a way that we simultaneously maintain that a Believer can perfectly attain salvation without receiving the said signs of the seal; namely, if he has never had the place or the means to be able to make use of them.

---

->Concerning Baptism and the Holy Supper.<-

*We have known no other Sacrament than Baptism and the Eucharist.* <note>original Occitan: "Nos non avèn conegù autre Sacrament que lo Baptisme, e la Eucharistia."</note>

<column-break/>

We have never known other Sacraments than the well-known Baptism and the Holy Supper <term>Eucharist</term>.

---

### 14. MAIN ARTICLE
->Concerning Submission to the Authorities.<-

*We owe honor to the Secular power, in subjection, in obedience, in readiness, and in payment.* <note>original Occitan: "Nos devèn honòr à la potesta Secular, en subjection, en obediença, en prompteffa e en pagamènt."</note>

<column-break/>

We have always held ourselves obligated to pay to the Worldly Power all honor, subjection, obedience, readiness, and taxes.

*The following Articles have been signed by all the Pastors and Heads of Families then present, who have sworn to believe them and to wish to hold to them, as recognizing them to be in conformity with the Holy Scripture, and containing the summary of the Doctrine which had been taught to them from father to son according to the Word of God, just as the faithful had done in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. Ezra chapter 10 and Nehemiah 9 and 10.* <note>original French: "Les Articles suivans ont esté soussignés par tous les Pasteurs & Chefs des Familles lors presens..."</note>

# Regarding the History of the Waldensian Churches.
<sig>Aa 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

*...righteousness through faith are established and formed, they must be sought from them.* <note>original Latin: "stitiam per faith instituuntur..." This is the conclusion of a sentence regarding the Holy Scriptures.</note>

*Furthermore, because they [the Scriptures] were delivered and inspired by God himself, as Peter and Paul among others affirm; and for this reason especially, so that they may be understood by all, they read and recite them in our churches in the common and native language, particularly the Gospels themselves and the Epistles, as was customary in the ancient Church: and from there also lessons and exhortations are frequently given publicly to the people, as circumstances and matters require.*

---

*Moreover, they say that the writings of the Doctors of the Church, especially the ancient ones, are likewise to be held as true and worthy of faith, and are useful for instructing the common people, yet only in those things where they do not deviate from the divine Scriptures. For they themselves wish their own works to be held in such a way that faith is placed in them only insofar as they agree with the divine Scriptures. Concerning this, Augustine says in the preface to book 3 of On the Trinity: "Do not," he says, "be a slave to my writings as if they were Canonical Scriptures; but in those [Scriptures], even what you did not believe, believe without hesitation once you have found it; but in these [my writings], what you did not hold as certain, do not hold firmly unless you have understood it to be certain." And elsewhere: "Do not believe my words or those of Ambrose as being equal to the Canonical Scripture." And this is held in the Decrees, Distinction 9.* <note>The "Decrees" refers to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law used in the medieval and early modern periods.</note>

<column-break/>

[...learned and] instructed, must only be drawn and proven from the same [Scriptures].

Besides this, that the same, as the Apostles Peter and Paul among others assure us, are given and inspired by God himself; and that they therefore primarily and especially use and read the Holy Gospels and Epistles, as they call them, in the mother tongue and known language—following the practice of the ancient Church—so that they may be better understood by everyone; and that finally from these, all teachings and admonitions, according to the requirements of the occasion and matters, and further Church sermons, are very often recited and given to the people.

They also say that the writings of all others, and especially of the ancient Teachers of the Church, should likewise be regarded as true and worthy of belief and are useful for instructing the people, yet only in those things where they do not deviate from God's Word. For they themselves wish that they be regarded in such a way, namely that they should only be used and believed so far as they are found to be in agreement with the Holy Pages. Concerning this, Saint Augustine has these words in the Preface to his 3rd book on the Holy Trinity: "*and be no slave*", he says, "*to my letters, as if they were Canonical Scriptures: but concerning these [Scriptures], believe without delay that which you yourself did not believe before, as soon as you have found it in them; but regarding those [my letters], never hold as certain that which you did not previously regard as such, until you have clearly understood it.*" And in another place: "*and never believe my words, nor those of Ambrose, as if it were the Canonical Scripture itself.*" Which is also cited in the <term>Decrees</term><note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Catholic Canon law.</note>, as they call them, at the 9th Distinction.

### II. CHAPTER.
->Concerning the Church Catechism.<- <note>original Dutch: "Vraag-oeffening", literally "Question-exercise," a term for catechizing by asking questions and receiving answers.</note>

**H**ence they teach the Catechism, *that is, this Universal and Orthodox doctrine of the Fathers; which is the Decalogue of God's commandments and the Apostolic Faith, arranged into twelve Articles.*

**H**ereafter they teach the Church Catechism, that is, this Universal and Orthodox Doctrine of the Ancient Fathers, contained in the *Ten Sayings* <note>original: "Tien-spreuk", referring to the Ten Commandments.</note> of God's Commandments, and in the *Apostolic Faith*, in twelve Head-parts.

It also introduces the use of the vernacular language in worship and the beginning of their formal catechism.</summary>

### General Memorial
<page-num>144</page-num>

...compiled and handed down in the Creed by the Nicene Synod <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the core beliefs of mainstream Christianity to combat heresy.</note>, and also confirmed and explained elsewhere; and finally, the Lord's Prayer. These, they constantly affirm, are the most holy things and represent the good and pleasing will of God.

Next, they teach that these Commandments must be observed in deed and heart, since the law is spiritual, and that all Articles of Faith must be believed without doubt and confessed with the mouth; and they fortify and strengthen these with the Scriptures to the best of their ability, attempting to explain the simple meaning of them—and if there is anything hidden or abstruse in them, or what its purpose is—extensively and openly from the same Scriptures.

Likewise, they teach that God is to be prayed to and invoked only through the name of Christ alone as Mediator <note>original Latin: "Mediatoris"; a theological term for Christ as the only go-between for God and humanity.</note>. They teach that men should pray not only for themselves, but truly for all Christians, wherever on earth they may be; for all leaders of the Church, and likewise for all placed in eminence and any power for ruling others.

But especially and first, they implore God with many prayers for the Highness and safety of the ever-August Emperor <note>original Latin: "Caesaris semper Augusti," the formal title of the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> and for the peak and success of your Royal Majesty, and for all Councilors, so that he may prosper and favor your Royal Majesty and Charles the Emperor <note>Referring to Charles V (1500–1558).</note>, ever August and invincible, in all things for the benefit of the whole Church, and extend the empire as widely as possible; so that toward all who are subject and obedient to your Royal Majesty, and are true worshipers of God and his Christ, he may deign to show a merciful and favorable heart. In short, according to the precept of Christ and the Apostles, and of the Primitive Church...

<column-break/>

...distinguished, established into a Church-rule by the Church-assembly of Nicaea and otherwise also frequently explained and confirmed, and finally in the Prayer of our Lord. So that they always place the good and well-pleasing will of God in these most holy things.

Thereby it is also a part of their Teaching, that while the Law is entirely spiritual, these her Commandments must be kept with heart and hand, and all the main parts of the Faith must be believed without doubt, confessed with the mouth, and always testified to with works; which they, according to their best ability, strengthen and empower with the Scripture, also attempting to explain and establish from the same as extensively and clearly as possible, what their simple meaning is, whatever is dark and hidden in them, and toward what all this is found to look.

They likewise teach that God must be prayed to and called upon only in the name of the Lord Christ alone, being the sole Mediator. What is more, they teach people to pray not only for themselves, but also in common for all Christians, in whatever corner of the world they may be hiding, and likewise specifically for all those who are placed in any highness or power to govern others.

But especially and in the first place, they pray to God with manifold supplications for the preservation and highness of the Emperor, always the Increaser of the Empire <note>original Dutch: "vermeerder des R. Rijx," a translation of the Latin 'Semper Augustus'.</note>, for the dignity and prosperity of Your Royal Majesty, and at the same time also for all your wise Councils; so that he may make all things succeed for the best of the whole Church for Your Royal Majesty and Emperor Charles, always the Increaser of the Roman Empire and Victor, and extend the Empire very widely everywhere, and finally also deign to give a merciful and favorable heart to Your Royal Majesty toward all those who are subject and obedient to the same and make it their work to serve God and the Lord Jesus in truth and uprightness. In a word, her Teaching brings this with it, that one, according to the command of our Savior...

<note>original vocabulary: Nicene Synod, Lord's Prayer, Mediator, Emperor Charles, Roman Empire</note>

# Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
<meta>catchword: Hence / Where-</meta>

...the Savior and his Holy Cross-ambassadors, and following the examples of the first primitive Church <note>original: "Gront-kerk," literally 'ground-church,' referring to the early apostolic church as the foundation.</note>, one must pray for all friends and enemies without distinction. And for this reason, they call the people together even more diligently to the solemn meeting places, so that they might encourage them there with all industry to fiery prayers.

Now in this healthy and Christian Catechism <note>original Dutch: "Vraag-oeffening," literally 'question-exercise,' a standard term for the practice of learning through questions and answers.</note>, not only those who have reached the age of maturity are instructed, but even the children themselves, so that they might become accustomed to it from their earliest youth and thus learn true religion and piety. For this reason, they also hold some separate meetings especially for them, admonishing the parents and godparents <note>original Dutch: "Doop-getuygen," or baptismal witnesses.</note> to diligently instruct them in this holy doctrine, and to offer their godly prayers to God for them, as well as for all other children truly dedicated to the Lord Jesus.

On the contrary, they reject everything that is found not to be in agreement with this godly and Christian fundamental teaching; and as the Lord of all things grants strength to each, they convince and refute the same with certain Scriptural proofs, and finally warn the people to be on their guard against it.

---

### III. MAIN CHAPTER.

->Of Faith in the Holy Trinity.<-

<column-break/>

Furthermore, they prove with Scripture that God is known through faith alone as One in the divine Essence and Threefold in Persons <note>The original Dutch uses "Self-standigheden" to translate the Latin "Personis," referring to the distinct individualities of the Trinity within one essence.</note>: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Regarding the Persons, a distinction can indeed be found, but regarding the Essence itself, nothing other than a distinct co-equality. This is also openly testified by the Universal Creed <note>original: "Al-gemeyn Geloof-schrift," likely referring to the Apostles' Creed.</note>, its agreement with the deliberations and decrees of the Nicene Council <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) which defined the nature of the Son's relationship to the Father.</note> and other Church assemblies, as well as the Confession or Creed of Saint Athanasius <note>A 4th-century statement of Christian belief focused on Trinitarian doctrine and Christology.</note>.

# General Memorial
<meta>catchword: many</meta>

*Hence they also teach the supreme power, wisdom, and goodness of that same one God; likewise his three most excellent works, which belong to him alone and to no one else besides him, namely the work of Creation, Redemption, and Preservation or Sanctification. They teach moreover, that this one true God, in one essence of Divinity and a blessed Trinity of Persons, is always to be adored, venerated, and worshipped with the highest reverence, honor, and praise, as the Lord of all and the supreme King, reigning forever; and that from him alone all things depend, are expected, and requested; to him alone the highest subjection, obedience, fear, and faith must be shown, and by him all religious worship must be sincerely observed; and he who does not do this acquires damnation for himself. Deuteronomy 6: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you worship. Again: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul and mind, and in short, with all your powers, both internal and external.* <note>original Latin: "Creationis, Redemptionis, Conservationis seu Sanctificationis."</note>

<column-break/>

Whereby they then also add an explanation of the power, wisdom, and goodness of that same single God, as well as his three most excellent works, which can be attributed to no one but him alone, namely the Work of Creation, of Redemption, and of Preservation or Sanctification. Beneath this they add this Doctrine, namely that this one true God in a single Essence of the Divinity and a blessed Trinity of Persons <note>original Dutch: "Self-standigheden," a literal translation of 'hypostases' or 'subsistences,' referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity.</note>, as a Lord and King of all, ruling in all eternity, must always be celebrated and adored, and honored with all reverence, with the highest honor and praise. That since all things depend on him alone, man must also request and expect everything from him. That consequently the deepest humiliation, fear, and faith must be given and shown to him alone, and for that very reason all divine service must be uprightly observed; and those who remain negligent in this, bring damnation upon their own necks. In Deuteronomy, in the 6th Chapter, it stands thus: *the Lord your God shall you adore, and him alone shall you honor and serve.* Again: *you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with your whole mind.*

---

### IV. CHAPTER
->Of Sin, of its fruits, and of Self-knowledge.<-

Here they teach that we should not be ignorant of sins, which are committed and occur both against our neighbors and against God. First, so that men might acknowledge themselves to be both conceived and born in sin, and to be sinners by their very nature and from the womb, and subsequently from their very childhood transgressing the Law of God in heart and deed, pressed and burdened by a mass of sins, as it is written: The Lord, when he looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see if there were any who either understood or cared for the Divine Power; here all had failed: all were likewise corrupted, none did what was right, not even one. Again: God saw that many <note>original: "multa," the Latin catchword for the next page.</note>

<column-break/>

Here they teach that one must not remain unaware of whatever sin it may be, whether one commits the same against one’s fellow man <term>neighbor: "eve-naasten" in Dutch, referring to those equal to oneself in the eyes of God</term> or against God himself. Firstly, so that all people might recognize that they are conceived and born in sins and are immediately sinners by nature and from their mother's womb; that they, not seldom even in their first childhood, have transgressed God's Holy Law with thoughts and deeds and subsequently go sinking under the heavy pack of sins, just as it is written somewhere: *when the Lord looked down from Heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were anyone who behaved wisely, or held God in any honor, they had all deviated here and were all equally corrupted: there was no one who did good, not even* <note>The Dutch text ends mid-sentence: "ook niet" (not even [one]).</note>

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.
<meta>catchword: sacrifices / shows</meta>

...the wickedness of men was great upon the earth and every thought of his heart was entirely turned toward evil at all times. And again: the Lord said to his heart; the sense and thought of the human heart are evil from its youth. Paul also: we were, he says, children of wrath by nature, just like the others. <note>These are references to Genesis 6:5, Genesis 8:21, and Ephesians 2:3, used here to establish the doctrine of original sin.</note>

Next, they teach from the Scriptures that men ought to acknowledge, because of this depravity and corruption of themselves and because of the sins born from this root, that a deserved and formidable destruction hangs over them, that the vengeance of God is imminent, and that the punishment of hell, worthy of their deeds, has been set before them. For the wages—as Paul says—of sin is death. Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: those who have done evil shall go into eternal punishment; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <note>original Latin: "Authoramentum... peccati mors," referring to Romans 6:23. "Authoramentum" specifically refers to a soldier's pay or a contractual wage.</note>

To this they teach that it is necessary that all should notice and know their own weakness, and the extreme poverty and evils into which they have been cast on account of their sins; and that they can save themselves in no way, nor justify themselves by any of their own works or studies; nor have they anything except Christ alone, through trust in whom they may redeem and free themselves from sins, Satan, the wrath of God, and eternal death; likewise that there is nothing in men by which one can bring help to another before God, since all are equally liable to sin and void of the justice of God, as he said through the prophet: bring to my memory (you, namely, man, whoever you are) and let us be judged; tell at the same time if you have anything, so that you may be justified. Your first father sinned and your interpreters have transgressed against me. Likewise; ceremonies and... <note>original Latin: "reduc mihi in memoriam... Pater tuus primus peccavit," quoting Isaiah 43:26-27.</note>

<column-break/>

...not even one. <note>This fragment likely completes a sentence from the previous page quoting Romans 3:10: "There is none righteous, no, not one."</note> Likewise in another place: *God saw that the wickedness of man was manifold upon the entire earth and that all the thoughts of his heart were at all times entirely inclined toward evil.* Again: *the Lord said within himself; the thoughts and intentions of man's heart are evil even from his early youth.* But the Apostle speaks plainly thus: *we were, like all others, by nature children of wrath.*

They prove the same in the second place, as before, from the Holy Scriptures, so that men might also acknowledge that, due to this their own worsening and corruption and due to the sins springing from this root, a deserved destruction is hanging over their heads, the terrible vengeance of God is approaching them, and finally the punishment of hell shall be given as a reward for their works according to their value. *For*, as the Apostle of the Gentiles <note>A traditional title for St. Paul.</note> says very well somewhere, *the wages of sin is death.* His Lord and Master had said it himself first with these words from the Gospel: *those who have done evil shall go away into eternal pain; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.*

Besides this they also teach that it is in every way necessary that everyone behold and know his weakness and utter poverty and the evils into which he has been plunged through his sins, as a result of which he cannot help himself in the least or make himself righteous with all his efforts and works; indeed, that he has nothing at all in the world outside of Christ alone, through whose power he can in some measure free and deliver himself from sins, from the Devil, from the wrath of God, and from eternal death. That likewise nothing is found in men with which one could help another before God, while they are *all equally subject to sin and deprived of the righteousness of God;* as he himself has testified somewhere through the Prophet thus: *bring everything to my mind (namely you, O man, whoever you are) and let us contend with one another. Speak up at the same time what you have to plead for yourself. Your Father first sinned against me and your mediators have shown rebellion against me.* <note>original Dutch: "middelaars" (mediators), referring to the "interpreters" or "teachers" mentioned in the Latin column's quote of Isaiah.</note>

# General Memorial
## V. HOOFT.
<meta>catchword: V. HOOFT.</meta>

...your sacrifices have displeased me, nor have I approved of your preparation of incense; neither have you satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. <note>original Latin: "sacrificia tua mihi diſplicuerunt..." This is a reference to Isaiah 1:11 or Jeremiah 6:20, where God rejects hollow ritualism.</note> *Paul also to the Hebrews:* You did not want sacrifice and offering, and you have not approved or required burnt offerings for sin. <note>Reference to Hebrews 10:5-6.</note>

Furthermore, they teach that all the troubles and afflictions with which we are shaken and distressed here are inflicted or set before men by God by most deserved right on account of sins—such as heat, cold, hunger, thirst, all labors, cares, misfortunes, sorrows, weariness, various ailments, and finally death itself; just as it is written: **On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.** And: **Cursed is the earth because of you; in labor you shall eat from it all the time, and all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall sprout for you.** <note>Genesis 2:17 and 3:17-18, establishing the biblical origin of human suffering.</note>

Yet they teach that all these troubles must be borne patiently by us, as we have deserved even heavier things. Not, however, that anyone might earn eternal life for himself through the endurance of such evils, however many they are, since the Apostle proclaims that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory which shall be revealed toward us; but so that through the greatness of their crimes and their own weakness and misery, all may know and understand how evil and bitter it is, as the Prophet says, to leave one's God, and so that, burdened and pressed by these evils, they might be awakened and stirred to seek the grace and help of God, who is merciful and compassionate and great in forgiving.

<column-break/>

...shows. Again: *your ceremonies and sacrificial animals have displeased me, and I have not accepted your preparation of incense from you as good. You have not satisfied me with the fat of your burnt offerings.* By St. Paul in his letter to the Hebrews we also have this concerning it: *sacrifice and offering you did not want; burnt offerings and offerings for sin have not pleased you, and you do not demand them.*

They also teach following this, namely, that all discomforts and miseries with which we wrestle and are continually afflicted here—such as heat, cold, hunger, thirst, all difficulty, worries, accidents, sorrows, displeasures, various weaknesses, yes, finally death itself—are very rightfully imposed and inflicted upon man by God on account of his sins, just as it stands written somewhere: *the day that you shall eat thereof, you shall surely die the death:* and: *cursed be the earth for your sake: with pain shall you eat of it at all times and all the days of your life; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you.*

Meanwhile, they also teach this: that one must nevertheless bear all those discomforts with patience, as we have deserved even much heavier than these; yet so that no one, by the enduring of these evils, however many there might be, can in any way win eternal life, because the Apostle openly proclaims, *that the suffering of this present time is not to be valued against the glory that shall be revealed in us;* but rather that they all might know and taste the greatness of their misdeeds, their weakness and misery—that which the Prophet says somewhere, *how evil, how bitter it is to leave one's God*—so that they, namely, being overburdened and pressed by these evils, might awaken and be moved to seek the grace and help of God with all diligence, as He who is merciful, compassionate, and generous in forgiving.

Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
Bb

### V. CHAPTER.
->On Repentance.<-

*In this place they teach that Repentance is that which is born from the recognition of sins and of divine wrath, which through the Law of God first strikes pain and terror into the conscience; namely, when sins are internally rebuked by the word of God, and the mind is rendered ill-conscious of itself, restless, exceedingly sad and despairing, and the heart anxious, broken, and fearful. This is such that a person can be lifted up by nothing of themselves nor find any consolation, but is entirely and most deeply afflicted, with a dejected and trembling spirit, shaken by a great horror at the sight of God’s wrath. As David says of himself: "Because there is no health in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin. I have become miserable and am bowed down excessively; I went about mourning all day long." <note>original Latin: "quoniam non est sanitas in carne mea..."—a quotation of Psalm 38:3, 6.</note> Meanwhile, they teach that those thus terrified and struck with fear should not despair; but that they should return to God with their whole heart and, through faith in Christ—which is also a part of repentance—embrace His mercy, grieving that they have sinned. For although they are empty of all righteousness, they may nevertheless implore divine grace and clemency, so that He might have mercy on them and forgive their sins for the sake of Christ and His merit, who for our sake was made sin and a curse, so that He might satisfy the justice of God for our sins. And the divine promises are to be instilled in those so affected: "Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me."* <note>original Latin: "in die tribulationis invoca me..."—a quotation of Psalm 50:15.</note>

*And they teach that this form of Repentance is to be maintained throughout one's whole life, whenever there is need. Also, those who thus repent,*

<column-break/>

In this place, their teaching is that this is true repentance, which arises from the knowledge of sins and of divine wrath, which first through the Law of God <term>Law of God (Wet Gots): referring to the Ten Commandments and biblical moral requirements which, in this theology, serve to show humans their failings.</term> drives a terror and anxiety into the conscience. This happens when sins are internally proven and rebuked by God’s Word, the mind is stirred up regarding them, becoming restless, over-sorrowful, and to some extent despairing, and the heart becomes anxious, broken, and afraid; so that the person can be raised up by nothing from within themselves nor find any comfort, but is completely and most highly oppressed, very dejected and trembling in spirit, and moved by an overwhelming fear upon considering God’s anger. This is just as the <term>Man after God's heart: a traditional title for King David.</term> depicted himself in a certain place: *Because of your wrath there is no health in my flesh, and my bones have no rest because of my sin. I have fallen into misery and stoop too low; all day long I go about mourning.* <note>Psalm 38:3–6.</note> Meanwhile, they also teach this: that those who are thus brought to fear and trembling must not therefore despair; but that they must turn back to God with their whole heart and, through faith in Christ—which is also a part of conversion—embrace His mercy alongside their sorrow for their sins. For though they are void of all righteousness, they can nonetheless call upon the grace and kindness of the Lord, so that through Christ and His merits He might have mercy on them and acquit and forgive them of all their sins. For this Savior has become a curse and sin for our sake, so that He might satisfy the justice of God for our sins. Indeed, they desire that one should rather instill the divine promises into those who are in this state: *Call upon me in the day of distress; then I shall deliver you and you shall glorify me.* <note>Psalm 50:15.</note>

They also teach that one can hold to this manner of remorse for sin, if it is necessary, all one's life. But to those who...

# General Memorial.

...they come to their senses <note>The Latin text here begins mid-word with *piscunt*, likely part of *resipiscunt*, meaning to recover one's senses or repent.</note> and teach what is written in *Isaiah*: that they should cease to act perversely and instead learn to do well. *The same is said by John*, the precursor of the Lord; "produce," he says, "worthy fruits of repentance." *Repentance consists mostly in this: that the old man be mortified and laid aside with his deeds and desires, and the new man be put on, who is created according to God, Colossians 3.* <note>The "old man" and "new man" is a common biblical metaphor for the transformation from a sinful nature to a life guided by faith.</note>

*They likewise teach that those repenting should approach a Priest and confess their sins to God himself in his presence (even though we do not command nor require an exhaustive list of sins), and ask him for counsel, a way of avoiding sins, and absolution through the keys of the Church; so that they may obtain the remission of sins through this ministry, as instituted by Christ.*

*Likewise they teach men to value absolution highly and believe without doubt that what is promised through the keys is truly done, since it is the voice of Christ expressed by his command in John 20: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive," etc. They should know that through the use and ministry of the keys, and by the authority of Christ’s words, all their sins are forgiven.*

*They also teach that those who are absolved—that is, those to whom sins have been forgiven through Christ—should be grateful for the grace of God received in Christ, lest they receive it in vain or fall back into sins, according to that saying: "Go, and from now on sin no more, lest something worse happen to you." Likewise: "If we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain terrible..."*

<column-break/>

...following the same in his conversion, they hold to what we find in the Prophet Isaiah, namely that they must stop doing evil and, on the contrary, diligently take up doing good. And truly that Holy Forerunner of the Lord <note>John the Baptist.</note> formerly looked to this when he said: "bring forth fruits worthy of conversion." *What is more, the whole of Repentance itself is primarily situated in this: that the old man be killed and laid aside with all his works and desires, and the new man be put on in his place, who is created after God, Colossians 3.*

They likewise teach that the repentant may well go to the Priest and confess their sins to God alone in his presence (though we do not prescribe or demand an enumeration of sins), to ask him for advice on how they might best avoid their sins, and to seek from him the release from the same through the Keys of the Church; so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins through this ministry, which was so established by our Savior.

Consequently, the people are also instructed by them that they must hold such an absolution <note>original Dutch: *quijt-slaging*, literally a "striking off" of a debt or guilt.</note> in high esteem and at the same time believe that what is promised through the aforementioned Keys will undoubtedly be fulfilled, because it is the very Voice of Christ, used explicitly by Him in this His command in John 20: *“receive likewise the Holy Spirit: whose sins you shall have forgiven,” etc.* and finally also to know that through the use of those Keys and Ministry and the power of Christ's words, all their sins are forgiven them.

Additionally, they teach that such Absolved persons—that is, all those whose sins are so forgiven through Christ—must be properly thankful for that grace of God received in Christ, so that they do not receive the same in vain or fall into their sins anew; just as is commanded by these words: *“go and do not sin again after this, so that nothing worse happens to you.”* Likewise: *“if we sin willfully, after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for the sins; but a certain terrible...”*

**Key Terms:**
<note>
*   **Repentance / Boet-vaardigheyt:** The process of turning from sin to God.
*   **Keys of the Church / Sleutels vande Kerk:** The authority given to the church (based on Matthew 16:19) to "bind and loose," or to declare sins forgiven or retained.
*   **Absolution / Quijt-slaging:** The formal act of pronouncing a person free from the guilt of sin.
</note>

It stresses that while confession is encouraged for spiritual guidance, a mechanical listing of every single sin is not required for forgiveness.</summary>

# Regarding the History of the Waldensian Churches.
<p align="right">Bb 2</p>

*...a certain terrible expectation of judgment and the intensity of fire.* <note>Original Latin: *ribilis quædam expectatio judicii & ignis vehementia.* This refers to the state of those who reject repentance, quoting Hebrews 10:27.</note>

*They also teach that the foundation and all the power of repentance consists in the merit of the death of Christ, Luke 24. Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day and to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name to all nations. And again: repent and believe the Gospel.* <note>Original Latin: *Etiam docent, fundamentum & omnem virtutem pœnitentiæ in merito mortis Christi consistere...*</note>

*Likewise they teach, that whoever neglects to perform repentance in God's name while alive, shall be destroyed with an evil end according to Christ's word: I tell you; unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish.* <note>Original Latin: *Item docent, ut qui in Dei nomine... pœnitentiam agere neglexerit...* quoting Luke 13:3.</note>

*...terrible expectation of judgment and the heat of the fire.*

They also hold this firmly as a part of their teaching: that the foundation and all the power of such <term>Repentance</term> <note>The Dutch uses *Berouw*, emphasizing the internal sorrow for sin.</note> depends solely on the merit of the death of the Lord Jesus, as we see in *Luke 24: Thus it behooved Christ to suffer and on the third day to rise from the dead, so that conversion and the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all peoples.* Again: *repent and believe the Gospel.*

Finally, they teach here also that those who, during their life, have neglected to turn themselves to repentance in God's name, shall (according to Christ's saying) perish most miserably; *I tell you, he says, unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish.*

### VI. CHAPTER.
->Concerning the Lord Christ and Faith in Him.<-

*First of all they teach, that a certain and firm faith must be held concerning Christ the Lord, namely that he is true God and man by nature, through whom all things in heaven and on earth were made, visible and invisible; whom John, calling him the eternal Word, interprets as being God the Light, the only-begotten Son, remaining in the bosom of the Father, full of grace and truth. The same in the 1st Epistle, chapter 5: he, he says, is the true God and eternal life: likewise concerning his works, performed for our salvation, his <term>incarnation</term> <note>The act of God becoming human in the form of Jesus.</note>, birth, passion, death, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God, and concerning his return to judge the living and the dead; and that through the Word and Sacraments good fruits are derived and emanate into us, so that we may be saved, as the secrets of the Scriptures contain and declare.*

They teach here above all things, that concerning the Lord Jesus one must believe firmly and with certainty: namely, that he is in fact both a true God and man, through whom all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created; and who, being called the *eternal Word* by Saint John, is elsewhere declared by him to be *a God who is the Light, the only-begotten Son, who remains in the Bosom of the Father, who is full of grace and truth.* So they also speak of his works, which he performed for our salvation: of the incarnation, birth, suffering, death, burial, resurrection, ascension to heaven, the sitting at the right hand of God, and his return to judge the living and the dead; and that these flow to us and are imparted as many good fruits for our eternal preservation through the Word and the <term>Signs of Faith</term> <note>Original Dutch: *Geloofsteykenen*, referring here to the Sacraments.</note>, just as has been revealed in the Mysteries of the Holy Scripture.

Furthermore, they teach that Christ, in that tangible and bodily manner in which he formerly dwelled on earth as a mortal man, willed to be betrayed, tormented with pains, and nailed to a tree...

*...forever, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth* <note>Original Latin: *Spiritum veritatis*</note>*, whom the world cannot receive, because it has not seen him, nor known him: but you know him, because he remains with you and shall be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you,* namely, through this Spirit of truth. *This understanding of the Scriptures is by no means a fabrication or a recent invention. For it was commonly taught and steadfastly held in the Early Church, as found in the Decretals* <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of canon law</note>*, distinction 2, chapter 1 (and these are the words of Augustine): until the world is finished, the Lord is on high; but nevertheless, the truth of the Lord is here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place; but his truth is spread in every place. For this reason, they teach that Christ the Lord is present in this, his second mode of existence (which we call invisible), in the Ministers of the Church, in the Word, and in the Sacraments; and through these, everyone must later receive him into themselves by faith, so that he may dwell within them through it, and be present through the Spirit of truth, of whom he said: he shall be in you; and again: I will come to you, etc.*

*Furthermore, they also teach that men are justified for free* <note>original Latin: *gratis*</note>*, by faith in Christ and through mercy, obtaining salvation and the forgiveness of sins without any human work or merit. They likewise teach that his death and blood alone are sufficient to abolish and atone for all the sins of all people. For thus Peter preaches in the Acts:* <note>Acts 4:12</note> *Salvation is in no other than in the one Lord Jesus, nor is there any other name given under heaven among men by which we must be saved. *...forever remain with you, namely the Spirit of truth, which the world cannot receive, as it has neither seen nor ever known him. But you know him, because he remains with you and shall be in you. I shall not leave you as orphans; I shall come to you,* namely through this spirit of truth. And this meaning of Holy Scripture is by no means fabricated or recently invented, since the same was taught throughout the early Church and steadfastly held, as can be seen in the Decretals, distinction 2, chapter 1, from these words of Saint Augustine: *the Lord is up there, as long as the world shall stand; but in the meantime, the truth of the Lord is always here with us. For the body with which he rose must necessarily be in one place; truth, on the contrary, is spread through all. Therefore, they also hold that the Lord Jesus is present in this second manner of being—which we call "invisible" to distinguish it—in the Ministers of the Church, in the Word, and in the Sacraments, and that thereafter each and every person must receive him through all of these by faith within themselves, so that he may dwell within them through the same and remain within them through the Spirit of truth, of whom he said: he shall be in you: and again; I will come to you, etc.*

Furthermore, this is also their teaching: that people are justified for free through the Lord Jesus and through faith in the same out of mercy, and obtain salvation and forgiveness of sins without any human work or merit. They also hold that his mere death and bloodshedding is sufficient for the annihilation and reconciliation of all sins that could ever be committed by all people. For so teaches Saint Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: *salvation is in no other than in the only Lord Jesus, and there is no other name given to men under heaven through which we must be saved. # Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

[...no man] <note>original Latin: *habere potest*; the beginning of the sentence is on the previous page</note> can have. It is indeed a gift of God, who, where and when it seems good to Him, works it through the Holy Spirit in man, so that he may perceive for salvation whatever has been rightly administered to him through the external Word and the **Sacraments**, instituted by Christ. Concerning this, **John the Baptist** says: *a man cannot have anything, unless it has been given to him from heaven.* And **Christ** himself: *no one*, he says, *can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, draws him: and a little further down; unless it has been given to him by my Father*, namely through the Holy Spirit.

They continue by teaching, *that by faith alone or trust in Jesus Christ men are justified before God, without any of their efforts, merits and works, as **Paul** says; furthermore, to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness. Again; but now apart from the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested, while it is confirmed by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets, and this righteousness is through faith in Jesus Christ etc. Elsewhere; through him everyone who believes is justified. And this sixth **Article** <note>original Latin: "Articulus"; original Dutch: "Hooft-lit"</note> is held by us to be the most important of all, as it is the sum of all Christianity and piety. Therefore our people teach and treat it with all diligence and study, and try to instill it into everyone.*

<column-break/>

[...abilities], <note>The Dutch text begins mid-word with "ten," likely "krachten" (powers/abilities)</note> will or desire can possess this faith. And truly it is a gift of God, who works the same at the place and time that pleases Him, through the Holy Spirit in man, in such a way that all that is properly presented to him through the external Word and **Sacraments**, solemnly instituted by our **Savior**, may be accepted for the salvation of the same. This the **Holy John** testifies very explicitly: *man*, he says, *can possess nothing, unless it be given to him from heaven.* The **Lord Jesus** himself says somewhere: *no one can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, draws him: and a week lower; <note>meaning "a little further down in the text"</note> unless the same were given to him by my Father*, namely through the Holy Spirit.

Finally they proceed in this way, that namely through sheer faith, or trust in **Jesus Christ**, they obtain a share before God in **justification** <term>Justification: The theological concept of being declared righteous or "right with God" through faith rather than deeds.</term>, without any of their activities, merits, or works coming into consideration, just as the **Teacher of the Gentiles** <note>A traditional title for the Apostle Paul</note> teaches that: *now to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness.* Again; *but at present the righteousness of God has been revealed without the Law, while it is strengthened by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets, and this righteousness is through faith in Jesus Christ etc.* Elsewhere it stands: *through him all those who believe in him are justified.* And this **sixth Article** is held by us to be the most foremost and weightiest, as it is a short summary of the whole of **Christianity** and all godliness. And therefore our people also teach it with all diligence and industriousness and strive to instill it into all people through such treatment.

---

# General Memorial

<column-break/>

...argues: <note>original Latin: *arguit*</note> why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your traditions? and: *in vain they worship me, teaching the precepts and doctrines of men.* Therefore they diligently warn that works established by men are not to be valued as highly as those which God has established and commanded. <note>The Waldensians were known for rejecting "man-made" church traditions in favor of direct biblical instruction.</note>

Likewise they teach that faith and charity—which is love for both God and neighbor—are the *fountains of all virtues and good works, as in 1 Timothy 1.* The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith. For without faith, *as the Epistle to the Hebrews has it*, it is impossible for anyone to please God. Without charity, however, nothing is profitable *1 Cor. 13.*

They teach furthermore that there is no one who fulfills the commandments by deeds of works, nor is there anyone who does not sin, however studiously he may exercise himself in good works and the Law of God, just as it is written: there is no man on earth who does good and does not sin. Therefore, for everyone perfect in Christ Jesus, life, righteousness, and salvation must be sought through faith from His merit and grace. *For whoever takes hold of Christ and hides and leans upon Him—who fulfilled the Law for every believer—all their sins are washed away through His blood: so that the transgressions of the Law cannot condemn the believers.* Hence the Apostle *Romans 8*: There is no condemnation for those who are grafted into Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Christ, therefore, is the satisfaction for all believers and, as Paul has it, wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

<column-break/>

...rebukes somewhere very severely those who go against this in any way: *why, says He, do you transgress God's commandment through your traditions? and; in vain they serve me, teaching commandments that are but human teachings.* From which they also diligently draw this observation: namely, that one must not regard the works of human institution as much as those commanded and prescribed by God.

This is likewise taught by them: namely, that faith and love, which consists in loving both God and our fellow man, are the origin of all virtues and good works; *in 1 Timothy chapter 1, the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and from an unfeigned faith.* For it is entirely impossible, as can be read in the letter to the Hebrews, for anyone to please God without faith. *Indeed, without love, nothing is profitable, 1 Cor. 13.*

Finally, they also teach this here in conclusion: that no one is found who can fulfill with his works what God has commanded man regarding works; that also no one is found who would not fall into sin, however carefully he may ever exercise himself in God's Holy Law and in the practice of good works; as it is written: *there is no man under the sun who does good such that he does not sin.* So that everyone in Christ Jesus can and must seek the perfection of the Law, life, righteousness, and salvation by the power of His merits and grace through faith alone. For all the sins of those who have accepted Christ, desired to hide in Him and lean upon Him—who fulfilled the law for all believers—are so washed off and out by His blood that such transgressions of the Law can never again condemn the believer. Why the Apostle speaks thus in *Romans 8: there is no more condemnation for those who, being grafted into Christ Jesus, walk no more after the flesh, but after the Spirit.* The Lord Jesus then alone is the satisfaction and, according to the saying of St. Paul, the wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption for all those who believe in Him.

### VIII. CHAPTER.
->Of the Holy, Universal Church.<-

They teach first, that *Christ the Lord, by his word, grace, and truth, is the head and foundation of the Church, in whom she is built up through the Holy Spirit by the Word and Sacraments, as Christ says to Peter: and upon this rock (that is, myself) I will build my Church: And Paul in 1 Cor. 3. no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. The same says elsewhere: he himself is the head of the body of the Church, who fulfills all in all.* <note>original Latin: *ipſe eſt caput corporis Eccleſiæ, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet*</note>

Also, they teach that one must believe and confess that the *Holy Catholic Church, as it is gathered in the world in its present state, consists of all Christians, wherever they may act on earth or wherever they may be dispersed, who through the sacred word of the Gospel have been gathered from all nations, peoples, tribes, and languages—of whatever rank, age, and tongue they may be—into the one faith of Christ and the Holy Trinity; as written by John in the Apocalypse: after these things I saw, and behold, a great multitude which no one could number, etc. And the Lord: where two or three are gathered in my name (among whatever nation and people), there I am in the midst of them. For wherever Christ is preached and accepted, wherever His Word and Sacraments are, and are dispensed and received according to His prescription and will; there is the Holy and Christian Church and the people of God, however great their number may be. But where Christ is absent and his word is rejected; there neither the true Church nor a people pleasing to God can exist.*

...[that he should] hold [to the Church], and embrace all its members with charity, and devote and consecrate himself entirely to its affairs and use, not bringing in sects, nor stirring up sedition; but that he should be engaged in it in the bond of peace and with the same consensus and spirit as all others: for such a person is a true member of the Church. They also teach, *that order must be preserved in the Church, so that no one strives only for their own benefit, nor thinks arrogantly of themselves; but each should seek the things of others, not their own, and be subject to one another for the sake of Christ and their own salvation. Of this the Holy Apostle speaks thus in his letter to those of Ephesus: *I urge you then, that you walk worthy of the calling with which you are called, bearing with one another out of love with all submission and gentleness, seeking to preserve the unity of the spirit through the bond of peace, etc.* Again: *each of us please his neighbor in what is good for edification and let nothing happen through strife or vain glory. But they hold and feel this regarding their own Assembly, namely that neither it, nor any similar one, however large or small they might be, is in any way the Holy Universal Church; but only a part and member of the same, as the Corinthians were in former times, of whom the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 12: *but you are the body of Christ and members in part.*

They likewise teach, that an orderliness must take place in the Church, so that no one regards only his own advantage or has a proud and bold opinion of himself; but that each may seek primarily that which belongs to another, and not his own, and for the sake of Christ and their own salvation, strive to subject themselves to one another. *Writing also to Titus and Timothy, Paul hands down the mode and norm of this Ordination: you therefore, my son, be strong in the grace which is through Christ Jesus, and in these things which you have heard from me through many witnesses: commit these to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others also. <note>original Latin: "Titum quoque ac Timotheum scribens Paulus Ordinationis hujus modum, normamque tradit..."</note> For this reason, among us, it is truly permitted for no one to perform the office of a Priest unless he has been properly called and established according to these precepts. Following the footsteps of those who have been thus called to the Ministry of the Church, they teach that their roles are to take diligent care of the souls entrusted to them, and to faithfully minister the word of the Gospel and the Sacraments according to Christ's institution and to show themselves as an example to be imitated by all; to pray to God for them, that they may be freed from sins and errors, and to search through the Scriptures for what His will may be in all things, 1 Peter 5. feed the flock of Christ which is among you, taking care of it not by necessity but willingly; not out of a desire for shameful profit, but with a mind naturally inclined. Again; be therefore a model for the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity, until I come. Pay attention to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine: do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of hands by the authority of the priesthood. Exercise these things, be in them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Pay attention to yourself and to the doctrine: persist in these things. For if you do this, you will save yourself and those who hear you.*
