### CHAPTER 10.
->Concerning the Word of God.<-

Furthermore they teach that the preaching of the Word of God, or the Gospel, is a Ministry instituted and commanded by Christ in the last chapter of *Matthew*: go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Likewise *Peter in Acts 10* <note>original Latin: "Petrus Actor. 10." Referring to Acts 10:42</note> says the Lord commanded us to preach. And this administration of the Word is held as the primary one among our people, and is practiced most of all, as something that contributes more to salvation and is more necessary than even the Sacraments themselves, as Paul says: Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, namely chiefly and first. For through the Gospel itself and its preaching, faith—suggested inwardly by the Spirit of God—is acquired; then his sense and will, and that of Christ regarding the Sacraments and other things that lead to salvation, are perceived.

They also teach to maintain a distinction between the power of the Law and the Gospel: that the former is indeed the administration of death, while the latter is the administration of life and glory through Christ, *2 Corinthians 3*: the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. And *John 5* <note>original Latin: "Johannis 5." This citation usually refers to John 6:63 in this context: "The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."</note>: the words that I speak to you are spirit and life.

Moreover, they grant that no one can attain true faith unless they hear the word of God, according to that saying of Paul: faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. And again: how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? Therefore our people devote every effort to teaching and preaching the Word of the Gospel in the Church, unmixed with human Traditions. Accordingly, [they read] the Gospels themselves, as well as the other Scriptures, in the common tongue in the churches

<column-break/>

Here they teach next that the Proclamation of God's Word or the Gospel is a service established by our Savior himself in the Gospel of Matthew, in the last chapter: *go through the whole world and proclaim the Gospel to every creature.* The same is to be taken from the words of St. Peter in *Acts 10*: the Lord has commanded us that we should preach. And this ministry of the Word is held by our people to be the most important, and is most in use of all, being even more necessary and useful for salvation than the Holy Signs of Faith <term>Sacraments; rituals like baptism and communion</term> themselves, just as the Apostle says somewhere: *our Savior did not send me to baptize, but to proclaim the Gospel everywhere*, namely primarily in the first place. For through the Gospel itself and its proclamation, faith is obtained by the inner inspiration of the Spirit of God, and furthermore His will and meaning—as well as those of the Lord Jesus regarding the Sacraments and other parts of salvation—are very clearly known and seen.

They also teach to make a distinction between the power of the Law and the Gospel, namely such that the former is held to be the ministry of death and this, on the contrary, the ministry of life and glory through Jesus Christ, *2 Corinthians 3*: the letter kills, but the Spirit makes alive; and *John 5*: the words that I speak to you are Spirit and life.

They furthermore also allow that no one can ever obtain true faith unless he first hears God's Word, according to Paul's saying: Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. And again: *but how can they believe in him of whom they have never heard anything?* This is also why our people apply all diligence to have the Word of the Gospel, pure of all human Traditions <note>The Waldensians emphasized "Sola Scriptura," rejecting man-made rules or traditions not found in the Bible.</note>, taught and proclaimed in every way in the Church. To which end they then also [use] the Gos-

### CHAPTER X.

->Of the Word of God.<-

<note>The left column contains the Latin text of the Waldensian confession.</note>
Furthermore, they teach that the preaching of the Word of God, or the Gospel, is a ministry instituted and commanded by Christ in the last chapter of Matthew: *go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature.* Likewise, Peter in Acts 10: *the Lord commanded us to preach.* And this administration of the Word is held as the primary one among our people, and is practiced above all else, as that which contributes more to salvation and is more necessary than the Sacraments themselves, as Paul says; *Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize,* namely chiefly and first. ### XI. CHAPTER.
->Of the Holy Sacraments, or Seal-signs of the New Covenant.<-

*They teach first of all that the Sacraments, instituted by Christ, are necessary for salvation, by whose benefit the faithful are made partakers and companions of the merits of Christ. If anyone, however, intentionally despises them, or does not value them worthily, or uses them in any other way than the will and command of Christ is, they say that he sins gravely against Christ, their author. If indeed it happens that someone truly desires to communicate in the Sacraments according to the mind and command of Christ, but is nevertheless hindered by something—imprisonment, illness, or led away captive to other nations, or oppressed by enemies or foes of the faith, etc.—and cannot obtain his salutary wish: this person, things being so, provided he believes the Gospel purely and entirely, will undoubtedly be saved through faith in Christ alone.*

*They teach next that the Sacraments by themselves, or as some say, <term>ex opere operato</term> <note>Latin: "by the work performed." <column-break/>

Here they teach before all things that the Holy Sacraments, instituted by the Lord Christ himself, are required as necessary for salvation, as through their contribution all believers can first become partakers of the merits of our Savior. They add this as well: namely, all those who intentionally despise them or have no proper high regard for them, or finally use them defectively in whatever other way it may be that does not agree with Christ's command or will, thereby sin very gravely against the Lord Jesus, the institutor of the same. For the Sacraments do not borrow their power from the one who distributes them, or from him who receives them, whoever both might be; but only from the arrangement and command of the Lord Jesus.

### XII. CHAPTER.
->Regarding Holy Baptism.<-

They likewise teach that Baptism is a saving administration, instituted by Christ and added to the Gospel, through which He Himself purifies, cleanses, and sanctifies His Church in His death and blood, as Paul says; *Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word.* And our Church ministers alone in the Kingdom of Bohemia and the Margraviate of Moravia <note>Bohemia and Moravia are historical regions in the modern-day Czech Republic, which were major centers for the Reformation movements described here.</note> have defended this faith concerning Baptism from the Scriptures against those who believe, confess, and write that Baptism only washes away the filth of the body, but profits nothing for the salvation of the soul.

<column-break/>

They teach here also, that Baptism is a wholesome ministry, which was instituted by the Lord Christ and added to the Gospel, through which He cleanses and sanctifies His Church in His death and blood according to the saying of Saint Paul; *Christ loved His Church so much, that He gave Himself up for her, that He might sanctify her, having cleansed her with the bath of water through the word.* And this view of Baptism has been maintained from Scripture only by our Church ministers in the Kingdom of Bohemia and the Margraviate of Moravia against those who believe, profess, and write that Baptism can only take away the impurities of the body and consequently do no good for the salvation of the soul.

### XIII. CHAPTER.
->Concerning the Holy Supper of the Lord.<-

They teach that the Lord's Supper, or the Sacrament of the Eucharist <note>original: "Sacramentum Eucharistiæ"</note>, is a ministry instituted by Christ, then given to the Apostles and through them, by His grace and goodness, to the entire Church for the common use and salvation of all. This is as the Evangelists testify, as does the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note>, whose words the whole Church recites: *For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, that the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread, etc.* and a little further down; *wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat (namely this Supper), tarry one for another.* <note>original: 1 Corinthians 11:23, 33</note>

*So also here, they teach that it must be believed with the heart and confessed with the mouth that the bread of the Lord's Supper is the true body of Christ, which was given for us, and the cup is His true blood, which was shed for us for the remission of sins, as Christ the Lord openly says: this is my body, this is my blood, etc.*

*They also teach that regarding these words of Christ—in which He Himself declares the bread specifically to be His body and the wine to be His blood—no one should add, mix, or take away anything of their own; but simply believe these words of Christ, turning neither to the right nor to the left. While the simple and genuine sense of these words was being attacked by certain people in the Kingdom of Bohemia and the Margraviate of Moravia <note>A historical region in the modern-day Czech Republic.</note>, and those whom it concerned remained silent instead of defending and vindicating it with the authority of the Scriptures; our people alone stood forth and proved from the Scriptures that faith should be placed simply in these words of Christ. For this reason, they endured many calumnies, sneers, mocks, insults, and open—*

<column-break/>

Here they teach that the Holy Supper, or the Sacrament of the *Eucharist* <note>from Greek *eucharistia*, meaning "thanksgiving"</note> or thanksgiving, is a ministry instituted by our Savior Himself and His Apostles. It is offered equally to the whole Church through these men, under His goodness and grace, for the common benefit and salvation of all, as the Evangelists testify and especially the Holy Apostle, whose words echo through the whole Church: *for I have received from the Lord, that which I also delivered unto you, that the Lord Jesus in the night in which He was betrayed, took bread, etc. and a little lower; so then, my brothers, when you come together to eat (namely this Supper), then wait for one another as is proper.*

Likewise, they also hold that one must believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that the Bread of the Lord's Supper is the true body of our Savior, which was given for us, and the Cup is His true blood, which was shed for us for the forgiveness of sins, as the Lord Jesus openly says: *this is my body, this is my blood, etc.*

This they also teach, namely that no one is permitted to add anything of their own to these words of Christ—with which He Himself assures us that the bread is His body and the wine specifically His own blood—nor to mix anything with them or to take anything away from them. Rather, one must believe them simply and plainly, without departing from them to the right or to the left. *In the Ancient Church, Paul taught; saying, let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats or drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body <note>original Latin: "non dijudicans corpus Domini"</note>. And elsewhere: examine yourselves, whether you be in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? unless indeed you are disqualified. But he who does not first descend into himself, nor previously consider with himself with what faith or with what mind he approaches this **Sacrament** <term>Sacrament: A sacred rite or "holy sign" of spiritual grace</term>, he treats the Sacrament itself with insult and despises this entire ordinance of Christ. Therefore, those who preside over the Churches among us admit no one to this Sacrament unless, as far as in them lies, they first prove and examine themselves, and behave themselves reverently toward this Sacrament. Moreover, where the communion of this Holy Supper is to be held, according to the custom of the ancient Church, a sermon is given concerning Christ and his death, concerning grace and salvation offered to all through faith by the intervention of his blood, and concerning the immense blessings which he himself works in believers through trust in his death and blood. And at the same time, prayers are offered with the whole assembly of the people. The Ministers, reciting the words of the Lord’s Supper, exhort the people to this faith, that they should believe the presence of Christ’s body to be at hand; and meanwhile, they distribute it to those kneeling on their knees. The people themselves receive it with thanksgiving, reflecting on the blessings of God in hymns and spiritual songs; they devote and exert themselves entirely to this, that according to Christ’s word they may do this in his **remembrance** <term>Remembrance: From the Greek 'anamnesis', a memorial act of worship</term>. This is indeed how Paul interprets it: as often as you shall eat this bread and drink of the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.*

### XIV. CHAPTER.

#### Of Church Authority, or the Keys.

And here they teach, so that it might be believed, that the Keys were delivered by Christ to the Church, about which he himself said to Peter on behalf of all: *I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven.* <note>original Latin: "tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum"</note> These, moreover, are the administration of Christ, delivered to the Church and its Ministers, which perseveres in it until the present day, and will not reach an end before the consumption of the world. The office and authority of this administration, according to the command and duty of Christ, as the divine letters relate, is to correct and bind the wicked and impenitent in the Church and to close the Kingdom of Heaven to them—that is, to exclude them from Christ and the use and participation of the Church; on the contrary, to absolve those who are truly penitent, to render them tranquil in conscience, to place them in certain hope of salvation and faith, and thus to open the Kingdom of Heaven to them and to strengthen and fortify them against all temptations and the assaults, terrors, and deceits of that Enemy <note>The "Enemy" refers to the devil or Satan</note>. This indeed they must do, not by their own power and will, but as Stewards of the Mysteries of God <term>Stewards: From the Latin 'dispensatores', those appointed to manage and distribute spiritual gifts</term>, Ministers and servants, by the authority of Christ, his Word, and the Sacraments. For the Lord, committing to them their office and duty, says thus in John ch. 20: *As the Father sent me, so I also send you. Receive the Holy Spirit. Whosoever's sins you remit, they are remitted to them; whosoever's sins you retain, they are retained.* And this use and authority of the Keys was declared in that incest of Corinth, because Paul himself, by the interdict of the Lord, together with the Church there, excommunicated and Sa-

<column-break/>

Here they teach especially, that one must believe that the Keys were given by the Lord Jesus to the Church, as he himself spoke these words to Peter in the stead of them all: *I will give you the Keys of the Kingdom of Heaven;* and that these same are an administration of Christ, given to the Church and its Ministers, which continues in the same until the present day and shall never cease before the end of the world. The office and power of this administration lies primarily in this: that according to the testimony of the Holy Pages <note>original Dutch: "H. Bladeren", referring to the Holy Scriptures</note>, following the command and in the name of the Lord Christ, they rebuke and bind the godless and unrepentant when they are found in the Church, and close the Kingdom of Heaven to them—that is, cut them off from the enjoyment and fellowship with Christ and his Church; and on the other hand, to acquit the sincerely penitent, to completely set their inner conscience at rest, to give them a sure hope and faith of salvation, thus subsequently opening the Kingdom of Heaven to them and finally preparing and properly strengthening them against all temptations, attacks, terrors, and deceits of that enemy. Which also can by no means be done out of their own will and power, but only insofar as they are Stewards of the Mysteries of God and Church Teachers or servants of the Lord Jesus, acting for the same through his word and Sacraments. For when the Lord laid these offices upon them, he used in John 20 only these words: *as the Father has sent me, so I also send you. Receive then the Holy Spirit. # General Memorial.

*...delivered [him] to Satan <note>original Latin: "tanæ tradidit", likely part of "Satanæ tradidit"</note>, who had committed this crime; and again, when by the grace of God he had come to his senses, he absolved him and received him back into the communion of the Church and the Sacraments. They likewise teach, *that the Keys of the Lord, or this administration and power of the Keys, was granted and delivered first to the leaders and Ministers of the Church, and then also to every Christian assembly, however few in number they might be, as the words of the Lord clearly testify: Truly I say to you; whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.*

After these things they teach, *that whoever uses these Keys, as often as there is need, through the Priest of the Church to which he is assigned, should believe as certainly that his sins are remitted by the virtue of the Keys as if he received absolution from the Lord himself present; since the Priest performs the office of the Lord and has this authority delivered by him, just as he himself says in John: whose sins you remit, etc. and again; he who hears you, hears me: and again; he who receives you, receives me, and he who despises you, despises me.*

They also admonish, *that those who are in the Ministry of the Church should use these Keys only according to the ordinance and will of Christ, as revealed in his Word, and not as they please according to the inclination of their own minds, lest that prophetic word be fulfilled in them: But now to you is this command, O Priests, if you will not lay it to heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts. I will send poverty upon you and I will curse your blessings and I will curse them, etc.*

<column-break/>

[The Apostle] in that place <note>referring to 1 Corinthians 5</note> excommunicated <term>excommunicated: "inden ban gedaan," literally placed under the ban, or excluded from the religious community</term> and delivered him to Satan: and when he, on the contrary, had obtained repentance through God’s grace, he [the Apostle] acquitted him of everything again and accepted him into the fellowship of the Church and the Sacraments. So that he also, in this manner, reopened the Kingdom of Heaven to him.

They likewise teach that the Keys of the Lord, or this power and administration of the Keys, is granted and given first and foremost to the Heads and Teachers of the Church, and thereafter also to all Christian assemblies, however small they might be in number, just as the words of our Savior state very clearly: *Truly I say to you, everything you shall have bound on earth shall be bound in heaven: for where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.*

Furthermore they teach, that everyone who uses these Keys through a Priest of the Church to which he belongs, as often as necessity requires, must believe that all his sins are as certainly forgiven by the power of the same as if he had the acquittal from God himself; since such a Church Teacher occupies God's place in this and derives all his power from Him, just as we have already cited these fine words from St. John above: *whose sins you shall have forgiven, etc.* So He himself says somewhere else: *all who hear you, hear me: and again; all who receive and accept you, receive me, and all who reject and despise you, despise me.*

To this they finally add a serious admonition: that those who are in such service to the Church may only use these Keys according to the will and institution of the Lord Christ, as it stands revealed in His Holy Word, and by no means according to their own pleasure or the impulse of their own minds, so that this saying of the Prophet might not be applied to them: *this command concerns you, O Priests; if you will not take this to heart, namely that you glorify my name, says the Lord of hosts, I shall send poverty to you, curse your blessings, and meet those with a curse, etc.*

# Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

### CHAPTER XV.
<note>original Dutch: "HOOFT-LIT.", meaning a main section or chapter.</note>

->Concerning Human Traditions.<-

They teach that human traditions, rites, and customs, which are in no way contrary to piety, should be observed in public gatherings, just as the Apostle warns: *let all things be done decently* (namely in the Church) *and according to order.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 14:40.</note> Elsewhere: *stand fast and hold the institutions* <note>original Latin: "institutiones", often translated as traditions.</note> *which you have learned either by word or by our Epistle.*

*But they teach that traditions, rites, or ceremonies of this kind, which obscure the glory and indeed the grace of Christ, lead the people away from the truth and faith and hold them back, or are equated with or preferred over divine precepts—or if anyone, in their name, should they transgress them, leaves the sincere use of the Word of God—these should be avoided and rejected. For the Lord harshly rebukes the Scribes and Pharisees, who were observers of these traditions, in Mark chapter 7: Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written; this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines that are the precepts of men. For neglecting the commandment of God, you hold the constitutions of men. And Paul also wants such traditions to be avoided in Colossians 2: see that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception according to the constitution of men, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ. Indeed, the Canons* <note>Refers to the "Decretum Gratiani," a collection of Canon law.</note> *also hand this down in Distinction 8, and especially in chapter 11, "Custom," where we read it written thus: we praise custom, yet only that which usurps nothing against the Catholic* <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox Christian faith rather than the Roman Catholic Church specifically.</note> *faith.*

<column-break/>

Here is their first opinion: that all human traditions, uses, and customs, which do not conflict with godliness in the slightest, must be maintained in the public gatherings, as the Apostle warns somewhere; *all things must (in the Church) happen decently and in order:* and elsewhere also; *persevere and hold yourselves to the teaching or institutions, which you have learned either from our reasoning or letter.*

On the contrary, they also hold at the same time, that one must avoid and reject all such traditions, uses, or ceremonies, which obscure the honor and consequently also the grace of Christ, lead the people away from the truth and faith and hold them back, or which are held in equal, and sometimes even in higher, esteem than God’s Word itself, or by whose transgression the true use of God’s Word is considered to be lost. Namely, the Lord himself punishes the Scribes and Pharisees very harshly in the Gospel of Mark in the 7th Chapter regarding the keeping of such human institutions, as he uses these arguments against them: *well has the Prophet Isaiah prophesied of you hypocrites, as it is written; this people honors me with the lips, but their heart stays far from me. But in vain they honor me, teaching doctrines that are commands of men. For neglecting the command of God, you hold the institutions of men.* St. Paul also explicitly wants in his letter to the Colossians, chapter 2, that one guards oneself well against such traditions: *see to it,* he says, *that no one carries you off as a prey through philosophy and empty deception according to the traditions of men, according to the first principles of the world and not according to Christ.* With which also the Rule-writings <note>The Canon Law or "Canones" mentioned in the left column.</note> of the Church agree, in which we read in Distinction 8 and especially in the 11th chapter, *Custom* <note>original: "Consuetudinem"</note>, regarding this matter: *we praise the use of the Churches, provided that it is such that it [does not go] against the universal* <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# General Memorial-script

**Page 180**

...is discerned. Wherefore our people teach that those rites and traditions—which promote and nourish faith, the worship of God, and other good things among the faithful, which reconcile and retain concord and peace among the people, and which establish a certain governance and harmony—should be observed, regardless of who their authors may be, whether a synod, a Pope, a Bishop, or anyone else. Indeed, no one should be offended by the authors of these traditions, nor should they be prevented from observing them, provided they carry no inconvenience. However, the greatest care must be taken lest they distract us from more serious and more principal matters. For in all things, divine matters are to be preferred over human ones. To these <note>the divine matters</note> the mind is chiefly to be directed, meanwhile disregarding traditions if they serve any impiety. For Christ in the Gospel thus rebukes the leaders of the Jews, who subordinated divine precepts to their own traditions: *you have left the weightier matters of the law: judgment, and mercy, and faith; these you ought to have done, and not to have omitted the others.* <note>Original Latin quote: "relinquiftis, quæ graviora funt legis, judicium, & mifericordiam ac fidem, hæc oportuit facere & illa non omittere." See Matthew 23:23.</note> And indeed, many ancient ecclesiastical rites are still retained among us today, such as certain fasts and appointed, established feast days on which the people assemble to participate in sacred things; morning and evening prayers, the Lord's Day, and the feast days of Christ's Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and so on. Furthermore, the memories of the Saints are celebrated, such as the most blessed Virgin, the Apostles, and others as well; but especially those whom Scripture mentions. All these things are done among us for the sake of the Word and divine worship. Although our people do not observe the rites and customs of everyone; because it is neither possible, nor is it necessary that the same rites and ceremonies be observed everywhere in all churches.

<column-break/>

...general faith is not found to be in any way offended. And for all these reasons, our people rightly maintain that such customs and traditions—which come to advance and nourish faith, religion, and other good things among the faithful, or which bring and preserve peace and unity in the congregation, or finally cause some state-order and mutual agreement in the same—must be maintained and followed; whoever it may be, whether a Church Assembly <note>original: "Kerken-vergaring", referring to a synod.</note>, Pope, or any other Bishop, who first instituted them. For their first inventors cannot give so great an offense that it should prevent them from being kept in value and use, as long as they do not drag any other inconvenience along with them. Here, however, one must take the highest care that they never pull us away from more necessary or weightier things. Always and everywhere, the divine must be valued and esteemed above the human. The mind must focus primarily on the divine and then simultaneously cast off <note>literally "give the shove"</note> traditions if they wish to serve godlessness. For the Lord Jesus thus rebukes the Authorities of the Jewish people in the Gospel, because they valued God's commandments much less than their institutions of the Elders; *you are*, he says, *neglectful regarding the weightiest things of the Law, such as justice, mercy, and faith. These things you ought to do, but the others you must not always leave out.* It is true, among us various old Church customs are still currently in existence, such as certain Fast-days, and instituted and set times at which the people come together for their worship, Morning and Evening prayers, Sunday, the Holy Days of Christ's Birth, Suffering, Resurrection, etc., together with the Celebration-days of the memories of the Saints, such as the blessed Virgin Mary, the Holy Apostles <note>original: "H. Kruyf-gefangen", likely a variant or error for "Kruys-gezanten" meaning Envoys of the Cross or Apostles.</note>, and others more, but principally all those who are in some way known in Scripture. But all this remains standing among us only because it seems to help God's word and Religion in some measure. And therefore not all of our...

*However, they do not oppose any good or pious rite, nor do they intend to oppose them. Even if some rites of this kind do not seem particularly necessary, provided they do not hinder piety nor detract from faith—which alone justifies and makes one blessed—they believe they should not be rejected.* <note>Original Latin: "Nullo tamen bono, pioque ritui adversantur..."</note>

Likewise they teach that the Church is not to be burdened with many traditions, as it was once under Moses. For the Apostles also forbade this to be done, as Peter said in the Acts to certain people who were urging the observation of legal matters: *why do you tempt God, by putting a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?* <note>Original Latin: "quod tentatis Deum..." See Acts 15:10.</note> And elsewhere Paul says: *see to it,* he says, *that you be not entangled in the yoke of servitude.* <note>Original Latin: "videte... ne jugo servitutis implicemini." See Galatians 5:1.</note> Christ also sternly threatened those who burdened the people with a mass of traditions, saying: *and woe to you lawyers, because you load men with burdens that they cannot carry.* <note>Original Latin: "et vobis Legisperitis væ..." Furthermore, they teach that human traditions ought not to be held as inviolable and eternal laws: but just as they are established for certain and just causes, so it is permissible to violate them without sin when other causes and circumstances arise that suggest otherwise. For the Apostles transgressed the traditions of the elders when they ate bread with unwashed hands, nor did they fast again with the others: but in both cases, since they were excused by Christ, they were without sin. And again in the Primitive Church <note>The early Christian church of the first centuries.</note>, the Apostles, gathered unanimously with other saints, decreed through the Holy Spirit that the faithful should abstain from things offered to idols, blood, and strangled meat; later however—

<column-break/>

...demonstrations and ceremonies have no place among us, all the more because it is impossible and unnecessary that one and the same usage should prevail everywhere in all churches. Nevertheless, we have never set ourselves against good and god-fearing outward practices and, on the contrary, never intend to change that opinion. Indeed, even though some of these do not seem so highly necessary, they still hold that one may not reject them, as long as they are not detrimental to godliness or to the faith, which alone can make a man righteous and blessed.

They likewise teach that the Church must not be overloaded at present with many traditions, as it once was in the time of Moses. For the Holy Apostles have also forbidden this to such an extent that Peter was forced to speak thus in the Acts of the Apostles to some who insisted rather strongly on the maintenance of the Law: *why do you test God, to lay a yoke on the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to carry?* and Paul says somewhere thus: *see to it, that you do not become stuck again to the yoke of slavery.* Our Savior himself even sternly threatens those who made the people bow under a burden of institutions: *woe to you,* he says, *you Scribes <term>Schrift-geleerde; experts in religious law</term>, because you lay burdens upon men that they will never be able to carry.*

Furthermore, they teach that human institutions may never be held as eternal and unbreakable laws; but that, just as they are established for certain and fair causes, they may likewise be transgressed without any sin upon occasion and if some new occurrences simply require it. Specifically, so the Apostles formerly acted regarding the Jewish traditions, when they dared to touch food with unwashed hands, and also did not want to fast as strictly as the others, without however committing any sin in the one or the other, because they were excused by the Lord Jesus himself regarding both. # General Memorial-Record.
<meta>catchword: XVI. CHAPTER-</meta>

*...but when those things for which it was then ordained cease, the precept also ceases.* <note>This refers to the early Christian dietary laws—like avoiding "strangled" meat—which were intended as a temporary compromise to maintain peace between Jewish and Gentile converts.</note>

*They teach thereafter that no one should be offended by others, nor should they despise, hate, or persecute one another on account of differences in ceremonies, customs, and rites—which may be seen among Christians in various Churches—as long as they do not protest against or hinder piety. Nor should they, by stirring up sects or seditions, alienate and tear themselves away from the unity of the Church; since the same rites have never existed in all Churches, nor do they exist now. This is also clearly shown by the Decrees of the Fathers (Distinction 12, Chapter "Scit"): "The Holy Roman Church knows that different customs according to place and time do not hinder the salvation of believers, provided that Canonical authority does not oppose them."* <note>The "Decrees of the Fathers" refers to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a famous 12th-century collection of Church law used by scholars to show that the Church historically permitted local diversity in worship.</note> *It should suffice for everyone in the Church for the peace of their conscience if all the faithful of Christ are endowed with one spirit; that is, if they agree in doctrine and faith. For he who does not have the Spirit of Christ, as the Apostle says, is not His, whatever rites, ceremonies, or traditions he may observe. Therefore, those who belong to Christ as members of one body ought to cherish, help, and bear with one another through charity, without which, as Paul says, nothing can be accomplished that will result in anyone’s salvation.*

<column-break/>

...to abstain from what is strangled, from blood, and from that which has been offered to idols. This command eventually ceased as soon as those things were removed that had been the cause of its establishment.

Finally, they draw from all this the following teaching: that one may not be offended by another, much less that they should despise, hate, or persecute each other because of any difference in ceremonies, customs, or practices, which are commonly found among Christians in various Churches, especially since they do not clash with godliness or are in any way harmful to it. Much less should any riot or schism be caused because of them, through which one would distance and separate oneself from the unity of the Church, since the exact same ceremonies have never been in all Churches, nor can they be at present. Thus we read in the Decrees, or the Ordinances of the Holy Church Fathers, that they clearly prove the same (Distinction 12, Chapter *Scit*): *the Roman Church,* it says, *knows very well that Church practices, differing according to time and place, can in no way harm the salvation of the faithful, as long as they are not specifically determined by the authority of the Canons.* <note>Original: "Regel-schriften" (Rule-writings), referring to official Church law.</note> This must then be enough in the Church for the peace of everyone's mind: that all believers are gifted with the same Spirit of Christ, that is, that they agree with one another in complete harmony regarding doctrine and faith (for whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, says the Apostle somewhere, does not belong to Him), no matter how much they may differ from one another regarding that other matter <note>i.e., external traditions and rituals</note>. In such a way, those who belong to our Savior must cherish, help, and bear with one another as members of one body out of love, without which, according to the words of St. Paul, nothing can be worked out for salvation.

### XVI. CHAPTER.

->Of the Secular Power.<-

It is taught here that we, according to the Scriptures, believe that the higher power, or secular Magistracy, is an ordinance of God, so that in those things which are political and temporary, the people may be governed. Concerning this, there is an illustrious passage from the Apostle Paul: *for there is no power, except from God; but those powers which exist, are ordained by God.* <note>original: "non enim est potestas, nisi a Deo; quæ vero sunt potestates, a Deo ordinatæ sunt." This is a citation of Romans 13:1, a cornerstone of Christian political theology regarding obedience to the state.</note>

They teach, in addition to this, that those who are in power and perform a public office or magistracy—whatever rank they may hold—should know that they perform not their own work, but the work of God. They should remember that He is their Lord and the supreme King of all others, to whom they must also render an account of their stewardship on the final day. This sentiment is discussed at length in the writings of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy; his works were often cited by early modern Christians to discuss the virtues of a just ruler.</note>, as well as by others elsewhere. They warn that the Magistrates should frequently recall the words of the Psalmist in this place: *And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in Him with trembling. Embrace discipline (or kiss the son, namely Christ, the King of all and supreme judge, with affection) lest the Lord at any time be angry and you perish from the way, when His wrath shall be kindled in a short time. Blessed are all they who trust in Him.* <note>This is a translation of Psalm 2:10-12. The text provides a Christological interpretation, identifying the "Son" whom the kings must "kiss" or honor as Jesus Christ.</note>

Furthermore, they teach that those who hold the Magistracy ought to be beneficent to men, as the Lord Himself says: *those who have power over others are called benefactors.* <note>A reference to Luke 22:25.</note> Moreover, the parts and duty of the Magistrates are to administer justice to all equally for the common use of everyone without respect of persons, to protect and procure public peace and tranquility, and to [act] concerning the wicked and the criminal,

<column-break/>

Here it is taught by our people according to the Scripture, that the higher Power or the secular Authority is an institution of God, so that the people in temporal and state-related matters may be governed righteously as is proper. Regarding this, we have an excellent passage from the Apostle Paul: *there is no power, but it comes from God, and the powers that be, are ordained by God.*

Additionally, they teach that all those who are provided with any power or high offices, or otherwise sit in the Council, at whatever level of dignity they might have climbed, must surely know that they perform not their own, but God's work, as He alone is a Lord and supreme King over them and all others; and that they consequently may freely consider that they shall one day have to give an account of all their conduct to Him on the last day. This view is found at length even in Philo and others besides, who at the same time admonish such persons that they should often call to mind the passage of the Royal Singer in Israel: <note>The "Royal Singer" is a traditional epithet for King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> *now then, you Kings, act wisely, let yourselves be disciplined, you Judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear and rejoice with trembling. Receive the discipline and instruction (or) kiss the Son, namely the Lord Christ, the King and supreme Judge of all, with uncommon affection and love) so that the Lord does not become angry and you perish on the way, when His wrath would burn but a little. Quite happy are all those who trust in Him.*

They also teach that those who hold the office of High Authority must be well-doing toward all men, just as is clearly commanded by the Lord: *those who have power over others must be beneficent.* And herein lies primarily their whole duty: that they do justice to everyone according to the requirements of the case, to work out and preserve the common rest and peace for the benefit of all and each person without regarding anyone’s status, [and to punish] the wicked and criminals, who the same [peace]...

<summary>This page outlines the Waldensian doctrine on secular government, asserting that civil authorities are ordained by God to maintain justice and peace. It emphasizes that rulers are "stewards" of God's power and will be held accountable at the Last Judgment for how they treat their subjects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter XVI, "Of the Secular Power." The text is presented in two parallel columns: the left column in Latin and the right column in Dutch. ->General Memorial-writing<-

*...of peace, to punish those who disturb it, and to protect all others from their violence and injustice. For it is certain that Magistrates serve God and perform His work, as they are even called "gods" <note>original Latin: "Dii vocentur." This refers to Psalm 82:6, where judges are called "gods" because they represent divine justice on earth.</note>; therefore, they must be allowed to carry out His will. For Paul also calls Magistrates the ministers of God, established for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.*

*They also teach that the Word of God commands all to be subject to the higher powers in everything, yet only in those matters that do not oppose God and His Word; first to Your Royal Majesty, and then to all others established in high office and the Magistracy, whether they be good men or unworthy and evil. They teach that all should honor and revere them in their respective jurisdictions and elsewhere, according to their rank and office, paying them everything that is due, such as taxes and tributes, as each person is required.*

*Regarding matters of the soul, faith, and salvation, they teach that one should listen only to the Word of God and His ministers, as Christ Himself said: "Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s."*

*However, if anyone should try to force them into things that conflict with and resist God and His Word (which endures forever), they teach that the example of the Apostles should be followed, who answered the authorities in Jerusalem: "It is necessary to obey God rather than men."*

*On this point, the decrees of the Church Fathers also exist, as found in Distinction 11, Question 3, Chapter "Si Dominus": "If a lord commands those things which are not contrary or adverse—"*

<column-break/>

...now and then disturb [the peace], to keep them in check with righteous punishments and thus seek to protect all others from their violence and injustices. For it is undoubtedly true that the Magistracy thus serves God and thereby performs His work, because they are even called *gods* and must therefore primarily ensure that they follow His will precisely in all things. Indeed, Saint Paul honors them with the title *servant of God* and says that they are appointed for the *praise of the good* and as an *avenger to punish those who do evil.*

In addition, they hold it to be prescribed in God’s commandments that all people must be subject to the Powers set over them (provided, however, that they never act against God or His Word because of it). Our people owe this first to Your Royal Majesty, and then to all others who are placed in any Authority or Council <term>Vroetschap: a council of "wise men" who governed Dutch cities</term>, whether they be good or bad. They must meet and serve them in their respective places and territories—or even outside of them—with proper honor according to their dignity and office, fulfilling all duties and willingly providing and paying all tolls and taxes that they owe.

They further add that regarding matters touching the soul, faith, and salvation, one must obey only God's Word and His Ministers, as our Savior Himself said: *Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.*

Finally, they teach that whenever someone would try to force them by violence to commit deeds that completely conflict with God and His eternal-abiding Word, they must then conduct themselves after the example of the Apostles, who gave this answer to the Council <note>original: "Kerkelijken Raat," literally "Ecclesiastical Council," referring to the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.</note> in Jerusalem in a similar circumstance: *We must obey God more than men.*

On this we also have the commandments of the Holy Early Fathers, which in Distinction 11, Question 3, Chapter *Si Dominus* <note>A reference to the "Decretum Gratiani," a standard collection of canon law. The chapter "Si Dominus" discusses the limits of obedience to secular lords when their commands conflict with higher spiritual laws.</note> read as follows: *if the lord commands such things as are not contrary*...

### XVII. C H A P T E R
->Of the Invocation of the Saints.<-

In the beginning they teach, *that since the creation of mankind there has never been anyone, nor is there now, nor shall there ever be, who by his own strength, merits, efforts, and works is holy or righteous, as Moses writes: no one is innocent before you of themselves. <note>Original Latin: "nullus apud te per se innocens est."</note> And blessed Job: what is man, that he should be stainless and appear righteous, born of a woman? Behold, among his Saints none is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight; how much more useless is man, who drinks iniquity like water? And by the Scriptures we are convinced that one and all, we are sinners by nature and from our very first origin, Psalm 13: All have turned aside, they have together become useless, etc. Whatever good there is in the Saints must be credited to the bounty and grace of God. For that the Saints are pleasing to God happens to them without any merit, solely by the lot of the divine will. For God, out of pure and unspeakable grace and the riches of his goodness, has from eternity chosen those whom he willed to enjoy glory with Christ, who have redemption, righteousness, and the remission of sins and a merciful God through the blood of Christ: by whose grace they were adopted as sons of God through faith, made Holy, cleansed from every stain, by good works and virtues as...*

<column-break/>

Here they teach first, that after the creation of the world no one has ever been found, nor is, or ever shall be, who through his own powers, merits, occupations, or works can be holy or righteous, since the Holy Moses writes somewhere: *no one is innocent before you by themselves.* The Holy Job has these words about it: *what is man, that he should be spotless, and he who is born of women, that he should consider himself righteous? Behold, there is no one among his holy ones without change, and even the heavens are not pure in his eyes, and what then would a useless man be, who drinks iniquity like water?* Indeed, we are convinced by the whole of Scripture that by nature and as we come into the world, every single one of us is a sinner: it is written, in the 13th Psalm, *or Church-song, <note>The Dutch "Kerk-sang" refers to the practice of singing the Psalms in communal worship, a hallmark of the Waldensian and later Reformed traditions.</note> they have all alike turned away, they have together become useless, etc.* In such a way that all the good that accompanies the saints must be attributed to God's generosity and grace. For even that they are holy and pleasing to God comes only through the will and providence of God, apart from all their merits. Namely, God has out of pure and unspeakable grace, through the sheer riches of his goodness, chosen those whom he willed from all eternity, so that they should enjoy the glory of Christ, after they should have had a share in redemption, justification, and forgiveness of sins through his blood, and consequently also in God as their reconciled Father. They become children of God through the accepted faith by his will alone, made holy, purified...

# General Memorial
<meta>catchword: com-</meta>

*...endowed as children of light, sealed by the Spirit of God; and who, after they have held the faith—the hinge of salvation <note>Original Latin: "salutis cardinem." The author uses this metaphor to describe faith as the essential point upon which the door to salvation turns.</note>—firmly until the very end of life, were finally received into heaven, where God crowns his own gifts in them.* <note>The phrase "God crowns his own gifts" is a classic theological expression, likely referencing Saint Augustine, meaning that when God rewards a Saint's merit, He is actually honoring the grace He gave them in the first place.</note>

*They also teach that certain Saints were gifted by God—who divides all things among all as he sees will be better for the future—with special graces, gifts, and virtues for the common progress of the whole Church above others. Ephesians 4: He gave some to be Apostles, some Prophets, others Evangelists, others Pastors and Teachers, for the restoration of the Saints, for the work of administration, for the building up of the body of Christ, which is the Church. The memory of these, and their works and fruits, remains in the Scriptures and the Church to this day.*

*Separately, they teach that it is necessary to believe and confess concerning the most blessed Virgin, mother of the Lord, as the Scriptures hold, that she was born of royal lineage from the house and family of David, chosen by God before the ages, blessed among women (as the Angel said to her), full of grace and the Spirit of God, and sanctified by Him to become the mother of the Savior; who, though he is the Son of God, nevertheless took on our flesh in her womb. This Virgin was a virgin before birth and a virgin after birth, and she called herself the handmaid of the Lord. Nevertheless, she was redeemed no less than the others by the blood and free merit of her Son, and made an heir of eternal blessedness, becoming a temple or dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, endowed with his distinguished gifts, virtues, and graces. For God did great things for her above all others; and therefore our Churches honorably celebrate her feast days to the praise and glory of God. Pious cautions also concerning her...*

<column-break/>

...[delivered] far from all contamination, endowed with good works and virtues as children of light, sealed by the Spirit of God; and after they have held the faith—that anchor of salvation—firmly until the end, they were finally taken up into Heaven, where the Lord then wishes to crown his own gifts in them.

They teach thereby, that various Saints from the Lord our God—who alone can distribute everything to everyone—are favored above others with special abilities, gifts, and virtues for the common benefit of the Church, just as he himself saw that it would be most advantageous: **Ephesians 4.** *and the same has given some as Apostles, and some as Prophets, and some as Evangelists, and some as Shepherds and Teachers, for the perfecting of the Saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, which is the congregation.* And truly, just as the memory of these remains perpetually fresh in the Holy Pages, so do their works and service remain in the Church to this very day.

But in particular they teach regarding the Holy Mother-Virgin of our Savior, that one must believe and confess according to the Scriptures that she is of royal stock, sprouted from the house and lineage of David, chosen by God before all ages, blessed among women according to the saying of the Angel, full of grace and God's Spirit, and by the same sanctified to be the mother of our Savior; who, being the Son of God, took on our flesh in her chaste body. And just as she was a virgin before her bearing, so has she remained so thereafter, and called herself a handmaid of the Lord. She is also, just like all others, redeemed through the blood and gracious merits of her Son, made an heir of eternal salvation, established as a house of God or dwelling of the Holy Spirit, and provided with his excellent and rich gifts, virtues, and graces. And while God has done very great things for her above all other people, our Churches very solemnly keep her feast days to God's praise and honor. They also compose concerning her...

## Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches
<meta>catchword: -rantes / the</meta>

...compose and sing these [songs] both privately and indeed publicly in the churches; in them they praise God and exhort everyone to the imitation of her faith, her other virtues, and her life and works. They also piously commemorate the labors she underwent for the sake of the Lord. Furthermore, they strive to emulate her as an exemplar of the most excellent life with all their might, and are by no means unmindful of her words: for they, together with the whole Church, proclaim her <note>Original Latin: "ebuccinant," literally meaning to "trumpet forth," implying a loud and joyful public declaration.</note> most blessed. Nor in these matters, as can be seen, is there any departure from the Scriptures.

Furthermore, they teach that the honor and worship due to God must not be transferred to the Saints, nor to their images, as is written in Isaiah: *Therefore, the Lord is my name; I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved images.* <note>Isaiah 42:8.</note> However, they teach that the Saints are to be honored in this manner: that at fixed and prescribed feasts and times, everyone gathering together to hear the Word of God and perform worship to God should celebrate their memory. They should commemorate the benefits and gifts which God conferred upon them and, through them, upon the Church. They should remember their faith, life, and conduct <note>Original Latin: "conversationis," referring to their manner of living or social dealings.</note> so that they may be moved to imitate them, in order that they may bear fruit in every good work through the Word of God. Additionally, by recollecting these things about the Saints, they give glory to God with praise and thanksgiving for such great gifts which He, out of His inexhaustible goodness, poured out upon them. They sing pious songs about them and exhort one another to live according to their example and pray to God that they might be made partakers with them in this life and the life to come. Nor in all these things is there any deviation from the Scriptures, as in Hebrews 13: *Remember those who rule over you, who have spoken the word of God to you; whose faith imitate, considering...*

<column-break/>

...very godly songs to be sung either privately by themselves or publicly in the Church, by which they praise the Lord on her behalf, properly exhorting all people to follow her faith, other virtues, life, and works, and finally piously counting and remembering all the difficulties she ever endured for her Lord. Lastly, they strive to follow her with all their strength as an example of a holy life, always keeping her words in mind; since they, with the entire congregation of the Saints, come to proclaim her most blessed. In all this, however, they do not deviate from the Scripture, as can be verified by everyone.

Furthermore, they teach that one may not show the service and honor, which belongs to God alone, to the Saints or their images, as it stands written by the Prophet Isaiah: *I the Lord (for that is my name) shall not give my honor to another, nor my praise to carved images:* <note>The Waldensians were known for their "proto-Protestant" views, which included a rejection of religious statuary and the belief that only God should receive "latria" (divine worship).</note> but that one can indeed honor the Saints in such a way that, meeting together at certain and set times and days to hear God's Word and perform His service, they simultaneously renew their memory, recount the manifold gifts and benefits He wished to show to them and through them to the Church, and finally tell of their faith, life, and conduct; so that all people might thereby be moved to imitation of the same and subsequently become fruitful in all good works through the Word of God. As also that, well-considering the things of the Saints, they might show honor to God with praise and thanksgiving for such great gifts which He, according to His inexhaustible goodness, poured out over them, singing spiritual songs of them, encouraging one another to a similar life, and subsequently praying to God that they might become their fellow-partakers both in this life and in the life to come. In all of which the Holy Scripture is also not opposed, since Hebrews 13 says: *remember your leaders, who [have spoken] to you the...* <note>Hebrews 13:7. The sentence cuts off at the end of the page.</note>

# General Memorial

<column-break/>

...considering the outcome of their way of life. <note>original Latin: "qui fuerint exitus conversationis illorum." This completes the citation of Hebrews 13:7 from the previous page.</note>

*Likewise, so that it may be known and believed, they teach that this should be understood not only of those Saints who lived in previous centuries before us and, having been released from these miseries, were received into the blessed life; but also of those who are now in the world. For all who believe in Christ, wherever in the world they may be, are saints; and all these, having been washed in the bath of regeneration <note>baptism</note>, are numbered among the children and heirs of God. Having been granted faith in Christ freely, justified, and burning with love toward all, they are cleansed from sins through faith and the ministry of the Church. They share in the body and blood of Christ, and they strive with all their might to perform the good works for which they were created, that they might walk in them. Indeed, Holy Scripture calls all these people "Saints" while they are still living here and clothed in mortal flesh, as seen in 1 Peter 2: "You are a chosen race and a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people acquired for a prize." <note>original: "vos estis genus electum & regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus, qui in lucrum accessit."</note> Likewise, Paul says in 2 Corinthians 13: "All the Saints greet you"; and elsewhere: "Greet all who are over you, and all the Saints," that is, the faithful, or Christians. For this reason they teach that, although we ought to embrace all Christians—even the bad ones—with charity and offer them a helping hand, especially in times of need; we must be of service most of all to those who have died <note>or "remain"</note> in the same doctrine and faith as us, and who express it through their deeds, in whatever matters we can. And since they follow Christian truth and doctrine, they are to be held in holy and brotherly society, and we should always think well of them, and honor them—as those from whom we may rightfully require, by the law of piety, that they pray for us—for the sake of Christ and Christian charity.*

<column-break/>

*...have spoken the Word of God, and follow their faith, beholding the outcome of their way of life.* <note>This column provides the Dutch translation of the Latin text on the left.</note>

They likewise teach that all that has been said must be known and believed not only of such Saints who lived in previous ages before us and, being delivered from these adversities, have been taken up into the blessed life, but also even of those who still live on the earth. For all those who believe in Christ are holy, wherever they may reside: since all such people have been washed through the bath of rebirth <term>regeneration: the spiritual renewal of a person through baptism</term>, accepted as heirs among the children of God, gifted freely with faith in the Lord Jesus and His righteousness, and being kindled with love toward all, are purified of all sins through faith and the service of the Church. Not to mention that they partake in the body and blood of our Savior and consequently exert all their strength to perform good works, for which they were created to walk therein. It is enough that Holy Scripture expressly gives the name of "Saints" to all such believers, even while they still live here on earth and are clothed with mortal flesh, as can be seen in 1 Peter 2: *You are,* it says, *a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people that is happily obtained for a prize.* So also the Apostle Paul calls them in his last [letter] to the Corinthians in the 13th chapter: *All the Saints greet you,* he says: and elsewhere; *greet those who are placed over you and also all the Saints,* that is, all Christians or believers. And for this reason they also teach that, although one is obligated above all people to love all Christians, even the evil ones, and so everywhere, but especially in times of need, to offer a helping hand; one must nevertheless be of service in a special way in everything possible to those who share the same doctrine and faith with us and openly show the same through their works; that one must take the same into company as brothers in a holy manner, insofar as they adhere to Christian doctrine and dignity, and always have a good opinion of them—

<summary>This page defines the Waldensian view of "Saints," arguing that the term applies to all living believers who are baptized and faithful, not just the deceased or canonized. It emphasizes that while charity is owed to all, special honor and fellowship are reserved for those who actively practice the faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Waldensian view on "Saints," transitioning from the duty to honor living believers to the proper conduct toward those who live immorally or err in doctrine. It then begins a new chapter on the practice of fasting.</meta>

**Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.**

...teach that they <note>Referring to fellow believers or "living saints."</note> should be treated with honor, and that their interests and affairs should be looked after; furthermore, they frequently exhort everyone to commend themselves to their prayers. <note>original Latin: "culum afficiendos, eorumque commodis & rebus consulendum docent; nec non, ut se quisque illorum precibus commendent, sæpius hortantur."</note>

*Moreover, regarding those who profess the name of Christ but live wickedly and impiously, or who realize they are wandering because they are entangled in false doctrine, they teach that as much as lies in each person, they should be corrected humanely and endured through charity; and that God must be prayed to, that He might recall them to the way of salvation, so that the Gospel of the glory of Christ may be adorned in all things.* <note>original Latin: "Istos autem, qui Christi nomen profitentur, verum nequiter ac impie vivunt..."</note>

[They should be honored] for Christ’s sake and because of the bond of Christian love (for we may, by virtue of godliness, request of them that they pray for us), showing them all honor and finally seeking their benefit and advantage in all things.

Lastly, this is their teaching: that those who indeed profess the name of Christ, but at the same time live very offensively and godlessly, or who are entangled in a wrong doctrine and acknowledge to some extent that they err, must be rebuked with politeness and corrected, and to some extent suffered and endured with love; yes, that one must pray to the Lord our God that He might bring them back to the way of salvation, so that the Gospel of the glory of our only Savior <term>Heiland</term><note>A traditional Dutch term for Savior, emphasizing the "healing" or "making whole" aspect of salvation.</note> may be glorified in all things.

### XVIII. CHAPTER

->On Fasting.<-

<column-break/>

*Our people teach that fasts are a certain external form of worship among the godly, to be offered to God alone, and that these may be observed by all and everyone according to the circumstances of persons, nations, places, and matters, even without superstition and hypocrisy. Nor are Scriptural passages lacking for this article; but from many, let these suffice: 2 Corinthians 6: "let us commend ourselves as ministers of God etc. in fasts." And Christ the Lord; "then," He says, "they shall fast." Again in another place, Paul: "so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer."* <note>original Latin: "Jejunia nostri cultum quendam externum in piis esse..."</note>

Here our people teach that Fasting among the godly is an external form of worship, which must be offered to God alone, and that it may be practiced by all and everyone according to the circumstances of the people, nations, places, and matters, without superstition and hypocrisy. This proposition is also not without a basis in Scriptural verses. Out of many, these present ones may be sufficient. 2 Corinthians 6: *but we, as servants of God, make ourselves acceptable in all things — in fastings, etc.* The Lord Jesus himself uses these words in a certain place: *then*, he says, *they shall fast.* Again, the Holy Paul in another place: *so that you may have time for fasting and prayer.*

*They teach further that fasting does not consist in the distinction of foods, but in the sparing consumption of them, in sobriety and temperance, and in the affliction and humiliation of one’s body before God. It matters, however, in total, with what spirit or will one fasts. That a fast is salutary, pleasing, and acceptable to God, is taught in Matthew chapter 6 and Isaiah 58.* <note>original Latin: "Docent deinde, non esse jejunium in discrimine ciborum..."</note>

In addition, they also hold that Fasting does not consist in the distinction of foods <note>The practice of eating fish instead of meat on certain days.</note>, but only in the small enjoyment of them, in sobriety and temperance, and in the paining and humbling of one's body before God. All of which, however, depends only on the will and the spirit with which one begins his fasting. Meanwhile, that Fasting is salutary and dear and pleasing to God, can be clearly gathered from what is written in Matthew 6 and Isaiah 58.

# General Memorial-Script
## XX. CHAPTER-

*...burning <note>original Latin: "ustione," a reference to 1 Corinthians 7:9, "it is better to marry than to burn."</note>, that is, if it should happen to him in Celibacy that he burns in such a way that he can neither tame nor restrain the burning by any counsel, teaching, chastisement, or warning. For just as he who has bound himself to marriage <term>matrimonio: the state of being wed</term> is no longer his own master as before; so also he who has devoted himself to Christ and His Church in ministry <term>ministerium: religious service</term> ought to prefer this ministry to all kinds of pleasures, for the sake of which he is bound to deny all things, even his own life. This chastity of life <term>castimonia: moral purity</term> and abstinence from pleasures has certain promises for this and the future life, Mark 10. Again: those who do not fight against the desires and affects of the flesh so as to seek to conquer them, these reject the gift bestowed on them by God, lose the Holy Spirit <term>Spiritum Sanctum</term>, and are a stumbling block to the Church, which they weaken and tear apart by their inconstancy.*

---

*Furthermore, they teach that the gifts of grace must be diligently preserved by all and with the greatest zeal. Thus they impose an intolerable yoke on no one that would cause an offense of conscience; but because everything in the Church ought to be done in good order and, as Paul says, according to a good arrangement. They judge it to be in the interest of the Church and helpful to the public utility that he who cannot remain continent should bring the matter to those presiding over the Church, and use their authority and counsel. For it is fitting for a minister of the Church to do all things by the authority of the Church and the Brothers, so that he may be a good example to others. And less sin is committed if you use the counsel of those who have the Spirit of Christ.*

<column-break/>

...became entirely on fire; <note>original Dutch: "geheelik aan 't branden raakte," referring to intense desire</note> that is, unless it should happen that this fire in time became so powerful that it could be dampened or kept within by no counsel, nor teaching, nor punishment, nor warning. For just as the one who has placed himself into marriage <term>houwelik: marriage</term> as into a slavery is no longer his own master, as before; so must he also, who has given himself to the service of our Savior and His Church, place the same above all types of pleasures, as he is obligated for the sake of that service to deny all things, even his own life. And this chastity <term>kuyſheyt: sexual purity</term> of life, this abstaining from all pleasures, therefore also has its promises for this and the next life, Mark 10. But at the same time we also read elsewhere: *those who do not fight against the desires and other urges of the flesh to subsequently be able to overcome them, reject the gift given to them by God, lose the Holy Spirit and serve as a great offense to the Church, which they weaken and tear through their inconstancy.*

Finally, they end with this Doctrine: that, just as one must diligently observe the gifts of grace <term>genade: divine favor</term> with all industry, one also may not impose any intolerable yoke with offense to the conscience on anyone. However, since everything must happen with good order and, as St. Paul <term>H. Paulus</term> speaks somewhere, due to the well-ordered state of the Church, they judge it to be very useful for the Church and serving the common peace that the one who can no longer restrain himself should bring the matter before the Heads of the Congregation to act according to their command and counsel. For it befits a minister of the Church, in order to give others a good example, that he do all things according to the approval of the Congregation. One also does not err so easily when one uses the counsel of those who are driven by the Spirit of Christ <term>Geeſt Chriſti</term>.

<summary>This page outlines the Waldensian view that while ministers should strive for celibacy to serve the church, those overwhelmed by passion should seek the counsel of church leaders to marry, maintaining order rather than causing scandal through inconstancy.</summary>

Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

### XX. CHAPTER.

->Of the Time of Grace, in which Divine favor must be sought and can be found.<-

Finally, in this place they teach *that men should know that, for as long as they are among the living, a time is granted to them by God, which is of grace, so that they may seek Him, and His grace, goodness, mercy, and gentleness, and thus by His promise find them and so attain blessed salvation.* Concerning this, Paul preaches in the *Acts*: *God preordains established times, and has fixed the boundaries of the habitation of men, that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel after Him and find Him.* <note>Acts 17:26-27</note> And the Lord says through the Prophet: *in an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time, behold, now is the day of salvation!* <note>Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2</note> Our people <note>The "our people" refers to the Waldensian authorities or authors of this confession.</note> diligently warn of the same, *that no one should abuse this time of grace; but that in the meantime, while one is in prosperous health, and while it is permitted through this time of grace, one should do penance for a previous life, be reconciled to God, and make one's Conscience peaceful, tranquil, and secure through faith in Christ and through His administration in the Church.* <term>administration: the local governing and spiritual guidance of the church community</term> *Hence, firmly believing that sins are forgiven and God is propitious <note>propitious: favorably inclined or merciful</note> because of Christ, in whose grace one is strengthened, and walking and progressing in good works, one ought certainly to expect that the soul, released from bodily bonds, will pass not into any punishment, but will be carried by the Angels into eternal goods like that Lazarus, and there remain forever with Christ the Lord, with whom is present whatever good there is and can be desired. Nor indeed will one fear the judgment of death on the last day; for one will be snatched up into heavenly life.* To this Paul wants us to strive, writing to the *Hebrews*; *exhort one another...*

<column-break/>

Finally they teach also at this place, that all men must know that, as long as they still live in the world, the time of grace is granted to them by God, so that they may seek and find him, his favor, goodness, mercy, and gentleness, and finally thus obtain salvation. About which Saint Paul also teaches thus in the Acts of the Apostles: *God has determined a set time and placed certain boundaries on the habitation of men, so that they should seek God, if they might perhaps touch and find him.* The Lord himself says somewhere through his Prophet: *at an acceptable time I have heard you and on the day of salvation I have offered my help. See, now is the acceptable time, see, now is the day of salvation!* Therefore our people also diligently exhort that they should by no means abuse this time of grace, but on the contrary, while their health still allows it and before the time has passed, show repentance <note>original Dutch: "berou," referring to the internal change of heart</note> for their previous life, reconcile themselves with God, and through faith in Christ and through his instruction in the Church, set their minds at peace, at rest, and beyond fear. In such a way that all those who firmly believe that all their sins are forgiven for Christ’s sake and that God becomes entirely merciful to them, being confirmed in this fine grace and walking and increasing in good works, must believe and wait without any doubt that their souls, released from bodily bonds, shall not pass over to any punishment: but as in former times that Lazarus <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 16:22, where the beggar Lazarus is carried by angels to heaven.</note> was carried over by the Holy Angels to eternal good, to remain there always with the Lord Jesus, with whom alone all good is to be found that can be thought of or desired by anyone. So that they do not even need to fear the sentence of death in the last hour, because they are snatched away to the heavenly life, for which the Apostle wants us to yearn fervently, as he writes this to the Hebrews: *exhort one another daily...*

<vocab>time of grace, Paul, Lazarus, Christ, repentance, salvation</vocab>

<summary>This page outlines the Waldensian doctrine of the "Time of Grace," emphasizing that the earthly life is the unique window for seeking God's mercy and reconciliation through the Church. It reassures believers that those who live in faith and good works will be carried to heaven by angels upon death, much like Lazarus in the biblical parable.</summary>
