# General Memorial-Script.
## Page 194

<meta>catchword: pec- (from the Latin 'peccatis' or 'peccatores')</meta>

...each other daily, as long as it is called "today," <note>original Latin: "vicem quotidie, quoad appellatur dies hodiernus"; Dutch: "malkanderen, ſoo lang het nog heden genaamt kan worden." This refers to Hebrews 3:13, urging believers to support one another while the opportunity for salvation remains.</note> lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we who have believed—that is, those of us who have listened to the voice of God in time—shall enter into the true rest.

They teach moreover, *that it ought to be most certain to everyone that, if he should depart in his sins without repentance and faith in the Gospel, his soul is made liable to eternal judgment after death, just like that of the impious Rich Man, <note>A reference to the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16); the Dutch uses the word "Vrek," meaning a miser or glutton.</note> for whom no grace remained. Those who thus depart this life unrepentant will hear with their own ears the horrible voice of God on the final day of the conclusion of all things: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which was prepared long ago for the Devil and his angels." This is also confirmed in the Gospel of John in the 5th chapter: "and those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of condemnation."*

They warn further, *that no one should delay their conversion to the Lord, the praying for forgiveness of their committed crimes, or the showing of repentance for them until old age or some illness; and in the meantime, sleeping quite securely on both ears <note>An idiom meaning to be completely unconcerned or complacent.</note> while indulging in the allurements of the flesh and the world and following one's own will in everything. For it is written: "do not heap one sin upon another, nor ever say: the mercy of the Lord is great, He will have mercy on the multitude of my sins. For His wrath approaches just as quickly as His compassion, and His indignation looks upon sinners. Do not be slow in converting to Him, nor put it off from day to day. For suddenly His wrath shall come, and in the time of His vengeance He will destroy you." <note>This quote is from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 5:5-9, a book of ethical teachings.</note> But above all, it is particularly dangerous for him who has already received a testimony of divine favor toward himself, and yet willfully and knowingly plunges himself into sins, and not only despises and tramples underfoot so many wholesome warnings to return to repentance in time, but who even foolishly and insolently abuses God's mercy—*

<column-break/>

*...each other, as long as it can still be called "today." That also no one among you should harden himself through the temptation of sin; for we all, who have believed—that is, who will have heard God’s voice in time—shall enter into the true rest.*

Furthermore, they also teach that everyone must be certain that, if he happens to die in his sins without repentance and faith in the Gospel, his soul—like that of the godless Glutton, who had no more mercy to expect—is immediately after death condemned to the eternal judgment. Those who so unrepentantly depart from the world shall on the last day of the conclusion of all things hear this terrible voice with their ears: *“Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which has long been prepared for the Devil and his angels.”* Which is also confirmed in the Gospel of John in the 5th chapter: *“and those who shall have done evil, shall reach the resurrection of damnation.”*

They admonish besides, that no one should put off his conversion to the Lord, the praying away of his committed misdeeds, or the showing of repentance for the same until his exhausted old age or some sickness, and in the meantime, quite carelessly with hands in lap, follow the enticements of the flesh and of the world and give obedience to his own will in everything. For there it is written: *“and do not heap one sin upon the other, nor ever say: the mercy of the Lord is big, He shall have mercy over the multitude of my sins. For His wrath approaches just as quickly as His compassion, and His indignation has the eye on the sinners. Be then not slow in converting yourself to Him, nor put it off from one day to the other. For His wrath shall come suddenly and in the time of His vengeance He shall destroy you.”* But above all, it is particularly dangerous for the one who has already received a testimony of divine grace towards him and yet willfully and knowingly plunges himself into sins; yes, who not only despises and tramples underfoot so many wholesome warnings to turn to conversion in time, but who even abuses God's mercy—

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches
## Page 195

<meta>catchword: These</meta>

*...if one has persisted in sins until the very last and now imminent moment of death, and only then first awakens, and out of horror and fear of impending death and hell begins to be wise too late: it is dangerous, lest he experience the fury of the Lord (as His words clearly testify) in his ultimate misfortune rather than His mercy; the Lord says in Micah 3 <note>Micah 3:4</note>: "they shall cry to me and I will not hear them, and I will hide my face from them at that time, just as they have acted wickedly in their pursuits"; since they would not hear my voice when I stretched out my hands all day long. It is indeed to be feared that he might receive the rewards worthy of his deeds, who so idly and ruinously used the time which God had granted him for repentance.*

---

*Nevertheless, they teach that no one should despair. For if even in the extreme danger of death a sign of true repentance appears—which, however, happens very rarely to such people (for Paul rightly says: "this," he says, "we will do, if God permits")—he is not sent away without the consolation of absolution <note>original Latin: "abſolutionis"; the formal declaration of forgiveness</note>. For the time of grace lasts as long as this life lasts. Let them remember this, which Paul says with the Prophet: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation on the day of temptation in the wilderness," etc. Admonished by these things, everyone should rest in time; even before the sun darkens and the mountains are covered with darkness, they should repent and, having left behind their old ways, return to God, and do everything so that they do not fall from glory; our people exhort this with the greatest zeal and care.*

<column-break/>

...foolishly and willfully misusing [God's] patience <note>original Dutch: "tigheyt," completing "langmoedigheit" from the previous page</note> and, based upon it, persisting in sins until the last and imminent moment of death; who then hardly begins to awaken and, out of terror and fear of the present death and hell, comes too late to reflection: whether such a person, instead of God's grace, shall not experience His wrath to their ultimate ruin, since these His own words clearly seem to say: *they shall call to me*, says the Lord himself by the Prophet Micah in the 3rd chapter, *and I shall not hear them; but I shall hide my face from them in that time, just as they have acted wickedly with intent, when they would not hear my voice, when I stretched out my hands to them the whole day.* Truly, it is somewhat to be feared that he shall receive the earned reward for his works, having so lazily and shamefully neglected the time granted to him by God for his conversion.

They teach this, however, in conclusion: that no one must fall into despair. For if even in the last danger of death a sign of true repentance <note>original Dutch: "boetvaardigheyt"</note> is seen—which, nonetheless, happens very seldom to such people; for according to the words of the Holy Apostle <term>Paul</term> *we can only do that if God shall will to permit it*—then they are not left without the comfort of absolution <note>original Dutch: "vryſpreking," literally "speaking free" or acquittal</note>. Namely, that time of grace lasts exactly as long as life itself. Meanwhile, everyone must always be mindful of what the Holy Paul says with the Prophet: *if you have heard his voice today, do not harden your hearts, as they were rebellious in the day of temptation in the wilderness*, etc. Wherefore our people also urge with all diligence and industriousness, that everyone, keeping themselves always admonished by all these things and giving faith to the same in time, before the sun be darkened and the mountains covered with a darkness, would show repentance and, after leaving the <term>Old Man</term> <note>original Dutch: "ouden mens"; a biblical term for the sinful nature or former way of life</note> might return to God and arrange everything in such a way that they may not miss out on eternal glory.

# General Memorial-Record
## Page 196

<meta>catchword: These</meta>

This [confession] has also earned this testimony, drawn from the Preface by Martin Luther, which he wrote in praise of the said Waldensians and their doctrine in the year 1535, placed before the same [confession]; which is contained in his own words as follows:

<margin>Testimony from Luther given regarding the orthodoxy of the Waldensians.</margin>
*Among these, however, there also occurred those Brothers whom they called Pighards <note>original Latin: "Pighardos"; a term often applied to the Bohemian Brethren, whom Luther here associates with the Waldensians</note>, who are no longer as hateful to me as they previously were during my time in the Papacy. Finally, I discovered in them that one and great miracle, almost unheard of in the Church of the Pope: namely, that having set aside the doctrines of men as much as they could, they meditated on the Law of the Lord day and night; and that they were skilled and ready in the Scriptures, whereas in the Papacy our Masters themselves entirely neglected the Scriptures—though they boast of that title—while some among them had never even seen the Holy Bible.* <note>original Latin: "Inter hos autem occurrebant & isti Fratres, quos Pighardos vocabant... nonnulli vero ex ipsis ne vidissent quidem Biblia Sacra unquam."</note> That is: among all these there also appeared to me those Brothers, whom people commonly call Picards, whom I no longer hate as I once did in my Papist days. At long last, I found in them that unique and exceedingly great wonder, almost unheard of in the Church of the Pope: namely, that having given the boot to human teachings, they contemplate the *Law* of the Lord day and night to the best of their ability, and are skilled and ready in the Scriptures; whereas in the Papacy our Lords Masters themselves habitually cast the Holy Scripture so completely aside <note>Dutch idiom: "agter de bank" (behind the bench)</note>—even though they brag about that honorable name—that many among them have not once in their lives looked into the Holy Bible.

These words are also very noteworthy, with which he ends the same: *I therefore commend in the Lord to all the godly also this Confession of the Brothers, in which they will see clearly with how much injustice they have been condemned and harassed by the Papists until now:* <note>original Latin: "commendo igitur in Domino omnibus piis & hanc Confessionem Fratrum..."</note> as if he said; I must therefore also praise this Confession of the Brothers to all the godly in the Lord according to its worth, because they will easily gather from it with what injustice the same have been condemned and persecuted by the Papist-minded until now: as well as these [words], which stand a little higher; *but now they come forward not a little more refined and free, not to say even more illustrious and better, so that I hope they will not be unwelcome, nor unlovable to all true Christians; so that it even behooves us to give the greatest thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the riches of his glory commanded this light of his Word to shine out of the darkness, so that he might once again destroy death in us and illuminate life;* <note>original Latin: "sed nunc prodeunt non paulo cultiores... ut sperem non ingratos... illuminaret vitam"</note> which in our language give this sense: but now they come forward somewhat more neatly and boldly, not to say even more gloriously and better, so that I dare to hope that they will thereby become very dear and very pleasant to all true Christians; even to the point that we are bound to show the highest gratitude to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the riches of His glory has commanded that the light of His Word should shine out of the darkness, so that He might once more destroy death and bring life into the light.

<margin>A remarkable testimony from Wesembecius.</margin>
In which, by fulfilling this saying of his, he has even gone before us all, since Wesembecius <note>Petrus Wesenbeck (1546–1603), a legal scholar and historian who wrote about the Waldensians</note> in his Discourse on the Waldensians on page 4 explicitly mentions that Luther, after reading the aforementioned Waldensian Confession of Faith, thanked God with great joy that He had granted them so much light, rejoicing with them that all occasion for hindrance—by which one might have been suspicious of the other—having been entirely removed, they had now approached each other so closely that, under the single Shepherd and Overseer of souls, they were equally brought together into one and the same sheepfold.

<margin>And from Philip Melanchthon.</margin>

# Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
## H h
<meta>catchword: ctis</meta>

### To the venerable man in Christ, Master BENEDICT, and the other Waldensian Brothers in Bohemia, grace and peace, etc. <note>Original Latin: "Venerabili Viro in Christo, D. BENEDICTO, cæterisque Fratribus Waldensibus in Bohemia gratia & pax, &c."</note>

I consider, most distinguished man, that your brothers in this meeting of ours have better known and perceived my opinion on many matters than I once seemed to myself to have understood your affairs. Therefore, since we agree on the principal articles of Christian Doctrine, let us embrace one another with mutual love. Neither should the dissimilarity and variety of rites and ceremonies divide our minds. Paul often preaches about ceremonies and forbids Christians from disagreeing because of a variety of rites and ceremonies, even though the world fights vehemently over ceremonies. The more severe exercise, or discipline, in your Churches certainly does not displease me; would that in our Churches a slightly more severe one could also be retained! Regarding my feelings toward you, you may think that I vehemently desire that those who love the Gospel and wish the name of Christ to be glorified should pursue one another with mutual charity and thus direct their doctrine by common efforts to the glory of Christ, lest they destroy themselves by mutual and domestic hatreds or discords, especially over those matters about which it is not necessary to cause a tumult. Fare well. Pray for me and for the glory of Christ. Given at Wittenberg in the year 1535. Philip Melanchthon. <note>Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a German reformer and a close collaborator of Martin Luther, known for his intellectual approach and efforts to find common ground between different religious groups.</note> Of which we provide this translation:

-> To the venerable man in Christ, the Lord BENEDICT, <-
-> and the further Waldensian Brothers in Bohemia <-
-> be grace and peace, etc. <-

I consider, most excellent man, that your brothers in this our assembly and meeting will have somewhat better grasped and understood my view on many matters; just as it now also seems to me that I do yours, beyond what I had previously imagined of them. For which reason we may also treat each other with mutual love, since we are in complete agreement regarding the principal points of the Christian Doctrine. And truly, the inequality and difference of ceremonies and customs <margin> *That one must grant leeway regarding the difference of some Church rites.* </margin> must not keep our spirits from one another, because St. Paul himself, very often teaching of such Church laws, clearly always forbids at the same time that one should ever alienate oneself from another because of any such distinction: although the world is currently mostly at odds because of them. It truly pleases me to the highest degree that you practice Church discipline <term>Church discipline (Kerk-tugt): The system of moral oversight and correction used by a church community to maintain its standards of conduct.</term> so strictly in your congregations: Oh, if only it were maintained somewhat more strictly in our Churches as well! <margin> *Praise of the severity of the Waldensian Church discipline.* </margin> Meanwhile, you can hold this as firm and certain regarding my sincere affection toward you: namely, that I very fervently wish that all those who love the Gospel and take the glorification of Christ's name to heart might show mutual love to one another, and so make their Doctrine tend toward the honor of their Savior with a common zeal, so as not to bring themselves to a secret ruin through internal hatred or strife, especially regarding such matters that do not even warrant such a fuss. Fare well. Pray for me and for the honor of the Lord Jesus. From Wittenberg in the year 1535. Philip Melanchthon.

<margin> *Testimony from Bucer.* </margin>
Here also must not be passed over what we find by Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551) was an influential Protestant Reformer based in Strasbourg who acted as a mediator between different reforming parties.</note> regarding this matter in his book called *Adversaria Latomi*, etc., in the chapter on Church power, p. 159, from which we transcribe the following words: "That method is certainly the best, which the Picard Brothers <note>The "Picard Brothers" (Fratres Piccardi) was a common, though sometimes derogatory, name used by outsiders for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren.</note> observe, who published their Confession of Faith, recently offered to King Ferdinand, in the year 1535 with a preface by Master Luther; who alone in the world have retained, along with purity of Doctrine, also the vigor of the Discipline of Christ among themselves. That we should grant them this praise and celebrate the Lord, who thus works in them, the matter itself compels us; even if those Brothers by the perversely learned..." <note>original Latin: "Illa certe ratio optima est, quam observant Fratres Piccardi... etiamsi Fratres illi a præpostere doctis"</note>

<summary>This page presents a letter from Philip Melanchthon to the Waldensians in Bohemia, expressing doctrinal unity and praising their strict church discipline. It also introduces a corroborating testimony from the reformer Martin Bucer, who highlights the purity of their doctrine and practice.</summary>

# General Memorial
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

"And let these things be despised by some. However, the reasoning they observe in this matter is this: Besides the Ministers of the Word and Sacraments, they have a certain Council of men, excelling in prudence and gravity of spirit, who perform the duty of admonishing and correcting sinning Brothers, reconciling those who disagree, and judging in their cases. However, they do not pronounce the sentence of excommunication unless the case is brought before the entire Church and judged by common vote, and this is done through the supreme Overseer of the Church. Saint Ambrose also wrote about such Elders in his commentary on the first Epistle to Timothy, chapter 5. From this, both the Synagogue and later the Church have always had Elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church, etc." <note>Original Latin: "Et is nonnullis contemnantur. Ratio vero, quam in hac re observant, haec est. Praeter Ministros Verbi & Sacramentorum habent certum Collegium virorum, prudentia & gravitate spiritus praecellentium, qui munus obeunt monendi ac corrigendi Fratres peccantes, componendi dissidentes & in causis eorum judicandi. Excommunicationis tamen sententiam non nisi causa delata ad totam Ecclesiam & communibus sententiis judicata ferunt, idque per supremum Ecclesiae Curatorem. De hujusmodi Senioribus scripsit & Divus Ambrosius in Epistolam 1. ad Timoth. cap. 5. Unde & Synagoga & postea Ecclesia Seniores habuit, quorum sine consilio nihil agebatur in Ecclesia. &c."</note> Which is to say in English: Indeed, that manner of proceeding is entirely praiseworthy which the Picardy Brothers <note>The <term>Picardy Brothers</term> or "Picards" was a common name for the Bohemian Brethren, a group that shared many beliefs with the Waldensians</note> follow, who had the Confession of their Faith—just as they recently presented it to King Ferdinand—printed with a preface by Master Luther in the year 1535. They are perhaps the only ones in the whole world who, alongside the purity of Doctrine, have maintained Christian Discipline; for which reason the facts themselves compel us to give them this praise and to properly glorify the Lord our God, who works so powerfully in them, no matter how much those Brothers are despised and criticized by some "wrongly-learned" men. Their practice in this matter is as follows. Namely, besides the Ministers of the Word and the Sacraments, they have a certain Assembly of dignified men, outstanding in foresight and courage of spirit, who alone carry out the office of admonishing the brothers who commit some lapse and bringing them to improvement, uniting those who quarrel, and sitting as judges over their affairs. Even so, they may not pass the sentence of the ban <note>The <term>ban</term> refers to excommunication or being cast out of the church community</note> unless the case is first brought before the whole Church and the verdict is given there by common vote; which is then carried out by the chief of the Church Overseers. Of such Elders, Saint <note>original: "H." for Heilige (Saint)</note> Ambrose also writes in the commentary on the first letter to Timothy in the 5th chapter. This is why, in the beginning, the Jewish congregation, as well as the Christian congregation thereafter, always had its Elders, without whose advice nothing happened in the Church. Which etc.

There is also found in the book of a certain Waldensian <note>original: "Wals"</note> teacher, George Morel, in which he described his conversation with Oecolampadius and Bucer, a letter still existing today from the latter, sent by him to the Waldensians, beginning thus: "Blessed be the Lord God and Father, who has preserved you until now in such great knowledge of His truth and who has now inspired you to the search for the same, having made you capable of doing so;" <note>Original French: "Le Seigneur Dieu & Pere soit benit, lequel vous a conservés jusqu' a present en si grande connoissance de sa verité & lequel vous a maintenant inspirés a la recherche d'icelle, vous ayant rendus capables de ce faire;"</note> that is, praise be to our Lord God and Father, who has kept you until now in such great knowledge of His Holy Truth and has even now driven you to the investigation of the same, having granted you sufficient ability for it. But what is worth noting in that long letter lies, among other things, primarily in this: that regarding their Confession of Faith, he uses these words; <margin>And of their antiquity.</margin> "Now here is the nature of true faith: it is that as soon as it recognizes in any part some spark of divine light, it carefully preserves the things which are given to it by God;" <note>Original French: "Or voicy quel est le naturel de la vraye foy; c'est que dès aussi tôt, qu'elle reconnoit en quelque part quelque étincelle de la clarté divine, elle conserve soigneusement les choses, qui luy sont données de Dieu;"</note> as if he said: now this is the nature of the true Faith, that as soon as it perceives any small sparks of the divine light, it carefully seeks to preserve the things it has received from God. In the same work one can also read a beautiful letter from the year 1530 to the Waldensians of Provence—who have always been one and the same body with those of the Valleys and, as we have proven, sprouted from the same—written by Oecolampadius himself. It is worth the trouble for us to copy the same word for word and insert it here. <margin>Notable testimony of Oecolampadius.</margin> "We have heard with much contentment from your faithful Pastor George Morel, what your faith and religion are and in what terms you speak of them. Now we give thanks to our most gracious Father, who has called you to such great light" <note>Original French: "Nous avons entendu avec beaucoup de contentement par vôtre fidelle Pasteur George Morel, quelle est vôtre foy & religion & en quels termes vous parlez d'icelle. Or nous rendons graces a nôtre Pere tresbenin, lequel vous a appellés a si grande lumiere"</note>

# Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

*“in this century & among the dark shadows, which are spread throughout the whole world, and the disordered power of the Antichrist. And yet we recognize that Christ is in you. Therefore we love you as brothers. And would to God that we could make you feel in effect what we would be ready to do for you, even if it were a very difficult thing to do! For the rest, we would not want what we write to be taken as if we were attributing some superiority to ourselves; but as words spoken to our brothers in charity and fraternal friendship. The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has granted you an excellent knowledge of his truth, more than to many other peoples, and has blessed you with spiritual blessing. If you persist under his grace, he has yet greater treasures with which he can enrich you and can make you perfect, so that you may grow into the measure of the inheritance of Christ;”* <note>Original French: "en ce ſiecle & parmi les tenebres obſcures, qui ſont épandues par tout le monde..." This is a letter from the Basel Reformer Johannes Oecolampadius to the Waldensians, likely from 1530.</note> which should be translated as follows: We have understood from your faithful Teacher George Morel <note>A Waldensian pastor who traveled to meet the Reformers</note> with great pleasure, how your faith and religion are and what words you use concerning the same. We thank God our merciful Father, that he has so kindly called you to such a great light in this world and in the midst of the thick darkness that is spread everywhere, and the disorderly power of the False-Christ <note>original Dutch: "Leuge-Chriſtus," referring to the Antichrist</note>. Therefore we also recognize that Christ is in you: indeed, we love you with a brotherly love. Oh, if we only had the opportunity to show in deed itself what we would certainly want to do for you, even if it were ever so difficult! In the meantime, we would not gladly see that what we write here were interpreted by you as if we were thereby assuming any superiority, since on the contrary these are but discourses held with our brothers in love and fraternal friendship. The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has shared with you, above various other peoples, an excellent knowledge of his truth and favored you very richly with a spiritual blessing. Nevertheless, he has yet greater treasures locked away, which he also wishes to give you, if you persevere under his grace, to enrich you with the same and to make you perfect, so that you might grow to the measure of the inheritance of our blessed Savior. The inscription <note>address</note> of that letter contained these words: *Oecolampadius desires the grace of God the Father through his Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit to the well-beloved Brothers in Christ, who are called Waldensians.* <note>Original French: "Oecolampade deſire la grace de Dieu le Pere par ſon Fils Jeſus Chriſt au S. Eſprit aux bien-aimes Freres en Chriſt, qu'on appelle Vaudois."</note> which gives this sense: Oecolampadius wishes the grace of God the Father through his Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit to his well-beloved Brothers, called Waldensians.

We add here yet another Confession of Faith, handed over to the Parliament, or State Council of Turin, and set against a certain Edict of the 23rd of the Spring-month <note>March</note> 1556, thundered by the same against the Waldensians. The content and short summary of what was proclaimed against those poor people by the same consisted of this: namely, that on behalf of the King and the illustrious Court of the High Council, all Jurisdictions, Societies, or Communities, the People and Inhabitants of Lucerna, La Tour, Villar, Bobi, Ville-neuve, Roras, St. Jan, Angronje, Lucernette, Bubiane, Fenil, Campiljon, Garcillane, Mombron (otherwise called St. Marten) and others of the Valley of Lucerna <note>These are towns in the Piedmont region of Italy, historically the heart of the Waldensian valleys</note>, as well as all other people, of whatever state or quality they might be, were expressly forbidden from taking into their land, housing in their homes or buildings, or henceforth hearing any Teachers coming from Geneva or elsewhere, much less those who are originally from the said places themselves, unless the same have been appointed for that purpose by the Most Reverend Lord Archbishop of Turin, his Deputy, or some other ecclesiastical Authority of those regions and approved by the well-mentioned Court of the Princely Council: and all this upon forfeiture of life and property. Regarding Auricular Confession <note>The practice of confessing sins privately into the ear of a priest.</note>, that they confessed their sins daily before God and, according to his command and that of our Savior prescribed to us in various places of His Word, prayed to Him for forgiveness for them in public and in secret. But regarding the claim that these traditions were prescribed by Councils, or Church assemblies, they replied that there are several which were not established by such high authority. Furthermore, even if they had such a magnificent origin, one must listen to no one—not even an Angel from Heaven—if he should command anything against God's Word. They noted that the aforementioned high Church Council had indeed prescribed several beautiful and holy Laws to appropriately guide the Teachers and the People, commanding for example, *that Church ministers who are scandalous through fornication, or drunkenness, or whatever else it might be, must be removed; that those who go to Mass with a whorish Priest must be excommunicated, etc.* <note>Original: "eſv." And truly, it can only be read with the greatest pleasure by those who love pure, clear, and concise Theology. But while it goes on at great length and yet contains nothing different in essence than the same Doctrine of the preceding and following confessions, it will be enough for me to place its arrangement here before your eyes and to cite the ways of speaking of some of the most prominent main articles as briefly as possible, especially regarding what concerns the disputes of Faith.

Let no Christian, then, imagine any fleshly union and communion between the Savior and his Elect; but rather, that they are nonetheless truly united with his body and blood, as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh. # General Memorial #

<meta>catchword: handed over</meta>

...handed over. Namely, in the time of Francis I, King of France <note>Francis I reigned 1515–1547; he was a contemporary of the early Reformation and fluctuated between tolerance and persecution of "heretics."</note>, who was then Prince of Piedmont and held his Royal Council in the city of Turin—presently the residence of the Dukes of Savoy—the Waldensians of the Valleys, both of Piedmont, as well as Dauphiné and Provence, submitted a Confession of their Faith. This is recorded unanimously by Jean Crespin <note>original: "Johannes Crispinus," a famous chronicler of Protestant martyrs.</note> in the 15th article of his *Monuments of Martyrs*, Book 3, in the life of Lancelot du Voysin, and by Lord De la Popelinière in the first book of his *Histories*, page 26 of the 1581 edition. They submitted it <note>original Latin: "quemadmodem ex omni memoria ætatum & temporum a Veteribus eam susceperant"</note>, that is, just as they had received it from their ancestors for many centuries. The same J. Crespin gives us in the cited third book another Confession of Faith, which the Waldensians of Mérindol and Cabrières <note>These villages in Provence were the site of a brutal massacre of Waldensians in 1545.</note> once delivered to the Provincial Council of Provence; he mentions that this other one was sent to the King of France in the year 1544, as we have said, and was publicly read in the Great Council of Paris in the year 1551. But to be brief, I shall skip the first one and be content with setting down the latter here word for word, especially since it contains in short what the others treat very extensively. It begins as follows:

### I.
->*Of God.*<-

<note>original French: "Nous croyons qu'il n'y a qu'un seul Dieu, qui est Esprit..."</note> *We believe that there is but one only God, who is Spirit, the Creator of all things, the Father of all, over us all, among us all, and in us all, who must be worshiped in spirit and truth, who alone can give life, nourishment, clothing, health, sickness, prosperity, and adversity; we love him as the author of all goodness, and fear him as the searcher of hearts.*

<column-break/>

We believe that there is but one single God, who is a Spirit, a Creator of all things, a Father of all, above us all, with us all, and in us all, and who must be worshiped in spirit and truth; who alone can give life, food, clothing, health, sickness, prosperity, and adversity; we love him as the giver of everything good and fear him as the searcher of hearts.

### II.
->*Of Jesus Christ, our only Mediator.*<-

<note>original French: "Nous croyons que Jesus Christ est le Fils & l'Image du Pere..."</note> *We believe that Jesus Christ is the Son and the Image of the Father, in whom dwells all fullness of Divinity, by whom we know the Father; that he is our Mediator and Advocate, and that there is no other name under Heaven given to men by which we must be saved. We call upon the Father only in his name, and offer no prayers to God except those contained in Holy Scripture, or at least those having the same meaning.*

<column-break/>

We believe that Jesus Christ is the Son and the Image of the Father, in whom all fullness of the Godhead is housed and through whom we know the Father; that he is our Mediator and Advocate and that there is no other name under Heaven given to men by which we must be saved. We also call upon the Father in his name alone, nonetheless offering no prayers to God but those included in Holy Scripture, or at least those having the same sense and content.

### III.
->*Of the Holy Spirit.*<-

<note>original French: "Nous croyons que nous avons le S. Esprit pour Consolateur, qui procede"</note> *We believe that we have the Holy Spirit as Comforter, who proceeds*

### IV.
->Of the *Holy Church*.<-

*We believe that there is a Holy Church, which is the assembly of all the elect of God, whom he has chosen from the beginning until the end of the world, of which the Head is our Lord Jesus Christ, which is governed by the Word of God, and led by his Holy Spirit. Within it all true Christians must dwell; it prays incessantly for all, it is pleasing to God, to whom it has its recourse, and outside of it there is no salvation.* <note>The phrase "outside of it there is no salvation" (extra Ecclesiam nulla salus) was a standard theological claim, here applied by the Waldensians to their own conception of the true, spiritual church.</note>

<column-break/>

We believe that there is a Holy Church, which is essentially an assembly of God’s elect <term>elect: those whom God has chosen for salvation from the beginning of time</term>, whom he has set apart for himself from the beginning to the end of the world, of which our Lord Jesus alone is the head; which is governed by the Word of God and led by his Holy Spirit. All true Christians must have their interaction within the same, because it prays without ceasing for everyone. The same is also very pleasing to God, to whom it therefore takes its refuge. Finally, outside of the same, there is no salvation.

### V.
->Of the *Church Teachers*.<-

*We hold this as resolved by us, that the Bishops and the Pastors must be irreproachable in their Doctrine, and in their morals, otherwise they must be deposed, and others established in their place, who fulfill their office. Now let no one attribute this honor to himself, unless he be called to it by God, not affecting dishonest gain as dominating over the heritages of the Lord, but being moved by a free heart, gives an example to pious persons in word, in conversation, in charity, and in chastity.*

<column-break/>

We hold this among us as fixed, that the Overseers <note>original: "Opsieners," a translation of the Greek "episkopos" or Bishop</note> and Teachers must be irreproachable in doctrine and life; indeed, that they must otherwise be deposed and better ones put in their place, who might better fulfill their offices. *In the meantime, no one may claim this honor for himself, unless he be called to it by God*, nor should he strive for shameful gain, as if exercising lordship over the heritage of the Lord; but rather, being driven to it by a willing spirit, he should give a good example to godly people in conduct, love, and purity.

### VII.
->*On Baptism.*<-

*We believe that the water in the Sacrament of Baptism is but a visible and external sign, representing to us what the Truth of God works within us, namely the spiritual renewal, and the mortification of our flesh in Jesus Christ, by which Christ also, we are made members of the Holy Church of God, in which we show the profession of our Faith, and the correction of our life.* <note>The "mortification of the flesh" refers to the spiritual struggle to overcome sinful desires.</note>

We believe that the water in the Sacrament of Holy Baptism is nothing other than an external and visible sign, depicting to us that which the truth of God accomplishes within us, namely the spiritual renewal and the killing of our flesh in Christ Jesus; through which Savior we also become members of the Holy Church of God, in which we demonstrate the confession of our faith and the improvement of our lives before everyone.

->*On the Holy Supper.*<-

*We believe that the Holy Sacrament of the Table of our Lord Jesus Christ is a holy memorial, and an act of thanksgiving for the benefits we have received by the death of Jesus Christ; that it must be celebrated in the assembly of the Saints, in Faith and Charity, and by the self-examination one has of oneself. And thus, by taking the Bread and the Wine, we have communion with the Flesh and the Blood of Christ, as we read in the Holy Scripture.*

We believe that the Holy Sign of Faith of the Table of our Lord Jesus Christ is a holy memorial and thanksgiving for all the benefits that we have received through the death of the Lord alone; that the same must be administered in the assembly of the Saints with Faith, Love, and self-reflection, and that by receiving the bread and the wine in this way, one comes to have communion with the flesh and blood of Christ, as the Holy Leaves <note>original: "H. ### X.
->*On Good Works.*<-

*We believe that pious and God-fearing persons should dedicate themselves to him to occupy themselves with good works, which he has prepared so that they may follow them. Now, these works are charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, moderation, temperance, and other works ordained in the Scriptures. On the contrary, we confess that we must be wary of false prophets, whose goal is to turn the people away from the religious worship due to the only God and Lord, and make them adhere to and trust in creatures, and not to do the works commanded of us in Holy Scripture, but to follow the inventions of men.* <note>original French: "Nous croyons que les personnes pieuses & craignans Dieu..."</note>

<column-break/>

We believe that holy and God-fearing people must dedicate themselves to him to be busy in **good works**, which he has prepared for them to walk in. These works are love, joy, peace, patience, goodwill, goodness, moderation, sobriety, and other such things that are prescribed for us in the Holy Scriptures. On the contrary, we also confess that one must be wary of false prophets, whose only purpose is to draw the people away from their upright godliness—which belongs to our Lord and God alone—and to make them cling to created things with full trust, so that instead of practicing the works commanded by God's Word, they might follow human inventions.

# General Memorial History

...observations which are recorded in the first book of the *Ecclesiastical Journals of the French Reformed Churches*, printed in Antwerp in the year 1580 by Jan Remy, page 42, concerning the year 1544. The first of these observations is as follows: <margin>Wondrous testimonies given to the Waldensian Confession of Faith by the theologians of a Bishop and a Monk.</margin> <note>The Dutch text uses "Wal-se," which could refer to "Walloon" (French-speaking), but in this context refers to the Waldensians or Vaudois of the Alps.</note> that the Bishop of Cavaillon <note>A town in Provence, France.</note> went to these same Waldensians to convert them. After having the main articles of their faith thoroughly reviewed by his theologians, he was so far from attempting to refute even the smallest part of them that he openly confessed *that in all his life he had never learned as much from Holy Scripture as he had in those eight days, during which he compared and reconciled the passages cited as proof with the text itself.*

The other observation is that after the same Bishop had gone to them a second time with four monks, newly arrived from the University of Paris, one of them—having heard how the little Waldensian children answered their teacher from the church catechism <term>Vraag-boek: a book of questions and answers used for religious instruction</term>—brought forth this public confession: *that he had never learned as much good in all the disputations he had either held himself or heard at the Sorbonne <note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note> as he had in listening to those little children.* Truly, that Bishop, that theologian, and that monk—being convinced in their consciences that the doctrine of the Waldensians was in agreement with Holy Scripture—gave them such a magnificent testimony. They were always little inclined to doubt the antiquity of the Waldensians or to criticize them in any way because they boasted (as we have seen) that they had just testified before Francis I, King of France and Governor of Piedmont, as well as before his High Court, that they had received this same faith from hand to hand from their ancestors, just as the elders of all ages and times had taught it to them.

And therefore (let me insert this in passing), the aforementioned chronicler, though ignorant of the exact time of their origin, begins the history of the Waldensians with these words from Book 1, page 35: *those who are commonly called Waldensians have opposed the errors of the Romish Church from time immemorial; and having proven that those of Provence originated from the Piedmontese Valleys and were beloved by the Roman Catholics because they were known as charitable, upright, and faithful people, and generally as enemies of all evil:* he adds a few lines lower: *that they had never been bound to the superstitions of the Papacy and for that very reason had always suffered persecution by the so-called inquisitors, etc. Indeed, it was a tangible miracle of the Lord that they had been able to remain standing in such a manner.*

Those of their fellow brothers who had fled to the lands of George, the Margrave of Brandenburg, also presented him with several Confessions of Faith in the years 1532 and 1538, which were drafted entirely according to the content of the preceding ones.

To all of these, we could now add many beautiful and concise *Apologies* <term>Apologies: formal written defenses of a religious doctrine</term> published by them in the years 1432, 1434, and 1508. But since they are all found to agree in sense with the following one, which belongs to the Duke of Savoy, and because this one is much shorter, it will be enough for me to present it here. It shall serve as a sample by which one may judge the larger works. See here then a Testimony of the Waldensians of the Meane Valley, St. Matthias, and the Marquisate of Saluzzo, made in the year 1603, when the Duke of Savoy drove them out of his territory and borders. We have faithfully transcribed the Italian original and translated the copy just as it was. Both read as follows:

*It is a known thing <note>original Italian: "Conciosa cosa"</note>, that at all times our predecessors, from father to son, have always been taught in the Doctrine and Religion, of which since our childhood we have always made open profession; and in that faith we have instructed our families, just as we learned it from our fathers. Why they were not compelled to write anything before the year 1120.
</margin>

I believe indeed that they did not need to issue such pieces of public defense earlier, which would serve as legal evidence and manifestos (*Factum* and *Manifest*) to shelter them from the storm of persecution or to place the justice of their cause before the eyes of the world; because they had never yet been publicly persecuted or openly subjected to violence. Prudence itself taught them to remain quiet, so as not to stir up those "dogs" against them—the same dogs who had so terribly barked at Claudius of Turin, their High Bishop <note>Claudius (died c. 827) was a Bishop of Turin known for his iconoclasm—the destruction of religious images—which the Waldensians viewed as a precursor to their own rejection of Roman Catholic practices</note>, who at the end of the eighth century (as we shall see hereafter) first drew them away from the Roman communion as soon as it wished to force them to become idolaters by accepting images; those dogs had since then fallen somewhat asleep. Consequently, it is very probable that, just as in the aforementioned year 1120 new efforts were made to force the acceptance of Roman traditions, they also had to add the mentioned Confessions of Faith and similar declarations to the document regarding the cause of their separation from the Roman Church, which we have produced elsewhere.

In the meantime, it is well worth the effort to see further whether the interval of 500 years, which has already passed since the making of that first one, has been able to change anything at all in the faith of our Waldensians. # General Memoirs

...principally to denigrate with infamous slanders the holy and salvific Doctrine which we profess: we are obliged, in order to enlighten the minds of those who might be preoccupied by such sinister thoughts, to make a brief declaration of our faith, as we have held it in the past and still hold it today in accordance with the Word of God; so that everyone may see the falsity of those slanders and with what injustice we are hated and persecuted for such an innocent Doctrine. <note>original Italian: "principalmente a denigrare... innocente Dottrina."</note>

...but especially to blacken with shameless slanders the holy and salvific Doctrine which we profess; so we are compelled, in order to give some light on the matter to those who might already be somewhat taken with such bad thoughts, to make a brief Declaration of our Faith, just as we have always held the same from of old and still today hold it in unison with God’s Word, so that everyone may see the untruth of that scolding and at the same time, with what a crying injustice we are hated and persecuted for such an innocent and righteous Doctrine.

->We believe then,<-

### I.

<margin>Of the Holy Trinity.</margin>
That there is only one God, who is a spiritual, eternal, infinite Essence, entirely wise, merciful, just, in short, entirely perfect; and that there are three Persons in that single and simple Essence, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. <note>original Italian: "Che vi, è un solo Iddio... Spirito Santo."</note>

<column-break/>

That there is one unique God, who is a spiritual, eternal, infinite, omniscient, merciful, righteous, in a word, a most perfect Being; and that in that same unique and simple Being three Subsistences <term>Selfstandigheden: a 17th-century Dutch term for the Persons of the Trinity</term> are found: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### II.

<margin>How God has revealed Himself.</margin>
That this same God manifested Himself to men in His works of Creation and Providence and furthermore in His Word, revealed from the beginning with oracles in various manners, then put into writing in the books called the Holy Scripture. <note>original Italian: "Che quello Iddio s'é manifestato... Scrittura Santa."</note>

That this same God has revealed Himself to men, both through His works of Creation and Divine Providence, as well as further in His Holy Word, in the beginning inspired in various ways by Oracles and thereafter left entirely in writing in the books called the Holy Scripture.

### III.

<margin>Of the Holy Scripture.</margin>
That it is fitting to receive, as we receive, this Holy Scripture as Divine and Canonical, that is, for the rule of our Faith and life, and that it is fully contained in the books of the Old and New Testament. That in the Old Testament there should only be included the books that God entrusted to the Jewish Church, by her always approved and recognized as divine, namely the five books of Moses, Joshua, the Judges, Ruth, the first and second of Kings, the first and second of Chronicles, or Para- <note>original Italian: "Che conviene ricevere... Para-" referring to Paralipomenon, an alternative name for Chronicles.</note>

That one must reverently hold and accept the same Holy Scripture as Divine and Canonical—that is, as a rule <term>Regt-snoer: literally a 'plumb line' or 'measuring cord'</term> of our Faith and Life—as we do; and also that the same is fully contained in the books of the Old and New Covenants. Also, that among those of the Old Covenant no others may be counted than those which God entrusted to the Jewish Church and were thereafter always unanimously judged and recognized by the same as divine: namely the five books of Moses, that of Joshua, the Judges, Ruth, the first...

### IV.

*That we recognize the Divinity of these Sacred books not only from the testimony of the Church, but principally from the eternal and indubitable truth of the Doctrine contained in them, from the excellence, sublimity, and majesty of the entirely divine whole which is demonstrated there, and from the operation of the Holy Spirit, which makes us receive with reverence the testimony which the Church gives us of it, which opens our eyes to discover the rays of celestial light that shine in the Scripture, and corrects our taste to discern this food with its divine flavor.* <note>original Italian: "Che riconoſciamo la Divinità... ſuo divino ſapore."</note>

<margin>
By which one knows its Divinity.
</margin>
That we recognize the divinity of those Holy Books not only through the testimony of the Church, but most especially by the eternal and unquestionable truth of the Doctrine which they contain in themselves, by the divine excellence, loftiness, and dignity which one perceives therein, and by the working of the Holy Spirit, who makes us receive the testimony that the Church gives us of the same with all reverence; who opens our eyes to discover the rays of that heavenly light that shines in the Holy Scripture, and finally enables our tongue <note>The Dutch text uses "tong" (tongue) where the Italian uses "guſto" (taste)</note> to be able to taste and distinguish the divine flavor of that food.

### V.

*That God has made all things from nothing by His will, which is entirely free, and by the infinite power of His Word.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' Iddio ha fatto... della ſua Parola."</note>

<margin>
Of the Creation.
</margin>
That God, through His most free will and through the infinite power of His eternal word, has created all things out of nothing.

### VI.

*That He conducts and governs them all with His providence, ordering and directing all that happens in the world, without Himself being the author or the cause of the evil which men do...* <note>original Italian: "Ch' egli le conduce... il quale ſanno"</note>

<margin>
Of Holy Providence and that God is not the worker of evil.
</margin>
That He conducts and governs everything through His providence, arranging and disposing all that happens in the world, without Him being, nonetheless, a worker or cause of the evil that men ever commit.

...committed, or that the guilt for it could or may ever be attributed to Him in any way. <note>original Dutch: "begaan, of datte schult daar van hem eenigermaten ooyt kan of mag geweten worden."</note>

### VII.

<margin>On the Angels.</margin>
*That although the Angels were all created pure and holy, some have fallen into an irreparable corruption and perdition; but that the others have persevered through an effect of divine goodness, which has sustained and confirmed them.* <note>original Italian: "Che gli Angeli eſſendo ſtati tutti creati puri e ſanti..."</note>

That although the Angels were all created pure and holy, some of them nevertheless fell into a helpless corruption and destruction, whereas the others remained in their first state solely through a work of divine goodness, by which He supported and confirmed them therein. <note>original Dutch: "Dat schoon d'Engelen altemaal ſuyver en heylig waren geſchapen..."</note>

---

### VIII.

<margin>On the Fall of Adam.</margin>
*That man, who had been created pure and holy in the image of God, deprived himself of that happy state through his own fault by giving credence to the deceitful discourses of the Devil.* <note>original Italian: "Che l'huomo, ilqual era ſtato creato puro e ſanto..."</note>

That man, who was created pure and holy after God's image, robbed himself of that blessed condition through his own fault, giving ear to the deceptive reasons of the Devil. <note>original Dutch: "Datte mens, die reyn en heylig na Gots beelt was geſchapen..."</note>

---

### IX.

<margin>And the corruption of the entire human race.</margin>
*That man in his transgression has lost the justice and holiness which he had received, and has incurred the indignation of God, death, and captivity under the power of him who has the empire of death, that is, the Devil; to such an extent that his <term>free will|libero arbitrio: The capacity to choose between good and evil, here described as lost</term> has become a servant and slave to sin; so that by nature all men, both Jews and Gentiles, are children of wrath, all dead in their failings and sins and consequently incapable of having any good movement toward salvation, even of forming a good thought without grace, all their imaginations being nothing other than evil at all times.*

That man in his transgression lost the righteousness and holiness that he had previously received, and fell into the displeasure of his God, into death and imprisonment under the power of the one who has the power of death, that is the Devil; also in such a way that his <term>free will|vrije Wille</term> has become enslaved and subject to sin. In such a way that all people, both Jews and Heathens, are equally by nature children of wrath, equally dead in their crimes and sins, and consequently equally incapable of any of the slightest good movement toward salvation, much less of having a good thought without <term>grace|genade: Divine favor bestowed without merit</term>, while even all their meditations are nothing else at all times but evil.

---

### X.

<margin>On Original Sin.</margin>
*That all the posterity of Adam is guilty in him for his disobedience, infected by his corruption and fallen into the same calamity, even the little children from the mother's womb: from which comes the name of <term>Original Sin|peccato Originale</term>.*

That the entire race and all descendants of Adam are guilty in him of his disobedience, infected with his corruption and plunged into one and the same misery, even down to the little children from the mother's womb; from which also the name of <term>Original Sin|Erf-sonde: The inherited state of sin and guilt resulting from the Fall of Man</term> comes.

### XI.

*That God draws from that corruption and condemnation those persons whom He has chosen by His mercy in Jesus Christ His Son, leaving the others according to the irreproachable reason of His freedom and justice.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' Iddio cava da quella corruttione..."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>On Election.</margin>
That God chooses only to pick out from that corruption and damnation those whom He has chosen according to His mercy in His Son Jesus Christ, while He leaves the others in the same state according to the incomprehensible reason of His freedom and righteousness.

---

### XII.

*That Jesus Christ, having been ordained by God in His eternal Decree to be the sole Savior and the only head of His body, which is the Church, has redeemed it with His own blood in the fullness of time and communicates to it all His benefits through the Gospel.* <note>original Italian: "Che Jeſu Chriſto eſſendo ſtato..."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>On the Redemption through our Lord Jesus.</margin>
That the Lord Jesus, being predestined by God’s eternal decree to be the only Savior and Head of His body the Church, has redeemed the same with His own blood in the fulfillment of time and makes it a partaker of all His benefits through the Gospel.

---

### XIII.

*That there are two natures in Jesus Christ, the divine and the human, truly united in one and the same person without confusion, without separation, without division, without change, each nature keeping its distinct properties; and that Jesus Christ is at once true God and true man.* <note>original Italian: "Che vi ſono due nature..."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Who is truly God and truly man.</margin>
That there are two kinds of nature in Jesus Christ, the divine and the human, without mixing, without separation, without division, without change, truly united in one and the same Personhood <note>The Dutch "Self-ſtandigheyt" refers to the theological concept of 'hypostasis,' meaning the individual reality of being</note>, in such a way that each of them always retains its distinct properties: as also that the Lord Christ is simultaneously truly God and truly man.

---

### XIV.

*That God so loved the world that He gave His son to save us by His most perfect obedience, especially that which He demonstrated by suffering the cursed death of the cross, and by the victories He achieved over the Devil, sin, and death.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' Iddio ha tanto amato..."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Died for our misdeeds.</margin>
That God so loved the world that He gave over His Son to make us blessed through His most perfect obedience, and especially through that which He showed in enduring the cursed death of the cross, and through the joyful victories He fought against the Devil, sin, and the world.

---

### XV.

*That Jesus Christ, having made the entire expiation of our sins with His most perfect sacrifice once offered on the cross, cannot, nor should...* <note>original Italian: "Che Jeſu Chriſto havendo fatta..."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>That His sacrifice cannot be imitated.</margin>
That, after our Savior has worked the complete reconciliation of our sins through His perfect sacrifice, once made by Him on the cross, the same, under whatever appearance it might be...

<term>Waldensian Churches</term>: A proto-Protestant movement following the teachings of Peter Waldo.
<term>Election</term>: The theological concept that God chooses certain individuals for salvation.
<term>Redemption</term>: The act of being saved from sin or error.
<term>Jesus Christ</term>: The central figure of Christianity, the Savior.
<term>Savior</term>: One who brings salvation.
<term>Gospel</term>: The teaching or revelation of Christ.
<term>Divine</term>: Relating to or coming from God.
<term>Human</term>: Relating to mankind.

<term>Reconciliation</term>: The restoration of friendly relations between God and man.

### Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
Kk 3
<meta>catchword: That</meta>

*...necessary for the faithful, who cannot reach the Kingdom of Heaven without performing them, considering that God has prepared them so that we should walk in them; thus we must flee vices and apply ourselves to Christian virtues, employing fasts and every other means that can serve us in such a Holy thing.* <note>original Italian: "necessarie a' fideli...". The Waldensians emphasize that while works do not "save," a saved person must naturally perform them.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Their necessity.</margin> ...are necessary, so that without the practice of the same they cannot reach the Kingdom of Heaven, seeing that God has prepared them so that we should always walk in them; and that we must consequently flee sins and dispose ourselves toward Christian virtues, using for that purpose both fasting and all other similar means that can be of service to us in such a holy matter.

---

### XXII.

<column-break/>

*That although our good works cannot merit anything, the Lord will not fail to recompense you with eternal life through a merciful continuation of His grace and by virtue of the immutable constancy of the promises He has made to us.* <note>The term "merit" refers to the Catholic doctrine that good deeds earn points toward salvation; the Waldensians argue instead that eternal life is a gift based on God's promise, not a wage earned by the believer.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Their fruits:</margin> That, although our good works can merit nothing, God will nevertheless not fail to reward the same with eternal life through a gracious perseverance of His grace and by the power of the unchangeable durability of His promises, which He Himself has made to us concerning this.

---

### XXIII.

<column-break/>

*That those who possess eternal life, as a consequence of their faith and their good works, ought to be considered as holy and glorified, praised for their virtues, and imitated in all the beautiful actions of their lives; but not adored, nor invoked, since one must pray only to one God through Jesus Christ.*

<column-break/>

<margin>And honor.</margin> That those who are already in possession of eternal happiness, on account of their faith and good works, must indeed be held as holy and glorified, praised for their virtue, and strictly followed in all the excellent works of their lives; but nonetheless never prayed to, or invoked; since no one, but God alone, through Jesus Christ, may be worshipped. <note>This marks a significant departure from Roman Catholic practice regarding the "Invocation of Saints."</note>

---

### XXIV.

<column-break/>

*That God has gathered for Himself a Church in the world for the salvation of men, and that she has only one single head and foundation, namely Jesus Christ.*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Church and her head.</margin> That the Lord, for the salvation of mankind, has willed to gather a Church in the world, and that the same has only one head and foundation, namely the Lord Jesus Christ.

---

### XXV.

<column-break/>

*That this Church is the company of the Faithful, who, having been elected by God before the foundation of the world and called by a holy vocation, come to unite themselves to follow the Word of God, believing that which He teaches therein and living in His fear.* <note>The "holy vocation" refers to the "effectual calling" or the internal pull of the Holy Spirit leading a person to faith.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Description of the Church.</margin> That this Church is the society of the Believers, who, being chosen by God before the foundation of the world and called with a holy calling, come to unite themselves to follow God’s Word, believing that which He teaches us in the same and living in His holy fear.

<meta>This page continues the confession of faith of the Waldensian Church. The previous page discussed the necessity of good works and the rejection of the idea that they can merit salvation. This page transitions into the doctrine of the Church and the Sacraments, specifically defining the nature of the Church as perpetual and detailing the two sacraments recognized by the Waldensians: Baptism and the Holy Supper (Eucharist).</meta>

<header>General Memorial-Record.</header>

### XXVI.

<margin>That which cannot perish.</margin>
*That this Church cannot fail to exist nor be reduced to nothing, but that it must be perpetual.* <note>original Italian: "Che quella Chiesa non puole mancar..." This reflects the Waldensian belief in their own ancient lineage and the theological concept of the "Indefectibility of the Church"—that Christ's true church will never vanish from the earth.</note>

<column-break/>

That this Church cannot diminish in such a way that it would fall away entirely to nothing, but that it must continually remain standing.

---

### XXVII.

<margin>The faithful must adhere to it.</margin>
*That everyone must join themselves to it and keep themselves in its communion.* <note>original Italian: "Che ognuno à quella deve congiungerfi..."</note>

<column-break/>

That everyone is obliged to join the same and to hold themselves to her community.

---

### XXVIII.

<margin>Of the Sacraments.</margin>
*That God does not only instruct us by His Word, but that He has furthermore ordained Sacraments to be joined to it as means to unite us to Christ and participate in His benefits; and that there are no more than two, common to all members of the Church under the New Testament, namely Baptism and the Holy Supper.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' Iddio non ci ammaestra solo..."</note>

<column-break/>

That God does not only instruct us through His Holy Word, but that He has established the signs of faith <term>signs of faith (Geloof-teykenen): the visible, physical elements used in the sacraments that represent spiritual grace</term> alongside it, to add them as means to the same, through which we might be united with our Savior and thus have a share and enjoyment in all His benefits: that there are also no more than two common to all the members of the Church under the New Covenant, to wit, Baptism and the Holy Supper.

---

### XXIX.

<margin>Of Holy Baptism.</margin>
*That He has established that of Baptism for a testimony of our adoption and that we are washed therein of our sins in the blood of Jesus Christ and renewed in holiness of life.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' egli ha stabilito quello del Battesimo..."</note>

<column-break/>

That He Himself has established that of Baptism as a proof and testimony that we are accepted by Him as children <note>This refers to "adoption" into the family of God.</note> and likewise through the blood of the Lord Jesus washed of our sins, as well as being renewed and recreated to holiness of life.

---

### XXX.

<margin>Of the Holy Supper.</margin>
*That He has established that of the Holy Supper, or Eucharist, for the nourishment of our souls, so that with a true and living faith through the incomprehensible power of the Holy Spirit, effectively eating His flesh and drinking His blood and joining ourselves most closely and inseparably to Christ, in Him and through Him we may have spiritual and eternal life. And so that everyone may clearly see what we believe in this chapter, we add here the same expressions that are found in the prayer we make before Communion, in our Liturgy, or form of celebrating the Holy Supper, and in the* <note>original Italian: "Ch' egli ha stabilito quello della santa Cena..."</note>

<column-break/>

That He has likewise given that of the Holy Night-meal, or *Eucharist*, (that is, Thanksgiving-meal) <note>original Dutch: "Dank-maal". The term "Eucharist" comes from the Greek word for "thanksgiving."</note> for the nourishment of our souls, so that we, with a true and living faith through the incomprehensible power of the Holy Spirit, truly eating His flesh and likewise drinking His blood—through which we are very closely and inseparably united with the Lord Jesus—might have eternal life in Him and through Him. ### XXXI.

<margin>Of the Teachers.</margin>
*That it is necessary that the Church have Pastors, judged well-instructed and of good life by those who have the authority, as much for preaching the Word of God as for administering the Sacraments and watching over the flock of Christ according to the rules of a good and holy Discipline, together with the Elders and Deacons, according to the usage of the Ancient Church.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' egli è neceſſario, che la Chieſa habbia de' Paſtori..."</note>

<column-break/>

That it is very necessary that the Church have her Teachers or <term>Shepherds (Harders): a common term for pastors, emphasizing their role in guiding the "flock" of the congregation.</term>, who are judged to be of good learning and life by those who have the management thereof; both to proclaim the Word of the Lord everywhere, as to properly distribute the Holy Sacraments and—according to the usage of the Ancient Church and following the prescription of a good and holy Church-discipline—to watch over Christ’s flock alongside the <term>Elders (Ouderlingen): lay leaders responsible for the spiritual oversight and discipline of the local church</term> and <term>Deacons (Diakenen): officers in the church dedicated to the care of the poor and the temporal needs of the community.</term>

### XXXII.

<margin>Of the Authorities.</margin>
*That God has established Kings, Princes, and Magistrates for the government of Peoples; that peoples must be subject and obedient to them by virtue of that ordination, not only for wrath, but also for conscience in all things, according to the Word of God, who is the King of Kings and the Lord of Lords.* <note>original Italian: "Ch' Iddio ha ſtabilito i Rè..." This article emphasizes that civil obedience is a religious duty, provided the laws do not contradict scripture.</note>

<column-break/>

That God has given Kings, Princes, and Authorities to rule the nations; that the people, by virtue of the aforementioned institution, must be obedient and subject to the same, not only because of punishment, but also for the sake of conscience in everything that corresponds with the Word of the Lord, who is a King of Kings and Lord of Lords.

# General Memorial-Script

<meta>catchword: Letter</meta>

### XXXIII.

*Finally, it is fitting to receive the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> as the fundamental writings of our faith and our devotions.*

*And for a more detailed declaration of what we believe, we reiterate here the protestation <note>original Italian: "proteſtatione," a formal public statement of faith or testimony</note> that we already published in 1603; namely, that we agree in sound Doctrine with all the Reformed Churches of France, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, and others, as it is represented in their Confessions, and even the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church (1530). By mentioning it, the Waldensians signal their desire for unity with all branches of the Reformation.</note> according to the declaration given by its author; and we promise to persevere in it by the grace of God, inviolably in both life and death, being prepared to subscribe to this eternal truth of God with our own blood, just as our ancestors have done since the time of the Apostles, and particularly in these last centuries. And therefore, we humbly pray all the Evangelical and Protestant Churches to hold us, despite our poverty and lowliness, as true members of the mystical body of Jesus Christ, who suffer for his name, and to continue toward us the help of their prayers to God and all other effects of their charity, as we have already abundantly experienced. For which we thank them with all possible humility, pleading with the Lord with all our heart that he himself might be their reward, spreading over them the most precious blessings of grace and glory in this life and in the one that is to come.*

<column-break/>

Finally, we are obliged to voluntarily accept the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the Ten Commandments as the foundational writings <note>original Dutch: "gront-ſchriften"</note> of our faith and religious duties.

Now, for a broader declaration of what we believe, we renew here our old testimony, which we already published in print in the year 1603; namely, that we agree in the sound Doctrine with all the Reformed Churches of France, England, the Netherlands, Germany, the Swiss, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, and others, just as the same is contained in the Confessions of them all, and even in that of Augsburg <note>The Augsburg Confession</note> according to the explanation of its author; and we promise to remain steadfast therein through God's grace, without transgression, in life and death, being ready to sign that eternal divine Truth with our own blood; just as our ancestors have also primarily done from the times of the Apostles and in these last centuries. For which reason we also very humbly request all the Protestant and Evangelical Churches that they, notwithstanding our poverty and contemptibility, please consider us as true members of the spiritual body of our Lord Jesus, who presently suffer for his name; and to persevere in the help of their prayers to God and the other fruits of their love, just as we have abundantly experienced them until now. For which we also thank them with all humility, praying to the Lord with all our heart that he himself might be their prize and reward, pouring out over them his most precious blessings of grace and glory in this and the other life.

# Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

*A brief defense regarding those points of which the Roman Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to high-ranking Catholic theologians and academics.</note> are accustomed to accuse our Churches and the other Reformed Churches; which are likewise condemned by all as being full of impiety and worthy of the abomination of Christians.*

We are ordinarily accused of believing:

1. That God is the author of Sin.
2. That God is not Omnipotent.
3. That Jesus Christ was not impeccable <note>original Italian: "impeccabile" — incapable of sinning</note>.
4. That Jesus Christ fell into despair upon the cross.
5. That man is like a stick or a stone in the actions to which he is moved for salvation by the Spirit of God.
6. That by virtue of predestination it is a matter of indifference whether one lives well or poorly.
7. That good works are not necessary for Salvation.
8. That penance and the Confession of sins are absolutely condemned among us.
9. That it is proper to reject fasts and other mortifications in order to live in dissolution <note>original Italian: "dissolutione" — a life of moral looseness or lack of restraint</note>.
10. That it is lawful for everyone to interpret the Scripture at their own whim and according to the movements of a private Spirit.
11. That the Church can fail entirely and be reduced to nothing.
12. That Baptism is of no necessity.
13. That in the Sacrament of the Eucharist there is no real communion with Jesus Christ, but only symbols.
14. That it is not proper to submit to Kings, Princes, and Magistrates, and to obey them.
15. That because we do not invoke the Holy Virgin and the men already glorified <note>The Saints</note>, we despise them; whereas we consider them blessed, worthy of praise and imitation, and particularly—
