### XXXIII.

*Finally, it is fitting to receive the Apostles' Creed <note>The "Simbolo degli Apostoli" or Apostles’ Creed is a foundational statement of Christian belief used across many denominations.</note>, the Lord's Prayer, and the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> as the fundamental writings of our faith and our devotions.*

*And for a more extensive declaration of what we believe, we reiterate here the protestation that we already had printed in 1603; namely, that we agree in sound doctrine with all the Reformed Churches of France, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, and others, as it is represented in their Confessions, and even to the Augsburg Confession according to the declaration given by its author <note>original: "Confessione d'Augusta." This refers to the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church. The "declaration by the author" likely refers to Philipp Melanchthon’s 1540 "Variata" edition, which was more favorable to Reformed views on the Eucharist.</note>; and we promise to persevere therein by the grace of God, inviolably in both life and death, being prepared to subscribe to this eternal truth of God with our own blood, as our ancestors have done since the time of the Apostles, particularly in these last centuries. And therefore, we humbly pray all the Evangelical and Protestant Churches to hold us, despite our poverty and lowliness, as true members of the mystical body of Jesus Christ, who suffer for His name, and to continue the help of their prayers toward God and all other effects of their charity, as we have already abundantly experienced. For which we thank them with all possible humility, supplicating the Lord with all our heart that He may be their reward, pouring upon them the most precious blessings of grace and glory in this life and in that which is to come.*

<column-break/>

Finally, we are obliged to freely accept the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the Ten Commandments as the foundational writings of our faith and godliness.

Now, for a broader declaration of what we believe, we renew here our old testimony, which we already published in print in the year 1603: namely, that we agree with all the Reformed Churches of France, England, the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, and others in the sound Doctrine, as the same is contained in the Confessions of them all, and even also in that of Augsburg <note>The Dutch text uses "Ausburg," a common spelling for Augsburg at the time.</note> according to the explanation of its author; and we promise to remain steadfast therein by God’s grace without transgression through life and death, being ready to sign that eternal divine Truth with our own blood; as our ancestors from the times of the Apostles and in these last centuries have also primarily done. Therefore, we wish to have all the Protestant and Evangelical Churches most humbly prayed that they please—notwithstanding our poverty and contemptibility—to hold us as true members of the spiritual body of our Lord Jesus, who presently suffer for His name, and to persevere in the help of their prayers to God and the other fruits of their love, as we have experienced them abundantly until now. For which we also thank the same with all humility, praying the Lord from our whole heart that He Himself be their reward and recompense, pouring over them His most precious blessings of grace and glory in this and the other life.

*Whosoever wishes to be saved, before all things, it is necessary to hold the Catholic <note>The word "Catholic" here refers to the "universal" or "general" Christian faith, rather than the Roman Catholic Church specifically.</note> Faith, which, if anyone does not keep whole and without doubt, he shall perish eternally. But this is the Catholic Faith: that we honor one God in Trinity, and the Trinity in unity, neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance. For there is one person of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit. The Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated, the Holy Spirit is uncreated. The Father is infinite <note>original: "mesurivol"; literally "unmeasurable."</note>, the Son is infinite, the Holy Spirit is infinite. The Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, the Holy Spirit is eternal. And yet they are not three eternals, but one eternal, just as there are not three infinites and three uncreated. Similarly, the Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Holy Spirit is almighty; and yet they are not three almighties, but one almighty. So the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and yet they are not three Gods, but one God. So the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, the Holy Spirit is Lord; and yet they are not three Lords, but one Lord. For just as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person to be God and Lord, so by the Catholic Religion, we are forbidden to say there are three Gods or three Lords. Truly, to finally close this long chapter, everyone who has even a spark of ingenuity and reason remaining must frankly admit with me that in matters of the Religion and Faith of any people, no one can know them better, no one regarding the same may be sooner believed, nor can more powerful evidence and documents be demanded from anyone, than from their own Catechisms <note>The Dutch "Vraag-oeffeningen" refers to the practice of learning through sets of questions and answers.</note> and Instructions in the Faith, which they cause their youth to consume as if with their mother's milk; the Church teachings delivered to them; the solemn Confessions of Faith which they hold as a rule <term>rule of faith: a standard or guideline for measuring doctrine</term> for their godliness; those which they hand over to their Sovereigns, which they make known throughout the whole world, and finally, those which they dare to seal with the shedding of their own blood. Nevertheless, to doom the Lords of the Roman persuasion to an eternal silence—those who, being ashamed to admit that they have so terribly persecuted and still daily persecute those poor Waldensians because of their Doctrine (which is so holy, so pure, and in such agreement with the Gospel), and who still do not cease to depict them as detestable Heretics and people of a wicked life—I shall, for the sake of abundance, go and clearly show through the most powerful Declarations one could ever wish for, drawn from the books of their greatest persecutors, that they have never held any other Doctrine than that which I have recounted of them until now, and that their holy conduct, defined by a Church Discipline and governed by those wonderful **Barbes** <note original: "Barbes">A specific Waldensian term for their pastors, derived from the word for "uncle" to distinguish them from "fathers" (priests).</note>, or Teachers, has always corresponded wonderfully well with the same.

While the wickedness and cunning of the haters of the Waldensians has at all times set everything in motion that earthly prudence could prescribe to make the world believe that their Doctrine was entirely heretical and monstrous—twisting it in a thousand and more ways and imputing to them a great number of various dogmas which they themselves loathed, let alone that they would teach them to others—it is my intention (so that they never again need to think they can make those who do not yet know the truth believe that what we have drawn from their own Writings is feigned or in any way twisted) to transcribe here from some books of their fiercest and most notorious enemies that which they, according to their own will, have written of their Doctrine themselves. Regarding which I also dare to assure myself that those who please to take the trouble to compare the same with all the samples we have drawn from the Waldensian Writings themselves, will have to sincerely admit with me that it is entirely one and the same Doctrine. # Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches.
[Signature Mark: Ll 3]

In the preface, he reveals that he had held the management of affairs under the three previous kings, namely Louis XI, Charles VIII, and Louis XII. Therefore, the whole world believed that a man of such great age, of such rare experience, of such great authority, and of such outstanding learning would be the most capable person to bring the wandering Waldensians of the Valleys back to the bosom of the Roman Church. For this purpose, he was also promoted from being the Bishop of Marseille to become the Archbishop of Turin <note>This refers to Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), a noted jurist and theologian who wrote against the Waldensians.</note>, so that, having the Waldensians under his own ecclesiastical jurisdiction, he might have a better opportunity to either convert or exterminate them. Being now their Archbishop, he wrote a book against them, which I still have in my possession; it was also almost entirely transcribed in the writing on the Waldensian Doctrine by Jacobus Cappel <note>Jacques Cappel (1570–1624) was a French Protestant professor of Hebrew and theology at Sedan.</note>, printed at Sedan in the year 1618. ,, Page 6. They say that they owe no tithes or first-fruits to the Clergy.
,, Page 7. They say that the consecration of churches, indulgences <note>The Roman Catholic practice of granting remission of temporal punishment for sins.</note>, and other similar blessings are but inventions of false priests.
,, Page 7. They also do not observe any Holy Days <note>Feast days dedicated to specific saints.</note>.
,, Page 7. They say that mortal men have no need for the help of the Saints, as their Christ is abundantly sufficient for them in everything.
,, Page 7. They say that everything spent to release the souls of the deceased from the punishments of Purgatory is useless, lost, superstitious, etc.

,, Page 54. They do not hold that the faithful are in any way obliged to give the Angel's greeting to the Mother of God <note>The "Ave Maria" or "Hail Mary" based on Luke 1:28.</note>, saying that it has no likeness to a prayer, but is merely a bare greeting. But it is in fact to ward off all worship of the Holy Virgin, as they say it is as unlawful to serve and pray to her as to all the other Saints.
,, Page 54. They say that no kind of Prayer may ever be accepted unless it appears that the same was composed by a specific writer <note>Meaning a biblical author.</note> and likewise approved by God, if one intends to obtain anything from God through it. Their Barbes have frequently taught this to abolish the service of the Virgin Mary and other Saints.
,, Page 56. They assert that the blessings of the Priests have no power.
,, Page 58. They say that one may not use holy water in the Church, because our Savior or the Apostles did not do or command the same, as if one were not allowed to say or do anything but what we read was done by them.
,, Page 61. They assert that Indulgences are of no value, even though they are openly granted by the Church.
,, Page 66. They say that the souls of the deceased, as soon as they depart from their bodies, immediately receive either joy or punishment without being tried in any way by any purification; and that the Clergy, blinded by their greed, have invented the Purgatory <note>The original uses "Suyver-burg," literally "Purification-fortress," as a mocking term for Purgatory.</note> near to Hell.
,, Page 68. They say that the Saints cannot know what happens here below on the earth.
,, Page 68. They reject and detest to the highest degree the Images and Crucifixes that we worship.
,, Page 73. They make no distinction between *Adoration of latria* <note>original: "Adoratio latriæ" — the supreme worship offered to God alone.</note> and *Adoration of dulia* <note>original: "Adoratio Douliæ" — the veneration or honor given to saints and angels.</note>.
,, Page 83. They assert that a lie is always a mortal sin.

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

Thus far, we have briefly transcribed from the book of the aforementioned Claude de Seyssel <note>Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), Archbishop of Turin and a prominent jurist and theologian.</note>, Archbishop of Turin, that which he relates concerning the teachings of the Waldensians—both when he allows them to speak for themselves and when he says of them what he pleases. The authority of such a distinguished man, who must have been over eighty years old when he wrote against them—having served under the three predecessors of King Francis I <note>Francis I of France (reigned 1515–1547). The predecessors would be Louis XI, Charles VIII, and Louis XII.</note>; who was endowed with such long experience and had the Waldensians living within his own Diocese—should be more than sufficient to fully prove the nature of their doctrine. However, since divine Providence has also placed in our hands a certain letter which one Claude Coussord <note>Claude Coussord was a 16th-century theologian at the University of Paris who defended the Catholic faith against "heresy."</note>, a theologian of the University of Paris, wrote to the said Archbishop regarding his stirring book against the Waldensians, in which he briefly runs through their entire doctrine, we can likewise see how he carries himself therein. "My Lord," he says to that <margin>*Testimony of Claude Coussord.*</margin> Archbishop, "In the book that you wrote against the Waldensians with the King’s privilege, granted on the 27th of February <note>original: "Sprockelmaant" (an archaic Dutch term for February).</note> 1547, you have these words at the beginning: 'I first intended to present the heresies of the Waldensians, having gathered them together, in a plain manner, just as they were equally condemned by a Roman Council held in the year 1211 and by the Friar Minor Rainier <note>Rainier Saccho (c. 1200–1259), a former Waldensian who became an Inquisitor and wrote a famous treatise against his former sect.</note>, who practiced the suppression of heresy two hundred and ninety-six years ago,' etc."

"The first error of the Waldensians, you say on page 41, is the despising of Ecclesiastical power.

"Page 42. The Waldensians maintain: 1. that they alone are the Church of Christ and his disciples; 2. that they consequently possess Apostolic power, as well as the Keys to bind and loose; 3. that the Roman Church is the Whore of Babylon; 4. and that all those, even the Clergy, who have given her their obedience since the times of Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335). The Waldensians traditionally believed the Church fell into corruption during his reign when it accepted the "Donation of Constantine" (wealth and temporal power).</note>, are all equally damned.

"Page 44. They say that the miracles performed throughout the Roman Church are lies, because they themselves do none. <margin>*False miracles.*</margin>

"Page 47. They reject all Saints’ days and Fast days, Vigils, the Priesthood, all Consecrations, Church Services, and similar things. <margin>*Against all Roman Traditions.*</margin>

"Page 48. They say that the Consecration of churches and cemeteries arose only through the greed of the Clergy, who made significant profit thereby.

"Page 51. They reject the Sacrament of Confirmation; and in place of that sign of faith, their Teachers merely lay hands upon their students.

"Page 52. They say that the Bishops, the Clergy, and other Religious <note>Monks and friars in holy orders.</note> are the Scribes and Pharisees, very cruel persecutors of the Apostles.

"Page 53. They say that the Body and Blood of our Lord is not a true sign of faith, but only consecrated or blessed Bread, which is called the body of Christ through such a figurative way of speaking, just as it is said somewhere that 'the Rock was Christ' <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 10:4: "and that rock was Christ."</note>.

"Page 58. They say that a Priest, being a sinner and therefore bound himself, cannot loose or in any way absolve.

"Page 60. They also reject Extreme Unction <note>The anointing of the sick/dying with holy oil.</note>, saying that it is a curse rather than a Sacrament. Marriage is also to them a 'beaten whoredom' <note>harlotry or fornication</note> when one does not live moderately within it.

"Page 60. They praise Moderation above all measure.

"Page 63. They say that there is no Purgatory, but that the dead go immediately either to Heaven or to Hell: consequently, the intercessions made in the Church for the deceased have no use in the world."

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.
Mm 2
<meta>catchword: That-</meta>

...against them, and they are acquitted by the aforementioned Archbishop, who had them under his ecclesiastical jurisdiction, who lived close to them, who saw them daily in his Diocese, and who, having reached a very great age as he then had, and having debated with them and written against them, must have had a firmer knowledge of them. We can see this, among other things, from these samples: While Claudius Couffard <note>Claude Coussord, a 16th-century Parisian theologian.</note> dares to say on page 78 *that they do not accept the Old Testament, but only the Gospels*; Claudius Seissel <note>Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), Archbishop of Turin, who wrote 'Against the Sect of the Waldensians'.</note> ensures the contrary, specifically on page 4, *that they accept nothing else than what is written in the Old and New Testaments*. This concerns their Doctrine; and it is the same regarding their life. When Claudius Couffard on page 60 dares to accuse them, *that they so praise Moderation, that they simultaneously deem Excess permissible*; Claudius Seissel answers him on page 48 on their behalf with these words: *They keep the Christian commandments better than the majority of our own persuasion. I set aside the things they teach against our Faith and Worship. Regarding the rest, they lead a holier life than all other Christians. They do not swear an oath unless they are forced to do so. They faithfully keep their Promises and live in great want and poverty.*

Let us also add here the remarkable testimony of an eminent Pope, I mean that of Aeneas Sylvius, who was Pope of Rome under the name of Pius II, and at the same time a great enemy of the poor Waldensians, as can be read in his Bohemian histories in the 35th chapter, and transcribed by *Jakobus Picolomineus Comment. lib. 6.*, by *Anthonius Bonfinius in Rer. Hungaric. Decad.*, and by *Bernh. Lutzenburg in the Catalog of Heresies, under the word Waldenses*. He speaks there only of those of Bohemia, whom he describes as descendants of the Valley Waldensians; using these words:

> <note>original: "Proruperunt in blasphemias &c..."</note> They burst forth into blasphemies, etc. Although they could perhaps have spoken ill of some lazy and vicious Priests, they began to bark at all Priests without distinction, and departing from the Catholic Church, they embraced the impious and insane Sect of the Waldensians. The dogmas of this pestilential and long-since condemned Faction are:

1. That the Roman Prelate <note>The Pope</note> is equal to the other Bishops.

2. That there is no distinction among Priests; that it is not dignity but merit of life that makes a Priest superior.

3. That souls, upon departing from the bodies, are either immediately plunged into eternal punishments or attain perpetual joys.

4. That no fire of Purgatory <note>The Catholic concept of a place of purification after death.</note> is to be found.

5. That it is vain to pray for the dead, and a mere invention of priestly greed.

6. That images of God and the Saints should be destroyed.

<column-break/>

<margin>Another testimony from Aeneas Sylvius.</margin>

They have burst forth in slanders, and where they could easily have spoken ill of some weak and wicked Priests, they have begun to bark at them without distinction, and departing from the Universal Church, they have chosen to follow the godless and mad Schism of the Waldensians. The teaching of this pestilential gathering, which has already been condemned for a long time, consists primarily of the following points:

That the Roman Bishop is no more than all the others.

That there is no difference between Priests: and that a better life, and not dignity, exalts one above the other.

That souls, as soon as they depart from the body, either immediately sink into certain punishments or receive eternal joys as their portion.

That no Hellish Purifying-fire <note>original: "Hels Suyver-vier", referring to Purgatory.</note> is to be found.

That it is futile to pray for the Dead and a blatant invention of the greed of the Priests.

That the Images of God and all Saints must be destroyed.

# General Memorial-Chronicle

7. <note>original: "Aquarum, Palmarumque benedictiones irridendas."</note> That the blessings of water and palms are to be mocked.

8. That the religious orders of mendicants <note>The "begging" orders of monks, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans, who lived on alms.</note> were invented by evil demons.

9. That priests ought to be poor, content with alms alone.

10. That the free preaching of the Word of God is open to everyone.

11. That no capital <note>mortal</note> sin should be tolerated, even for the sake of avoiding a greater evil.

12. That whoever is guilty of a mortal fault should possess neither secular nor ecclesiastical dignity, nor should he be obeyed.

13. That Confirmation, which the Pontiffs <note>Bishops or Popes</note> perform with chrism <note>consecrated oil</note>, and Extreme Unction <note>the "Last Rites" for the dying</note> are not to be included among the Sacraments of the Church.

14. That auricular <note>whispered into the ear of a priest</note> confession is a trifle; it is enough for each person to confess his sins to God in his own chamber.

15. That baptism should be received in the water of a river without any added mixture of Holy Oil.

16. That the use of cemeteries is an empty practice invented for the sake of profit: it matters not where human bodies are covered by the earth.

17. That the temple of the wide-reaching God is the world itself; those who build churches, monasteries, and oratories confine His majesty, as if the Divine goodness were found more favorably within them.

18. That priestly vestments, altar ornaments, palls, corporals, patens, and vessels of this sort are of no importance.

19. That a priest in any place and at any time can prepare the Holy Body of Christ and administer it to those who ask: it suffices if he only says the Sacramental words.

20. That the prayers of the Saints, reigning in Heaven with Christ, are sought in vain, as they cannot help us.

<column-break/>

That the consecration of Water and Palm branches is ridiculous.

That evil spirits invented the Order of the Mendicant Monks.

That priests must be poor and satisfied with alms.

That the proclamation of God's Word stands open and free to everyone.

That one may never commit a cardinal sin, even if it were to avoid a greater evil.

That those who have committed a mortal sin may hold neither worldly nor ecclesiastical offices, and that one must not be obedient to them.

That Confirmation, which the Pope brings about through anointing, and the Holy Unction <note>Last Rites</note> can in no way be counted among the Sacraments of the Church.

That Auricular Confession is but a trifle; and that it can fully suffice for each to lament his sins to God on his bed.

That Baptism must be served and received with pure stream-water without any added mixture of Holy Oil.

That the vain use of graveyards was invented through greed: and that all bodies are equally worthy once the womb of the earth contains them.

That the world itself is the House of God, whose power extends everywhere; and that those who build Churches, Cloisters, and Houses of Prayer—as if His divine goodness were enjoyed there more amply than elsewhere—in some way limit His great almightiness.

That priestly garments, the decoration of altars or consecration-blocks, stoles, tunics, chalices, platters, and other such vessels can be of no use anywhere.

That the priest at all times and places can prepare the holy body of Christ and distribute it to those who come to request it; since it is enough alone that he merely speaks the sacramental words, as they call them, over it.

That the favor of the Saints, who reign in Heaven with Christ, is obtained by men in vain, because they can do them no service.

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

21. <note>original: "In canonicis horis cantandis, dicendisque frustra tempus teri."</note> That time is fruitlessly wasted in the singing and saying of the canonical hours <term>The set times of day—such as Matins or Vespers—appointed for prayer and the reading of the breviary.</term>.

22. <note>original: "Nulla die ab opere cessandum, nisi quæ Dominica nunc apellatur."</note> That one's work need not be stopped on any day, except for that which is presently called the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>.

23. <note>original: "Celebritates Sanctorum prorsus rejiciendas."</note> That the feast days of the Saints must be utterly rejected.

24. <note>original: "Jejuniis quoque, ab Ecclesia institutis, nihil inesse meriti."</note> That there is no merit in fast-days, even if they were instituted by the Church.

<column-break/>

That in the reading and singing of the hours, one’s time is completely and unprofitably wasted.

That one need not cease their work on any day, except for the one currently called Sunday.

That one must entirely reject the feast days of the Saints.

That fasting days are of no merit, even if they have been established by the Church.

---

The historiographers of Magdeburg relate in their twelfth *Century* <term>Referring to the "Magdeburg Centuries," a massive 13nd-century Protestant work organized by centuries of church history.</term> or Hundred-year cycle, in the 18th chapter, pages 1206 and 1207, that the Waldensians hold these following positions, just as they present them *from an ancient manuscript book*:

<column-break/>

1. <note>original: "In articulis Fidei summam esse Sacræ Scripturæ autoritatem..."</note> In the articles of Faith, the authority of the Holy Scripture is supreme, and for that reason, it is the rule of judgment: so that whatever does not agree with the word of God must rightly be rejected and avoided.

2. <note>original: "Patrum & Conciliorum dogmata..."</note> The dogmas of the Church Fathers and the Councils are to be approved only insofar as they agree with the Word of God.

3. <note>original: "Sacrarum Scripturarum Lectionem..."</note> The reading and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures is free and necessary for all people, both the laity and the clergy; indeed, the writings of the Prophets and Apostles should be read rather than the commentaries of men.

4. <note>original: "Duo esse Ecclesiæ Christi Sacramenta..."</note> There are but two Sacraments in the Church of Christ: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

5. <note>original: "Utriusque speciei usum..."</note> The use of both kinds <note>Referring to the practice of the "laity" receiving both the bread and the wine during Communion, which was then reserved only for priests in the Catholic Church.</note> for Priests and Laity was instituted by Christ.

6. <note>original: "Missas esse impias..."</note> That Masses are impious, and it is madness to perform masses for the dead.

7. <note>original: "Purgatorium esse figmentum hominum..."</note> Purgatory is an invention of men: for believers enter into eternal life, while unbelievers enter into eternal damnation.

8. <note>original: "Sanctorum mortuorum invocationes..."</note> The invocation of dead Saints and their worship is nothing but pure idolatry.

9. <note>original: "Romanam Ecclesiam esse Meretricem Babylonicam."</note> That the Roman Church is the Babylonian Whore <note>A derogatory term used by reformers, referencing the Book of Revelation, to describe the perceived corruption of the Papacy.</note>.

10. <note>original: "Papæ & Episcopis non obtempe-"</note> That one [should] not obey the Pope and the Bishops...

<column-break/>

<margin>And that from the Centuries of Magdeburg.</margin>
That in all the main points of Faith, the authority of the Holy Scripture alone must hold place, and that it is therefore a rule of conduct by which to judge, so that everything that does not agree with God’s Word must rightly be rejected and avoided.

That the teachings of the Holy Church Fathers and the Church Councils can only be accepted and approved insofar as they agree with God’s Word.

That the reading and knowledge of the Holy Scripture is permitted and necessary for all people, both laypeople and clergy; indeed, that the writings of the Holy Prophets and Apostles ought to be leafed through and handled rather than the new books and fables of men.

That there are only two Sacraments in Christ’s Church: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

That the receiving of the latter under both forms <note>bread and wine</note> was instituted by our Savior for both Priests and laypeople.

That the Masses are very ungodly, and that it is madness to perform them for the dead.

That Purgatory is a find and institution of men, since the believers receive eternal life and the unbelievers receive damnation as their portion.

That the calling upon the deceased Saints and the worship of images is nothing other than simple idolatry.

That the Roman Church is the Whore of Babylon.

That one [should not obey] the Pope and his Bishops...

12. <note>original: "Ecclesiam Christi esse, quæ sincerum Christi Verbum audiat & Sacramentis, ab ipso institutis, utatur, ubicunque locorum ea existat."</note> *That the Church of Christ is that which hears the sincere Word of Christ and uses the Sacraments instituted by Him, wherever in the world it may exist.*

13. <note>original: "Vota esse hominum figmenta, Sodomam nutrientia."</note> *That vows are human figments, nurturing Sodom.* <note>A reference to the biblical city of Sodom, here implying that monastic vows of celibacy lead to immorality.</note>

16. <note>original: "Conjugium Sacerdotum esse licitum & necessarium."</note> *That the marriage of Priests is lawful and necessary.*

...one must not give them a hearing, because they are but wolves of Christ’s Church.

That the Pope is not permitted to exercise dominion over all the other Churches of our Savior, and that he in no way possesses the power of the spiritual and worldly sword.

That this alone is the Church of our Lord: that which hears only the pure Word of Christ and properly uses the tokens of faith <note>The Sacraments</note> instituted by Him, wherever they may be gathered.

That the monastic life was invented by men, and it does nothing but provide nourishment for Sodomy.

That the life of a monk is but a stinking carcass.

That all those superstitious dedications of churches, the memorials of the deceased, the blessing of other creatures, those pilgrimages, all those forced fast-days, all those unnecessary feast-days, all that shouting of unlearned people, and the maintenance of all those further ceremonies—which very markedly weaken and hinder the teaching and institutions of God’s Holy Word—are nothing other than devilish inventions.

That the marriage of Priests is necessary and permitted.

<meta>catchword: Writing-</meta>

*...they even ascribed it to the evil Demon.* <note>original Latin: "etiam malo Dæmoni adscribebant." This is the conclusion of a point from the previous page regarding the origin of certain church ceremonies.</note>

6. *They rejected the Roman Pontiff and the Prelates of the Church, to whom they believed no obedience was due.* <note>original Latin: "Rejiciebant Pontificem Romanum & Prælatos Ecclesiæ, quibus nullam obedientiam credebant esse debitam."</note>

Sylvester I was Pope during the reign of Constantine the Great; the Waldensians often dated the "fall" of the Church to the era when it first acquired worldly wealth and power.</note>

8. *They taught that the festivals of the Saints should not be tolerated in the Church; nor could the Saints be worshipped or invoked without offending God.* <note>original Latin: "Docebant, Sanctorum festa in Ecclesia non debere ferri; nec posse Sanctos sine Dei injuria coli aut invocari."</note>

9. *They taught that Masses, alms, prayers, and intercessions for the deceased were of no benefit to them at all.* <note>original Latin: "Docebant, Missas, eleemosynas, orationes & suffragia pro defunctis iisdem nihil omnino prodesse."</note>

10. *Finally, they so detested Images that they cried out that it was manifest idolatry for them to be tolerated in the Churches of Christians.* <note>original Latin: "Denique Imagines ita aversabantur, ut manifestam idololatriam clamarent, quod in Ecclesiis Christianorum tolerarentur."</note>

<column-break/>

...of which they made the evil Spirit the inventor.

They rejected the Pope of Rome and other Guardians of the Church, to whom they believed they owed no obedience.

They taught that the Church, from the time of Sylvester (who was Pope of Rome), had become so corrupted that all those who held to its faith would never reach salvation.

They taught that Holy Days could not be suffered in the Church; nor could the Saints be served or called upon without insulting God in the highest degree.

They taught that masses, alms, prayers, and atonements for the deceased were in no way advantageous to them.

Finally, they so loathed Images that they cried out that it was open idolatry to tolerate them in Christian Houses of God.

<margin>
And that from the Carthusian Peter of the Valley of Cernay.

A certain Peter, from the Monastery of the Valley of Cernay (*Vallis Sernensis* or *Clairvaux*) of the Carthusian or Cistercian order, also relates in his book, titled *History of the Albigensians and the Holy War* <note>original Latin: "Historia Albigensium & Sacri Belli"</note>, undertaken against them in the year 1209—that is, a History of the Albigensians and the holy war waged against them in the year 1209, in which he says on pages 1, 2, and following, that he was personally present. He says there, among other things, that the City of Toulouse in Languedoc was never free from that pestilential Heresy of the Waldensians, but that it was always *passed down from father to sons, with the poison of infidelity successively spreading* <note>original Latin: "a patre in filios fuit propagata, veneno infidelitatis successive diffuso"</note>; and a few lines later, that the Doctrine was *a torch of ancient wickedness* <note>original Latin: "antiquæ vitiositatis fax"</note>, whose beginning and origin he cannot find. Though he willfully falsifies his description in many parts, he was forced by the power of truth to record that they believed, among other things: I. That the Roman Church was nothing other than "a den of murderers and the Whore of the Apocalypse; II. That it was permitted to baptize with "rainwater and that the holy host of the body of our Lord "is but bread; indeed, that if it were true that one always "actually ate the body of our Savior, it would have been finished long ago, "even if it had been as large as the Alpine mountains; III. That Confirmation and Auricular Confession "are but trifles; IV. That, although they could not "reach the perfection of holiness of life, they nevertheless hoped "that they could be saved through their faith; and V. That they said the Images standing in the Churches "were nothing other than idolatry, etc. It is true that he also accuses them of permitting lewdness, and that they consider it enough for salvation to pray the Lord's Prayer just once shortly before death, etc. But in the main chapter, where we deal with the Discipline, Life, and Manners of the Waldensians, we shall so powerfully convict him of lying that he shall come away with nothing but shame; just as has already happened to him through the Declarations of those Bishops and others of the same kind.

I would never be finished if I had to gather here all that others...

# General Memorial-Script.

<column-break/>

...writers of the Roman Catholic persuasion have generally touched upon the Waldensian doctrine in their books. It would also be a quite unnecessary labor, since one could not wish for more powerful testimonies than the preceding ones, and those by contemporary Roman Catholics would be of even more weight, having been produced and given by their own renowned scholars, Archbishops, and Popes. Nevertheless, the reader should please keep in mind regarding these same authors that the opponents of the Waldensians speak therein, who generally overlook their best arguments or, in order to evade their force, commonly distort them; indeed, they often accuse them of things that do not apply and of which they have more than sufficiently cleared themselves, both through their own writings and through other more similar opponents—the one asserting that they hold to the doctrine of the Holy Apostles, briefly contained in their Creed, and the other that they are only to be punished because they so markedly slander the Roman Church.

And truly, Reinerus Sacco <note>An inquisitor and former Waldensian who wrote "Summa de Catharis et Pauperibus de Lugduno" around 1250.</note>, appointed by the Pope as an inquisitor <term>original: "Dwing-ketter" — literally a 'forcer of heretics,' a term used for an Inquisitor</term> against those of the Valleys and consequently fully credible in this matter, is himself forced to confess this, as can be seen in that book written by him against them and very often cited by us as a proof of antiquity in the continuation of this work; where he plainly makes this assurance, namely: *that the Waldensians believe all things well concerning God and understand all the articles contained in the Creed; they only blaspheme and hate the Roman Church and call it the church of the malignant* <note>original Latin: "quod Valdenſes bene omnia de Deo credunt & omnes articulos, qui in Symbolo continentur, capiunt; ſolam Romanam Eccleſiam blaſphemant & oderunt & vocant Eccleſiam malignantium."</note>.

<margin>
1. Worthy observation by the Inquisitor Reinerus Sacco.
</margin>

He subsequently also has them proceed thus: that the same began to fall away just after the times of Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (314–335 AD), often cited by reformers as the point when the Church became corrupted by worldly wealth under Constantine.</note>; that the poison of worldliness was already raging within her then; that she is the Whore of Revelation; that she has departed from the Evangelical doctrine to adhere to traditions. He adds further that they again reject Exorcisms; that they make a mockery of the Mass, as something which the Holy Apostles did not know; that they want the service in the mother tongue; as well as that the change of forms in the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note> does not happen through the hand of the consecrating Priest, but only in the mouth of him who receives the same worthily. And that all this came from the fact that they would accept nothing but the Bible—no Decretals <note>Papal decrees.</note>, no Legends, etc. That they reject the invocation of Saints, the worship of the Cross, Confirmation, the *Agnus Dei* <note>Wax medallions blessed by the Pope.</note>, Purgatory, etc.

With this agrees Roger of Hoveden <note>An English chronicler (died c. 1201).</note> on page 318, letter b, of the second part of his Annals, where he relates how the Waldensians had been accused of being Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> and Manicheans <note>A dualist sect that believed in two opposing powers of good and evil.</note>, and against those accusations they merely presented the following Confession, which I faithfully transcribe and translate here:

And from Hoveden.

### General Memorial-Writ

<margin>2. Remark concerning the same.</margin> One must also very carefully observe, regarding the faith of the Waldensians, that their opponents never attack what the Waldensians actually believe, but only what they *do not* believe; this serves as clear proof that they have not been able to critique or undermine the fundamental principles and truths of their faith in the slightest. Where, for instance, does one ever see attributed to them that they believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Or that there is one holy, universal Church; that the blood of our Savior cleanses them from all sin; that one must call upon God the Father through the merits of Jesus Christ, confess one's sins to the Lord, apply oneself to good works, and, alongside the teachers who proclaim God’s Holy Word, be obedient to the authorities and pay their taxes? They only say that they do not believe in the Saints; that they reject the Roman Church, as well as Purgatory, the invocation of the Saints, Auricular Confession <note>The practice of private confession to a priest</note>, the merit of works, and all works of supererogation <term>works of supererogation|Acts performed beyond what is required by God's law, which were believed to earn extra merit in the Catholic tradition</term>; that they will not submit themselves to the Pope or his clergy, etc. Thus, they are condemned and persecuted not so much for what they fundamentally believe, but only for what they, so to speak, *do not* believe. And truly, how could Rome have pursued them with fire and sword merely for the established articles of their faith, when Rome itself professes to believe those same things with one accord, and when the Pope himself boasts of believing what they believe? How then could he condemn them for what they actually believe? Indeed, they are never cast out for their true faith, except when people wish to make the world believe they hold views which they actually loathe with all their might—such as the claim that God is the cause of sin, that the Lord Jesus fell into despair on the Cross, that because of Predestination it matters not whether one does good or evil; that good works, the confession of sins, and repentance are not necessary; that they despise the Saints and even the Holy Virgin, etc. These are nonetheless the main points concerning which they themselves gave testimony at the end of their Confession of Faith, which they published in the year 1655 and which we have inserted previously.

### CHAPTER XIX.

->Regarding the Refutation of those who claim the Waldensians are descended from the ancient Arians, Manichaeans, Cathars, and other such Heretics.<-

It seems somewhat unnecessary, after so many proofs brought forward in defense of the Waldensian doctrine—drawn both from their opponents and from themselves—to occupy oneself with refuting various heresies with which some of their enemies have tried to smear them before the whole world. They say, most notably, that the Waldensians are nothing but a remnant of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, Manichaeans <note>A dualistic sect believing in two opposing gods of good and evil</note>, and Cathars <note>A medieval sect often confused with the Waldensians due to their shared opposition to Rome</note>, who, according to the opinion of various writers, are all one and the same. But since even today various people, seemingly even among the Reformed, hold this opinion—indeed, I have spoken to many such persons of status and learning who had perhaps only seen that Hovedenus <note>Roger of Hoveden, a 12th-century English chronicler</note>, in the second part of his *Annals* for the year 1176, so mingles the Arians, Manichaeans, and Waldensians together that he makes but one doctrine of them; or that one Jacob de Riberia <note>James de Ribera, a 16th-century scholar and secretary to the King of France</note> in his *Collection of the Histories of Toulouse* calls them a...

<margin>
*Of Du Haillan.*

# General Memorial Script

*Many wicked opinions were attributed to them, from which they were entirely foreign* <note>original Latin: "plures nefariæ affingerentur eis opiniones, a quibus omnino fuerant alieni"</note>: which carries this meaning; even if they had held some very bad views, this would not have brought down upon them the hatred of the Pope and other Princes as much as that freedom of speech with which they were accustomed to loathe and criticize the vices and unbridled morals of the aforementioned Princes and Clergy, and even the life and works of the Pope himself. And from this, it especially followed that they became a target for everyone's hatred; this was also the sole reason that many grizzly opinions were wrongly attributed to them, for which they had a total aversion. We can certainly add here what Nicolaus Vignierus <note>A 16th-century French historian and royal physician</note> testifies to us in good faith in his *Ecclesiastical Chronology* <note>original: "Kerkelik Tijt-boek"</note> regarding the year 1206. 

<margin>
Concerning Nicolaus Vignierus.
</margin>

*A certain man,* he says, *worthy of trust from Novempopulania in Gaul <note>An ancient Roman province in what is now Gascony, southwest France</note> affirmed to me that he had read one of their Confessions, written in the old Gascon language and presented to Chancellor Hospitalius <note>Michel de l'Hôpital (1507–1573), a French statesman known for his religious tolerance</note> shortly before the second civil disturbances in France; which completely agreed with the doctrine of the Waldensians, with no trace of Manichaeism <note>An ancient religion that taught a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness; its followers were often accused of rejecting the Old Testament</note> appearing. They expressly declared that they receive the Canonical books of both the Old and New Testaments, and reject all Doctrine that did not have its foundation in them or contained anything contrary to them:* <note>original Latin: "homo quidam... fide dignus e Gallia Novem-populana mihi affirmavit..."</note> that is, a certain honest and credible man from Guyenne <note>A historic province in southwest France</note> told me himself that he had read one of their Confessions, written in old Gascon and given to the Chancellor or Great-Seal-Keeper Hospitalius shortly before the second troubles of France, which completely corresponded with the Waldensian Doctrine, so that no resemblance to Manichaean Heresy was to be found in it. On the contrary, they testified very explicitly that they accepted all the Canonical books of the Old and New Covenant and rejected all Doctrine at once that was not grounded upon them, or also contained something contradictory. A little further down he speaks thus: *they repudiated and condemned all ceremonies, traditions, and ordinances of the Roman Church, saying that it was a den of thieves and the Whore of the Apocalypse:* <note>original Latin: "omnes Romanæ Ecclefiæ ceremonias... fpeluncam effe latronum & Meretricem Apocalypticam"</note> they rejected and damned all ceremonies, traditions, and institutions of the Roman Church, saying that it was a den of murderers and the Whore of Revelation. 

Let us not forget here, among so many good testimonies, that of the notorious Jesuit Gretserus <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625), a prominent Counter-Reformation scholar and polemicist</note>, 

<margin>
Concerning the Jesuit Gretserus.
</margin>

which he gives to the Waldensians on page 300 of the book he published against them. Likewise: you shall only do what I command you and you shall never add anything to it, or take away from it. The same Monk also says further, ,, that they use the passages of Isaiah 29 and Matthew 15 in the same matter; in vain do men serve me, teaching for all Doctrine the commandments ,, of men. Is it now conceivable, dear Reader, that if the Waldensians had been accustomed to reject the Old Covenant as Manichaeans do, that Jesuit would have forgotten to reproach and charge them with that? But he saw for himself that they served themselves all too well with it to liberate themselves from the Institutions of the Popes. From this can now also very easily be discovered the falsehood of the slander—invented not by Matthew Paris <note>A 13th-century English chronicler and Benedictine monk</note> himself, but by those whom he blindly followed—consisting of what he relates for the year 1203, namely that the Albigensians, being besieged, [told] the besiegers

Following the previous page’s discussion of the Albigensians and the dismissal of Manichaean charges, the author now uses the testimony of the Inquisitor Reynerus to show that even their enemies recognized their moral uprightness and orthodox belief in God, distinguishing them from more radical dualist groups.</meta>

->### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.<-

...teachers threw the Gospel back at them with these words: "Be gone with your law; we have nothing to do with it; go and be merry with it." Yet, on the contrary, they were persecuted above all because they read God’s Holy Word so diligently. Their enemies could not endure that they refused to be fed with [fanciful] Legends and Decretals <note>Decretals are papal letters that formulate decisions in church law; the author contrasts these man-made laws with the "Holy Word."</note>. This makes the author’s claims look entirely ridiculous, specifically another story he tells concerning the year 1234. He claims they renounced the Christian faith and denied the Mystery of the Incarnation of our Lord. He argues this because the Pope, who persecuted them cruelly, had asserted that to deny Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: The Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ during Mass</term>—as all the Waldensians did—was nothing other than lying about the Incarnation itself. 

Indeed, the frequently mentioned Reynerus <note>Rainier Sacconi (c. 1200–1262), a former member of the Cathars who became a Dominican friar and a prominent Inquisitor</note>—who, as we have discussed more extensively elsewhere, spent nearly his entire life enforcing the suppression of heresy against the Waldensians— <margin>Concerning Reynerus.</margin> also highly exonerates them from these false accusations. We can see this in his own testimony cited earlier. He uses a third reason to describe their sect as more dangerous than any other: *that, while all other sects (namely the Cathars and Manichaeans) cause horror through the enormity of their blasphemies against God, this sect of the Leonists <note>Leonists was a common name for the Waldensians, derived from their legendary founder Peter Waldo of Lyon</note> has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men and believe all things well concerning God, and all the articles contained in the Creed. They only blaspheme and hate the Roman Church, to which the common people are easily inclined to listen.* 

He further adds that this was the reason why, whenever he presided over the Inquisition to legally interrogate these heretics, he found forty-one of their schools in the Diocese of Padua and ten at Babac or Clemna. Shortly before this, he notes that in all the cities of Lombardy, in Provence, and in other kingdoms and lands, there were more classrooms of these same heretics than there were theologians. There were also many of their listeners who openly debated with the people, convinced them in formal disputes, and preached in the fields, in the marketplaces, and on the rooftops without anyone daring to disturb or prevent them. 

Now, it is clear that by "these heretics" he always means the Waldensians and never the Cathars or Manichaeans. This is evident from what he says later in the sixth chapter, pages 71 and 72 of his aforementioned work. He assigns to these heretics (whom he, along with many writers, considers to be one and the same) no more than six churches or congregations in total. He finally concludes regarding them, using these or similar words: "Say boldly, O reader, that in the whole world, of every kind, there are not four thousand Cathars to be found; *but those Believers and Faithful ones are without number*" <note>original Latin: "sed credentes & fideles illi sunt innumeri"</note>. 

But if you want to know, dear reader, who those may be whom that persecutor calls *Fideles* and *Credentes*—that is, properly "the Faithful" and "the Believing"—he will tell you himself in the ninth chapter of the mentioned book. There he gives a prescription for how one should behave in the interrogation of those who might ever be caught as Waldensian heretics. He explicitly maintains that it is not enough to address them thus: "Are you a heretic, or of the Leonist faction, etc.?" but that one must also, primarily, ask them if they are not *Fideles* or *Credentes*? By which he makes it clear enough that by those "Faithful" or "Believing" ones he means nothing else...

# General Memorial-Script

[page 240]

*...many wicked opinions were attributed to them, from which they were entirely foreign:* <note>original: "plures nefariæ affingerentur eis opiniones, a quibus omnino fuerant alieni"</note> which means that even if they had held some very poor views, this would not have brought down the hatred of the Pope and other Princes upon them as much as that freedom of speech with which they were accustomed to loathe and denounce the vices and unrestrained morals of the aforementioned Princes and Clergy, and even the life and works of the Pope himself. And it is from this, in particular, that they became a target of everyone's hatred; this was also the sole cause for many grizzly opinions being wrongly attributed to them, for which they actually felt a total aversion. We can well add here what Nicolaus Vignierus <note>Nicolas Vignier (1530–1596) was a French royal historiographer and physician.</note> testifies to us in good faith in his *Ecclesiastical Chronology* regarding the year 1206. <margin>Regarding Nicolaus Vignierus.</margin> *A certain man,* he says, *worthy of trust from Novempopulania in Gaul <note>Novempopulania was a Roman province in southwest France, later known as Gascony or Guyenne.</note> affirmed to me that he had read one of their Confessions, written in the old Gascon language and presented to Chancellor de l'Hôpital <note>Michel de l'Hôpital (1507–1573) was the Chancellor of France who sought to promote religious tolerance during the Wars of Religion.</note> shortly before the second civil disturbances in France; which plainly agreed with the doctrine of the Waldensians, with no trace of Manichaeism appearing at all. Indeed, they expressly declared that they received the canonical books of both the Old and New Testament, and rejected all doctrine which did not have a foundation in them or contained anything contrary to them:* <note>original Latin: "homo quidam, fide dignus e Gallia Novem-populana mihi affirmavit, legiffe fe unam ex Confessionibus eorum... nihil... Manichæifmi comparente vestigio."</note> that is, a certain honest and trustworthy man from Guyenne told me himself that he had read one of their Confessions, written in Old Gascon and given to the Chancellor or Great-Seal-Keeper de l'Hôpital shortly before the second unrest in France, which completely agreed with the Waldensian doctrine, so that no resemblance to the Manichaean heresy <term>Manichaeism: an ancient dualist religion that was often used as a smear label for medieval heretics to suggest they rejected the physical world and the Old Testament</term> could be found in it. On the contrary, they testified very explicitly that they accepted all the canonical books of the Old and New Testament and rejected all teachings together that were not grounded in the same, or contained something contradictory to them. A little further down, he speaks thus: *they repudiated and condemned all ceremonies, traditions, and ordinances of the Roman Church, saying that it was a den of thieves and the Apocalyptic Whore:* <note>original: "omnes Romanæ Ecclesiæ ceremonias, traditiones & ordinationes repudiabant ac condemnadant, dicentes, eam fpeluncam esse latronum & Meretricem Apocalypticam"</note> they rejected and condemned all ceremonies, traditions, and institutions of the Roman Church, saying that the same was a den of murderers and the Whore of Revelation.

Among so many good testimonies, let us now not forget that of the notorious Jesuit Gretserus, <margin>Regarding the Jesuit Gretserus.</margin> <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625) was a German Jesuit author and a leading figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> which he gives to the Waldensians on page 300 of the book he published against them. In the seventh error he blames them for, he explicitly makes those people say that they are in no way obligated to observe the institutions of the Bishops, because they are not divine but only human traditions; for it is written in the book of Deuteronomy: *you shall not add to this Word that I speak to you, much less take anything away from it.* Also: *you shall do only that which I command you, and you shall never add anything to it, or take anything away.* The same Monk says further that they use the passages from Isaiah 29 and Matthew 15 in the same matter: *in vain do they serve me, teaching for all doctrine the commandments of men.* Is it now conceivable, dear Reader, that if the Waldensians had been accustomed to rejecting the Old Testament as Manichaeans do, that Jesuit would have forgotten to reproach and charge them with that? But he saw for himself that they served themselves all too well with it to protect themselves from the institutions of the Popes. From this, the untruth of the slander can now also be very easily discovered—not invented by Matthew Paris <note>Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259) was an English Benedictine monk and chronicler.</note> himself, but by those whom he blindly followed—consisting of what he relates in the year 1203: namely, that the Albigensians, being besieged, [told] the besiegers

### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

Nn 3

The slanderers threw the Gospel at their heads with these words: "Be gone with your law: we have nothing at all to do with it; make merry with it yourselves." On the contrary, they were persecuted above all because they very diligently read God’s Holy Word, being unable to tolerate those who forbade it in order to feed the people with legends and decretals. <note>Decretals are papal letters that formulate decisions on points of canon law.</note> Thus, he makes himself altogether ridiculous through another account he gives of them regarding the year 1234, saying that they abjured the Christian faith and denied the Mystery of the Incarnation of our Lord, allegedly because the Pope (who cruelly persecuted them) had said that denying **Transubstantiation** <term>Transubstantiation: the Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</term> or Change of Substance—as all the Waldensians did—was nothing other than lying about the Incarnation. Indeed, the oft-mentioned Reynerus—who, as we have noted elsewhere at greater length, spent nearly his entire life practicing the suppression of heretics against the Waldensians— <margin>And from Reynerus.</margin> also speaks of them as being highly free from those untrue accusations, as we have also been able to see from his testimony cited earlier; when he uses this third reason to present their sect as more dangerous than any other: *“because all other sects (namely the Cathars and Manichaeans), while they cause horror by the enormity of their blasphemies against God, this sect of the Leonists has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men and believe all things well concerning God, and all the articles contained in the Creed. They only blaspheme and hate the Roman Church, to which the multitude is easily inclined to believe”*; <note>original: "quod, omnes aliæ (Sectæ ſcilicet Catharorum & Manichæorum) quum immanitate blaſphemiarum in Deum horrorem inducant, hæc Leoniſtarum magnam habet ſpeciem pietatis, eo quod coram hominibus juſte vivant & bene omnia de Deo credant & omnes articulos, qui in Symbolo continentur. Solam Romanam Eccleſiam blaſphemant & oderunt, cui multitudo facilis eſt ad credendum"</note> namely because, where all others (he seems to speak of the Cathars and Manichaeans) strike terror into people through the horror of their blasphemies, the **Leonists** <note>Leonists: another name for the Waldensians, likely derived from "Lyon," where their founder Peter Waldo lived.</note> have a beautiful appearance of godliness, because they live righteously before men, believe everything rightly concerning God, and even all the main points of the Apostles' Creed. They only blaspheme and hate the Roman Church, for which the common people so readily have an ear. He further adds that it resulted from this that, when he occasionally stood in the Inquisition for the legal interrogation of those heretics, 41 of their schools were counted in the Diocese of Padua and 10 in Babaca or Clemna: and a little before, that in all the cities of Lombardy, in Provence, and in other kingdoms and lands, there were more lecture rooms of these same heretics than there were of theologians; as well as very many of their listeners, who openly disputed with the people, convinced them in formal disputes, and preached in the fields, in the marketplaces, and on the rooftops without anyone daring to disturb or hinder them. Now, that by these heretics he always means the Waldensians and never the Cathars or Manichaeans is clear from what he says thereafter, namely giving in the 6th chapter, pages 71 and 72 of his aforementioned work to the said heretics (whom he, with many writers, considers one and the same) no more than six churches or congregations in total. He also finally concludes regarding them, using these or similar words: say boldly, O reader, that in the whole world, of all kinds, not four thousand Cathars are to be found; *but the believers and the faithful are countless*: <note>original: "ſed credentes & fideles illi ſunt innumeri"</note> but those believing and godly folk are without number. By which he clearly enough indicates that by those "Faithful" or "Believers" he means nothing other than...

### General Memorial-Script.

...others and believes, like an uncountable number of Waldensian Nicodemites <note>Nicodemites were people who secretly held certain religious beliefs—in this case, Waldensian ones—while publicly appearing to conform to the established Church, named after the biblical Nicodemus who visited Jesus by night.</note>, who indeed believed the teachings of the Waldensians inwardly, but because of the persecution did not dare to reveal themselves. Among other things, it is also to be noted here that he complains about an infinite number of such people immediately at the beginning of the thirteenth century.

<margin>Ridiculous reason for the same accusation.</margin>
But we have not yet finished with this. The same Reynerus cites yet another reason why they were called Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism was an ancient dualistic religion; the label was often used as a slur for any group that practiced extreme asceticism or criticized the material wealth of the Church.</note>; it was namely, he says in the 5th chapter as before, page 87, because they rejected the state of marriage, saying that married couples come to sin unto death when they unite and join one another without hope of children. Does that not seem to you to be a fine proof that one can rightly call them Manichaeans? A pagan poet is slandered by no one because he once sang:

->That is:<-

->children satisfies you. That which goes further must hinder.<-

The Empress Zenobia is still praised because she did not want to be touched by her husband as soon as she felt that she was pregnant. I do not bring up this saying or this example here as if I wanted to slander such an unpolluted sleep or the moderate enjoyment of wine; but only to show thereby both the innocence and simplicity of those Waldensians and the heinous wickedness of their accusers, who, for lack of other crimes and heresy, want to seek them in such things that they themselves cannot deny to be very praiseworthy in those of their own kind, which they can still maintain today and could then.

<margin>Another regarding the name Leonists.</margin>
But here something comes to mind regarding that last testimony of Reynerus, who elsewhere traces the origin of the Waldensians back to the time of Constantine the Great and places them at the same time as Sylvester; namely, that one may observe here in passing, which is quite important to know, that when the aforementioned writer (along with many other distinguished men cited on various occasions in this work) calls them *Leonists*, <note>Leonists was a common medieval name for the Waldensians, often attributed to a legendary companion of Pope Sylvester.</note> he intends thereby to make them descendants of a certain Leo, who lived very familiarly with the mentioned Pope and, not being able to endure that the aforementioned Emperor honored him and the entire Christian Church in general with such an abundance of riches, splendor, and worldly dignities—since he very easily foresaw the great ruin that those treasures and that pride would drag along with them—would not have wanted to participate in it, withholding himself from his company, even though he was already Bishop of Rome then, in order to hold himself only to the poverty and simplicity of the Apostles. Which indeed is all the more probable because one can generally read in the Waldensian writings, and especially in the writing *Of the Lying Christ* and in that of the *Noble Lesson* <note>original: "d'Uytstekende Lesse" refers to the 'Nobla Leyczon', a famous Waldensian poem from around 1100 AD.</note>, that within Rome after the times of Sylvester, no true and upright Apostolic Bishop has sat anymore. But let us finally return now to our supposed Arians and Manichaeans.

# Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

<meta>catchword: Charles</meta>

<margin>Refutation of the accusation of Manichaeism by De la Popeliniere.</margin> Indeed, if our Waldensians had ever been infected with those filthy heresies, if they had ever followed the Arians <note>Arians believed that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, Manichaeans, etc., how could Monsieur De la Popeliniere <note>Lancelot Voisin, Sieur de La Popelinière (c. 1541–1608), was a French historian known for his attempts at objectivity during the Wars of Religion.</note>, in the second volume of his *French Histories*, pages 38 and 245 of the 1581 edition, have given us this assurance: namely, *that the religion of the ancient Waldensians was very little different from that which the Protestants hold today; and that this is evident from several fragments and monuments written in their own language, and even from a solemn dispute by M. Arnolt, Minister of Lombardy, against the Bishop of Pamier, the acts of which still exist to this day and are set down in a language that seems more like Catalan than French. Indeed, several people,* he adds further, *have assured me that they have certainly seen their Articles of Faith engraved on old marbles found in the city of Albi, and that they are consistent with those of the Protestants* <note>original: "la Religion des anciens Vaudois étoit fort peu differente de celle, que tiennent aujourd'hui les Proteſtans, & qu'il en conſte par pluſieurs fragmens & monumens, écrits en leur propre langue, & même par une diſpute ſolemnelle de M. Arnolt, Miniſtre de Lombardie, contre l'Evêque de Pamier, dont les actes ſubſiſtent encore juſques a ce jour d'hui & ſe trouvent couchés en une langue, qui ſamble plutôt la Catalane, que la Françoiſe. Voire pluſieurs... m'ont aſſeuré, qu'ils ont aſſeurement veu leurs Articles de Foy, gravés ſur de vieux marbres, qui ſe trouvent en la ville d'Albi; & qu'ils ſont conformes a ceux des Proteſtants"</note>: [meaning] the religion of the old Waldensians differed very little from that which the non-Romans <note>The author uses "onroomse" (non-Roman) to refer to Protestants.</note> have adopted today, and that this can still be seen from various remains of old pieces described in their own language (which strongly reinforces the weight of the handwritten books from which we have gathered their Doctrine), as well as most notably from a formal debate held between Monsieur Arnolt, a <term>Minister</term> <note>A Protestant clergyman.</note> of Lombardy (he was undoubtedly from the valleys of Piedmont, as that area formerly belonged to old Lombardy) and the Bishop of Pamier, of which the writings still exist today, composed in a language that resembles Catalan more than French. What is more, several people have also assured me that they saw the articles of their Faith with their own eyes, as they were contained on old marble stones which can still be seen in the city of Albi, and that they entirely agree with those of the Protestants.

<margin>And Thuanus.</margin> This also agrees very well with what Monsieur Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a high-ranking French statesman and historian famous for his massive history of his own times, "Historiae sui Temporis."</note> dares to assert in the 5th book of his chronological work for the year 1550. Namely, after he recounted there that the Alpine Waldensians, and consequently especially those of the Valleys, taught that the Roman Church is that "great whore" because it has kicked away the faith of Christ; that one must not give ear to the Pope or the Roman Clergy, who hatch all errors; that the monastic life is vain and only fit to put the shameful impurities of young people beyond reproach; that the fire of <term>Purgatory</term> <note>original: "vier van 't Helvoorburg" (fire of the forecourt of hell). A common Protestant polemical term for Purgatory.</note>, the solemn sacrificial consecration of the Mass, the invocation of Saints, and prayers for the deceased are but inventions of the Devil, etc., he adds these words: *to these principal and certain heads of their doctrine, others have been falsely added concerning marriage, the resurrection, the state of the soul after death, foods, etc.* <note>original: "his præcipuis ac certis eorum Doctrinæ capitibus alia ſunt afficta de conjugio, reſurrectione, animæ ſtatu poſt mortem, de cibis, &c."</note> That is; to these prominent and certain points of their Doctrine, others have been fabricated regarding marriage, the resurrection, the condition of the soul after death, foods, and other such things. And what could he have cited more clearly to clear them of heresy, and especially that of the Manichaeans? But it should still be noted here that <margin>Reason for the mentioned accusation.</margin> this was very stubbornly and generally held against them because it could easily seem quite plausible to the eyes of the simple-minded; this was due to the fact that several of their teachers or <term>Barbes</term> <note>A term for Waldensian pastors, meaning "uncle."</note> never actually married, so that they could more conveniently be sent from their Valleys to Apulia, Calabria, the land of Alsace, Bohemia, and elsewhere for the proclamation of God's Word, as can be found and read in the chapter *On the Barbes* and throughout this work; and that they moreover led uncommonly sober lives. Why almost all the world finally cried out that they, like the Manichaeans, posited "two Principles" of all things, clearly shows the learned, God-fearing, and pious...

Header: General Memorial

Since this Waldensian Doctrine is held to be so innocent and free from the heretical opinions of the Manichaeans, the Arians, the Cathars, and others—not only by the Lutherans themselves and the Calvinists, but even by the Roman Catholics—it shall in no way be necessary for me to dwell upon this at any greater length. Freeing myself, then, from the labor of writing more on this, and sparing the reader from having to read a new heap of other testimonies on the same subject as the preceding ones—namely, to further confirm the purity of the Doctrine of the ancient Waldensians, although more than enough has already been done on that in the first part—I shall presently turn my attention to answering that difficult question: how it could possibly have been that this holy and upright Apostolic Doctrine has been able to maintain itself, and has in fact remained standing, in the Valleys since Italy first accepted the Gospel through the ministry of Saint Paul and his immediate successors <note>original: "bevangers"; refers to those who took up the mantle of the Apostles</note>, despite so many corruptions, superstitions, and prevailing idolatries, considering: 1. the great power of the Roman Popes, 2. the weakness of those Valley Churches, and 3. their proximity to Rome. And I hope to do this so clearly that all those who are willing to read the following Chapters without the distorted spectacles of their passions or prejudices will be inclined to follow my view on the matter.

### CHAPTER XX.

->Concerning the absurdity of those who demand that the<-
->Apostolic Succession of the Waldensian Churches<-
->be proven before the seventh century.<-

Undoubtedly, one would be worthy of laughter if they tried to convince a group of simple folk that they were not of Adam’s race simply because they could not easily prove, through their family tree or a continuous succession from father to son, that they were descended from him. Anyone who would then try to assert, as a result, that they had either fallen from Heaven, or sprouted up like a bunch of mushrooms in a single night <note>A common historical idiom for groups appearing suddenly without historical roots</note>, or were finally a new breed of humans, would certainly be considered more ridiculous than clever. This is because we understand from God’s Word that the entire human race took its beginning from one and the same blood; and finding in them the same human nature as in all others, one can rightly and boldly conclude that they all grow from the same trunk. It is exactly the same with our Waldensians. For since Holy Scripture openly testifies to us that the true Church has always been the same from the beginning of the world, and that those who hold the true faith—which it diligently teaches us—must be considered its legitimate children; so too are our Valley-dwellers, without any contradiction. On the one hand, they prove very concisely that they have always confessed that Faith and still confess it today; and on the other, the true Succession <note>original: "Bevang"</note> of the Church depends not so much on the place, or even the people themselves, as it does on the Faith and sound Doctrine, just as the Holy Spirit sufficiently teaches us in Mark 3, John 8, Romans 4, 9, and 11, etc. This is also stated by Gregory Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), an Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the Four Great Fathers of the Eastern Church</note> in his funeral oration for Saint Athanasius, saying that all those who follow the Faith of Abraham are the true children of Abraham. Now, all the world must grant me, without my needing to provide proof of the lineages and descendants of every household, that as long as the Roman Church remained with the true Faith and Religion—just as it was established by the Holy Ambassadors of the Cross <note>The Apostles</note>—

Imagines adorari debere; quod omninò Ecclesia Dei execratur..."</note> **In the year 792 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus, Charles, King of the Franks, sent a synodal book to Britain (he means the second, false <term>Council of Nicaea</term> <note>The Second Council of Nicaea (787 AD), which restored the use and veneration of icons.</note>), which had been sent to him from Constantinople. In that same book, oh sorrow! many unseemly things were found that were contrary to the true Faith, especially that by the unanimous assertion of nearly all the Eastern Doctors, and no fewer than—if not more than—three hundred Bishops, it was newly confirmed that Images ought to be adored; which the Church of God completely abhors. Consequently, Alcuin <note>Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), a leading scholar and advisor to Charlemagne.</note> wrote a letter against it, wonderfully fortified by the authority of the Holy Scriptures; and he brought it back to the aforementioned Great Majesty <note>Charlemagne</note>, along with the said book, in the name of all our Bishops and Princes.**

<margin>3. And also in Upper Germany and France.</margin> One cannot likewise say that England and Spain alone remained untainted by that abominable Idolatry, for one can clearly see that Upper Germany and France together had a similar aversion to it. From which it then necessarily follows (to mention this in passing) that the <term>Valley Churches</term> <note>The Waldensian or Vaudois churches, located in the Alpine valleys.</note>, which have always belonged—and still today belong—to the same body as those of the Dauphiné <note>A former province in southeastern France.</note>, who are situated on the soil of present-day France, just as they themselves are located in the <term>Cottian Alps</term> <note>The Latin "Herwaarts-Alpis" refers to the side of the Alps facing France/Italy.</note>, had also kept themselves pure from the same. Now, for this I desire no more striking proof than the well-known Church assembly held at the end of the eighth century—that is, in the year 794—by the command of Charlemagne, both Emperor and King of France, at Frankfurt am Main. Specifically, this assembly, despite the Eastern Council of Nicaea and the raging of Pope Adrian and Irene the Empress, brought about with three hundred Bishops that <note>original: "Pseudo-Synodus Græcorum, pro adorandis Imaginibus habita & falso Septima vocata, ab Episcopis omnino damnata est"</note> **the false Synod of the Greeks, held for the worship of Images and wrongly called the Seventh, was entirely condemned by the Bishops,** as Walafrid...

Strabus <note>Walahfrid Strabo (c. 808–849), a Benedictine monk and advisor to the Carolingian kings.</note>, the Monk of Angoulême, who has left us the life of Charlemagne <term>Karel de Groote; King of the Franks and later Emperor, who united much of Western Europe</term>, as well as Ado of Vienne and Regino of Prüm, all explicitly recount the same history. Regarding this rejection, a considerable book was written, which I read at the court in my youth, and which was thereafter sent by the same Emperor through certain Bishops to Rome.**

Maintained perseverance, from various letters to the Pope.
