It would also conflict with the truth if one were to pretend that this good sentiment descended into the grave with that great Prince. For in the year 822, Louis the Pious <note>Ludovicus Pius; Charlemagne's son and successor.</note> and his eldest son Lothair (whom his father had declared co-regent of the Empire), being prompted by Michael Balbus, Emperor of Constantinople, to speak regarding the Images, desired to give him a more binding and powerful answer. To do so, they gathered the most excellent teachers of that time whom they could assemble, especially those from Francia, at Paris. The outcome of this meeting can be judged no better than from the words of those very theologians themselves, which they used against the Pope regarding the aforementioned Council of Frankfurt: <note>original Latin: "talia quippe quædam sunt quæ in illorum objectionem opposuit, quæ remota Pontificali autoritate & veritati & autoritati refragantur"</note> **such are nearly all the things that he (Pope Adrian I) comes to raise against them, that when one sets the Papal authority aside as is proper, they run contrary to all Church power and reason.** One also finds in the Imperial Law-books, cited by Goldastus on page 750 *concerning the Worship of Images* <note>original: "de Cultu Imaginum"</note>, a magnificent Letter from the two aforementioned Emperors, which they dispatched to the Pope of Rome through an Italian Bishop, Jeremiah of Siena, and a certain Jonas, Bishop of Orleans. Through this letter, they stood as firmly as ever by the Frankfurt Decisions and commanded the said Bishop-envoys—who were to speak not merely on their own behalf, but to some extent in the name of that venerable assembly of scholars—to maintain their views and those of the said Synod against the Pope and his Clergy: <note>original Latin: "patienter ac modeste cum eo de hac causa disputando, ne nimis resistendo eum in aliquem irrevocabilem pertinaciam incidere compellerent"</note> **disputing with him about it modestly and gently, so that they might not, by too harsh an opposition, drive him into an irreformable stubbornness.** Regarding this, it may also be noted in passing that even as late as the ninth century, the Pope of Rome was not yet recognized as the supreme and indispensable arbiter of faith disputes whose pronouncement everyone was blindly bound to follow; rather, men dared to boldly reject his views following a lawful investigation according to Holy Scripture, whenever they found them to be in conflict with it.

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

Pp
<meta>catchword: wil-</meta>

Furthermore, we also find in the *Life of the highly esteemed Prince Louis the Pious* <term>Lodowijk de Goede; Emperor of the Romans and King of the Franks (r. 814–840), son of Charlemagne</term>, as published by Petrus Pithæus <note>Pierre Pithou (1539–1596), a French lawyer and scholar known for his work on Gallicanism and ancient manuscripts.</note>, that when Pope Gregory IV behaved as if he intended to place both the Emperor and his bishops under the ban <term>excommunication; a formal exclusion from the church and its sacraments</term> at the same time, they declared outright against him that they would by no means follow his whims. Instead, if he came to cut them off from the Congregation, he would return cut off himself, since the authority of the ancient Church laws was quite otherwise: *we will in no way submit to his will; but if he should come to excommunicate us, he himself would depart excommunicated, for the authority of the ancient Canons stands differently.* <note>original: "nullo modo ſe velle ejus voluntati ſuccumbere; ſed ſi excommunicaturus veniret, excommunicatus abiret, quum aliter ſe habeat antiquorum Canonum autoritas."</note>

But of particularly great importance in this matter is the excellent letter of Gunther and Theutgaud <note>Gunther was Archbishop of Cologne and Theutgaud was Archbishop of Trier; both were deposed by the Pope in 863 over their support for King Lothair II's divorce.</note> (it is found in the *Annals of France* for the year 863, as collected by the same Pithæus), which they wrote to Pope Nicholas I. This was after he had deposed the one from his Archbishopric of Trier and the other from Cologne, and subsequently cast them out of the Church because they had supposedly set themselves against all his new fabrications and pretended power. They mocked his commands with sufficient cause, as is clearly evident from this language, which they used among other things: 

*Such a wicked sentence, so far removed from the zeal for righteousness, so unjust and unreasonable, and so contrary to the Canonical laws, we by no means receive. Indeed, with the entire assembly of our brothers, we despise and reject it as a desecration and a curse, pronounced in vain. And we truly refuse to communicate with you—a patron and associate of the excommunicated and of those who have been cast out and have despised the sacred Religion—being content with the communion and brotherly fellowship of the whole Church, which you, arrogantly exalting yourself, despise, and from which you separate yourself, making yourself unworthy through the swelling of your pride. Therefore, by the temerity of your own levity, you have inflicted the blow of the curse upon yourself, crying out: "Whoever does not keep the Apostolic precepts, let him be cursed." For you are known to have violated the divine laws in many ways, at once trampling upon and, as much as lies in you, nullifying the sacred Canons, refusing to follow the footsteps of your predecessors, the Roman Pontiffs.*

*Now therefore, we who have experienced your deceitfulness and cunning also recognize your indignation and swollen power. We yield nothing to you or your pride, with which you hurried to overwhelm us to satisfy the wishes of our enemies, whom you favor. You shall know that we are not your clerics, as you boast and exalt yourself, whom you ought to have recognized as brothers and fellow-bishops, had your pride permitted it. And these things we answer to you, not being ignorant of our own order and compelled by your excessive wickedness; not as if provoked by the insult offered to us, but inflamed with ecclesiastical zeal against your iniquity. Nor do we look upon our own lowly persons, but keep before our eyes the whole universality of our order, upon which you attempt to inflict violence.*

That is to say: we hold nothing at all of such a godless sentence, which is so far removed from an upright zeal, so unjust, so unreasonable, and so contrary to the Church Laws; indeed, we despise and reject the same with the whole company of our Brothers as a desecration and a curse, unjustly pronounced. Nor do we wish to have anything at all to do with you, who maintain fellowship with and support those banished from the Church and those who reject and despise the true Religion. We are satisfied with the communion and brotherly union of the entire Congregation, which you, exalting yourself most arrogantly, trample underfoot, and from which you rightly separate yourself, since through your swollen pride you make yourself entirely unworthy of it. 

According to your own words, you have therefore caused the punishment of the curse to fall upon your own head through your light-minded recklessness, crying out that those are surely cursed who do not maintain the Apostolic Commands; while it is very well known that you yourself still violate the divine laws in many ways and have violated them in the past, trampling equally upon the holy Church statutes, frustrating them to the best of your ability, and not following the footsteps of your ancestors, the Popes of Rome, to their reproach...

wishing to enter. Furthermore, where we had previously only experienced your deceit and craftiness, we now also find your spitefulness and lust for power. <margin>From St. Agobardus; concerning Images.</margin>Here we can now add what a famous jurist from Paris, Papirius Masson <note>Jean Papire Masson (1544–1611) was a French scholar who discovered and published the long-lost manuscripts of Agobardus in 1605.</note>, has shared with us through the publication of the works of that Bishop of Lyon, St. Agobardus, which he had printed in Paris in the year 1605 with the King's privilege. Namely, after he showed in the Preface which he intended for the said book, that St. Agobardus lived under Charlemagne <note>The text places Agobardus under Charlemagne, though he also served prominently under Louis the Pious.</note>, just like Claudius of Turin <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827) was a bishop famous for removing all crosses and images from his diocese, arguing they led to idolatry.</note>—of whom we shall treat in the following chapter—and proved that he was a man full of divine knowledge and great holiness: he further describes him as one who had discovered and very courageously fought against the error and idolatry of the Greeks regarding Images and Paintings, denying that one should pray to them, etc. Thereafter, he lets the Holy Bishop speak for himself; for in a certain book written against Images and published by the same Masson, as has been said, he essentially used the same language that the aforementioned Claudius had used shortly before him, and which the Orthodox could still speak against the Roman Catholic Lords today. But see here the words themselves right at the beginning of the cited book. God says in the First Commandment of the Law:

<margin>And in his work itself page 212.</margin>> I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no foreign gods before my face. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of anything that is above in Heaven, nor of anything that is below on the earth, nor of anything that is in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them, nor serve them.

To which words St. Augustine, in a certain sermon on the book of Exodus, adds the following (as he says) for clarification; by this Commandment, all representation of God is equally forbidden that man might wish to make of Him; not as if God resembled nothing: but because no image of God may be served, etc. By which saying, this Holy Ancient Father comes to point out to us briefly and concisely how this Commandment and those like it must be understood. For when it is explicitly forbidden that one shall make no image or likeness of anything that is in Heaven, or on earth, etc., it is easy to notice that it speaks not only of the images of Idols; but even of those of all heavenly and earthly creatures, which human ingenuity might ever find to honor the Creator. This is why Moses also quite openly uses this reasoning toward the people: when He also spoke to you out of the midst of the fire, you heard the sound of His words; but you saw not the least likeness: *since it is distinctly stated that no likeness should be made of all things that are in heaven, or that are on earth, or that are under the earth, it is not understood as being said only concerning the likenesses of foreign gods; but also concerning heavenly creatures, or what human sense could [devise] in honor of the Creator* <note>original: "cum diſtincte dicatur, non faciendam ſimilitudinem omnium, quæ in cælo ſunt, aut quæ in terra, vel quæ ſub terra, non de ſolis ſimilitudinibus alienorum Deorum intelligitur dictum; ſed & de cæleſtibus, creaturis, aut quæ in honore Creatoris humanus ſenſus potuit"</note>

# Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

to devise. For which reason Moses also speaks openly to the people, saying: *the Lord spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of his words and you did not see his form.* <note>original: "locutus eſt Dominus ad vos de medio ignis: vocem verborum ejus audiſtis & formam ejus non vidiſtis." See Deuteronomy 4:12.</note> Finally, after such a concise reasoning against the misuse of introducing images as anyone could ever make—and one which is so aptly supported by St. Augustine in the 10th book of the *City of God*, <margin>P. 249.</margin> in the 1st chapter—he finally concludes with these dignified words: *if the works of God’s hands are not to be adored and worshipped, not even in honor of God; how much more are the works of human hands not to be adored nor worshipped, even in honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be?* <note>original: "ſi opera manuum Dei non ſunt adoranda & colenda, nec in honorem Dei; quanto magis opera manuum [hominum] non ſunt adoranda nec colenda, nec in honorem eorum, quorum ſimilitudines eſſe dicuntur?" The Latin text contains a likely printer's error, repeating "Dei" (God) where it should say "hominum" (men), which the Dutch translator correctly identified in the following sentence.</note> Which has this translation: if one may not then pray to the works of God's hands, even to God's honor; how much less can it be permissible to honor, serve, and pray to the works of men's hands, merely pretending therein to honor those whose images they are said to be?

From this idolatrous misuse of Images, he moves on to the invocation of the Saints; about which he also comes to write most strikingly. <margin>The invocation of the Saints.</margin> The summary-heading alone of the first chapter can give us sufficient judgment of the whole work. See here then the own words of the Holy Writer: *that between God and men no other Mediator should be sought, except him, who is both God and man;* <note>original: "quod inter Deum & homines nullus ſit alius Mediator quærendus, niſi ille, qui Deus eſt & homo;"</note> as if one said; that between God and men no other Mediator may be sought, but the one who is simultaneously God and man. These words from the second chapter are no less noteworthy: *that no creature, worshipping God, wishes to be worshipped in His place, to whom it is itself subject;* <note>original: "quod nulla creatura, colens Deum, velit pro illa coli, cui & ipſa ſubdita eſt;"</note> that no creature, who itself honors God, can wish to be honored in stead of Him, to whom it is itself subject. He also ends that Writing in this sense: just as one must offer to God alone, so must one also call upon God alone.

Thereafter follows his work against all kinds of Church-robbery <note>Sacrilege or the misappropriation of ecclesiastical property.</note> and Simony <note>The practice of buying or selling spiritual offices or roles.</note>, which he even then <margin>Church-robbery and Simony.</margin> began to observe in the Roman Church.

Finally, he concludes with another against the Antichrist and the Merits <margin>Antichrist and merits of works.</margin> of works, which he destroys with such zeal and power as any Calvinist could ever have done. Which can easily be seen even from reading that uncommon book.

But who could now still doubt whether—while such a prominent Bishop, from the eighth Century to the beginning of the ninth, in the second most prominent City and the largest trading city of all France, the neighborhood of Provence, of Languedoc, and of the Valleys, indeed the only and rich staple <note>A central marketplace or commercial hub where goods were collected for export.</note> for all merchandise that was constantly transported from France to these latter regions—dared to attack the increasing abuses of the Roman Church in such a manner and so courageously advocated for and maintained the purity of the Evangelical Doctrine; this holy seed is entirely the same that grew so powerfully and miraculously in those regions during the eleventh and twelfth Centuries, being unable to be entirely stifled in the tenth, because it was immediately watered by the ample preaching of the divine Word and warmed by the zeal-discipline and fire of Peter Waldo, or to put it better, <term>Waldenis</term>? <note>The author connects the 9th-century reforms of Agobardus directly to the 12th-century Waldensian movement led by Peter Waldo (Valdes).</note> We shall hereafter always note that he did not begin to teach in that famous City until those other open places had become, as it were, too small for the innumerable multitude of his zealous disciples and listeners; whose dispersal has indeed provided all corners of Europe and even a part of Asia with true Teachers, with Pastors and Evangelists.

See there then, how not only the Bishops and Churches of England and <margin>And finally especially in Italy and Piedmont.</margin> France, but even those of Germany still dealt with the Pope and his novelties in the ninth Century. # General Memorial-Writing

Situated in Italy, namely in Lombardy (to which Piedmont belongs), and furthermore in the vicinity of Rome, they would not have dared to concern themselves with it so well, or ward off image-worship and other abuses without needing to openly depart from the Roman Church because of it (we shall confirm hereafter that this finally occurred anyway); but let all the world know that, while keeping the sound doctrine of the Holy Scriptures and the ancient Orthodox Councils, they could not have lost the right to persevere in that free rejection of everything that was presented to them to the contrary, just as they have always practiced it: so it must be very diligently observed that they made their complaints not only to Rome and to the Pope himself, but also—which is very remarkable—to the Churches of the East. This is testified beyond contradiction by that glorious letter which the Bishops of Italy wrote concerning this to the Overseers <note>The author uses "Opzienders" (Overseers), a common Reformation-era term for Bishops or Superintendents.</note> of the Eastern Congregations, the contents of which appear from this [letter] by Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, as it is cited in the Annals of Baronius for the year 863, § 42. where he makes them speak in this sense, among other things: *From the regions of Italy a certain Synodical Letter was brought to us, containing countless evils and crimes, about which those who inhabit Italy complain against their own Bishop; offering us also countless entreaties with a great threat of the wrath of God, so that we might not overlook them, so miserably lost and oppressed by such a great and heavy tyranny. Moreover, they tell of priestly laws and all Ecclesiastical rules being trampled underfoot, etc.* <note>original Latin: "ex partibus Italiæ Synodica quædam Epistola ad nos allata est, sexcenta continens mala & dilecta, quæ adversus proprium ipsorum Episcopum illi, qui Italiam incolunt, conqueruntur; sexcentas etiam obtestationes cum magna iræ Dei comminatione nobis adhibens, ne ipsos prætermittamus ita misere perditos & tanta & adeo gravi tyrannide oppressos. Sacerdotales præterea leges & omnes Ecclesiasticas regulas conculcatas narrant, esv." The term "sexcenta" (six hundred) is used idiomatically in Latin to mean "countless."</note> that is, from the regions of Italy a certain letter has been delivered to us, which was written by their Church assembly <term>Synod: a formal meeting of church leaders to decide on doctrine or administration</term>, containing a thousand wickednesses and villainies, about which the inhabitants there complain against their own Bishop; using toward us a thousand kinds of testimonies and supplications with added threats of God’s great wrath, so that we might not now reject them, since they are so miserably corrupted and oppressed by such great and heavy violence. He also maintains that all priestly laws and Ecclesiastical regulations have been trampled underfoot, etc.

It is therefore so far from the truth that all of Italy would have accepted all the novelties that the Popes began to introduce, that even toward the end of the ninth century, Synods were explicitly held to solemnly oppose them; as can be seen from these words of the cited letter: *But now indeed, as I said above, various letters from various people have come from there, full of such tragedies and countless evils; of which we have attached some copies to these letters of ours, according to their requests and entreaties (for they asked with dreadful oaths that they be sent to all Patriarchal Sees, as the letters themselves, when read, will make manifest to you): so that concerning these things also, when a Holy Universal Synod is gathered in the Lord, what pleases God may be confirmed by common opinion and the great peace of the Church of Christ may be restored;* <note>original Latin: "nunc vero, ut superius dixi, diversæ literæ diversorum inde venerunt, hujusmodi tragœdiæ & sexcentorum malorum plenæ; quarum exempla juxta eorum preces & obtestationes (ad universas enim Patriarchales Sedes illas dari cum horrendis obtestationibus rogarunt, ut ipsæmet literæ, cum legentur, manifestum vobis facient) his nostris literis adjecimus: ut de his rebus etiam, Sanctâ Universali Synodo in Domino congregata, quæ placuerint Deo, communi sententia confirmentur & magna pax Ecclesiæ Christi restituatur;"</note> which means this: but currently also, as I have begun to touch upon above, various letters from various [people] have come from there, full of a thousand such tragedies and similar evils; of which we, at their request and prayers (for they have requested with terrible oaths that they might be sent around to all Patriarchal Churches, as the letters themselves, when read, shall be able to testify), have enclosed some copies in our present [letter]: so that, when the holy general Synod shall be assembled in the Lord, that which pleases God may be decided with a common sentiment and the great peace of Christ’s Church may be restored.

# Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

### CHAPTER XXI.

#### Concerning Claudius, Archbishop of Turin and the Valleys; and how he, along with the same, at the end of the eighth Century, openly left the fellowship of the Romish and Papal Church.

Although it is sufficiently clear from what we have just so convincingly and clearly proven, that—despite all the efforts of the Romish Church and those of the Pope, who sought to introduce various new superstitions into the world—various Churches, regions, and even entire Kingdoms refused to accept them even until the end of the ninth Century, but instead valiantly contested them; and that those who refused to accept them could by no means be forced to do so (just as indeed, according to the prophecy of the Holy Revelation, the whole world was not to follow after the Beast, worship its image, or finally receive its mark on hand and forehead, on pain of otherwise not being allowed to buy or sell <note>The author refers to Revelation 13:16-17, interpreting the "mark of the beast" as a loss of civil and commercial rights for those who resisted the Roman Church's authority.</note>, that is, to be persecuted and stripped of all freedom of trade, before the thousand years had expired, at the end of which Satan would be loosed), yet one must especially adore here the unutterable wisdom and wonderful Providence of God. For, in keeping for Himself a good number of faithful witnesses to oppose that Son of Perdition <note>A biblical term for the Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3).</note> with more power and preparation as soon as he should be fully revealed, He furthermore desired from time to time to raise up various great Men who would openly and zealously oppose the Anti-Christ as soon as he was born and began to emerge through the introduction of Idolatry. Namely, God could then make use of such valiant and courageous Champions to assault him, as it were, in the cradle. What is more, He even kept on foot several very significant Churches in the Alpine Valleys for this purpose, in which the torch of the Gospel always shone most gloriously, even when it was once more surrounded on all sides by thick darkness. It also seems that the Spirit of God <margin>The ancient coat of arms and Motto of the Valley of Lucerna.</margin> from of old desired to give a sort of prelude to that merciful privilege which He reserved for these Valleys: namely, to establish them as a perpetual Goshen in Egypt <note>In the Book of Exodus, the Land of Goshen remained in the light while the rest of Egypt suffered a plague of darkness.</note>. For it is found that even in the time of Heathenism, they bore as a coat of arms a lit torch with seven stars in the midst of a great darkness, still having this Motto, *Lux lucet in tenebris*, <note>Latin: "The light shines in the darkness" (John 1:5).</note> the light shines in the dark. From which also the most prominent of these, namely the Valley of Lucerna, seems to have derived its name <note>The name "Lucerna" is related to the Latin word for lamp or light.</note>. However that may be, in the time of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, <margin>Concerning Claudius, the Archbishop of Turin and the Valleys.</margin> that is, at the end of the eighth and the beginning of the ninth Century, the Teachings of Claudius, Archbishop of Turin, were very strongly in vogue throughout almost all of Italy. Under his ecclesiastical jurisdiction belonged not only the Valleys that now belong to the Dukes of Savoy, as certain Princes of Piedmont, but even—which the reader should well note—those situated in Dauphiné and on French soil toward the side of Provence, that is, on the other slope of the Alpine mountains. Indeed, they were influenced there by that renowned Bertramus <note>Likely Ratramnus of Corbie, a 9th-century theologian known for his views on the Eucharist.</note>, the learned Godeſchalcus <note>Gottschalk of Orbais, known for his teachings on predestination.</note>, and Felix of Urgel <note>Felix of Urgell, a Spanish bishop who was a contemporary of Claudius.</note>, who was a comrade of Bertramus and a teacher of Claudius, and other great Lights of their century.

"Claudius," he says, "the Bishop of Turin, was very famous in the time of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious; in whose favor he stood very well long before he even attained that high Church office. Against this Claudius, a certain Jonas, a Bishop of Orleans, published a slanderous writing after Claudius's death, during the time of Emperor Charles the Bald. In this book, he set down various things that he had drawn from a certain work by Claudius. And even though these were likely not transcribed too faithfully, and the most important proofs seem to have been skipped over, I nevertheless believe it is worth the effort to set them together here for a second time and give them to the reader to read. The cautious and godly reader will always be able to easily gather from them how glorious and useful his entire work must have been. But the ill-will of the Papists has, along with countless other writings against the widespread errors of the Church, begrudged us that work and made away with it."

But among other writings of the aforementioned Claudius of Turin, the said Jonas, Bishop of Orleans, mentions one in his cited work by this name: *Apologeticum, sive Rescriptum, Claudii Episcopi adversus Theodemirum Abbatem*, that is, *The Defense or Answer of Bishop Claudius against Abbot Theodemir*. See then the very words and their faithful translation:

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

...against the rule of the Catholic Faith <note>original: "contra regulam Fidei Catholicæ"</note>, which is entirely false. Nor is it a wonder if those members of the Devil have said such things of me, who proclaimed our Head <note>A reference to Jesus Christ.</note> himself both a deceiver and demon-possessed. For I do not teach a Sect, I who hold the truth and proclaim the truth; but Sects and Schisms and Superstitions and heresies, as much as I was able, I have suppressed, crushed, fought against, and to fight against them, as much as I am able, I do not cease, with God's help.

---

And because I alone began to destroy what men were worshiping. ** For since it is distinctly said, *that a likeness is not to be made of anything that is in heaven, or that is on earth, it is understood to be said not only of the likenesses of foreign Gods, but also of celestial creatures.* Those against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church say: *if you write on a wall, or paint Images of Peter & Paul, Jupiter & Saturn, or Mercury, neither are these Gods, nor those Apostles, nor these, nor those men.* But by this the name is changed; yet the error remains always the same, both then and now. Certainly if they were to be adored, they ought to have been adored while alive, rather than as you have placed them—not an effigy of beasts, or (what is truer) of stones, or wood, lacking life and sense and reason. From which matter it must be most highly considered; because if the works of God's hands are not to be adored and worshiped, how much more are the works of men's hands not to be adored and worshiped at all, not even in the honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be? Because if the Image which you adore is not God (because not only he who worships visible figments and Images, but also...

<column-break/>

...tried to establish; which is entirely untrue. It gives me no wonder, however, that those members of the Devil speak so of me, since they themselves formerly cried out against our Head <note>Referring to Christ, whom his enemies called a deceiver (Matthew 27:63).</note> as a deceiver and one possessed. Meanwhile, it is so far from the case that I, who hold to the truth and cry out the truth everywhere, should cause any division; rather, I have always suppressed, trodden down, and overcome all self-willed factions <note>Dutch: "Selfgeſintens", referring to those who create their own private dogmas or sects.</note> and Schisms and Superstitions and Heresies to the best of my ability, and with God's help, as much as is possible for me, I never cease from doing that.

<margin>
He accuses image-worship of open Idolatry.
</margin>
And because I, you go on to say, *alone begin to overthrow that which men until now have rendered service and honor.* ** For here it is explicitly said, *that one may make no image of all that is in heaven, or on the earth;* thus it cannot be understood to be said only of the bare likenesses of foreign gods, but even also of the heavenly creatures. But to this say those against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church: although one draws or paints the images of Peter and Paul, of Jupiter and Saturn or Mercury on the wall, they do not thereby immediately become such Gods, nor those such Apostles, or neither of them in any way men. But to this fits the answer, that namely by so doing the name is somewhat changed, but nevertheless both then and now the same error always remains. And truly if they ought to have been worshiped, it would have better suited them living, than in the state in which you want to place them—that is, not insofar as they are representations of beasts or (what is truer) of stone, or wood, deprived of all feeling and reason. From which this stands in the highest consideration; if one may not pray to or show honor to the works of God's hands, how much less may the same in any way happen concerning the works of men's hands, even not in honor of those whose Images they are held to be? Furthermore, if also the Image that you come to pray to is no...

# General Memorial-Writings

...even any creature, whether *heavenly*, *earthly*, *spiritual*, or *bodily*, worships in the place of God's name and hopes for the salvation of their soul—which comes from God alone—from them: it is of these people that the Apostle <note>Referring to Saint Paul in Romans 1:25.</note> says: *they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator* <note>original Latin: "coluerunt & servierunt creaturæ potius, quam Creatori"</note>. Why do you humble and bow yourself before false images? Why do you bend your captive body before foolish likenesses and earthly figments? *God made you upright and, while other animals are prone and pressed down toward the earth in their posture, you have a sublime status and a face turned upward toward heaven and the Lord.* <note>This argument—that humans are uniquely built to look at the sky while animals look at the ground—was a popular philosophical and theological point in the Middle Ages to discourage idolatry.</note> Look there, raise your eyes there; seek God in the heights. So that you may be free from the depths, lift your heart up to high and heavenly things. Why do you cast yourself into the fall of death along with the senseless image you worship? Why do you fall into the ruin of the Devil through it and with it? Preserve the nobility in which you were born; remain as you were made by God. But these followers of false religion and superstition say: "We worship, serve, and adore a painted cross in memory of our Savior and as an image in his honor." To these people, nothing else is pleasing in our Savior except what also pleased the godless: the reproach of the passion and the mockery of his death. They believe the same about him as godless men—whether Jews or Pagans—do, who lack faith in his resurrection; they cannot think of him as anything else, except to believe and keep him in their hearts as entirely dead and always placed in suffering. They do not attend to, nor understand, what the Apostle says: *even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.* <note>2 Corinthians 5:16. Claudius uses this to argue against focusing on the physical suffering of Jesus's human body.</note> God commanded one thing; these people do another. God commanded us to carry the cross, not to adore it; these people want to adore it because they are unwilling to carry it with them, neither spiritually nor bodily. To worship God in such a way is to depart from him. To whom it must be answered: that if every wooden [cross]...

<column-break/>

...is no God <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous page: "how much more is it the case that a thing made by man] is no God."</note> (so it is not only those who call upon visible images or tangible carvings, but also those who invoke all sorts of both heavenly and earthly, both spiritual and bodily creatures in the place of God's name, and hope for the salvation of their souls—which can come from God alone—from the same; they belong to the number of those to whom the Apostle applies these words: they have served the creature rather than the Creator). To what end do you humble yourself? Why do you bow then before those false images? To what end do you bend your slavish body before those earthly fictions and trifling likenesses? The Lord created you upright; and where all other animals, leaning forward, remain as if creeping very close to the earth, there you have received an exalted stature and a face looking up toward heaven and the Lord. Look only there then, for your eyes are directed there; seek your God only above. Lift your high thoughts to those exalted and heavenly things, so that you may learn to do without these lowly things. Why do you cast yourself down with that mad image that you honor, into a fall of death? Why do you fall with and through the same into a destruction of the Devil himself? Retain the dignity with which you were born. Remain such as you were made by God. But those followers of the untrue religion and superstition dare to answer the following to this: "We honor, serve, and worship a painted cross for the memory of our Savior, which is portrayed in his honor." By which they always, above all, make known that nothing more in our Savior appeals to them than that which also pleased the godless therein: namely, the reproach of his suffering and the mockery of his death. They also believe only that of him which godless people—be they Jews or Heathens—do, who give no faith to his resurrection; and they can hardly think anything of him, unless they simultaneously believe and hold in their hearts that he is entirely dead and always remains stuck in his suffering. Yes, and they do not understand, nor regard, what the Apostle says somewhere: "Though we had known the Lord Jesus according to the flesh, yet [now] we know him..."

<note>original Latin catchword: ruit (falls); catchword: Christus (Christ)</note>

*...made by the cross, they wish to adore it because Christ hung on the cross; and many other things apply to them which Christ did through his physical body. For he hung on the cross for barely six hours; yet he was in the Virgin's womb for nine lunar months and over eleven days, which together are two hundred and seventy-six lunar days—that is, nine months and six days. Therefore, let young virgins be adored, because a Virgin gave birth to Christ. Let mangers also be adored, because as soon as he was born, he was laid in a manger. Let old rags also be adored, because immediately when he was born, he was wrapped in old rags. Let ships also be adored, because he frequently sailed in ships and taught the crowds from a small boat and slept in a ship and ordered the net to be cast on the right side of the vessel, when that great catch of fish was made by those who were previously struggling. Let donkeys be adored, because by sitting on a young donkey he reached Jerusalem. Let lambs be adored, because it is written of him: "behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world." <note>John 1:29</note> But these cultivators of perverse doctrines want to devour living lambs while adoring those painted on the wall. Let lions also be adored, because it is written of him: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered." <note>Revelation 5:5</note> Let rocks also be adored, because, when he was taken down from the cross, he was placed in a stone tomb; and of him the Apostle says: "and the rock was Christ." <note>1 Corinthians 10:4</note> But Christ was called a "rock," "lamb," and "lion" figuratively, not literally; by what they signify, not by their physical substance. Let the thorns of the briars also be adored, because from them a crown of thorns was placed on his head at the time of his suffering. Let reeds also be adored, because his head was struck with blows by the soldiers using them. Finally, let spears also be adored, because one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear.*

<column-break/>

...yet we do not know him in that way anymore. God has commanded something else, and they do otherwise. God has ordered not that one should honor the cross, but take it up; <note>Referencing Matthew 16:24: "Whoever wants to be my disciple must... take up their cross and follow me."</note> they, on the other hand, wish to worship it because they refuse to carry it in both a spiritual and physical manner. To serve God in such a way is to turn away from him. 

This answer can also be given to them: namely, that if they desire that every kind of wood endowed with the form of a cross must be worshiped because Christ hung on the cross, they will likewise have to honor various other things by the same right, because the Lord Christ, during his humanity, is found to have done something regarding them. And truly, he was stretched out on the cross for barely six hours, whereas on the contrary, he was enclosed in the womb of the Virgin for nine months and eleven days, which together makes two hundred and seventy-six days—I say, nine months and six days. 

Let them rather worship young virgins, because a Virgin gave birth to the Savior. Let them likewise worship the mangers, because right after his birth he was laid in a manger. Let them worship the old rags, because having just come into the world, he was wrapped in old cloths. Let them also worship the ships, because he was often on ships and taught the people from a small boat, and slept in a ship, and had the net cast on the right side of the ship when they were so busy with all those fish during that good catch. 

Let them worship the donkeys, because he rode to Jerusalem on a young donkey. Let them worship the lambs, because it is written of him: *Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.* Indeed, those followers of perverse doctrines would well like to gobble up the real sheep and yet they honor those painted on the wall. Let them likewise worship the lions, because we read of them: *The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered.* Let them also worship the rock-stones, because having just been taken from the cross, he was laid in a rocky grave; and because the Apostle says of the same: *Now that rock was Christ.*

# General Chronicle

...he fell; from where flowed blood and water, the Sacraments, from which the Church is formed. <note>original Latin: "unde fluxit sanguis & aqua, Sacramenta, unde formatur Ecclesia."</note> All these things are ridiculous and to be mourned rather than written down; we are forced to propose against fools and against hearts of stone not the arrows or sentences of the Word, but to hurl stony blows. Return, you transgressors, to your heart—you who have retreated from the truth and love vanity and have become vain yourselves: you who crucify the Son of God again and hold him up to contempt. Through this, you hold the souls of miserable associates of demons in throngs, alienating them from their Creator through the unspeakable sacrilege of idols, casting them down and throwing them into perpetual damnation.

<margin>Against the Pilgrims.</margin>
*As for what you say—that I forbid men to go to Rome for the sake of penance—you speak falsely. For I do not approve of that journey, and as if explaining why you said it, you add: "because I know that it does not hinder all, nor profit all, nor benefit all, nor harm all." First, I want to ask you yourself: if you know that performing penance <note>penitence/repentance</note> is going to Rome, why have you lost so many souls over such a long time, whom you kept in the monastery and received into the monastery for the sake of penance? And you did not send them to Rome, but rather made them serve you? If things are as you say—that penance is going to Rome—what will you do about the sentence...*

<column-break/>

Christ. And to tell the truth, our Savior is called a rock, a lamb, and a lion figuratively and not literally; only according to the meaning, and not according to the essence. Let them adore the thorns of the hedges, because at the time of his suffering a crown of thorns was woven for his head from them. Let them also adore the reed alongside it, because the soldiers cruelly struck his blessed head with it. Finally, let them also adore the spears, because one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, from which also blood and water flowed out—the two <term>seal-signs</term> <note>refers to the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist</note> from which the Church consists. Meanwhile, all those ridiculous things are rather to be wept over than written about; and we are somewhat compelled to shoot out stony shafts against those foolish and stony hearts, instead of the arrows or sayings of the Word. Return then, you rebellious ones, return to your senses—you who, having deviated from the truth, love vanity and have become vain; who crucify the Son of God and put him on display anew, and thereby have made the souls of many miserable people in heaps into companions of the Devils, alienating them from their Creator through the ghastly <term>profanations of images</term> <note>idolatry</note> causing them to fall and plunge into eternal damnation.

But concerning your claim that I supposedly hinder people from traveling to Rome for penance <note>original: "penitentie"</note>: you falsely attribute these words of mine to me, for I do not at all support such journeys. And then, as if wishing to speak somewhat more clearly, you add these reasons of mine: *because I know that they neither help all people, nor harm all, nor are they advantageous to all, nor disadvantageous to all.* But I have only something to ask you about that. If you know well that <term>penitence</term> consists of making a <term>pilgrimage</term> <note>original: "Be-vaarden"</note> to Rome, why then have you for so long a time allowed so many souls to be lost, whom you have kept in your monastery—indeed, have taken into the same to show penitence? Why have you not rather sent them to Rome, instead of keeping them under you for your service? If it stands as you say, that *it is performing penance when one travels to Rome*, then where do you stand with that saying...

<margin>How they were able to preserve themselves in purity during the terrible corruption of the 10th century.</margin>
If ever a century was born in which the good seed of sound doctrine could have been entirely smothered in the Valleys, it must necessarily have been the tenth, which Cardinal Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), an influential Catholic historian</note> himself called a dark, sullied, and unfortunate century; one in which superstition—which was never greater—had gained the complete upper hand through the help of ignorance, which was hardly ever found to be so coarse. This is why Werner Rolevinck, a Carthusian <note>A member of a strictly enclosed religious order</note> from Westphalia, gives it the name of "scandalous times" according to the testimony of the well-known *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Fasciculus Temporum", a famous 15th-century world chronicle</note>; times in which the fine luster of gold was lost, the Saints were missing, and the obscured truths vanished from among the children of men. In the same writing, it is recounted a little further down that when Emperor Louis was presented with a monstrosity—which had a human body with a dog's head—he said that the monster well-represented the deformed state of those times, because men in that age, as if they had no head, were staggering from all sides and barking like dogs. To this is added the testimony of Nicolas Vignier, historian to the King of France, who relates that the brutishness and ignorance of the free arts and studies, regarding both the Divine and the human—which then held the field much more than in any preceding centuries—caused the heaviest misfortune at first; so much so that in that century, no famous teachers or Councils were found. Nevertheless, even though in this same century the error of a certain monk of Corbie, Paschasius Radbertus <note>A Frankish regent and theologian</note>—who was the first of all at the beginning of the ninth century to try to introduce the belief in Transubstantiation into the Church, that great pillar of the idolatry currently practiced in the Mass—began to creep forward gradually and imperceptibly, it had very little or no following. Namely, it had already been powerfully attacked by the oft-mentioned teacher Bertramus <note>Also known as Ratramnus of Corbie (died c. 868)</note>, likewise a monk of Corbie, who, by order of King Charles the Bald <note>original: "Carolus Calvus"</note> of France, wrote an excellent book (which I still have) to stifle this heresy in its birth. He was also significantly bolstered in this by Amalarius, Heribaldus, Rabanus, John Eriugena, Walafrid Strabo, Florus, Lupus (Abbot of Ferrières), Prudentius (Bishop of Troyes), Christian Druthmar, Johannes Scotus, Trudegarius, and Remigius, who were almost the only great men of that time. Not to mention that the aforementioned Paschasius was also condemned as a heretic by the Council of Quierzy <note>original: "Cressi"</note>. One also finds a beautiful Church sermon <note>homily</note> which, in the time of the Emperors Henry the Fowler <note>original: "Henricus Auceps"</note> and Otto the Great, his son, around the middle of the tenth century, used to be recited and read in all the churches of Saxony and England on Easter Day; in which these very words are explicitly found, entirely agreeing with the faith that the Communities of the Valleys (steadfastly followed thereafter by all the Reformed) have held there since ancient times, expressed in this sense—

...the: <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a quotation from the previous page.</note> "There is a great difference between the body in which Christ suffered, and the body which is consecrated in the host. <note>original: "multum interest inter corpus, in quo passus est Christus, & corpus, quod in hostia consecratur"</note> Truly, the body in which Christ suffered was born of the flesh and blood of Mary, and was structured with bones, skin, nerves, human members, and a rational soul; but his spiritual body, which we call the host, is gathered from various grains, without blood, bones, members, and soul. — The body of Christ, which suffered death and rose from death, will never die thereafter, but is eternal and impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or feeling pain</note>; but that host is temporary, not eternal, corruptible and divided into various parts, crushed by teeth and sent into the belly. — This mystery is a pledge and a figure; the body of Christ is the truth itself." <note>This long Latin passage is from the writings of Ælfric of Eynsham, an Anglo-Saxon abbot.</note> — That is, there is a great difference between the body in which the Lord Jesus suffered, and the body that is consecrated in the host. Namely, the body in which our Savior suffered was born from the flesh of Mary and endowed with human blood, bones, skin, nerves, limbs, and a rational soul; but his spiritual body, which we call the host, is joined together from various grains without blood, bones, limbs, and soul. — The body of our Lord, which endured death and rose from death, can thereafter never die, being eternal and free from all suffering; but that host is temporary and not eternal, perishable, divided into various parts, crushed with the teeth, and swallowed into the stomach. — This mystery is a pledge and an image; but the body of Christ is the truth itself. Now, to be upright, is there anything to be found here that in any way reeks of the <term>Sacrifice of the Mass</term>? <note>The Catholic doctrine that the Eucharist is a literal re-offering of Christ's sacrifice.</note> Nevertheless, this Church teaching—as can be seen in Ussher, <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a famous chronologist.</note> the excellent and accurate English Chronicler, in his book *The Weightiest Questions* <note>original: "graviss. quæst."</note> page 53 of the Hanau edition of the year 1658—was even translated into English by a certain Ælfricus, who from being Abbot of Malmesbury became Bishop of Crediton, and to whom King Edgar, in a certain document given to the Monastery of Malmesbury in the year 974, adds the title of honor of a very learned man who was uniquely well-versed in all Church affairs.

We also have from a high-minded Prince <note>Referring to the source of the discourse, likely meaning King Edgar or the authority behind the Bishop.</note> a beautiful Discourse, which he gave in the name of Wulffinus, Bishop of Sherborne, <note>Wulfsige III, Bishop of Sherborne (c. 992–1002).</note> for the Clergy of the Saxons in their own language, in which he repeats the known Teaching regarding the Holy Supper of the Lord with these following words: "That host is Christ's body, not corporally, but spiritually: not the body in which he suffered, but the body of which he spoke when he consecrated the bread and wine into the host on the night preceding his passion, and first said of the consecrated bread: 'This is my body'; and again of the sacred wine: 'This is my blood, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.'" <note>original: "hostia illa est Christi corpus, non corporaliter, sed spiritualiter... hic est sanguis meus, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum"</note> which in our language have this meaning: that host is indeed the body of our Lord, yet not in a bodily, but a spiritual way; not the body in which he suffered, but the body of which he spoke when, on the last night before his suffering, he sanctified the bread and wine into the host and first said of the sanctified bread: "This is my body"; and again of the holy wine: "This is my blood, which is shed for many for the forgiveness of sins." He presents the same Doctrine once more in almost as many words in another similar, fine Discourse, which he first gave in Latin and then in Saxon for the Priests themselves, and published by order of Wulfitanus, the Archbishop of York. <note>Wulfstan, Archbishop of York (died 1023).</note> Consequently, men at that time still knew a great difference between "the Bread the Lord" and "the Bread of the Lord," <note>A theological distinction: the bread itself being the Lord (Transubstantiation) versus the bread belonging to the Lord (Sacramental presence).</note> by which, as anyone can easily see, the Mass with all its appendages could not possibly remain standing. Indeed, there is no one who does not well know that this <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>The author uses "Wesen-verschepping," literally "essence-transformation."</note> could only be counted and established as a chief article of Faith in the thirteenth Century, namely in the year 1215, under Innocent III at the Council of the Lateran.

## Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

<meta>catchword: would</meta>

It is then also difficult to imagine that the Churches, which had already shaken off the Roman yoke since the eighth and ninth preceding centuries, would have voluntarily taken it upon themselves again in the tenth; all the more so since they were in no way disturbed in this regard, while the Popes—according to the testimony of almost all historians—were content to give themselves over to all kinds of shameful lusts. I also believe that one cannot have even the slightest suspicion of this with any reason in the world, once I have proven that it was then so far from the case that the Popes of Rome were concerned with properly taking action against the rejecters of their Church laws and the despisers of their Power; that, on the contrary, entire Church assemblies in the middle of Italy, even within Rome itself, and whole Kingdoms—which had not yet left her communion as the Valley <note>The "Valley Churches" refers to the Waldensians, a pre-Reformation group in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont.</note> Churches already had—openly rose up against her and boldly despised her letters, decrees, and commands; in short, they rejected all her new doctrines and oral laws, which the former brought forward and which did not please the latter.

To prove this now more clearly than the sun, it is only necessary to observe what we find regarding it from the famous chronicler Luitprandus <note>Liutprand of Cremona (c. 920–972), a historian and diplomat whose works are a primary source for 10th-century Italian history.</note>, who can never be suspected by the lords of the Roman-minded. This man, in the 6th book of his History, in the 9th and 10th chapters concerning the year 963, gives us the letter of the Emperor Otto the Great and the Council, solemnly described by him at Rome against Pope John XII (the biographer Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a Renaissance historian famous for his "Lives of the Popes."</note> calls him John XIII and "a most wicked man, or rather a monster" <note>original: "hominem sceleratiffimum ac potius monstrum"</note>); contained in these very words:

*To the Supreme Pontiff and universal Pope, Lord John: Otto, by divine clemency Emperor Augustus, together with the Archbishops of Liguria, Tuscany, Saxony, and France, greetings in the Lord. Coming to Rome for the service of God, when we inquired of your sons—namely the Roman Bishops, Cardinals, Priests, Deacons, and the entire populace—concerning your absence, and what the cause might be that you did not wish to see us, the defenders of your Church and yourself; they brought forth such obscene things about you that, if they were spoken of stage-performers, they would make you feel ashamed. And so that your Greatness might not be unaware of all these things, we describe some of them to you briefly, since, if we wished to express everything by name, a single day would not suffice us. Know therefore, that not by a few, but by all—of your own order as well as others—you have been accused of the crimes of murder, perjury, sacrilege, and incest with your own kin and with two sisters. They say another thing, horrific even to hear: that you have drunk wine in love of the Devil; and that in a game of dice you have asked for the help of Jupiter, Venus, and other Demons. We therefore earnestly pray your Paternity that you do not delay coming and purging yourself of all these things. If by chance you fear the violence of the reckless multitude, we affirm to you by oath that nothing shall be done except according to the sanction of the holy Canons. Given on the 8th Ides of November.* <note>original: "Summo Pontifici & universali Papæ, Domino Johanni, Ottho... Data VIII. Idus Novembris:"</note>

Which, through faithful translation, comes to give this meaning: Otto, by the grace of God Emperor and always Enlarger of the Empire, as well as the Archbishops of Liguria, Tuscany, Saxony, and France, wish the High Priest and universal Pope, Lord John, health and salvation in the Lord. And so that your Mightiness may not remain hidden from them all, we shall only describe a few of them very briefly here, while a whole day would not be enough

### XXIII. CHAPTER.

#### Concerning the Revelation of the Antichrist in the Eleventh Century.

From what we have seen until now, it is easy for us to conclude that, while Satan was not yet entirely loosed to deceive all the inhabitants of the earth, nor the Antichrist fully revealed—and while, regarding the errors that then began to intrude into God’s Church, everyone might accept or reject everything according to their own mind—the Churches of the Valleys <note>The Alpine valleys of Piedmont, the historical home of the Vaudois/Waldensians.</note> could very well have maintained the purity of the Apostolic Doctrine, even if they had not so openly left the Communion of Rome, just as we have seen happened during the latter part of the eighth century. One must be all the more certain that they also did the same, because it has appeared so clearly to us that they were not only separated from Rome, but that they dared to denounce the same before all the world as superstitious, its worship as untrue, its ceremonies as idolatry, and its Popes as both un-Apostolic and specifically as Scribes and Pharisees who only "sat in the seat of Moses," <note>A reference to Matthew 23:2, implying the Popes held the position of authority but lacked the spirit of the law.</note> etc. And finally, that just as their Doctrine was such in the eighth century, they also subsequently persisted in the same throughout the ninth and tenth, as we have seen among others that the Great Rorengo <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo (1600–1681), the Prior of Lucerna and a prominent Catholic historian and polemicist against the Waldensians.</note>—being himself a member of the Council *for the extirpation of Heretics* <note>original: "exftirpandis Hæreticis"</note>—made a solemn account of this explicitly to the courts of Turin and Rome in two books, having spent his entire life in that investigation. He was a native of the Valleys, a Co-Lord of those of Lucerna, and possessed the approval and consideration of the entire Clergy of Turin for his books and testimonies.

But likewise, it remains for us to observe how they conducted themselves in the aforementioned eleventh century during the time of the loosening of Satan and the revelation of the Antichrist; that is, how they not only did not drink from the cup of the Great Whore, nor returned to the spiritual Babylon, but even on the contrary, more courageously exposed her nakedness far and wide, brought her abominations to light, and contested her errors. Now, so that this may be done by us with more clarity, we shall abundantly prove, even through the most famous writers of the Roman Catholic faith: 1. That the full rise of the Antichrist must truly be brought to that time, and 2. That the Waldensian Churches, or rather primarily the inhabitants of the Valleys, then also began to thwart his tyranny that much more fiercely.

# General Chronicle

<margin>Fictions forged, as may be seen in Ranulphus Cestrensis. <note>Ralph Higden (c. 1280–1364), a Benedictine monk and chronicler known for his work *Polychronicon*.</note></margin>Likewise, around that same time, certain fictitious Revelations were especially invented, which, added to those deceptive lying-wonders, caused that profit-bringing <term>Purgatory</term> <note>original: "Vage-vier," literally "cleansing fire," a place of temporary punishment for souls.</note> to be ignited, and subsequently also the Masses for the departed souls, who were imagined to still be tormented there. ### CHAPTER XXIV.

#### Concerning the State of the Church at the time of the agitated Revelation of the Antichrist; and how the faithful Witnesses of Jesus Christ, particularly the Waldensians, or Inhabitants of the Valleys, strongly opposed his tyranny and faithfully preserved the pure Doctrine.

<margin>The sad state of the Church concerning the revelation of the Antichrist according to the testimony of St. Augustine and Gregory.</margin>
I must then acknowledge that the condition of God’s Church in such dark times could not have been anything but sorrowful, as it was even foretold by God Himself that the whole world would follow after the Beast and receive his mark on hand and forehead. This went so far that St. Augustine, in his 80th letter to Hesychius, noted the following regarding this matter: "The Church shall not be visible, as the ungodly persecutors will then be raging beyond measure" <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia non est apparitura, impiis tunc persecutoribus ultra modum sævientibus*</note>. And the Holy Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a pivotal figure in early medieval theology.</note>, in the 19th book of his moral commentary on Job, in the 29th chapter, wrote the following maxim: "The Church, as if weakened by a certain old age, shall by no means be able to bear faithful children through the free proclamation of the Word" <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia quasi quodam senio debilitata, per prædicationem filios minime erit paritura*</note>. With this also agrees a certain <margin>Ephrem.</margin> Ephrem the Syrian <note>A 4th-century deacon and prolific Syriac-language hymnwriter and theologian.</note>, when he assures in his sermon on the end of the world and the Antichrist that at that time, one person shall most earnestly ask another whether the Word of God is still hidden and preserved in one corner of the world or another, etc. But above all, regarding the teachers of the Gospel of that time, these words of the English Teacher Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> are very noteworthy, which he wrote among other things concerning the 9th and <margin>And St. Thomas.</margin> 10th chapters of Revelation: "In the beginning, when the Antichrist is born, before he has expanded his power, preaching will still occur. <margin>Their condition in the Valleys.</margin>

It also has quite some probability that, in order to have proof of this, he took a consecrated host and sacrificed it to the fire, as Matthew Paris and even Cardinal Benno testify to us, who, being contemporary with him, could well have known of the true occurrences. Whatever the case may be, it is not easy to believe that he [the Pope] believed in Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: the Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual substance of the body and blood of Christ.</term> or that the true body of the Lord was in the Mass-wafer, since he even dared to throw it into the fire.

They had spread the doctrine far beyond the Valleys and had come to form a very significant group, all unanimously rejecting the Doctrine of Gregory. # General Chronicle

<margin>That the Doctrine, just as the revelation of the Antichrist occurred, received new strength through Peter of Bruys.</margin>...of one Peter of Bruys, a Priest of Toulouse and a prominent teacher of those who, in the majority of historical records, bear the name of Albigenses <note>A medieval Christian sect in Southern France, often associated with the Waldensians by later Protestant historians.</note>, also nicknamed Petrobrusians. They began to reveal themselves more openly, being also—beyond all contradiction, as is confirmed in several places in this work—none other than the same Waldensians. For they, like that great man of God <note>Referring to Peter of Bruys.</note>, were not satisfied with merely rejecting more and more of the Roman decrees, courageously opposing the Pope and entirely refusing to ever return to his fellowship; but they also gave reasons for this in a particular book, which they published in their mother tongue under the title *Aiço es la caofa de noftre despartiment de la Gleife Romane* <note>original Occitan: "This is the reason for our departure from the Roman Church."</note>. The historian De Serres <note>Jean de Serres (1540–1598), a French humanist and historian.</note> says he preserves this among his books for the year 1223, and of which we ourselves still have irrefutable copies, written in an Old German-style script <note>Likely referring to Gothic blackletter script.</note> on parchment and kept in the famous University of Cambridge.

In these writings, they completely reject Purgatory, images, the invocation of saints, the sacrifice of the Mass (which people were then already starting to introduce), Transubstantiation <note>The belief that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>, the power of the Pope, and his church commands. <margin>A short summary of the same.</margin> They taught that Baptism brought no salvation insofar as it was merely a ritual, as if grace were bound to the water, but rather that one must be included in God’s Covenant through it. They taught that Masses for the dead were nothing but folly and godlessness; that priests and monks should rather marry than burn in unchaste flames of desire; that the Cross should not be worshipped or honored; that it was superstitious to forbid anyone from eating certain foods on certain days; and that one should never accept any teaching unless it agreed with the Rule of Scripture, etc.

But because handwritten books can easily be brought into doubt, even those that could give us samples of the doctrine of those Petrobrusian Waldensians, I will refrain from bringing many others of the same kind here, even though they are equally contrary to the traditions of Rome. I am satisfied that I have cited the aforementioned, because they are recognized and known even by one of their greatest enemies, namely one <margin>Confirmed by Petrus Cluniacenfis.</margin> Petrus Cluniacenfis <note>Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156), Abbot of Cluny, who wrote against the Petrobrusians.</note>, who speaks of this in his first and second letters, etc., just as Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer and historian.</note> notes in the 15th book of the *Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth*. In that place, he also recounts that the said Peter of Bruys—after he had steadfastly continued for over twenty years in Languedoc, Provence, and Dauphiné, as well as especially in the Dioceses of Gap and Embrun, being hemmed in by the valleys between the Alps, yet moving somewhat more toward the heart of France—finally sealed these mentioned articles of faith with his blood at Saint-Gilles in Languedoc. <margin>And Davity.</margin> The chronicler Davity <note>Pierre Davity (1573–1635), a French historian and geographer.</note>, who also mentions this on page 350 of his *Writings on Heresies*, says that this happened in the year 1124, which is more than fifty years before the time of Waldo of Lyons <note>Peter Waldo, often credited as the founder of the Waldensians, though this author argues the movement is older.</note>.

<margin>Subsequently defended by many other great men, especially by one Henricus.</margin> The death of Peter of Bruys did not diminish the number of those who came to adhere to his doctrine, while the same was continually upheld by Theucholin or Tudemus, Peter of Blois, John Rosalin (a very learned man and one of the principal restorers of the Academy of Paris), the highly learned Peter Alexander, a certain man called Arnoldus (who was finally executed at Paris according to the account of Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a papal historian.</note>), and among many other great men, especially one Henricus <note>Henry of Lausanne, a 12th-century reformer and student of Peter of Bruys.</note>, a disciple of the said Peter of Bruys. As Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay <note>A Cistercian monk and chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade.</note> acknowledges in the preface of his *Albigensian History*, and Davity along with others in the cited place, Henricus followed in his footsteps in all things. Indeed, this last man championed the cause with such courage and luster, that whereas they were previously called Petro-

# Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

...Bruysians were called, they received from this Henry the surname Henricians. St. Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note>, undoubtedly poorly informed about his teaching, also rails terribly against him in his 65th and 66th Church-teachings <note>Sermons on the Song of Songs.</note> regarding the Song of Songs; wherein he nonetheless—which is very noteworthy—calls his disciples *Apostolics*, as they boasted greatly that they were the upright descendants of the Apostles and faithful preservers and followers of their doctrine. He likewise insults them as simple and dull people, "whom nonetheless many of the Clergy and Bishops, indeed even many secular Princes, deign to favor" <note>original Latin: *quos tamen multi de Clero & Episcopis, imo etiam de Laïcis Principibus, fovere dignantur*</note>. Finally, he attributes to them, among other things, that they teach that the fire of Purgatory is but a dream, since souls, immediately after departing the body, go straight to rest or damnation; that one may not pray for the deceased; and that the Papal Synagogue of Rome is in no way the Church, etc.

<margin>Antiquity of the Waldensians.</margin>
Now this last point alone, which St. Bernard forces upon them—namely, that they say the Roman Synagogue is not the Church, while they present themselves as the true Church, being truly Apostolic—must be more than sufficient to the judgment of all reasonable people to prove convincingly that they then no longer recognized the Roman Church as the upright Church. Rather, they had separated themselves from it as from a heretical Synagogue in order to hold to the pure doctrine of the Apostles. Regarding this, I cannot refrain from once again asking the kind reader to take this brief observation in passing concerning the antiquity of the doctrine of these Petrobrusians and Henricians (whose summary we have just touched upon). That is, one cannot deny (even the Roman Papists themselves do not deny it, but even dare to confirm it as the truth, as we see in Gretserus <note>Jakob Gretser (1562–1625), a Jesuit historian and polemicist.</note>, etc.) that it is one and the same as that of the Waldensians; and they themselves were called among one another without distinction by the name of Waldensians and were condemned under the same, even though Peter Waldo of Lyons had not yet appeared at that time. This can then also be added to those other clear and irreproachable proofs that we already presented in the 2nd chapter of this book—where we traced the origin of the name <term>Waldensian</term> <note>The author argues the name comes from "valleys" rather than Peter Waldo.</note>—as well as the account of Waldo, who was contemporary with Berengarius. From this it follows necessarily that they did not first begin to be called Waldensians after that Waldo of Lyons, but had of old in their language the name of *Valdenfes* or *Valdesi*, because the word there means <term>Valley-dwellers</term> <note>original Dutch: *Valleyenaars*</note>; and that in all that space between the Alpine mountains, which is called habitable vales or valleys, located both down in Piedmont and in France, they always harmoniously confessed the same religion beyond human memory.

<margin>Confirmed by the lifetime of Bernard.</margin>
But to confirm this truth somewhat more closely, let the reader please note this briefly: namely, that St. Bernard—even according to the chronology of Genebrardus <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegite and historian.</note> and other trustworthy chroniclers of the Roman persuasion—was made a Saint in the year 1165, twelve years after his death, and subsequently died at 63 years of age in the year 1153. And as he was born at the end of the 11th century (that is, in the year 1090), he was already in high regard by the year 1120. Because all that is so, it is also necessary that this Henry of whom he speaks, and to whose disciples he gives the title of honor "Apostolics"—people whose faith was supported by many Clergy, by Bishops, and Princes—had maintained himself and increased significantly long before, as they were already making such a stir in his time. One also does not see that he ever reproaches that school of teaching (as he chooses to nickname them) for their novelty; but rather, he speaks of them as of a doctrine that is deeply rooted. But

# General Chronicle

<meta>catchword: toward</meta>

...taken however, that this Henry only revealed himself around the time of St. Bernard, that is around the year 1120; it is nevertheless so, that since his teacher Peter de Bruys—according to the account of his sworn enemy Peter of Cluny <note>Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156), Abbot of Cluny, who wrote "Against the Petrobrusians."</note>—had already presented the same Doctrine long before him with such luster, that they were already called Petrobrusians after his name twenty years prior and had become such a multitude that the Roman Court feared them so much that it convened Council after Council to oppose them; these Churches also necessarily remained active in the tenth and eleventh centuries, that is, before the times of St. Bernard and the birth of the Antichrist <note>Protestant writers of this era often used "the birth of the Antichrist" to refer to the period when the Papacy reached the height of its political and spiritual power.</note>, as we have sufficiently proven, and between 70 and 80 years before the aforementioned Waldensis or Waldo of Lyon <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1205), often credited as the founder of the Waldensians, though the author argues the movement is older.</note>, they had already publicly stood against his [the Pope's] tyranny.

<margin>And by the Council of Tours.</margin>
Whatever the case may be, Pope Alexander III as early as the year 1167 at the Synod of Tours <note>The Council of Tours was actually held in 1163; the author’s date may reflect a different calendar or source.</note> had an article established, by which he, among others, gives the Teaching of the Waldensians the name of *damnada Hæresis, quæ jamdudum emersit* <note>original: "a damned heresy, which emerged long ago"</note>, a damned heresy that had crept into the world long before. In this, one should take good notice of the word *jamdudum*, or "long ago." For since he could not very well point out its exact beginning, it must have been of a respectable age, all the more so as the said church rule also states that they had not only traversed the entire region of Toulouse, Languedoc, and Provence, as well as Lombardy, by then, but had even spread through Gascony and other provinces and taken deep root; all of which is recounted by one William of Marpurg <note>Likely referring to William of Malmesbury (c. 1095–1143), a famous English historian.</note> in his second <margin>And the 1st Lateran.</margin> book of the affairs of England. But this is not all. Namely, even in the documents of the first Lateran Council, held eight years before that of Tours—that is, in the year 1159 <note>The Third Lateran Council was in 1179; the chronology here reflects the author's specific historical sources which vary from modern consensus.</note>—which Rome has wanted to place at the top of all the general Church Councils of the East, it is found that the same Teaching of the Waldensians was already condemned as a doctrine that was already old at that time, deep-rooted, and spread everywhere.

<margin>Likewise newly propagated by one Arnold. As Rorenco himself admits.</margin>
After the death of the aforementioned Henry, a certain Arnold of Brescia, one of their prominent Teachers, further advanced the same Doctrine through Italy and especially renewed it throughout all of Lombardy, to which the Valleys of Piedmont also belong. This is even admitted by the Chief Abbot Rorenco <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo (died 1664), the Prior of Lucerna and a major Catholic opponent of the Waldensians.</note> (who is still living), their most bloody persecutor as a member of the Council for the *exstirpandis Hæreticis* <note>original: "the extirpation of heretics"</note>, in the second chapter of his book entitled *Memorie historiche* <note>original: "Historical Memoirs"</note>; who, following many other historians, also ensures that they were called Arnoldists after the name of this Arnold. But having finally gone to preach in Rome against the Pope and his Clergy, according to the account of [Otto of] Freising in the 20th chapter of the *Deeds of Emperor Frederick*, the fury of the Roman Court against this great Man of God was so great that, having gotten him into their clutches, they were not satisfied with nailing him to a cross—as they say the Heathens also did to St. Peter—but in the year 1155, having taken him from the cross, they burned his body to ashes.

> by the Esperonists one must understand the same fellow believers who are otherwise
