# General Memorial

...tirely driven from their paths and were forced to do so; it seems to me sufficient to answer that it was for the same reasons why the Lords did not wish to throw their long-standing local subjects into unrest, as those regions had always been inhabited by them, and they had professed the same Faith from generation to generation since time immemorial. If one wishes to see this more clearly, the following powerful reasons might also apply.

It happened, then: 
I. <margin>1st reason.</margin> because several of those Lords held a very good opinion of the Teaching, acknowledging specifically that it was in agreement with the Holy Scriptures. 
The II. <margin>2nd reason.</margin> reason is the good life of these people: their uprightness, piety, love, and loyalty, to which even their greatest enemies give many excellent testimonies, as we shall see later in the 30th chapter of this book. This caused even high-ranking people within the Roman Catholic <note>original: "Roomfse Gefinte"</note> community to consider it no small blessing to have servants or maids from among these people. They openly declared that such virtuous, moderate, and loyal people were to be found nowhere else. This continued, despite various oppositions raised by the Clergy, until the year 1640. I could provide countless examples and testimonies of this here as well. I could even show that the same Lords and other prominent Catholics used every effort to get Waldensian <term>nurses<gloss>wet-nurses or nannies</gloss></term> for their children. Finding none willing to leave their own households, the nobles placed their children with the Waldensians, even in the highest mountains. But since those troubled times, the <term>oppressors<gloss>original: "dwingketters," literally those who force or persecute regarding heresy</gloss></term> and especially Her Royal Highness have imposed so many ecclesiastical and civil fines on anyone keeping such servants or nurses, that no one dares employ them now, for fear of being immediately labeled a "half-heretic" by everyone. 
The III. <margin>3rd reason.</margin> reason—which helped prevent even those Lords who might otherwise have disliked these poor people from persecuting them cruelly—is the matter of self-interest (this is the great law of state for almost all men). They recognized the great income and unbelievable rents they gained from the preservation of these people, which would be ruined and lost with their destruction. No one can doubt this truth who knows anything of the geography and current state of that land, and who considers the labor, management, and way of life of these people.

Specifically, the places in the *Great Valley of Luserna*, where freedom of religion has remained in effect from all time, or from time immemorial <note>original: "da ogni tempo" or "da tempo immemoriale"</note>—as they have always demonstrated to their Princes through the petitions presented to them, without this phrasing ever being criticized by anyone—are the entire communities of Angrogna, Rora, and Torre Pellice from St. Margaret’s bridge upwards, as well as Villars and Bobbio.

Between the Valley of Luserna and the Valley of Perosa lies the dale and the community of Rocheplatte.

In the Valley of Perosa itself, one finds the places St. Germain, Pramollo, Grand-Dublon, Le Taluc, and Le Pis.

In the Valley of St. Martin are the communities of Faetto, Salsa, Massello, Rodoretto, and Prali.

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

VV 2

In the Marquisate of Saluzzo are located the lands or mountains of Pravillelm, Biolet, Biëtonnet, Festiona, etc.

I shall remain silent regarding the Valleys of Chisone <note>original: "Cluſon"</note>, or Pragelato, Queyras, Freissinières, and Val-Poutane or Vallouise, which almost all border those of Piedmont and are always nestled between these same Alps.

Finally, in the Valley of Susa, we find the valleys of Meana, Mattie, and several others.

Among all these places, some lie in the mountains, which commonly remain buried under snow for seven, eight, and indeed often nine months of the year; these regions previously gave shelter only to wolves and bears, being generally covered with forests that are mostly such high-standing woods that they are barely possible to approach or pass through. These poor people have also known how to manage and cultivate these lands with unthinkable effort, so much so that they are now filled with many inhabited villages, though nothing more than a little rye, barley, or oats can be harvested, and even that is often so scarce that they can hardly recover their own seed. This, however, only happens to them when the snow surprises them before the ground has frozen properly. 

Meanwhile, the menfolk usually depart for the entire winter, leaving their wives and children with the few meager resources they have for their sustenance, and go into foreign lands to earn a living. One occupies himself with rope-making, another with cabinetry or carpentry, a third with masonry, and finally others with sawing heavy trees into planks and crossbeams by hand. From there they return home around Easter, bringing with them the little money they have been able to save, which is often the only means to sufficiently protect their livestock and small household goods—which they may still possess—against the seizures of the <term>tax collectors<gloss>officials who collected "schatting," a type of land or property tax</gloss></term>. 

In like manner, the women and daughters of these poor mountain folk go to Pinerolo, the nearest city in Piedmont (which currently belongs to the King of France), and carry there long poles of *larch* <note>original: "Meleſe"</note>, a wood very suitable for supporting the high vineyards of those who live in the plains. They travel thus, going and returning, between 20 and 24 miles on foot to earn a few pounds of salt, which is exceedingly expensive in those regions. They also go so heavily burdened with that load that no stranger could see them without having great pity for them, and all this for less than a French guilder, or a <term>quart d'écu<gloss>a silver coin worth a quarter of a crown</gloss></term>; upon which they must then live for three whole days, which they necessarily spend on the road. 

Also, the other places situated somewhat lower in more fertile and warmer regions are so unsuitable and difficult regarding labor (I speak now not of the very few households inhabiting the small plains of San Giovanni and Torre Pellice, who pay richly for their convenience with the heavy burden of tolls and taxes), so sharp, so mountainous, and so ungovernable; because there is not one where one could use any wagons, and many others where one cannot even put horses or mules to work in carrying all sorts of loads. The backs of those wretched people must serve as all the wagons and strong beasts of burden, and they themselves must carry their hay, wheat, wood, wine, must, etc., often not only for many hours but sometimes even for entire days' journeys, wherever necessity requires. 

But this is most worthy of wonder: namely, that in several places where there was nothing but a single cliff and where one could find little or no earth in the gaps between the rocks, all of them sloping almost equally steeply, they have raised small stonework, like steps <note>meaning terraces</note>, and brought much soil there from elsewhere. For therein they have even planted their vines, which they maintain with unbelievable...

Where they, when the snow and ice begin to melt, are in constant danger of being overwhelmed and covered by *avalanches* <note>original: "avalanches"</note>, that is, large clumps of snow that slide down from the top of the Alps and roll downwards, sweeping away everything they encounter; often uprooting not only strong trees and some houses, but also sometimes entire villages, as there are all too many sad examples of this, especially when it happens that a large pile of trees or accumulated rocks causes them to jump outside their defined space and set valleys, like some streams over their banks? <margin>Why the Clergy did not persecute those poor Waldensians from the beginning. 1st reason.</margin>...it must be asked how, since those simple folk so boldly rejected the institutions of Rome, the clergy of the surrounding areas—or even the priests and popish clerics of the districts, who in various places lived not only in their neighborhood but even among and under them—could have left them somewhat at peace? To which it can be quite pleasantly answered: I. That those regions were always devoid of Jesuits, "converting monks," heresy-suppressors <note>original: "Dwingketters," referring to inquisitors or those who used force to compel religious conformity</note>, and other such spies and deadly persecutors of non-Catholics, except for the last three hundred years. This is shown to us by the good Grand Prior Marco Aurelio Rorenco di Lucerna <note>A 17th-century Catholic official and historian who wrote about the Waldensians</note> on page 127 of his *Historical Notes*, printed with approval in Turin in the year 1649. He shows there that the first monastery in the Valleys was only founded in the fourteenth century, and likewise the first abbey, which was built in the year 1228 in the community of Villars in honor of St. Christopher, was also only given to the Order of St. Benedict—that is, to the heresy-suppressors—around the year 1444. It is therefore no wonder that those poor people were not yet spied upon, harassed, or suppressed by those "locusts of Revelation" <note>A biblical reference to the agents of destruction in the Book of Revelation, here applied to the inquisitorial orders</note>, who today are the great agitators and tools of His Holiness of Rome.

<margin>2nd reason.</margin>II. Regarding the priests and the aforementioned district clerics themselves, some among them knew the truth well enough, though they kept it hidden; others "played the Nicodemus" <note>Referring to the biblical figure who followed Jesus in secret; used here to describe people who hid their true beliefs to avoid trouble</note>, being neither cold nor hot, and stayed on good terms with both sides, adapting themselves to everything just to keep their positions. There were even others who, while keeping their honorable titles and miters unchanged, boldly taught the Truth to their parishioners, even if they "howled with the wolves" elsewhere. So, since a good number of such priests were still found, the *Barbes* <note>original: "Barbes," the traditional title for Waldensian pastors, meaning "uncles" in their dialect</note>, or teachers of the true believers, overlooked their weaknesses and nonetheless embraced them as brothers. From this, it easily followed that these same teachers often took the names of Priests, Shepherds, *Barbes*, and even Bishops without distinction.

<margin>3rd reason.</margin>III. But finally, the primary reason that forced the most ill-willed of those priests and clerics to remain quiet was that they feared losing both their church and their tithes, and consequently their "fat morsels" <note>original: "vette sopjes," a Dutch idiom for an easy income or comfortable lifestyle</note>; as they could not avoid this if they caused their entire districts to be broken up.

### XXVI. CHAPTER.

#### Concerning a certain Testimony about the Antiquity of the Waldensian Church, otherwise those of the Valleys of Piedmont, drawn from their own Writings.

Up to this point, we have seen: 1. how the Valleys were able to maintain the purity of the Gospel without changing any article of faith until the eighth century, and indeed did maintain it; 2. how, at the end of that same century—when people were already being forced to accept images, the invocation of saints, relics, and pilgrimages; in short, when superstition and idolatry were being pushed into their midst—Claudius, their own High Bishop <note>Claudius of Turin, a 9th-century bishop famous for his opposition to the use of religious images</note>, courageously resisted it, prevented his diocese from being infected by it, and openly separated himself from Rome, calling it a false religion, contrary to the universal Faith and the pure...

It also introduces the historical role of Bishop Claudius of Turin as a defender of their "pure" faith against Roman innovations.</summary>

->General Memorial<-

,, Truth, a new choice of doctrine <note>Dutch: "Leerkeur," referring to a confession or set of selected beliefs</note>, going far beyond the Apostle’s Faith, who as well as the Pope himself can be held as Apostolic; of whom he said, that they sat upon the Seat of St. Peter just as formerly the Pharisees sat upon that of Moses: in a word, how he already then taught that which is currently called **Calvinistery** <note>A term used by opponents to describe Calvinism</note>, or the teachings of Calvin, just as we have proven even with the complete agreement of the Roman historians. 3. How also his teachings, during the ninth, tenth, and eleventh centuries in the Valleys of Piedmont and surrounding places—standing nevertheless under the same Church jurisdiction—were very wonderfully preserved, although they were then in all other regions suppressed almost to the point of choking; and how they primarily gained great strength again in the following period and were spread over Dauphiné and Provence, provinces of France situated near the Valleys, and thereafter were strongly distributed in Lyon: and finally how these, through the scattering of the **Waldensians of Lyon**, were set forth even more broadly through almost all of Europe, as formerly through all of Asia upon the occasion of similar persecution arising in the time of the Holy Martyr Stephen. From all of this, it seems to me, the reader should now be able to see clearly enough what is to be held regarding the true Apostolic origin <note>Dutch: "bevang," meaning the reach or succession</note> of the Waldensians and their upright antiquity. Nevertheless, I intend for good measure, with God’s help, to give him much more light and certainty regarding this, and with three types of arguments—of which one alone would be more than sufficient to convince and compel all gainsayers to surrender to the truth—to strengthen him even more powerfully and immovably in that right opinion. For all these being joined together, they shall forever and always stop the mouths of those who, maliciously misusing these words from **Tertullian** in his *Prescription Against Heretics* <note>original: "de praescript. contr. Haeret."</note>, constantly shoot at us the insulting, mocking words of which he speaks, saying: *Who are you? Where did you come from? Where have you been hiding so long?* <note>original Latin: "qui estis vos? unde venistis? ubi tam diu latuistis?"</note>

<margin>
Three types of arguments for the Antiquity of the Waldensians.
</margin>
The first then of these proofs we shall draw from the own writings of the Waldensians, not so much in view of their expressed time of writing, but primarily from the language they use therein, which very clearly makes known whether they were outsiders <note>Dutch: "Afdoditen," likely a corruption of "Aphroditischen" or a similar term for pagans/outsiders</note> or true children of Abraham; and especially from that which they themselves have so clearly shown regarding their antiquity to all powers, both Clerical and Secular, with whom they ever had anything to do, so that they never received any contradiction against it. The following shall be taken from many distinguished chroniclers and non-Roman teachers who recognized that pure antiquity, thanking God that He had so miraculously preserved it like a torch, from which nearly all the Orthodox <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the Protestant Reformed churches</note> churches of Europe have borrowed their light, either medially or immediately. But the last and most decisive proof, which like a ball of pitch <note>A reference to the story of Daniel and the Dragon, using pitch to stop a beast's mouth</note> could stop the maw of the hellish Dragon himself and prevent him from ever biting or making a noise again, I shall take from the multitude of testimonies of the famous opponents of those poor believers, and even from the heresy-suppressors who were appointed to root them out and wipe their memory entirely from the earth; as these shall give us more proof of the antiquity and the Apostolic origin of the Waldensians than they themselves and all the Romans put together.

<margin>
The first from the preface of the first French Bible.
</margin>
To begin then with the own writings of the Waldensians: those of the Valleys thank God in the Preface of the first French Bible that ever appeared whole and unadulterated in the world, written from the Alps on the 17th of February <note>Dutch: "Sprockelmaant," an old name for February</note> in the year 1535, because *from the time they were enriched with the treasure of the Gospel by the Holy Apostles, or their near successors, they had always* <note>original French: "dès qu'ils furent enrichis du thresor de l' Euangile par les SS. Apôtres, ou leurs proches successeurs, ils en avoient toûjours"</note>

### Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

*...always preserved the full enjoyment* <note>original French: "toujours conservé l'entiere fruition"</note>, after they had once been enriched with the treasure of the Gospel by the Apostles or their immediate successors, they always maintained the complete enjoyment of the same.

<margin>From *The Noble Lesson*.</margin> One of their writings, called *The Noble Lesson* <note>original title: "La Noble Leiçon," a famous 12th-century Waldensian poem</note>, the original manuscript of which (a sample of which can be found earlier in the 4th chapter of this book) is kept in the renowned University of Cambridge <note>original: "Cambritz"</note> and in Geneva along with others that we cite in the list of names in the 3rd preceding [part]; it bears the date of 1100—that is, from the eleventh century—as can be seen immediately at the beginning on the sixth line. And to say it here, the subject matter and writing style of that work entirely resemble that of the Apostles. For every kind of sin is strictly rebuked therein, and conversely, all Christian virtues are wonderfully well-described and praised; the reading of God's Word is prescribed, the invocation of the only God to the exclusion of all creatures, perseverance under the cross, and the rejection of false teachers and all emerging errors are strongly impressed upon the reader. The Antichrist <note>A term used by the Waldensians to describe the perceived corruption within the medieval Papacy</note>, who was then certainly being born, is very accurately depicted from life, and the remission of sins given by priests for money is thoroughly exposed as one of his new inventions. All of this is written with such a grace that one can clearly see from it that they had always steadfastly rejected the Roman traditions, which they had never accepted, and even then rejected them entirely; nor were they ever minded to accept any doctrine besides that of our Savior and his Apostles, which they had received from hand to hand and from generation to generation. Consequently, I should henceforth no longer need to be concerned with bringing forward many broad proofs to show that the Waldensians (for so they are already named in that writing) had not learned their doctrine from a certain **Peter Waldo**, as they already called it *Ancient* and *Apostolic* in the year 1100 and set it against the new inventions of Rome.

<margin>And the writing of the Antichrist.</margin> But the same is also remarkably confirmed by the excellent *Treatise on the Antichrist*, which you have found inserted in its entirety in the same book concerning the doctrine of the ancient Waldensians, even though it was published in the year 1120 and thereafter—more than fifty years before Waldo. Anyone who will take the trouble to notice how the believers therein are armed in advance against the new church laws of Rome and all incoming errors must certainly confess that such a style of writing can only be used by such people who would sooner choose to die than to allow the precious treasure of the pure and truly apostolic doctrine to be snatched from them by anyone in the world. Why it was also impossible that the slightest novelty could be talked into them, who remained so firm by it and wished to preserve the same without any change or mixture. But he who has no desire to read that entire wonderful *Tract on the Antichrist* may just cast his eye on the one place where this note stands in the margin: *reasons why they are separated from the Roman Church*, and which begins thus: *Now therefore we take care to note what the causes of our departure are, etc.* <note>original Waldensian: "or donc nous ordonnon notar, quals sian las caosas del nostre departiment. esv."</note> since he will be able to learn there that it happened only to maintain among them and in their assembly, as they say, *the essential truth of the faith, worship appropriate to God alone, the merit of Jesus Christ with all sufficiency of grace and righteousness, the true remission of sins, true repentance, etc.* <note>original Waldensian: "la Verità essential de la fé, Cultivament convenivol al sol Dio, lo Meric de Jesu Christ cum tota sufficientia de gratia & giustitia, la vera Remission de li peccà, la vera Penitentia, esv."</note> which is contrary to all the corruptions that Rome sought to introduce.

These documents are used to prove the Waldensians maintained an 'Apostolic' faith independent of Roman Catholic innovations.</summary>

# General Memorial Writing

<margin>And that regarding the Invocation of the Saints.</margin>In the meantime, the magnificent book against the invocation of the Saints <note>The practice of praying to saints as mediators, which the Waldensians rejected in favor of praying to God alone</note> must be even older than the previously mentioned work on the Antichrist. This is because it is explicitly noted that it was composed as soon as the doctrine of worshipping Saints began to increase in the Church—at the very moment men sought to move the faithful away from a respectful commemoration of the Holy Martyrs <note>original: "H. Bloetgetuygen," literally "blood-witnesses"</note> (who confirmed the truth of the Gospel with their own lives to encourage steadfastness during persecutions) and toward treating them as minor deities, or at least as advocates and mediators between us and God; in a word, as beings to be worshipped. For it calls that doctrine *the new intercessions, introduced by the Man of Sin* <note>original Occitan/Old French: "las novas intercessions, entermenà per l'homme de peccà"</note>—that is, the innovations that the "Man of Sin" <note>A biblical reference to the Antichrist, here associated with the corruption of the Roman Church</note> sought to drag into and establish within the Church. Now, those even slightly familiar with Church History know for certain that this superstition first crossed into the Latin <note>Western/Roman</note> Churches precisely in the sixth century, during the time of the Roman Bishop Gregory the Great. While previous practices (for there were already some beginnings of this in the Greek Church around the year 476) were not only approved but accompanied by new additions. It was then that saints were made into minor gods, and churches and feast days were consecrated to them. Though such invocation of saints was still practiced by some in private and was even slandered and contradicted by the largest and best part of the Church, it began to become public when the aforementioned Gregory included the Holy Virgin in the Litany <note>The standard communal prayers of the Church</note>. Following this, over time, the same status was obtained for other saints, until this evil had infected almost the entire North by the eighth century. Consequently, the mentioned writing that the Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenfen"</note> composed against this emerging or "new" doctrine of invoking saints must necessarily have been written before the aforementioned work on the Antichrist. Be that as it may, the entire content and discourse clearly show that its only goal was to preserve the doctrine of the Lord Jesus and His Apostles <note>original: "Kruyf-gesanten," literally "ambassadors of the Cross"</note> purely and entirely, and to oppose everything introduced secretly against it from time to time. As soon as one reads it, one is completely convinced of this.

<margin>Another old handwritten book</margin>Furthermore, the reader may find in one of the old handwritten books dated to the year 1587 (which is kept in safety at Cambridge <note>original: "Cambritz"</note> according to the catalog) an answer to a question posed to the Waldensians of the Valleys: *How long has this religion been preached in the Valleys?* <note>original Italian/Vaudois: "quanto tempo è, che la religion è stata predicata nelle Valli"</note>. The answer given is: *About five hundred years, as can be gathered from many histories; but according to the belief of the inhabitants of the Valleys, from time immemorial, and from father to son even from the time of the Apostles* <note>original: "circa cinque cento anni, come si può raccogler da molte Historie; ma secondo la credenzo de gli habitanti delle Valli da tempo immemoriale & da padre in figliuolo indi dal tempo de gl' Apostoli"</note>. Truly, the mention of such books speaking only of "about five hundred years" (which would then place their origin around the year 1087) arises only because they were not yet universally persecuted—for reasons we have touched upon elsewhere in this book—and thus their name had not yet become so famous. Even so, this would still be 100 years before Peter Waldo of Lyon.

<margin>A letter of the Walden-</margin>With this, a certain letter agrees well, which those of Provence sent in the year 1530 through George Morel and Pierre Masson, two of the teachers <note>pastors or "barbes"</note> of the Valleys...

# Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches

<margin>Letters to Oecolampadius.</margin>...ley, have written to Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), a major Protestant Reformer in Basel</note>, charging him to hold a broad mutual discussion with him, Bucer <note>Martin Bucer, reformer of Strasbourg</note>, Capito <note>Wolfgang Capito</note>, and Haller <note>Berchtold Haller, reformer of Bern</note> regarding several ceremonies about which they were in doubt. For in these letters, regarding their antiquity, they use these very words: "for so that you may understand once and for all, we, such as we are, teachers of a poor and small people, who have remained for more than four hundred years among the most cruel thorns, yet not without the great favor of Christ, as all the faithful would easily judge; for the people have been frequently delivered by the said favor, even when they were most pricked and tormented by the said thorns" <note>original Occitan: "car açò que tu entendas una vèz, nos tals, quals enſegnador d'un poble pavre & petit, liqual an demorà plus de quatre cent ans entre las crudeliſſimas ſpinas, ma emperçò non ſenza grand favor de Chriſt, come legierament jugerian tuit li fidels; car es iſtà delivrà ſovenderament par la dicta favor, point & tormentà de las ditas ſpinas"</note>. Now, in this letter from the Waldensians to Oecolampadius, the reader should please note that it is not said that they had enjoyed the purity of the Gospel for only 400 years; but rather, that for more than 400 years they had been persecuted and "entangled in thorns," from which they were nonetheless delivered from time to time by Christ's grace. This period also coincides exactly with the times in which Satan was "unbound" and the Antichrist was revealed to wage war against the Saints—a war that has never ceased, first wounding and tearing them through excommunication and later, as we shall see in the first chapter of the following book, through fire and sword.

<margin>And their Confession of Faith from the year 1120.</margin>To confirm this same great antiquity, their Confession of Faith, written in the year 1120, also serves wonderfully well. It was previously inserted here in full among the examples of their Doctrine; such that anyone who chooses to consider both the simplicity and conciseness of the writing style, as well as the age of the document itself, must also confess that nothing can be found that more closely resembles the language of the Apostles.

<margin>Yet another from the year 1544.</margin>They further testify in their confession, which they presented in the year 1544 to the French King Francis I for their defense, that it was entirely the same as that which they had received from hand to hand from their ancestors, just as their forebears had taught it to them from time to time. This is recounted by one Johannes Crispinus in *Monuments of the Martyrs, Book 3* <note>original Latin: "Monum. Martÿr. l. 3."</note>, which is confirmed by a certain Lancelot du Voisin, as well as by Lord De la Popelinière in the first book of his *French Histories* from the year 1581, on page 26.

<margin>And the style of their petitions and demonstrations.</margin>The Great Prior Rorenco, after having spoken in his chronological notes in the 38th chapter, page 128, about a mission of the Jesuits sent to the Valleys in the year 1580, and subsequently the petition which the excesses of those "new guests" had caused them to present to their Prince in this sense: "Most severe Duke, etc. There appear most humbly at the feet of Your Royal Highness your most faithful, etc.," saying that certain Jesuits, at the time and place of their assemblies, and especially on Sundays, had for some time been forcing their way in to take the churches away from them and to disturb their ministers in their service—even using the boldness to find themselves accompanied by various crowds of Roman Catholics, with the Judge, or Governor, and even sometimes with the Lords of the Valleys, specifically arming themselves with a letter written by Your Royal Highness on the 20th of December of this current year, etc. Having set this out at length, he shows among others these words: "it is a true and notorious thing, most serene Duke, that his said subjects and their ancestors have been taught for several hundred years in the true Christian Religion by their Ministers, whom they honorably called <term>Barbes</term> <note>The word "Barbe" means uncle in the local dialect; it was the respectful title given to Waldensian pastors to distinguish them from the Roman Catholic clergy</note>," <note>original French/Occitan: "c'eſt choſe vraye & notoire, ſereniſſime Duc, ſes dits ſujets & leurs anceſtres avoir été enſeignez dés pluſieurs centaines d'années en la vraye Religion Chreſtienne par leurs Miniſtres, qu' ils appelloient honorablement des Barbes"</note>

# General Memorial

...—bes, and that they sometimes taught them in secret and nightly assemblies in imitation of the primitive Church to flee the persecution of the Clergy: but since then, seeing that pretexts were being taken to slander them at any price, they wished to preach publicly the Holy Doctrine, which they had from all antiquity and handed down from their fathers, etc. <note>original French: "...bes, & qu' ils les ont par fois enseignes en des assemblées secrettes & nocturnes a l'imitation de la primitive Eglise pour fuïr la persecution des Ecclesiastiques : mais du depuis voyant, qu'on prenoit de la pretexte de les calomnier, a quel prix que ce fût, ils ont voulu precher publiquement la S. Doctrine, qu'ils avoient de toute ancienneté & de main en main imbue de leurs peres, esv."</note> That is to say: it is true and well-known, most severe Duke, that your aforementioned subjects and all their ancestors for several hundred years already have been instructed in the true Christian Religion by their Teachers, whom they, as a sign of respect, called <term>Barbes: an old Occitan term for "uncles," used by the Waldensians for their pastors to protect their identity during times of persecution</term>, or Uncles; and that these [teachers] occasionally taught them very secretly in hidden night-gatherings in order to avoid the persecution of the Clergy, following the example of the early Church; but that afterwards, seeing that people sought opportunity to insult them with slander, they wished to teach in public the Holy Doctrine, which they had received from all antiquity and from hand to hand from their parents, etc.

The same Rorenco <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo, a Prior of Lucerna who wrote against the Waldensians but documented their historical claims</note> further cites in the aforementioned book on page 132 another petition from the 19th of November <note>original Dutch: "Slagtmaant," an old name for November, the "slaughter month"</note> in the year 1599, where he, among other things,
,, has them say that they have not merely possessed the knowledge of the
,, pure truth for some fifty years; but that on the contrary, it was
,, known to everyone that they had already taught exactly one and the same
,, doctrine for more than five to six hundred years previously.
Regarding this, the reader should please note that they speak plainly of the Doctrine as if it had been very clearly taught in the Valleys by their ancestors, and moreover that they had persevered in it since the year 900—which is precisely the time at which I have proven that they separated themselves from the Roman Communion.

Also in the year 1603, the Waldensians of the Valleys of Meana and Mattie, living near the side of Susa, which is also located in Piedmont, submitted a lengthy Petition to their Sovereign Charles Emmanuel, the Duke of Savoy, who by a very severe Edict <term>Plackaart: a formal public decree or proclamation</term> had commanded them to leave the country (which they indeed did, losing all their property just to be able to keep the pure Doctrine); in this [petition] they very clearly brought to his mind, among other things, that the Faith for which he banished them was no newly-
,, invented Religion, but indeed the true Doctrine of the Apostles, and which
,, their ancestors from of old and from generation to generation had always
,, very openly confessed, just as they had received the same from their fathers, etc.

I could here pile up more than a hundred such documents of request and petition, just as those poor Waldensians drew them up at various times and, on various occasions that presented themselves, delivered them to various Sovereigns and Councils of State; as well as just as many defense documents made against the Clergy of Rome, in which they continually use the same language. Indeed, since the year 1644, I have written more than thirty myself, which have been delivered both to the Royal Princess and his Royal Highness currently reigning, as well as to their Commanders and Princely Councils, following therein nothing other than the same style of all my ancestors. Nevertheless, it has never yet happened that either the Sovereigns, or their Commanders, or any of their Councilors have ever said anything against these repeated answers: **from time immemorial, from father to son, even from the time of the Apostles** <note>original Italian: "da tempo immemoriale, da padre in figlivolo, inde del tempo degl' Apostoli"</note>. Instead, they have always passed over the same with a deep silence. Which then sufficiently indicated that they were inwardly convinced of it, just as all Petitions, open Letters, and Edicts issued, signed, and annotated (as they say) by them or their Councils of State and Chambers of Accounts perfectly prove the same. So far was it from them that they [should deny] these...

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

Xx 2 CHAPTER XXVII.

...these other reasons would ever have been refuted or nullified, which they [the Waldensians] still brought forward to persuade them to allow them to remain in the possession of the exercise of their Religion, which they had always enjoyed *since time immemorial* <note>original Italian: "da tempo immemoriale"</note>; consisting namely in this: that they had already long possessed it before the Dukes of Savoy were even Princes of Piedmont, and subsequently, regarding their Faith, they had never been persecuted for it, except that they might be left in the same state in which they had been found. I still have in my possession a copy of a Petition in which I myself use these words: *before the Dukes of Savoy were Princes of Piedmont, etc.* <note>original Italian: "dinanzi che li Duchi di Savoya foſſero Principi di Piëmente, eſv."</note> And although the Council President Truchis—considered one of the shrewdest men in the Land and therefore, contrary to the custom of appointing a simple legal advocate, was made a President in Turin out of pure favor and given high authority over everything concerning the affairs of the Valleys—has attempted to refute that document from beginning to end in writing; he nevertheless, like the Marquess of Pianezza, never dared to touch that matter of Antiquity. But truly, those men would have had to be much sharper than all the Land-Councilors of the old Emmanuel Philibert, who was himself one of the most sensible Dukes and Princes that Savoy and Piedmont ever had. For look here at the words that the inhabitants of the Valleys used with him in their beautiful and noteworthy letter of the year 1559, just as we shall transcribe it in full in the 3rd chapter of the following book: *May it please Your Highness to consider that this Religion in which we live is not merely our own, or devised only a few days ago, as is falsely imputed to us; but that it is the Religion of our Fathers and of our grandfathers and of our great-grandfathers and of our other most ancient predecessors, and of the Holy Martyrs, Confessors, Apostles, and Prophets. And if there is anyone who can demonstrate the contrary, we are ready, etc.* <note>original French: "que V. A. conſidere, s' il luy plaît, que cette Religion, en laquelle nous vivons, n'eſt pas ſeulement nôtre ou controuvée depuis peu de jours, comme on luy impute fauſſement; mais que c'eſt la Religion de nos Peres & de nos ayeuls & des ayeuls de nos ayeuls & autres plus anciens nos predeceſſeurs & des Saints Martyrs, Confeſſoren, Apôtres & Prophetes. Et s'il y a qui puiſſe montrer le contraire, nous ſommes prêts, eſv."</note> That is to say: may it please Your Highness also to take note that the Faith in which we live is not only ours, or picked up yesterday or the day before, as people wish to insist against the truth; but that it is the Religion of our Fathers and of our grandfathers and of our great-grandfathers and of our other older ancestors, indeed of the holy Martyrs <note>original Dutch "Bloedgetuygen": literally "blood-witnesses"</note>, Confessors, Apostles, and Prophets. And if there should be anyone who would wish to prove the contrary of this, we are ready, etc. Now, would that great Prince and his entire Court have been able to tolerate in any way that those poor people dared to challenge them so boldly, if there had been any shred of cleverness or understanding <margin>of his Royal Highness's [council]</margin> to be found that would have given them the courage to contradict them in this and to maintain that they were not thus descended from generation to generation from the Martyrs, Confessors, and even from the Holy Apostles?

# General Memorial

### CHAPTER XXVII.

->Concerning certain proofs of the aforementioned Antiquity, drawn from the Writings of those of their Faith.<-

<margin>
*Non-Roman Teachers testify to the Antiquity of the Waldensians.*
</margin>
It is now no wonder that, following such striking proofs of the true Apostolic Antiquity of the said Waldensian Churches, drawn from the foundational documents of their own books, a great number of Teachers and Historians—who followed the same Faith yet spoke without passion—have recognized them as the Mother Churches of all the Right-believing, or *Reformed*. They adore God’s wise and merciful providence, which so miraculously preserved that "smoking flax" <note>A biblical reference to Isaiah 42:3, signifying something fragile but still burning with life.</note> against all kinds of storms. God prevented this holy seed, which would one day bring forth so much fruit to the world, from being choked by the weeds with which the enemy had sown the field of the Lord on all sides, while men lay unhappily buried in deep sleep. To speak here of their testimonies as promised, the first place belongs to that of one **Robertus Olivetanus**, that godly and distinguished man. At the expense of the Piedmont Valleys, he himself translated the first French Bible that was ever seen in the world in a complete and pure form, and had it printed in Neuchâtel <note>original: "Nieu-kasteel"</note> in Switzerland in the year 1535 <note>The text says 1537, but Pierre Robert Olivétan’s Bible was famously published in 1535; the author may be citing a later printing or slightly misremembering the date.</note>. I say *the whole* Bible, because although the Waldensians—in addition to the New Testament—had already transcribed some books of the Old, such as Genesis, the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job, several centuries earlier, they did not yet have the rest ready. Such particular pieces are still found, written by hand on ancient parchment, but never the entire Bible in one place. I also say *pure and faithful*, because the old books previously found among the Papists were full of all kinds of corruptions. This is what Théodore de Bèze <note>A major French Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> also stated in his book of *Illustrious Men* <note>original Latin: "Icones", here translated as "Uytmuntende Mannen"</note>, in the chapter on the Waldensians: that everyone must admit that France, through the efforts of the Valley Waldensians, still possesses and lives by the Bible in its own language today. Now, this holy man Olivetanus acknowledges with thanksgiving to God, in a certain Preface he placed before that Bible, that since the torch of the Gospel was first lit among the Waldensians or inhabitants of the Alpine Valleys (for to him these are always one and the same) in the time of the Apostles or their immediate successors, it has never been entirely extinguished in that Gascon <note>Refers to the Occitan or Waldensian vernacular; the translator notes it remained lit in their specific region.</note> region. "This poor people," (so his words go when he speaks of the said Churches—he who, as one of their most distinguished Teachers, knew their condition better than anyone in the world) "has always had the full possession and enjoyment of the heavenly Treasure of Truth, which is locked within the Holy Scriptures, ever since they were once gifted and enriched with it long ago by the Holy Apostles <note>original: "Kruyfgesanten", literally 'ambassadors of the cross'.</note> of our Lord Jesus Christ." Somewhat further down, he adds the following: "this is the small, invincible corner, the small, triumphant army of our Savior, to whom He, as a true field commander, has given courage and fearlessness through His wisdom, and from whom He has driven away all fear and timidity through His living and powerful word." He then continues, turning his speech toward God's Church...

Theodore Beza.</margin> Johannes-Theodore Beza spends a whole chapter in his book, titled *The Images of Eminent Men both in Piety and Learning, whose labor God has used in these recent times to restore true Religion in various lands of Christendom* <note>original: "de Afbeeld-fels der voortreffelyke Mannen..." referring to Beza's work *Icones*</note>, in which he tries to prove that especially by means of the Piedmontese and neighboring Valleys, the Gospel was spread nearly throughout all of Europe. He says among other things that it is they, above all, who have always maintained the true Faith without ever allowing themselves to be entirely overturned by any temptation, etc. The Waldensians, he says afterward, were so named because they lived in the Valleys and narrow passes of the Alps: and one can say with truth that they are a remnant of the pure Christian primitive church <term>Grontkerk</term> <note>literally "ground-church," referring to the foundational or apostolic church</note>, while it is certain that those people, through a wonderful providence of the Lord during so many adversities, have remained so well upright that for the span of many hundreds of years, through the ruses of the Bishop of Rome—who lamentably brought the East to ruin—they have set the whole world in motion. Nevertheless, despite the terrible persecutions with which he <note>the Pope</note> has distressed them, he could never bring them under the idolatry and tyranny of the Antichrist <note>A common Reformation-era term for the Papacy</note>; but against the will of the Devil and all his efforts, they still possess today no small number of flourishing churches, both in terms of Doctrine and the examples of a very sincere life; I mean now primarily those of the Alpine Valleys, of which some belong to the King of France, and some again under the Duke of Savoy. It is meanwhile not easy to describe how variously those Princes, incited by the Popes, have sought to root out those Waldensians, who were nevertheless preserved by their poverty from the violence of highwaymen and, through an irreproachable conduct loved and approved by everyone, have nullified countless false slanders with which people wrongly tried to smear them.

<margin>3. Sleidanus.</margin> Sleidanus, that famous Historian and one of the most esteemed in all of Europe, to whose knowledge and faithfulness those of the other Faith <note>likely referring to Catholics or non-Protestant scholars</note> give broad testimony regarding so many books on the state of the Faith and that of the Commonwealth; he, I say, treating in his *Histories of Charles V* in the 16th book, page 534, regarding the Waldensians, testifies of the same that by ancient custom they never wished to recognize the Pope of Rome and always adhered to the pure Doctrine; *these, by ancient* <note>original Latin: "hi vetusta"</note>, these are his own words, *custom, do not recognize the Roman Pontiff at all and have always held the purer Doctrine* <note>original Latin: "consuetudine Pontificem Romanum nequaquam agnoscunt & puriorem habuerunt semper Doctrinam"</note>. Wherein the Reader should also note this: that this great man himself cannot find out since when that people rejected the Roman Pope, and is therefore satisfied simply to say that it was so *by ancient custom* <note>original Latin: "vetusta consuetudine"</note>.

->### 309<-

->#### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.<-

If they had already cast off the Pope, they must by necessary consequence have already existed in essence right at the start of the eleventh century, eighty full years before Waldo of Lyons <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205), often credited as the founder of the Waldensians, though this text argues the movement is older</note>. This is especially evident from a certain note by Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer and historian</note>, where in the nineteenth book of his *Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth* <note>original: "Naamtaf. vande Getuyg. der Waarh." referring to the *Catalogus Testium Veritatis*</note> he states that Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague did nothing other than restore the teachings of the Waldensians—or rather the Gospel of Christ—to its previous standing, just as they had previously received it through the efforts of Wycliffe, whom he considers a contemporary of Nicholas of Lyra, who lived in the year 1322.

<margin>5. Comenius.</margin>
The venerable, learned, and godly Comenius <note>John Amos Comenius (1592–1670), a Czech philosopher and the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren</note>, the sole survivor of all the orthodox bishops who escaped the persecutions in Bohemia, says on page 70 and following of the histories he wrote about those events—drawn from the yearbooks and journals of that land, which he so miraculously saved from the fire and still preserves today in Amsterdam; he says, I say, that the believers of Bohemia and Moravia, who had withdrawn themselves from the fellowship of the Papists and Calixtines <note>A moderate faction of the Hussites who demanded the cup (chalice) for the laity during communion</note>, having chosen three teachers from among themselves, were highly concerned regarding their ordination. But having heard that some Waldensians lived on the borders of Moravia and Austria, they decided to completely remove the difficulties from their minds and those of others, both now and for the future, by sending a certain Michael Zambergius <note>Michael von Žamberk, also known as Michael Bradacius</note>—one of their teachers who had once received the priesthood from the Bishop of Rome himself—thither with two others to visit those Waldensians and relate to them what had occurred among them, and especially to ask for advice on what they should do in this matter. They found there a certain Waldensian Bishop named Stephen, who, along with several teachers, called for another to come; in their company, he showed the delegates from Moravia and Bohemia that his doctrine and that of the other Waldensians dated from the times of Constantine <note>Constantine the Great (reigned 306–337 AD), a reference to the Waldensian claim that their church separated from Rome when the Church became wealthy and politically powerful</note>, explained its main points, and told of the terrible persecutions that his beloved brothers in Italy and France had endured. Finally, this Stephen, together with the others mentioned before, gave the calling and ordination through the laying on of hands to those three teachers who had been sent to him, with the charge and command to likewise do the same for others as the occasion arose. From then on, those of Bohemia and Moravia wished to join into one body with the Waldensians: which is why it also happened that they were themselves called Waldensians. Further, on page 75, he also confirms that neither the Bohemian nor Moravian churches have ever denied that they received the power of the laying on of hands and the outward succession from the Waldensians. One sees clearly from this that not only do the Waldensians very soundly prove that their doctrine was already known by the fourth century, when Constantine the Great lived, but also that entire nations, such as those of Bohemia and Moravia, after powerful conviction, hold the same to be true.

<margin>6. The French Histories.</margin>
The Ecclesiastical Histories of the orthodox churches of France, called *of the three hammers* <note>original: "des trois marteaux," likely referring to an early Protestant history such as the work by Jean Crispin or similar martyrologies</note> and printed in Antwerp in the year 1558, speak in the first part on page 35 with these words of the antiquity of the Waldensians: the Waldensians, as they are called, have from time immemorial courageously opposed the abuses of the Romish Church, and despite the raging of the whole world, the Lord has so protected them that they have always remained together in the Valleys of Piedmont: from which, however, some divided themselves approximately 270 years ago into the lands of Provence, especially at Mérindol, Cabrières, Lourmarin, etc. And

...and a little lower: "concerning their faith, they have never adhered to the ecclesiastical laws of the Pope." And truly, if they never held to those Papal church commandments, they must necessarily have departed from the Roman communion as soon as it sought to impose those traditions upon them which were contrary to Scripture; and consequently, it was also never necessary for them to be "brought back" <note>This refers to the "reformation" of a church; the author argues the Waldensians didn't need a Reformation because they never fell away from the original Gospel</note> to the right path in any way.

<margin>7. Amyraut.</margin>
This is also the opinion of Mr. Amyraut <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a highly influential French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur</note>, who in his life was a minister and professor at Saumur and is still very famous for his learned writings. He himself declares this in a sermon he gave on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 10, verse 15; where, having spoken of the ignorance, error, and superstition that still held the upper hand in the time of Luther, Calvin, and other Reformers who lived before them, he also uses these words: "It is by no means unknown to you, beloved Brothers, how greatly all those things were still in vogue throughout all of Europe then, except for one small corner of the world, hidden in the Valleys of the Alps and among the rocky cliffs of Provence, where the Gospel of our Lord was preserved in its entirety."

<margin>8. Drelincourt.</margin>
Mr. Drelincourt <note>Charles Drelincourt (1595–1669), a famous minister of the Reformed Church of Paris known for his popular devotional works</note> agrees with this in his second *Familiar Dialogue*, offering these or similar reasons: "Finally, from time immemorial, there have always been believers in the Valleys of Piedmont who never wished to follow the Roman church laws or participate in any way in her grossest abuses." This is why a certain Italian monk named Belvedere, in his book printed in Turin in the year 1636 under the title *Relatione alla Congregatione de propaganda Fide* <note>original: "Relatione alla Congregatione de propaganda Fide," meaning "Report to the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith," a Vatican department</note>, dared to say in so many words that these same people have constantly and at all times been stuck in their heresies. For those people immediately brand as a heretic anyone who wishes to hold only to the Doctrine of the Apostles and the purity and simplicity of their service.

<margin>9. Heinrich Pantaleon.</margin>
This was also the reason why one Heinrich Pantaleon <note>1522–1595, a Swiss physician and historian</note>, commonly known as the chronologer of Basel, sought to apply the aforementioned words of Sleidanus <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), the historian of the Reformation</note> somewhat more broadly in the fifth book of the *Ecclesiastical Acts*, page 111. "These," he says, "by ancient custom do not acknowledge the Roman Pontiff and have always preserved a somewhat purer doctrine. And especially the people who dwell at the foot of the Alps (these are those of the Valleys) and at Merindol and Cabrières <note>Towns in Provence that were the site of a brutal crusade against the Waldensians in 1545</note>, have always lived so piously and modestly that in their whole conduct and way of life the fear of the Lord has most greatly shone forth and the highest faith and justice have been clearly seen." <note>original Latin: "hi vetusta consuetudine Pontificem Romanum non agnoscunt & aliquanto semper puriorem Doctrinam conservarunt. Et maxime populus, qui ad pedem Alpium & Merendolii, Cabrieræque degit, ita pie ac modeste semper vixit, ut in eorum tota consuetudine ac vitæ ratione timor Dei maxime eluxerit & summa fides & justitia perspecta fuerit"</note> These Waldensians, by old custom, do not know the Pope of Rome and have always maintained the Doctrine somewhat more purely. But especially the people who live at the foot of the Alps, at Merindol and Cabrières, have always lived so godily and modestly that in their whole social interaction and way of life, the fear of the Lord has shone out to the highest degree, and very great faithfulness and justice were to be perceived.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

#### Concerning similar testimonies, drawn from the writings of their most famous opponents.

Nemesius <note>Nemesius (c. 390 AD) was a Christian philosopher and Bishop of Emesa</note>, a friend of Gregory Nazianzen <note>One of the "Great Cappadocian" Fathers of the early Christian Church</note>, while intending to bring forward a testimony from Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and famous opponent of early Christianity</note>—his great enemy—in the third chapter of his book *On the Nature of Man* to confirm the Christian faith, once said "with great reason, that the proofs we derive for ourselves from our enemies are very powerful against them and beyond all contradiction." This will undoubtedly also hold true for those whom we are about to highlight here, in order to confirm with even greater abundance and irrefutability what we have already clearly proven regarding the antiquity of the Evangelical Waldensian Churches, or those of the Valleys. We may begin with the Monk Belvedere <margin>Testimony of the Monk Belvedere.</margin>, who was very famous, especially in Italy, and who was the head of a large company of proselytizing priests <note>The original term "Bekeerpapen" refers to Catholic missionaries sent specifically to convert Protestants</note> sent by the Pope to the Valleys in the year 1630. He wrote a certain book, as mentioned before, to give a thorough report to Rome regarding the origin and growth of the alleged Waldensian heresy, titled *Report to the Council for the Propagation of the Faith and the Extirpation of Heretics* <note>Original Latin: *Relatione al Consiglio de progaganda Fide & extirpandis Hæreticis*</note>, which was published in Turin in the year 1636. Seeking in that work—and indeed, in his own opinion, having found—the origin of many other heresies, he comes to the alleged heresy of the Waldensians of the Valleys and asserts "that it is nothing other than that of Calvin and Luther." Afterward, while excusing himself and his fellow companions for the fact that they had found no way to root them out, nor had been able to bring a single one of those allegedly erring people back to the bosom of the Roman Church, he uses this simple reason: that the heresy had struck roots too deep in those places for anyone to think they could be reached, since *the Valleys of Angrogna have always and at all times held heretics* <note>Original Italian: *le Valli di Angrogna semper ed in ogni tempo hanno havuto heretici*</note>. Now, it is clear that by these "Valleys of Angrogna" he does not only mean Angrogna itself—which we have seen is but a single community among those of Lucerna—but also all the other neighboring ones, which are commonly included in that name, as we have previously shown from Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian</note> and many other historians. This testimony must therefore be of great weight, as it comes from one of the most prominent wandering monks who was employed against the Waldensians; he reports his experiences to the Roman Council, whom he would surely be careful not to deceive in favor of the Waldensians.

But let us also look once more at the testimony of another very famous <margin>From the Inquisitor Reinerio.</margin> Inquisitor <note>The Dutch "Ketterdwinger" literally means "Heretic-compeller"</note> who was also intentionally set against them. I mean Reinerio Sacco, who neglected nothing—neither in trying to destroy the Waldensians in the Valleys and throughout all of Italy, nor in thoroughly investigating the nature of that alleged heresy and its doctrines, which daily did so much damage to the Pope and, by his own account, had already been in the world for about 500 years. For since he nevertheless does not have the impudence to deny, in a certain book he wrote on the subject (which was also included by the Jesuit Gretser in his *Library of the Fathers*), that the Waldensians have their origin from the times of the Apostles; his...

# General Memorial-Writings

This testimony is so valuable that it is well worth being read here word for word in its own language. <note>original Latin: "Inter omnes Sectas, feyt hy, quæ adhuc funt, vel fuerunt, nulla fuit perniciofior Ecclesiæ, quam Leonistarum, idque tribus de causis. Prima est, quia est diuturnior; aliqui enim dicunt, quod duravit a tempore Sylvestri, aliqui a tempore Apostolorum: fecunda, quia generalior; fere enim nulla est terra, in qua hæc Secta excepta non fit: tertia, quia, cum omnes aliæ Sectæ immanitate blasphemiarum in Deum audientibus horrorem inducant, hæc magnam habet fpeciem pietatis, eo quod coram hominibus justé vivant & bene omnia de Deo credunt & omnes articulos, qui in fimbolo continentur, obfervant. Solummodo Romanam Ecclesiam blasphemant & clerum, cui multitudo Laïcorum facilis est ad credendum:"</note> "Among all the Sects," he says, "that still exist today, or have ever been, none has been more destructive to the Church than that of the Leonists <note>Leonists was a common medieval term for the Waldensians, named after their association with Peter Waldo of Lyons.</note>, and this for three primary reasons. The first is because it has lasted longer than any other; for some say that it has existed since the time of Pope Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335 AD), during whose time the Waldensians believed the Church became corrupted by wealth and power.</note>, and some even since the time of the Apostles. The second is because it is more widespread than any other; for there is hardly any land in which this Sect is not established. The third is because, while all other heresies <term>Kerkfcheuringen: literally 'church-splittings' or schisms</term> incite horror in the listeners through the monstrosity of their blasphemies against God, this one, on the contrary, has a great appearance of godliness, because they live justly before men, believe all things well concerning God, and accurately hold all the chief parts of the Creed. They only blaspheme the Roman Church and the Clergy, to which the multitude of the laity is very ready to give credence."

It is as if he were saying: among all the religious sects that are still in existence today, or have ever been, none has been more harmful to the Church than those of the Leonists, and that specifically for three kinds of reasons. The first, because they have endured longer than any; for some say they were already there in the time of Pope Sylvester, some even in the time of the Apostles. The second, because they have spread more than any; for there is scarcely a country where this faith has not taken up residence. The third, because, where all other schisms strike terror into the listeners by the horror of their blasphemies against God, these on the contrary have a great appearance of godliness, because they live righteously before men, believe everything well of God, and strictly maintain all the fundamental tenets of the Faith. They only slander the Roman Church and the Clergy, whom the majority of the secular world very easily believes.

Truly, that notorious Reinerio <note>Reinerius Saccho (c. 1190–1259) was a former Cathar who became a Dominican friar and an Inquisitor. His writings are frequently cited by Protestants as evidence of Waldensian antiquity.</note> was not so far removed from the time of Waldo of Lyons—whose disciples he calls Leonists here and whom he acknowledges to be Waldensians—otherwise he would have been able to find him without any trouble if he had been the first founder of that alleged Sect. He would not have needed to climb back in his search for their origin to the times of Sylvester or Constantine the Great, the first Christian Emperor, or even to the times of the Apostles, seeing as he lived in the year 1254, which is only 80 or 90 years after the time of Waldo. One must also admit that for an Inquisitor <term>Dwingketter: literally 'heresy-forcer' or persecutor of heretics</term> he still shows some sense of conscience, since he so uprightly acknowledges that there was nothing to be said against either the life or the doctrine of those poor Waldensians, except that they thundered very fiercely against the Roman Church and the Clergy.

I also do not wish to withhold from the reader that the Jesuit Gretserus <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625), a German Jesuit theologian and prolific polemicist against Protestantism.</note>, in a certain book he wrote against the Waldensians (Chapter 8, page 39), in order to evade the force of the previous declaration, dared to say that the writer did not bring that forward <note>original: "ex fua, fed ex aliorum fententia"</note> from his own opinion, but only according to the opinion of others. However, far from weakening that glorious testimony, he actually makes it much more weighty. He not only exposes himself publicly when he tries to make people believe that the author would not have stated his own opinion directly there—where he nonetheless clearly and firmly asserts what he says in that matter, as if Gretserus could have penetrated the thoughts of that Teacher better than the man himself—but also when he adds that he presented this not so much as his particular belief, but as the common view of others. Truly, one could not speak more clearly to testify that it was then no longer just the opinion of that Teacher or Inquisitor (who in such a capacity had not failed to take accurate notice of the same, while he had already sought to give a certain report to the Roman Court about it), but that it was also the opinion of other Teachers and Inquisitors—indeed, the public opinion of all others—that the Faith of the Waldensians originated with the times of the Apostles, or at least with those of

# Concerning the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

Sylvester had taken a beginning, upon which they then firmly established that it was the oldest of all, *longer-lasting than all* <note>original Latin: "omnium diuturnior"</note>, attributing no other origin to it in their writing than that which it has in common with the Apostles themselves. Furthermore, even though he states that Reinerio only follows the judgment of others when he speaks in such a way of the antiquity of the Waldensians; he nevertheless confesses that he—however it may be—has spoken in these words: "among all Sects that still exist, or have ever been, this is the oldest of all" <note>original Latin: "inter omnes Sectas, quæ adhuc sunt, vel fuerunt, est diuturnior omnium"</note>, *according to his own opinion*. By which he must again admit that they have been in existence since time immemorial, and consequently that it was no new Teaching that the aforementioned Waldo began to teach around the year 1160 or 1180; which same fact, that it was *originally introduced into the world and wonderfully multiplied in its ways* <note>original Latin: "primitus in mundum introducta & nivius in modis multiplicata"</note>, had been around since ancient times. This forced the aforementioned Gretserus <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625), a Jesuit scholar and polemicist.</note> on page 38 of the same Work to also confess that it was no new Teaching that the Waldensians and Albigensians <note>The Albigensians were another group of medieval dissenters in Southern France, often associated by their enemies with the Waldensians.</note> maintained around the year 1160, and which has since grown so uncommonly.

<margin>From the Teacher Rainerus.</margin>
A certain High German Teacher, also a papist, named *Rainerus* (whose book on the historians of Bohemian affairs is published, specifically on pages 222 and 223), repeats almost word for word, or at least with very little change, the testimony of the previously mentioned Italian and thus gives it a new strength. For his words are as follows: "There have been many Sects of Heretics since ancient times: among all these Sects, which are or have been, none is more harmful to the Church of God than that of the Poor Men of Lyons: for three reasons. First, because it is longer-lasting: Some say it has lasted since the time of Sylvester; others say from the time of the Apostles. The second is because it is more general: for there is almost no land in which this Sect does not creep. The third is because, while all others bring horror through the monstrosity of their blasphemies against God, this one of the Leonists has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men and believe all things well concerning God and all the articles contained in the Creed. They only blaspheme and hate the Roman Church; to which the common people are easily inclined to believe." <note>original Latin: "Sectæ Hæreticorum ab olim fuerunt multæ: inter quas omnes Sectas, quæ sunt, vel fuerunt, non est perniciosior Ecclesiæ Dei, quam Pauperum de Lugduno: tribus de causis. Prima, quia diuturnior: Quidam dicunt, quod duraverit a tempore Sylvestri; alii dicunt, quod a tempore Apostolorum. Secunda est, quia generalior: fere enim nulla terra est, in qua hæc Secta non serpat. Tertia, quod, omnes aliæ cum immanitate blasphemiarum in Deum horrorem inducant, hæc Leonistarum magnam habet speciem pietatis, eo quod coram hominibus juste vivant & bene omnia de Deo credant & omnes articulos, qui in Symbolo continentur. Solam Romanam Ecclesiam blasphemant & oderunt; cui multitudo facilis est ad credendum."</note> As if he said: there have indeed been various Sects of Heretics in ancient times; but among them all, none has ever been found that was so detrimental to God's Church as that of the Poor of Lyons, and that primarily for four reasons. The first, because it is by far the oldest: for some say that it has lasted since Sylvester's times, others even since the times of the Apostles. The second is because it possesses more people; for there is hardly a province to be found where it has not crept in. The third is because, where all others are terrifying through gruesome blasphemies, this one of the Leonists shows a great appearance of godliness, while they outwardly live very honestly, believe everything properly about God, and accept all the points of the Summary of Faith <term>Hooftbegrip des Geloofs: The Apostles' Creed, the basic statement of Christian belief.</term> as good. They only speak ill of the Roman Church and bear a very great hatred toward it; to which the common folk very easily lend an ear.

One must therefore no longer find it strange that Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> has maintained above that the name *Vaudois* (Waldensian) originally comes from *Vaux*, or Valleys, not from Waldo, but that on the contrary Waldo even takes his name from the Valleys, while both the mentioned Arch-Inquisitor <term>Dwingketter: literally "compeller of heretics," used here as a pejorative for an Inquisitor.</term> Reinerio, and his follower that High German Teacher, assure us that the Leonists and Poor of Lyons—whom we have already seen are Waldensians—lived already in the time of Pope Sylvester, or even from the Apostles.

### General Chronicle

<margin>Splendid saying of the Jesuit Campian.</margin>Change your language then, you gentlemen of the Roman Catholic persuasion; no longer insult as "new" the Doctrine of those who have been in the world so long that you ought rather to recognize them as your ancestors, just as the Jesuit Campian <note>Edmund Campion (1540–1581), an English Jesuit priest and martyr.</note> does plainly in a certain book concerning the marks of the Church, in the explanation of the third reason; there he quite explicitly calls them *Waldensians, our ancestors* <note>original Latin: "Valdenses, majores nostros"</note>. To this we might well say: yes, your ancestors indeed, but from whom you have become entirely degenerate and bastardized. Now, if this their Teaching—according to the opinion of that same Jesuit—was the same as that of today’s <term>Calvinists</term> <note>Followers of the Reformed tradition of Protestantism.</note>, how can you continue to reproach them with the "novelty" of their faith?

<margin>From the Archbishop of Turin, Claude de Seyssel.</margin>But this antiquity is also significantly confirmed by a testimony of such striking weight that it shall impose an eternal silence even upon the most cunning and malicious <term>nitpickers</term> <note>Dutch: "muggesifters," literally "mosquito-sifters."</note> through its respectable power. Namely, the oft-mentioned Claude de Seyssel, Archbishop of Turin, in a certain book that he wrote specifically against the Waldensians—published first with a fine privilege from Francis I given on the 27th of February <note>Dutch: "Sprockelmaant"</note> in the year 1547—uses these words: *the Waldensian Sect took its beginning from a certain Leo, a very religious man, in the time of Constantine the Great, the first Christian Emperor: who, having detested the greed of Sylvester and the excessive generosity of Constantine, chose rather to follow poverty in the simplicity of faith than to be defiled with Sylvester by a fat and rich benefice. To which Leo all those joined themselves who felt rightly regarding the Faith* <note>original French: "la Secte de Vaudois a pris son, commencement d'un certain Leon, homme tres religieux, du tems de Constantin le Grand, premier Empereur Chrétien: qui ayant detesté l'avarice de Sylvestre & l'excessive largesse de Constantin, aima mieux suivre la pauvreté dans la simplicité de la foy, que d'être avec Sylvestre souillé d'un gras & riche benefice. Auquel Leon s'étoient adjoints tous ceux, qui sentoient bien de la Foy"</note>. We have previously cited the same from Bernard of Luxembourg’s *Catalog of Heretics* <note>original Latin: "Catalog. Hæretic."</note> under the entry for Leonists, from Thuanus's *History, book 5*, and from Goldast’s *Rationale of the Imperial Constitutions, 1607 edition, p. 78.* But however one takes this excellent Declaration by the aforementioned Archbishop—whether as his own opinion or merely as a report of what others believed—this necessary conclusion follows: that this Archbishop Claude de Seyssel, who had investigated the origin of the Waldensians with such diligence, does not attribute the foundation of the so-called <term>heresy</term> <note>A belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious doctrine.</note> of the Waldensians to that Waldo of Lyons (who lived at the end of the twelfth century). In this, he is like the aforementioned Reinerio Saccho, who was specifically appointed as Inquisitor against them, especially in the Valleys as was said before, and wrote a book solely on that subject. He proves here that the sect comes from so far back that its origin or beginning cannot be certainly pointed out, and they only agree on this: that they have set themselves against the Roman Bishop from time immemorial. This is why on page 7 of the same book, after having long racked his brains searching for the first root of the Waldensians, he sufficiently testifies that it was impossible for him to discover it because of its antiquity. Trying to excuse himself for not being able to provide more light on the matter, he is satisfied to add only these words as a conclusion: *it must be that there are great and effective causes and occasions for which this Waldensian Sect has already lasted so many centuries* <note>original French: "il faut bien, qu'il y ait des grandes & efficacieuses causes & occasions, pour lesquelles cette Secte Vaudoise a déja duré tant de siecles"</note>. This he wrote in the year 1500, and after so much research, he still frankly confesses that he himself does not know for how many centuries the Waldensians had already been active before that time—

For against the opinion of everyone they have always remained victors and entirely invincible* <note>original French: "toutes sortes de gens en divers tems par un tres grand effort ont en vain essayé de les arracher. <margin>Of Eneas Sylvius.</margin>Let us now also bring to bear those great and excellent testimonies of a high <term>Prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note>, I mean Eneas Sylvius, who under the name of Pius II was a Roman Pope and a great enemy of the Waldensians. The dogmas of this pestilential and long-since condemned Faction are: that the Roman Prelate etc.* <note>original Latin: "proruperunt... in blasphemias &, quum aliquibus ignavis fortasse ac vitiosis maledicere possent, in omnes latrare Sacerdotes cœpere & ab Ecclesia Catholica recedentes impiam Waldensium Sectam atque insaniam amplexi sunt. The Doctrine of this pestilent gathering, which has been condemned of old, consists particularly in the following points: that the Bishop of Rome etc.

<margin>Of the Council of Vaus in Languedoc.</margin>Upon that testimony of the Pope follows very appropriately this one from a Council. Petrus of the Monastery of the Valley of Sernay <note>Pierre de Vaux-de-Cernay, a 13th-century Cistercian monk and chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade.</note> sets down in the 66th chapter of his aforementioned *Albigensian History* a certain letter from the Church assembly of Vaus, written to Pope Innocent II <note>likely Pope Innocent III, who reigned during the Albigensian Crusade.</note> to incite him so that he might root out and destroy the wretched Waldensians of the regions of Languedoc, Provence, and Dauphiné to the last man. In this, that fine <term>firebrand</term> <note>Dutch: "stokebrant," someone who incites trouble or conflict.</note> of a Church assembly uses no more powerful motive to bring His Holiness to the execution of that his disastrous resolution than this bare representation: that they had brought onto the stage such a heretical pestilence, which had been sown long ago and had grown immensely in former and ancient times; *it concerned the Heretical pestilence, sown of old, which has long since and from ancient times grown immensely.* <note>original Latin: "agebatur de peste Hæretica, antiquitus saminata, quæ in immensum succreverit jamdudum & ab antiquis temporibus."</note> Truly, such a <term>Synod</term> <note>A council or assembly of church officials.</note> would never have dared to use such language to such a prominent Pope as it wrote to in the twelfth century, if that Doctrine had then been only new, or if it had known how to name its origin or find its first founders.
