Is that not a clear enough admission that they were, and truly still are, the pure seed of the original Christian Church? That they have always held solely to the Doctrine of our Lord without ever tolerating any mixture therein? That they departed from the fellowship of the Roman Church as soon as it sought to oblige them to accept its Traditions, and began to rise up against the Church of Rome just as it sought to quietly take its place within the Church—given that no other beginning of their separation can be found?

<margin>And from M. A. Rorenco.</margin> Here may now follow another witness, who alone ought to be enough to silence even the boldest detractors and to prove irrefutably that the Waldensian Churches are truly Apostolic. They have never bowed the neck under the yoke of idolatrous Rome and consequently never had need to be cleansed of errors or improved in any way; rather, they only needed to ensure that from then on they always, as before, guarded themselves so that [the Roman errors] did not force their way into their midst. This witness is again the illustrious Marco Aurelio Rorenco <note>A 17th-century Prior of St. Roch in Turin and a primary historical source for the history of the Waldensian valleys; though an opponent, his writings are used by Waldensian historians to prove their antiquity.</note>, whom we have already seen above; he is the Lord of the Luserna Valley, Grand Prior of St. Roch, and regarded by the Roman Catholic lords as the most diligent, shrewd, and powerful instrument they could obtain in this century to cause trouble for those poor people of the Valleys. He was considered the most cunning man in the world for providing advice and means for their destruction, having spent his entire life in this business until he was quite elderly. 

This man then complains very bitterly in his book titled *Narratione dell' introduttione delle Hereſie nelle Valli* <note>original Italian: "Narrative of the introduction of Heresies into the Valleys"</note>, printed in Turin with approval and privilege in the year 1632; he states that the Heresy of the eighth century (he speaks clearly of the aforementioned Doctrine of Claudius, the Archbishop of Turin <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827) was a bishop famous for his opposition to the use of religious images and the authority of the Pope, often cited as a precursor to the Reformation.</note>, and it pleases him to label it heresy in this manner) had remained continuously in the Valleys throughout the following ninth and tenth centuries. This is precisely the interval of time that elapsed from the same Claudius of Turin until the aforementioned Peter Waldo of Lyons, whose disciples, having fled in part to the same Valleys, had also strengthened the churches there. 

Since he has so clearly shown before how the sound Doctrine of our Savior and His Holy Apostles had always been preserved in the Valleys and remained free of all corruption until the eighth century; and since, at that time—namely the era of Charlemagne <note>Latin: *Carolus Magnus*</note>—this Claudius, with a good number of other pious teachers, so powerfully opposed the introduction of Images, the Invocation of Saints, Pilgrimages, and Indulgences that he kept his Bishopric free and pure of them; and since the Prior himself confesses that, although the same [doctrine] was somewhat stifled in other places during the ninth, tenth, and following centuries, it nevertheless always remained in existence in the Valleys, where it emerged with a new luster in the eleventh century just as it still is today: it can therefore in no way be denied that it has been preserved there since the times of the Apostles without any interruption. 

Furthermore, the same <term>Prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy.</note> confirms the whole matter to us in one of his other books, published in Turin in the year 1649 with the approval of the ecclesiastical authorities under nearly the same name, *Memorie Hiſtoriche dell' Introduttione delle Hereſie* <note>original Italian: "Historical Memoirs of the Introduction of Heresies"</note>, and solemnly dedicated to Vittorio Amedeo, father of the Duke who still reigns today...

[Coming] a bit closer; when he, having said that in the eighth century *the enemies of the sacred Images* <note>original Italian: "li nemici delle sacre Imagini"</note> (they were very fiercely attacked and at the same time very courageously rejected only by the people of the Valleys) first appeared, he finally adds these words: *in the ninth century there was no new Sect, but indeed a new promoter of the preceding ones. Among whom was Claudius, Bishop of Turin, a disciple of Felix, who denied reverence to the Holy Cross, as also the veneration and invocation of Saints, and was a primary detractor of Images* <note>original Italian: "nel nono secolo non vi fù nuova Setta, ma ben nuovo fomentatore delle precedenti. Fra quali fù Claudio, Vescovo di Torino, discepolo di Felice, che negava la riverenza alla Santa Croce, come anche la veneratione ed invocatione de Santi, e fù principal destrattor dell' Imagini"</note>; in the ninth century no new sect arose, but rather new champions of the previous ones. Among these was also Claudius, Bishop of Turin <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827) was a teacher and bishop famous for his iconoclastic views, often cited by later Protestants as a forerunner of the Reformation</note> and a student of Felix <note>Felix of Urgell, a Spanish bishop known for the Adoptionist heresy, though here linked to the rejection of image worship</note>, as one who refused to give the Holy Cross its honor, as well as the service and worship of deceased Saints, and was one of the foremost Iconoclasts <term>Beeldstormers: literally "image-stormers," those who destroyed or removed religious icons</term>. For even assuming that this High Bishop was neither the first nor the only one who sought to prevent the worship of the Cross, the invocation and honoring of the Saints, and the service of Images—as this Gentleman [Rorenco] takes for granted—he undoubtedly had his eye on the aforementioned Emperor **Carolus Magnus** <note>Charlemagne (742–814), King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor</note>, who, having been promoted to the Empire in the year 768, wrote four magnificent books against Images <note>The *Libri Carolini*, a work commissioned by Charlemagne to refute the pro-image decrees of the Second Council of Nicaea</note> which are still found today; and on all the Bishops of the **Council of Frankfurt** <note>Held in 794, this council, called by Charlemagne, condemned the worship of images</note> that was called by him specifically to condemn that practice in that region, as we have already seen above. Indeed, he [Rorenco] would then have to reveal either his ignorance or his malice, since that Claudius was already from that time one of the foremost advisors of the highly esteemed Emperor, and had even written on [the Emperor's] command against the Images and other errors of the Romish Church. Thus, he would only give more strength to our proof and more strongly confirm that the misunderstandings regarding the honoring of the Cross and Images and the invocation of Saints—which in the eighth century, when the oft-mentioned Claudius began to rise in prominence, had already begun to set foot in the Church—had been very fiercely attacked by many others whom he does not name. This was even more fierce at the beginning of the ninth century, when he [Claudius] was called by the Emperor **Ludovicus** <note>Louis the Pious (778–840), son and successor of Charlemagne</note> to the dignity of the High Bishop of Turin and of the Valleys; and likewise, his Teachings remained active throughout that entire century. Furthermore, so that no one might think that in the thick darkness of the tenth century [his teaching] had in any way changed or been extinguished, he immediately adds in the following discourse that *in the tenth century nothing else was discovered* <note>original Italian: "nel decimo secolo non si scoprì altro"</note>; also in the tenth century nothing else came to light, nor was there even the slightest change. One must then conclude from the declaration of that High Bishop that the resistance used in the eighth century against those emerging errors never ceased in the following ninth and tenth centuries, and that the Doctrine of Claudius himself was already considered very old then, since he himself confesses that it was not new, *that it was not a new Sect* <note>original Italian: "che non fù nuova Setta"</note>. Now, while by his own confession it was new neither in itself nor in the Valleys during the eighth and ninth centuries, I would like to see it proven to me that its origin was any later than the times of the Apostles. And truly, that Bishop himself, being ashamed to confess to his own disgrace that the Doctrine of the Waldensians had arisen in the time of the Apostles, yet being unable to find any other beginning for it, concludes on page 60 of the previously cited book his entire argument with these words: *one cannot have certainty of its entry into the Valleys* <note>original Italian: "non si può haver certezza del suo ingresso nelle Valli"</note>; that is, one can have no certainty as to when it forced its way into the Valleys. It is from this that it also followed that, although he always—and especially in his **Chronological Notes** <term>Tijdfchriftige Aanteykeningen: refers to Rorenco's "Memorie Historiche"</term>—criticized and refuted the writings of those poor people of the Valleys as much as possible, and the Petitions [presented] by them to their Sovereigns even during the life of the old...

...begun to spread, they might cease to reproach us for that novelty <note>The "novelty" refers to the common Catholic accusation that Protestantism was a new invention of the 16th century.</note>. This latter point many famous Roman writers have even been forced to acknowledge; in addition to what has already been seen occasionally in various proofs of antiquity, we shall set some of them down here.

<margin>The Reformed Doctrine is the same as that of the old Waldensians according to the testimony of Hosius and Lindanus. And of Gualterus.</margin>
Cardinal Hosius <note>Stanislaus Hosius (1504–1579), a Polish Cardinal and leading figure of the Counter-Reformation.</note> then, in the first book of the *Heresies of our Time*, admits alongside Lindanus <note>Wilhelmus Lindanus (1525–1588), Bishop of Roermond and a staunch Catholic apologist.</note> in his *Analytic Tables* <note>original Latin: "tabul. anacl.", referring to Lindanus’s *Tabulae Analyticae*.</note> that the doctrine of the non-Romans in Bohemia was nothing else than the blasphemy of the Waldensians, which had infected all of Bohemia; for the largest part of the Bohemian Kingdom, following the doctrine of Waldo (who we have seen had fled to Bohemia) with one accord, separated itself from the Roman Church.

The Jesuit Gualterius <note>Jacques Gaultier (1560–1636), a Jesuit author who wrote against Protestantism.</note> asserts the same in his *Chronographical Table* concerning the twelfth century, chapter 15, page 494, where he has recorded the agreement between the doctrine of the Waldensians and those whom he calls the "deceived servants of Calvin," in twenty-seven principal articles.

<margin>And of Claudius Rubius.</margin>
Claudius Rubius <note>Claude de Rubys (1533–1613), a magistrate and historian of Lyon who was fiercely anti-Protestant.</note>, speaking in his *History of the City of Lyon*, book 3, page 269, regarding the Lutherans and Calvinists, also says among other things that the heresies which have arisen in our time are grafted onto the old ones of the Waldensians.

<margin>And of Aeneas Sylvius and J. du Bravius. And of T. Walden.</margin>
We have also seen that Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), who later became Pope Pius II.</note>, and likewise Johannes du Bravius <note>Jan Dubravius (1486–1553), Bishop of Olomouc and historian of Bohemia.</note> in his *Bohemian Histories*, dare to assert the same thing quite plainly.

Thomas Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), an English Carmelite who was a leading opponent of the Wycliffites.</note>, writing against the doctrine of Wycliffe, says in the 6th part of *Concerning the Sacraments*, title 12, chapter 10 <note>original Latin: "de Sacramentalib. tit. 12. cap. 10."</note>, that it is the doctrine of the Waldensians which had crept into the regions of France and England.

<margin>And of De la Popeliniere.</margin>
The well-regarded Lord De la Popeliniere <note>Lancelot Voisin, Seigneur de La Popelinière (1541–1608), a French historian.</note> explicitly confirms this in the first of his aforementioned books: that the Waldensian doctrine was shared by the inhabitants of the land of Alby (called Albigenses) with the English—who were their neighbors at that time while they held all of Guyenne—and was subsequently brought to the minds of many who later carried it into England. He states that from hand to hand it finally embedded itself in the thoughts of one Wycliffe, a very famous theologian from the Academy of Oxford and Lincoln <note>referring to the Diocese of Lincoln, which then included Oxford.</note>. Through his eloquence and rare scholarship, Wycliffe knew how to win the hearts and minds of various English people so well that even the most prominent among them came to embrace it. Furthermore, a certain student had taken a book by this Wycliffe, namely *On Universals* <note>original Latin: "de Universalibus"</note>, with him to Prague. This book presented and explained that doctrine—which had long ago, in the time of Waldo himself, been promoted in Bohemia by Waldensian refugees—in such a way that many of the people, the scholars, the nobility, and indeed even many of the clergy began to adhere to it.

<margin>And of Bellarmine.</margin>
To this is added Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation.</note>, who gives no less striking or powerful testimony in a word or two regarding the excellent spread of the Waldensian faith among the English; in the 2nd part of his *Works*, chapter 26, page 86, he asserts that Wycliffe had nothing of his own that he added to the doctrine of the Waldensians.

<margin>And of Eckius.</margin>
Eckius <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543), Martin Luther’s principal theological opponent.</note> knows of nothing else to reproach Luther with in his *Commonplaces*, chapter 28 <note>original Latin: "Locor. Commun. cap. 28."</note>, than that he has only hauled up anew from the gutter the long-condemned heresies of the Waldensians, Albigenses, Wycliffe, and Jan Hus, thus admitting that all those people professed but one and the same doctrine.

<margin>And of Alphonsus de Castro.</margin>

<margin>That the Greek Churches have more right to the Apostolic succession than the Roman.</margin>
But to add this here while the opportunity serves: even if it could not be shown that God, through the agency of the Waldensians, had kept the torch of His pure Gospel burning continuously and successively in our Europe, this new Roman Church still could not rightly claim for itself true antiquity or the Apostolic succession <term>Apostolic succession: the claim of a continuous line of spiritual authority descending from the original Twelve Apostles</term>. <margin>As also those of Armenia, Russia, and Muscovy.</margin>
These views have always been held, and are still followed today, by the Armenian, Muscovite, and Russian Churches, which have never turned to the idolatry of the Roman Church. This can be seen in the description of Muscovy <note>An old name for the Grand Duchy of Moscow, the precursor to the Russian Empire.</note> by one Jan Fabri, sent to the Emperor Ferdinand, and in the books of Paulus Jovius and Matthias Michou, as well as in a certain description of Sarmatia in the 4th chapter of the 2nd book. For the Grand Prince of Muscovy (whose realm, by its sheer size, covers a good half of Europe) recognizes to this very day neither the Pope of Rome, nor Purgatory, nor Transubstantiation; though he and his people do not for that reason cease to have faith in the Lord Christ, which they believe they received through the teaching of the Holy Apostle Andrew and have always steadfastly maintained. The Ruthenians, or Russians, their neighbors, who possess a very great stretch of land extending almost to the North Pole, undoubtedly practice the same religion. Always on the other side, in the land of Ethiopia among the Abyssinians <note>The historical name for people of the Ethiopian Empire.</note>—located not far from Egypt, a land much larger than all those in Europe that follow the Pope—the Christian faith is held to be far less contaminated with idolatry than in the Roman Church. There they know of no "private Masses," much less do they wish them to be a sacrifice for the living and the dead; rather, they are solely a remembrance of the suffering of our Lord Jesus, just as the Reformed <note>The author is likely referring to the Protestant/Calvinist tradition here.</note> have in the Holy Supper, and they serve the same to the people under both kinds <note>Providing both the bread and the wine to the congregation, rather than just the bread.</note>. No host is worshiped there, nor is anything known of Transubstantiation, Purgatory, the Pope, or the Renunciation of Marriage <term>Renunciation of Marriage: the practice of clerical celibacy</term>. All these notes can be confirmed by the 5th and final chapter of the 2nd book of Marco Polo of Venice, by the Ethiopian Histories of Francisco Alvarez (who particularly describes the faith of the Abyssinians), and others besides. The preface of Leunclavius <note>Hans Leunclavius (1533–1593), a historian who translated many Ottoman and Greek sources.</note>, which he placed at the start of his Turkish Histories, the monk Brother Brocardus in his description of the Holy Land and its inhabitants, and many other historians also indicate that many Christians live among the Turks and Muslims, such as the Zifiers, Bulgarians, and Albanians...

# Concerning the History of the Waldensian Churches
### Chapter 30

[Arnaut]laren <note>original: "laren"; completing "Arnautlaren" or Albanians from the previous page.</note>, Georgians, Jacobites <note>Members of the Syrian Orthodox Church.</note>, and similar groups who have never wished to recognize the Pope; and that the Nubians, Chaldeans, Syrians, Armenians, Maronites, Ethiopians, but above all the Numidians and Gabians <note>Likely referring to groups in Upper Egypt or Abyssinia.</note>, still adhere today to the true Evangelical Doctrine, which they claim to have received through the preaching of the Holy Apostle Matthew. The aforementioned Brocardus <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a 13th-century Dominican monk and traveler.</note> expressly assures us that in Lesser Armenia, or Cilicia, the majority are Christians who live under the rule of the Tartars <note>The Mongol Empire.</note>.

<margin>And a great number of others from the East Indies.</margin>The mentioned Venetian, Marco Polo, tells us in the 1st book of his *Travels to the Eastern Lands*, chapters 45, 47, 48, 62, and 63, and again in the 2nd book, chapters 39, 62, 64, and 66, that in his time (which is now about 150 years ago <note>Marco Polo actually lived much earlier; the author may be referring to a specific 15th or 16th-century edition of his travels.</note>) a great multitude of such Christians lived in many regions and among various peoples of the Tartars. They also had numerous churches there, such as in the great cities of Quinsai <note>Modern-day Hangzhou, China.</note>, Samarkand, Cigigni, and Saicoion; as well as in the lands of Castar, Carcham, Chinchintales, Suchur, Tangut, Calai, Egrigaia, and Thenduth, where Prester John <note>Paap Jan: a legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European medieval chronicles.</note> formerly held his court, as well as in the kingdoms of Ergimul and Corguth and several others. Indeed, one of the Eastern islands, called Abasia <note>Likely Abyssinia or Ethiopia, often confused with islands in early geography.</note>, has four Christian kingdoms out of only seven in total; and in Calicut, Cochinchine, as well as in the city of Cranganore and its surrounding places, there are no small number of them.

<margin>As also from the West Indies.</margin>The same is also seen in various places in the West Indies <note>In this period, "West Indies" could refer to the Americas or be used broadly for distant Western territories.</note>, Mesopotamia, and other distant lands, with whose description I do not intend to occupy myself for long here. Those who desire more extensive reports from witnesses who are beyond reproach even to Rome can consult the oft-mentioned Marco Polo the Venetian in his 1st book, chapter 14, and in his 3rd book, chapter 43; one Aloyfius Cadamustus <note>Alvise Cadamosto, a Venetian slave trader and explorer.</note> in the 18th chapter of the 2nd book of his *Travel*; Alisius Cadanisi in his 3rd book, chapter 78; Josephus Judas <note>Joseph the Indian, a 15th-century Syrian Orthodox priest from India who traveled to Europe.</note> in the 132nd, 133rd, and 134th chapters of his *Travels*; Ludovicus Romanus Patricius <note>Ludovico di Varthema, an Italian traveler.</note> in his 6th book, chapters 2, 14, 15, 37, and 38; and Andreas Masius in the letter of dedication concerning the *Liturgy of St. Basil*, written to the ambassador Ogier de Busbecq.

While all these Christians have never known the Pope or the Roman Church, much less accepted her traditions, Mass, Purgatory, and so on—because they have always held to the Doctrine of the Gospel, though slightly changed by many church rituals—is this not more than enough, especially if one adds these notes to those we have just presented regarding the Apostolic origin of our Waldensians? Does it not show how ridiculous all that boasting is of those who call themselves the "only-universal Roman-Apostolic Church"? They pretend there is no Catholic <term>Catholic: meaning "universal" or "whole," here used in its original sense rather than as a title for the Roman Church.</term> or Apostolic Church other than that which simply and blindly gives place to the decrees of modern Rome, her Councils, and above all, her Popes. Let us now move on to the life and customs of our Waldensians.

### CHAPTER XXX.

->On the Life and Manners of the Waldensians.<-

It is not enough that we are generally convinced of the purity of the Waldensian doctrine, both through their own public and private writings and those of their most severe opponents. If the Life does not harmonize with the Doctrine, it is but clanging brass and a tinkling cymbal <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1, emphasizing that outward profession without love or virtue is hollow.</note>, the voice of Jacob and the hands of Esau; in short, breaking down with one hand what is built up with the other. Woe to those (as the Lord Christ once said to the Jews as a reproach) who speak much and do nothing. For far from being saved by their words, they would only increase and hasten their damnation, making themselves equal to that wicked servant in the Gospel who was punished with more lashes than the ignorant one. Just as many bells hung from the hem of the robes of the ancient Priests, there were no fewer pomegranates <note>Reference to Exodus 28:33-34. The bells symbolized the sounding of the word, while the pomegranates symbolized the fruit of good works.</note>, to teach them that one should do no less than one says. Faith is active through Love; and it is the work of hypocrites to boast of possessing faith without having works in any way. *Faith without Works is dead.* Since we have investigated until now what the Faith of the Waldensians was throughout the ages, it now follows for us to see how it stood with their works, life, conduct, manners, and discipline. It is true that in various places, drawn and cited from the writings of their opponents regarding their Faith, such beautiful and respectable declarations of the sincerity of their lives are found that they should be sufficient to clear them of all slander. However, to bury these slanders once and for all, it is necessary that we add the following striking and irrefutable proofs; the more so because there has always been, and still is today, a great number of ignorant or wicked people who ceaselessly bark at those poor Waldensians as if they were a pack of monsters and pests of the Land and Church, in order to incite the powers to the destruction of their remnants—exactly in the same manner as the ancient Heathens used to do toward the Believers of the Early Church. And truly, when I imagine how the Marquis of Pianezza <note>Andrea Gastaldo, Marquis of Pianezza (1611–1675), the commander responsible for the "Piedmontese Easter" massacre of 1655.</note> boasted in the Turin Council *for the propagation of the Faith and the extirpation of Heretics* <note>original: "de propaganda Fide & exstirpandis Hæreticis"</note>, shortly before he had those outrages committed in the Valleys in the year 1655 (he showed in that Council the humble petition that the Deputies of the Valleys had handed to him to deliver to their Sovereign, or Madame Royale <note>Christina of France (1606–1663), the Duchess of Savoy and mother of Duke Charles Emmanuel II.</note>, His Highness’s Mother, in which they complained of several hardships inflicted upon them; without the said Deputies themselves, or their agent Gibellyn, being heard in any way before he had fallen on his knees before the Lord Archbishop, who was the head of that assembly, and in that state asked him for permission), I do not doubt—and the outcome has only too much shown and confirmed it—that he uttered words nearly identical to those with which Cecilius, in the writings of Minutius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix was a 3rd-century Christian apologist; his dialogue "Octavius" defends Christianity against the Roman Cecilius.</note> (whom St. Jerome calls a great Orator of Rome), sought to wipe the name and memory of the poor Christians from the earth:

...could have given [this account], or ever sent it to the Roman Court, if he had not been more than sufficiently convinced of the truth? <margin>A certain Inquisitor according to Freherus's Writers.</margin>
Yet he is not the only one who speaks so explicitly in their favor in this matter. A certain writer who, along with others, was published in Hanau by one Freherus under the title *Rerum Bohemicarum Scriptores* <note>Latin: "Writers of Bohemian Affairs." Freherus refers to Marquard Freher (1565–1614), a German jurist and historian.</note>, reports on page 231, line 44, about another Inquisitor, formerly appointed against those Waldensians from whom the Bohemians had received their doctrine—being subsequently, as we have proven elsewhere, exactly the same as those from the Valleys—that he begins a certain book written by him against the Leonists <note>Leonists: A common medieval name for the Waldensians, likely derived from their association with the city of Lyon or their leader, Peter Waldo.</note>, or Waldensians, with these very words: *cognoscuntur Hæretici per mores & verba: sunt enim in moribus compositi & modesti, superbiam in vestibus non habent* <note>Latin: "Heretics are known by their manners and words: for they are composed and modest in their behavior; they have no pride in their clothing."</note>: the Heretics are recognized by their customs and words: for they are very modest and restrained in their lives, and they do not practice pride in their clothing. So also on page 232, line 42, and page 1602, line 48: *casti sunt Leonistæ: qualibet naturæ turpia devitant & suos subditos ad eadem diligenter informant* <note>Latin: "The Leonists are chaste: they avoid all natural shames and diligently instruct their subjects in the same."</note>: that is, the Leonists conduct themselves purely and avoid everything that nature deems shameful, diligently instructing those under them in the same.

<margin>Thuanus.</margin>
With which the testimony of Thuanus <note>Jacques-Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman.</note> in the 27th book agrees very well, in which he gives this assurance: *præcipue castitatis cura & honos inter Valdenses, adeo ut vicini, qui alioqui ab eorum religione alieni erant, ut filiarum suarum pudicitiæ consulerent, vim a licentioso milite veriti, eas Valdensium curæ ac fidei committerent. — omnem a se & suis cœtibus iniquitatem eliminabant* <note>Latin: "Chastity is especially cared for and honored among the Waldensians, so much so that neighbors, who were otherwise strangers to their religion, would commit their daughters to the care and faith of the Waldensians to preserve their modesty, fearing violence from licentious soldiers. — they eliminated all iniquity from themselves and their assemblies."</note>: as if he were saying: especially among the Waldensians, chastity is held in esteem and honor, so much so that the neighboring peoples, who otherwise kept themselves distant from their religion, entrusted their daughters to the care and loyalty of the Waldensians, in order to better ensure their purity, for which they were fearful in view of the unrestrained soldiers. — They cast out from themselves and from all their gatherings all godlessness and unrighteousness.

<margin>Baronius.</margin>
Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian who wrote the "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> also reports concerning the year 1270, volume 12, no. 10: *Valdenses tactum omnem mulierum refugisse* <note>Latin: "The Waldensians fled from all contact with women."</note>, meaning that they always very diligently fled all intercourse with women—that is, dishonest or impure contact.

<margin>Rudolph of Coggeshall.</margin>
But their chastity is also proven particularly by a specific incident involving a girl, described by a certain English monk, Rudolph of Coggeshall, and cited by Boxhornius <note>Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a Dutch scholar and historian.</note> on pages 717 and 718 of his *General Memorial-Book*, where he also confirms what he had said regarding the holiness of the Waldensians' life; consisting in this: that the same girl, finding herself very strongly pressured by a lustful and wanton young man to commit fornication, gave these words in response: "Heaven forbid, o good companion, that I should ever make such an acquaintance with you, or with anyone in the world. For I know well that if I lost my honor in this way and defiled my body, I would have to expect eternal damnation." Hearing which, he continues, our Master Gervase immediately concluded that she was of the filthiest sect of the Publicans <note>Publicans: A derogatory term used in the Middle Ages for various heretical groups, including the Waldensians and Cathars.</note>, or Waldensians, etc. *Quod audiens Magister Gervasius... intellexit protinus, hanc esse de impurissima Secta Publicanorum* <note>Latin: "Hearing this, Master Gervase... immediately understood that she was from the most impure sect of the Publicans."</note>, etc. (these are the monk's own words). See here once again in passing, dear reader, by what sign that clever teacher could recognize the "filthiness" of the Waldensian doctrine: namely, by the exemplary chastity of their young maidens.

## General Memorial-Script

<margin>The Dominican Monk Lielenfinius.</margin>
The holiness and integrity of life has consistently shone through among the Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement that sought to return to apostolic simplicity, often persecuted by the established Church.</note> in such a way that a certain Dominican, Jacobus Lielenfinius <note>Also known as James of Reutlingen, a 15th-century inquisitor.</note>, a sworn enemy of the Bohemians—who were disciples of the Waldensians—frankly admits that they were then, as before, good in life and morals, truthful and sincere in their speech, and united in brotherly love; only their faith is incorrigible and most evil, as has been shown in my book: "good in morals and life, truthful in speech, united in brotherly love; only their faith is incorrigible and most evil, as appeared in my treatise." <note>original Latin: *boni in moribus & vita, veraces in fermone, in charitate fraterna unanimes; fed tantum fides eorum est incorrigibilis & pessima, ut patuit in tractatu meo.*</note> What can Slander itself find to criticize here in the declarations of such stubborn heretics? If all words must be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses, then these witnesses should certainly not always be suspect to you. Now, what could be said more gloriously of the believers of the purest and first foundational Church itself, than that they were pious, upright in life and conduct, truthful in their words, and that regarding their brotherly love they were but "one soul and one heart"? Is that not exactly the same testimony given to them in the Acts of the Apostles?

<margin>Thuanus.</margin>
And although it cannot be said of this last writer that he speaks only of the Bohemian Waldensians—while the people of the Valleys <note>The Alpine valleys where the Waldensians (Vaudois) lived.</note> might not be so easily cleared, since he takes none to be their disciples in either life or doctrine—we may nevertheless hear what Mister President Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian and statesman known for his monumental work *Historia Sui Temporis*.</note> will specifically say about it in the 27th book of his Histories, which shows us the state they were in in the year 1560. He speaks of it with such dignified words that they are worthy of being read here. "They observe," he says then, "the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, in which the rule of a holy and pious life is handed down. They eliminate all iniquity from themselves and their assemblies. They shun and detest with their whole heart illicit swearing, perjury, dire imprecations, insults, quarrels, seditions, gluttony, drunkenness, fornication, divination, sacrilege, enchantments, theft, usury, trickery, and other such things." <note>original Latin: *Observant Decalogi præcepta, quibus regula sanctæ & piæ vivendi traditur. Omnem a se ac suis cætibus iniquitatem eliminant. Illicitas pejerationes, perjuria, diras imprecationes, contumelias, rixas, seditiones, crapulas, ebrietatem, scortationes, divinationes, sacrilegia, incantationes, furta, usuras, præstigia & id genus alia aversantur ac toto pectore detestantur.*</note> That is to say, they keep the laws of the Ten Commandments, in which alone a guideline for a holy and godly life is to be found. They ward off all unrighteousness from themselves and their community.

<margin>Their own Archbishop Claude Seyssel.</margin>
What is more, the oft-mentioned Claude Seyssel <note>A 16th-century jurist and theologian who became Archbishop of Turin; he wrote extensively against the Waldensians while acknowledging their virtue.</note>—whom we have seen was made Bishop of Marseille and then Archbishop of Turin and the Valleys because he was judged the most capable man in the world to bring them back to the bosom of the Roman Church—likewise admits in explicit words in a certain book that he published in the year 1500 against those poor Waldensians; "that as for their life and their morals, they have been blameless among men, devoting themselves with all their power to the observation of the Commandments of God," <note>original French: *dat pour leur vie & leurs mœurs ils ont été sans reproches parmi les hommes, s' addonnans de tout leur pouvoir a l' observation des Commandements de Dieu.*</note> they have been irreproachable before men regarding their life and morals, applying themselves with all their might to the keeping of God's commandments. Has anyone ever been able to give a more honest and dignified testimony in the Mother Church <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> to the most faithful blood-witnesses <note>Martyrs.</note> of our Lord Jesus?

It would now, after such confessions and declarations given in favor of the good morals and exemplary conduct of the Waldensians—and particularly those from the Valleys—be nothing other than a desire to unnecessarily fatten this book if one were to gather a multitude of other similar testimonies here, which would be easy to do. Meanwhile, if the curious wish to go somewhat deeper into this, they need only look up what The

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

<margin>De Serres, Perrin, etc.</margin> Serres <note>Jean de Serres (1540–1598), a French humanist and historian.</note> describes, under the reign of Louis VIII, the history of the Waldensians and Albigensians <note>Two medieval Christian groups often targeted by the Inquisition for their rejection of certain Catholic doctrines.</note> from the 5th chapter of the 1st book by Paul Perrin, the accounts of the Monk of Vallis-Sernensis <note>Pierre de Vaux-de-Cernay, a chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade.</note>, from Jacob de Riberia, the records of Toulouse, the annals of Burgundy, Hologaray, Ussher <note>James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, known for his historical and chronological works.</note> regarding the most significant dispute, and many other such sources.

And then they shall boldly conclude with the aforementioned Bernard Girard <margin>Bernard Girard.</margin>, who is also a good Roman Catholic, in the 10th book of his *French History*, that there is nothing, to tell the truth, that so provoked the hatred of the Pope and Princes against them as the free-spokenness with which they rebuked their errors and, especially, the lawlessness of the Clergy. This alone is the true cause that made them so mortally hated, and why people have always sought to smear them with many horrific opinions. 

<margin>William Paradin.</margin> Similarly, William Paradin <note>A 16th-century French historian.</note>, in his *Yearbooks of Burgundy* in the 2nd book concerning the year 1209 (pages 247 and 248 of the Lyon edition of 1566), states that the errors and crimes charged against them were nothing but fictions, which had been very wickedly devised. He claims they had committed none of the things they were falsely accused of, except that they criticized the corruption and sins of the Prelates a bit too freely.

<margin>Barbe Vignaux.</margin> It is then no wonder that one of the most prominent *Barbes* <note>The term "Barbe" (meaning uncle) was used by the Waldensians for their pastors and teachers to distinguish them from Catholic "fathers."</note>, or Valley Teachers, named Vignaux, in the book of his *Notes*—which he left us regarding the state in which he still found those Churches shortly before the Reformation was introduced in France—gives this good testimony to those good people on page 4: namely, that they were people of a good and holy life, manners, and religion, temperate and great enemies of sin. 

And a bit further down: "We live in the valleys of Piedmont among one another in peace and holy concord; but we nevertheless make no such mixture that we ever take the daughters of those of the Roman Church for our sons, nor give our sons to their daughters. Meanwhile, our manners and life please them so much that the Nobility, who are lords of the places, and other Roman-minded people would rather have servants and maids from our people than from their own." 

And who knows if it was not also because of this faithfulness and humility in performing their service that they were given the names *Boni homines* <note>original Latin: "Boni homines" (Good Men).</note>, *Humiliati* <note>original Latin: "Humiliati" (The Humbled).</note> and *Patarini* <note>A term often applied to those in the poverty movements of the Middle Ages.</note>, <margin>Hu- Nic. Bertrand. de gest. Thol. p. 31. also calls them Perfecti and consolati for the same reason.</margin> <note>Nicolas Bertrand, in his history of Toulouse, also calls them "Perfecti" (The Perfect ones) and "consolati" (The Consoled) for the same reason.</note> as if to say that they were pious, humbled, and much-oppressed people. One can always see from the history of the Persecutions they endured with what goodness they actually behaved in the years 1560 and 1561 toward their treacherous abusers, and how far they were from satisfying a lust for revenge or repaying violence with violence, or evil with evil. For after a simple defense of their fortifications, during which they were attacked for quite a long time, they were satisfied to see their enemies driven to flight in terror and shame. They made it a matter of conscience not to fully exploit the victory and pursue them, when they would have had to do nothing but kill them since they found no resistance; and they blessed God while others did nothing but vomit curses, mockeries, and slanders against them.

<margin>Davity.</margin> Therefore, the historian Davity <note>Pierre Davity (1573–1635), a French geographer and historian.</note> also says very well near the end of his writing on Piedmont, where he speaks of the Valley Waldensians and wishes to give some reason why the Dukes of Savoy have always been willing to tolerate them there—as one must indeed admit that they never persecuted them except when they were forced to do so by the Roman Clergy; that this happened because of the...

# General Memorial-Record

> "...great goodness and sincerity of those people and the taxes <note>The author highlights that even as "heretics," the Waldensians were valued by the state for their productivity and tax contributions.</note> that they extracted from them."

<margin>Monsieur de Birage and the clergy and laymen of his Council.</margin>
When Monsieur De Birage <note>Renato di Birago (1506–1583), a diplomat and later Cardinal who served the French crown.</note>, the King’s Governor in the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>A territory in the Piedmont region of modern-day Italy, then under French control.</note> during the time of the deadly atrocities in France occurring in the year 1572 <note>A reference to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, where thousands of French Protestants (Huguenots) were killed.</note>, received orders from His Majesty to execute all the most prominent Waldensians within his territory at the first opportunity; and when he presented this to his Council—consisting not only of the most distinguished politicians of Saluzzo but also of the Head Dean and other clergy—even that Head Dean, who was by no means as cruel as his fellow lords, dared to offer these reasons to halt the execution of that sorrowful decree,
"saying this among other things: 'Certainly His Majesty has received some false and evil reports against these poor people, and if he had received better information, it would undoubtedly grieve him that this
"sentence against them had been carried out. One can take all those people into custody and
"fill the dungeons with them, keeping them in strict confinement for a time: but
"postpone their execution until His High Majesty has been informed that they are pious and honest people, very loyal in
"his service and living very peaceably with their Catholic neighbors, in
"whom, in a word, nothing else is to be rebuked except that they are of that Religion.
"If His Majesty remains determined to put them to death after that, there will always be time enough for it.'" This opinion of the Archdeacon was followed because of its reasonableness; and those miserable people, though heavily imprisoned, finally escaped with their lives.

<margin>The Emperor Frederick II.</margin>
It would also not be fitting to suggest that Emperor Frederick II <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1194–1250) who issued several harsh edicts against heretics.</note>, who specifically established certain laws against the Waldensians, would have forgotten to include their errors and crimes in those laws if he had known of any; for by doing so, he could have justified to posterity why he had dealt with them so severely. Nevertheless, he does not know how to accuse them of anything else therein, except that they had long ago separated themselves from the Roman Church, its service, and ceremonies, as can be read in the 2nd book, letters 25, 26, and 27, of Petrus de Vineis <note>Pier delle Vigne (c. 1190–1249), the diplomat and chancellor to Frederick II.</note>, his Chancellor.

Truly, if the opponents of the Waldensians from the Valleys grant them such excellent praise and so openly confirm the honesty of their lives, one can no longer deny them belief when they themselves—through various defensive writings presented as circumstances required to Kings of France, Dukes of Savoy, and finally to more distant Princes—have cleared and acquitted themselves of everything. This book would swell to an unnecessary thickness if I were to include them all here. However, I must not skip over the fact that their brothers-in-faith formerly defended themselves so well before Vladislaus <note>Likely Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary (1456–1516).</note> (they call him Lancelot), King of Bohemia and Hungary, against the most prominent and shameful slander with which they had ever been stained—namely, the claim that they gathered like a pack of animals and committed all kinds of impurities <note>This "animalistic gathering" refers to the common medieval "Slander of the Sabbat," where heretical groups were falsely accused of ritual orgies.</note>.

<margin>Complaint and petition, presented by the Waldensians to the King of Bohemia and Hungary.</margin>
See here what language they use in a certain letter, the original of which Mr. Perrin <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a 17th-century historian of the Waldensians.</note> declares in the 4th chapter of his *Waldensian History* to still have in his possession, and of which I myself have a certified copy in the mother tongue that is still spoken in the Valleys today (this is a powerful and clear proof that those Bohemian Waldensians had recently come from the same stock, as they had not yet been able to learn any other language), in which they complain about their adversaries who willfully sought to blacken their names; see here their own way of speaking: *Entro las autras cosas* <note>original: "Entro las autras cosas" (Occitan/Piedmontese dialect); translates as "Among other things."</note>, they say, *illi predican en* <note>original: "illi predican en"; translates as "they preach in..."</note>

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

"...like troublesome and barking dogs <note>original: 'ayma cans moleſtos & renòs'</note>, who claim that we hold this as a law among us: 'Give yourself to anyone who asks you'; and that we then satisfy our unchaste and hot lusts in dark and hidden caves with the first women who encounter us, whether it be our mother, or daughter, or wife, or sister. Yet, for more than forty years together, God has so protected and preserved us that one has not even heard of any fornication—let alone any adultery—among us in all that time. In this way, our lives and good works shame and nullify their lives and accusations." It is also very easy to perceive what a loathing they had for wantonness and, conversely, what high regard they held for honorable marriage, when one reads in a book titled *The Book of the Remedy for the Sin of Lust* <note>original: 'Libre del remedi del peccà de luſſuria'; This was a moral treatise written in the Waldensian language, a dialect of Old Occitan.</note>, specifically written against it, what they say in the 21st chapter with these words:

<column-break/>

*The sin of Lust <note>original: 'Lo peccà de Luſſuria'</note> pleases the Devil greatly, is most shameful to God, and injurious to one's neighbor; because the man obeys the most base part of his body more than God, who has forbidden it. A loose woman robs a fool not only of his possessions but of his very self. He who works in this vice keeps faith with no one; thus David had his faithful servant killed because of his wife, and Amnon corrupted his own sister Tamar. This vice takes away the inheritance of many, as is said of the prodigal son, who dissipated his substance by living lustfully. Balaam chose this sin above all others to cast down the children of Israel by making them sin; for which sin twenty-four thousand men died. This sin blinded Samson and perverted Solomon: and many have perished through the beauty of women. Fasting and prayer are the remedy for this sin, and drawing oneself back! For other vices can be conquered by fighting: but this one is conquered by fleeing and not making oneself familiar with it.*

<margin>
Teaching of the Waldensians against lust.
</margin>

As if it were written there: the sin of Lust <note>term: 'Geyligheyt' (Dutch) or 'Luſſuria' (Occitan) — in this 17th-century context, it refers to sexual immorality or lewdness.</note> is highly pleasing to the Devil and is no less displeasing to God; indeed, it insults our neighbor in no small way. Namely, in it, man obeys the despised member of his body more than God, who has forbidden it. Such a frantic woman robs the fool not only of all his goods but also of himself. This sin also causes their faithful lovers to break all trust and faith in every circumstance. Thus did David <note>A reference to King David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband, Uriah.</note> bring about the death of his faithful servant on account of his wife; thus did Amnon violate his own sister Tamar. This sin consumes the inheritance of many, as we see in the Prodigal Son, who spent his goods through a lustful life. Balaam <note>A biblical figure who, according to tradition, advised the Moabites to entice the Israelites into sexual immorality to bring God's judgment upon them.</note> also chose only this sin out of all others to plunge the children of Israel into all wickedness and evil together: at which time this sin caused as many as 24,000 men to lose their lives miserably. This sin made Samson blind and turned Solomon astray: in a word, many have perished through the beauty of women. Now, fasting and prayer, as well as the cutting off of all familiarity, are a remedy against this sin. For while one can bring down other sins while fighting them, this one is conquered without needing to be present—indeed, even by fleeing: as we can see...

---

<margin>And concerning Marriage.</margin>
Concerning the practice of Marriage, they use these words, which may be read in certain of their books regarding the Virtues, in the chapter on marriage: *Marriage is an indissoluble bond <note>Original: "Matrimoni es ligam non desligivol"</note>, which cannot be untied until death, except, as Jesus Christ says, by reason of fornication; and Saint Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7: do not separate the wife from the husband, nor the husband from the wife. Marriage was ordained by God in Paradise; it is a remedy to avoid fornication, and of this St. Paul says: let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband; for the husband must love his wife as Christ loves His Church, and the married must live holily with their children in the fear of God.* Marriage is an unbreakable bond, which—according to the words of our Savior—cannot be dissolved before death except in cases of adultery. St. Paul wrote these words in the 7th chapter of his first letter to the Corinthians: the woman, he says, shall not separate herself from the man, nor the man from the woman. Marriage was first instituted in Paradise as a means for avoiding harlotry, and therefore the aforementioned Apostle speaks thus: let every man have his own wife and every wife her own husband, etc.; and again, let the man love his wife just as the Lord Jesus loves His Church. Those who are married are therefore obliged to live holily with their children in the fear of the Lord.

<margin>Notable history.</margin>
Finally, one must not overlook what Charles du Moulin <note>A famous 16th-century French jurist known for his work on customary law and his leanings toward the Reformation.</note> relates on pages 56 and 57 of his book on French Sovereignty. He describes how Pope Innocent III, through his legate Julian, did not cease to urge Louis XII, King of France, to utterly root out the remnants of the Waldensians, or Albigensians <note>The Albigensians were a religious group in Southern France targeted by the Catholic Church during the Albigensian Crusade; they were often grouped with the Waldensians by later historians.</note> of Languedoc and Provence, from the face of the earth. The Pope proclaimed, he says, that they were sorcerers, practitioners of incest, and similar folk, and that the King would earn great merit before God and the Roman See if he completely destroyed those abandoned, godless people and gave no ear to their appointed delegates. To this presentation, the King gave this answer: "Even if I were at war with the Turk, or the Devil himself, I could not refuse to hear what he had to say." Whereupon the delegates of the Waldensians from Mérindol and Cabrières, having obtained a hearing, boldly spoke these words before the King:
> Sire, it will not be of your own volition, but only through the instigation of the Pope, if you fall upon us with war; for he is our false accuser, because we do not recognize him as that which he usually wishes to represent himself, nor do we listen to him in any way, as he does his best to lead us astray through his errors. Meanwhile, we believe the Gospel, the Word of God contained in the Holy Bible and the Apostles' Creed <note>The "Apostels Hooftbegrip des Geloofs" refers to the core tenets of the Christian faith used by many denominations.</note>, just as your Majesty and his people profess to believe; in confirmation of which we also baptize our children. We also accept and observe the Commandments of the Lord. If we are then found to believe or live otherwise, we are most willing to die. But if the matter is different, as it is in deed and truth, we most humbly pray your Majesty that, before we are put to death, it may be diligently investigated whether the situation is so or not. The King then sent to them the Lords N. Fumet, who usually [handled] his petitions—

> „ ...finally <note>French: *son Maître de Requêtes*, a high-ranking judicial officer in the French court</note> and one William Parvy <note>original: Willem Parui</note>, of the Order of Saint Dominic and a Doctor of Theology from the Sorbonne, accompanied by his own Confessor. Having searched the districts and churches of the Waldensians, they found no images <note>In this context, religious idols or statues</note> at all therein, nor could they see the slightest trace of the service of the Mass <note>Dutch: *Misdienst*</note> or any preparation for church ceremonies that were customary among the Roman Catholics. Having thereafter also conducted a very thorough investigation of their lives and alleged crimes, it was so far from the case that they heard or saw even a shadow of them, that on the contrary, it appeared clearly that they celebrated Sunday very piously, baptized their children according to the custom of the early Primitive Church, and were very thoroughly instructed in the teaching of the Apostles' Creed <note>Dutch: *Apostels Hooft-leerbegrip*, literally "The Apostles' Main Principle of Doctrine"</note> and the Law of the Lord. Is that not also a beautiful declaration from an upright Roman Catholic?

It would now be very easy for me to bring forward many other such passages, drawn both from the own writings of those Waldensians and from those of their opponents, to powerfully refute such and similar lies by which their enemies have always sought to turn the whole world against them. I even dare to declare outright that not a single error in doctrine, or disorder and vice in life, has been held against them, which I could not even more broadly convince of untruth through their own books and declarations, both from enemies and friends. But would it not be unnecessary, after so many concise and undeniable examples of evidence that I have cited for that truth, to further abuse the patience of the readers? Truly, it cannot enter my mind that there could still be any Papist (to say nothing of the Reformed), however biased and one-sided, who would not now give in, or be quite convinced in his conscience—whether he dare confess it or not—that although people have spread every conceivable evil about those poor Waldensians, the same, as our Savior once said, happened through nothing other than lying. # General Chronicle
### 338

<meta>catchword: they say;</meta>

Was it not also predicted of the Church of the New Covenant long ago, that piety in the same would so far decline and iniquity increase, that when the Son of Man should return, He would no longer find faith on the earth? To this, one can give as an answer: that namely, besides the excellent <term>Church Discipline</term><note>Dutch: *Kerktugt*; the system of maintaining moral and spiritual order within a congregation</note>, to which they always strictly adhered and which helped not a little in preventing the disorders of life, the constant practice and contemplation of the Holy Scriptures—with which they were continually occupied—was primarily very useful in bringing them to the practice of a holy life, as can be gathered from various testimonies that we have already brought forward.

<margin>That it comes from good Discipline and Contemplation of God’s Word.</margin>

We can also add here, in abundance, what is cited in a certain book called *Menippus* by Johann Valentin Andreae in the 35th Dialogue, taken from an old writer of the Roman Catholic faith, which we faithfully translate into our language thus: "All men and women," he says, "both small and great, instruct there night and day and learn from one another. By day, the plowman teaches his companion while plowing, or otherwise receives instruction from another; and by night, all the time they can remain awake is spent entirely in learning together. They even instruct without books. When someone has been a pupil for seven days, he already begins to seek others to teach them in turn, as much as he himself has already increased in knowledge. If occasionally someone is found who seeks to be excused under the pretense that he cannot easily learn by heart, they encourage them with these words: 'Just learn a single word day by day, and so by the end of the year you will still know many sayings, and finally, persisting on that footing from year to year, you will at long last increase somewhat.' I have even seen with my own eyes and heard with my own ears that one of those miserable Peasants recited the entire book of Job by heart without missing a word. I have also known several who knew the entire New Testament perfectly." If they also find anyone among their own who does not live well, they discipline him strictly according to their Church Discipline, always reminding him of this: "The Apostles never led such a life, and we, who endeavor to follow their lives, must also live quite differently." They wish to indicate by this that what they had retained from the Doctrine of the Apostles had also given them the incentive to follow, as much as was possible, the holiness of their lives—just as, in deed, faith and true Religion are shown through works according to the testimony of Saint James.

<margin>Testimony of an old Catholic Writer.</margin>

For this reason, the aforementioned Henrik Pantaleon also says in the 5th book of what occurred in the Church—after he had noted the Waldensians, and especially all the people living at the foot of the Alps, as constant possessors of the purest Religion—that they were also so godly and modest of life, that in all their dealings and way of living, the fear of the Lord always shone forth, and among them a perfect faithfulness and justice was constantly found.

<margin>From Henrik Pantaleon.</margin>

And truly, their busy contemplations of the Holy Scriptures must have been quite considerable, since their great persecutor, the <term>Inquisitor</term><note>Dutch: *Dwingketter*; a polemical term used here to describe Reinerio, a famous persecutor of "heretics"</note> Reinerio, in his book against the Waldensians in the 5th chapter, page 58, has these words concerning it: "The Waldensians know the text of the New Testament and a large part of the Old in the common tongue by heart" <note>original Latin: *Valdenfes Testamenti Novi textum & magnam partem Veteris vulgariter fciunt corde*</note>; as if he said: the Waldensians know the whole New Testament and a good part of the Old in their Mother tongue by heart; adding further with these words, that they also wish to be taught nothing else: "for whatever a Preacher does not prove through the Old and New Testament, they say is a lie;" <note>original Latin: *nam quidquid Prædicator per Vetus & Novum Testamentum non probat, mendacium esse dicunt*</note>

<margin>And from Reinerio.</margin>

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches

<meta>catchword: French-</meta>

*they say*; for everything that the Teacher does not confirm with the Scriptures of the Old or New Covenant, they regard as almost nothing else than a lie.

I confess, however—and sad experience shows it only too clearly—that the Christian Churches (we may even freely say those who call themselves <term>Reformed</term><note>Protestant churches following the traditions of Calvin or Zwingli</note> among the Christians) would be found quite unsightly in their morals if one were to compare them to the <term>Apostolic Foundation Church</term><note>The original Christian church as established by the Apostles</note>; and that, since corruption, greed, bragging, pride, and other worldly vices have penetrated even into the sanctuary, the golden candlestick has great need of the snuffers. For this reason, I do not intend to advocate for my <term>Waldensians</term><note>A medieval Christian movement that preceded the Reformation, known for their devotion to poverty and the Bible</note> in such a way as to deny they were human, and consequently subject to the same weaknesses as others. Indeed, I even confess and sigh before God—since they are my brothers according to the spirit and the flesh—that the Waldensians of this time have strayed quite far from that great holiness and world-renunciation which were the daily work of our blessed ancestors. Nevertheless, I can say this with truth to the honor of the Giver of all good gifts: that taken as a whole and compared to all non-Roman or <term>Doctrine-reformed</term><note>Protestant</note> peoples who have ever come to my knowledge, they are not only surpassed by none (if I did not speak of my fatherland, I would say no one even comes close to them) in sincere zeal for God’s Holy Word and holy steadfastness in the same—confessing it at the risk of life and limb and the shedding of their blood in every occurrence, as all the world has seen in many glorious and nearly continuous displays—but also in simplicity and sincerity, in truth, in faithfulness of conduct, in sobriety of life, and in constant diligence in their labor. This has been especially visible since the <term>Jubilee Year 1650</term><note>1650 was a year of renewed Catholic pressure and "jubilee" decrees aimed at converting the Waldensians or restricting their rights, leading to the "Piedmontese Easter" massacres shortly after in 1655</note>, when those calamitous decrees were taken against them, and is still seen every day on various occasions. Furthermore, they abstain from every kind of game, except for the exercise of arms—especially that of the <term>firelock</term><note>Dutch: *vierroer*; an early firearm or musket</note>—of <term>palet</term><note>A traditional game involving throwing disks at a lead target</note>, of running, and occasionally (though this happens rarely) the honest use of the <term>broad handball</term><note>Dutch: *wyde handkaats*; an early form of handball or tennis</note>. They further reject all games of cards, dice, and other such things, which are even unknown and foreign to them. One could also live among them for a hundred years before hearing them swear an oath by God. They have an aversion to dancing, drunkenness, fornication, and in general to all those "crying sins," holding those who once fall into them as forever dishonorable and despised. The practice of bickering, haggling, and litigating has been so banished from them since antiquity that <term>Thuanus</term><note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian</note>, writing of the customs of the Waldensians of the <term>Angrogna Valleys</term><note>A primary Waldensian stronghold in the Piedmont region</note>, asserts that the first lawsuit ever heard of among them occurred only in the sixteenth century. This happened because a certain farmer, a little richer than his neighbors and desiring to have his son study Law, sent him to the <term>Academy of Turin</term> for a long time; and that boy, having come home "new-wise," filed a complaint before the judge against one of his fellow farmers, demanding compensation or payment for his cabbages, which the other man's herd of goats had eaten. Otherwise, they generally settle their disputes through <term>arbitrators</term><note>Dutch: *goe-mannen*; "good men" or informal mediators chosen from the community</note>.

# General Memorial

living toward Italy from France, that such people, I say, in those places more than all others deviate from that good rule of guidance, as if some of those <term>new Canaanites</term><note>A biblical metaphor referring to the "corrupting" influence of worldly neighbors, similar to how the ancient Israelites were warned about the Canaanites</note>, among whom they have their dwelling, had infected these strangers whom they host. Nevertheless, everyone must confess with me that the magnificent and good **Church Discipline**, which has always been followed very strictly among them, has at all times been the primary cause that these good people have remained so upright within the boundaries of their sworn duty. And truly, a good discipline is the strong skeleton which keeps that body standing upright, and the nerves which move it and make it work. If those bones are crushed, it must necessarily fall to pieces; if those nerves are injured, there must necessarily follow many strange contractions or even a total stroke. Let us then here observe how the Church Discipline was in former times and how it still is today, under which the Waldensians of the Valleys still live and have always lived.

#### Concerning the Pastors.

*All those who are to be received as Pastors among us, while they are still with their people <note>Their families or original communities.</note>, they pray—if it pleases our people—that they be received into the ministry, and that it may please them to pray to God afterwards that they be made worthy of so great an office: but those making the request do not do the aforementioned things for any other end, except to demonstrate humility.*

<column-break/>

#### Concerning the Teachers.

<margin>How one treats those who aspire to the Church Office.</margin>
All those who shall be called to be Teachers among us, request—while they are still with their parents or friends—that it may please us to accept them into the Church service and to pray to God for them, so that they may be made worthy of so great an office. This same request is nevertheless made by those seekers only to show their humility thereby.

<margin>What they have to learn.</margin>
Thereupon we give them very heavy lessons, making them learn by heart all the main chapters of the Holy Matthew and John, and all the Epistles of the Holy Scripture which are called Canonical <note>Referring to the standard books of the Bible accepted as authoritative.</note>, along with a good portion of the writings of Solomon, David, and the Prophets.

<margin>How they are accepted.</margin>
If they thereafter receive good testimony, they are confirmed into the Teaching office by the imposition of hands.

<margin>Their conduct and way of doing.</margin>
He who is accepted later is permitted to do nothing without the leave of the one who arrived before him; and likewise, the earlier one may perform nothing without the consent of his companion, so that everything among us happens with good order.

### Of the Priests, Elders, or Teachers, of the general Alms and Church Assemblies.

<margin>Of the Heads, or Elders of the Church.</margin>
**T**he Heads and Priests, or <term>Teachers</term><note>The Dutch "Leeraars" refers to the Waldensian ministers, often called 'barbes'.</note>, are, as has already been said, chosen from the people according to the variety of workings in the unity of our Lord. <margin>How the Synod is held.</margin>

### V. CHAPTER.

#### Concerning Church Discipline.

<margin>The Necessity of Discipline.</margin>
Similarly, corrections must be made to instill fear so that the unfaithful may be punished and turned away, either from a life of evil alone, or from evil doctrine—whether it be against Faith, against charity, or against hope—or from every kind of evil together. And the Lord Jesus teaches that this must be done through correction. <note>original: "Semeillament devon esser faict corrections..." The first column is written in the Waldensian dialect (Old Occitan/Provencal), which the Dutch author provides for scholarly comparison.</note> *If your brother sins, go and correct him between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother.* The Apostle confirms this same thing, saying to the Galatians: *If a man be overtaken in any fault or sin, you who are spiritual, teach him in such a manner in a spirit of gentleness.* <note>Referencing Matthew 18:15 and Galatians 6:1.</note>

<margin>How to use the same against secret rebels.</margin>
But because not everyone receives correction with love, the Lord teaches what the spiritual leaders <note>original: "regidors spirituals"</note> ought to do, saying: *If he will not hear you, take with you one or two more, that every word may be established in the mouth of two or three witnesses.*

<margin>How against public ones.</margin>
And the Lord intends this for when the fault is not known to many. But it is much more serious when someone sins openly, and the sin is made manifest to all. For such a person, the correction must be made publicly. The Apostle shows this, saying: *Rebuke those who sin before everyone, so that others may also have fear.*

<column-break/>

#### Concerning Church Discipline.

<note>This second column is the 17th-century Dutch translation of the Waldensian text in the first column.</note>

Disciplines <term>Tugtingen</term> <note>The Dutch "Tugt" or "Tugtingen" refers to the formal system of moral and spiritual correction used to maintain the purity of the church community.</note> should also be in use to instill a fear in the people and to punish and turn away the unbelieving, either only from their evil life, or from their unfounded Doctrine, which runs against the faith, against love, or against hope; or finally from both those evils together. Now, that these same things are very highly necessary, the Lord Jesus himself teaches us: *so*, he says, *if your brother sins, go and rebuke him between you two alone; and if he then hears you, you have won your brother.* With this, that which the Apostle writes somewhere to the Galatians agrees very well: *if a man is found in any crime or sin, it is fitting for you, who are spiritual, to instruct him in the spirit of gentleness.*

But since all men do not accept these rebukes in love, our Savior teaches us furthermore how the spiritual heads <note>The leaders or elders of the congregation.</note> should conduct themselves against such persons, when he adds these words: *but when he will not hear you so, take one or two more with you, so that every word remains firm and certain in the mouth of two or three witnesses.* This is nevertheless understood by the Lord to apply only as long as the sin is not yet known to many.

To be sure, the situation is quite different when an open sin is committed and it is considered as such by everyone. For then the Discipline must also occur publicly, just as the Apostle clearly shows in this sense: *rebuke those who sin so in the presence of all, so that the others may be brought to fear thereby.*

-># Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.<-

Ccc 3

<meta>catchword: VII. CHAPTER-</meta>

### VI. SECTION.

| On Excommunication. <note>original: "De l'Excommunication." Written in the Waldensian dialect, an Old Occitan variety used by these communities in the Alpine valleys.</note> | Concerning the Church Ban or Exclusion. |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------|

But, because all those in such a reprimand do not want to have sufficient amendment, nor abandon the evil: Christ teaches that we must do with such people—if he will not hear those of the Church, that is the rectifiers <note>original: "endreiçador," referring to the church elders or governors.</note> by whom the Church is ruled and preserved—that he be under the scourge of punishment, especially for his contumacy <note>stubborn refusal to obey authority.</note>. And the Apostle confirms this same thing: *For I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged as if present, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus;* and again: *If anyone who is called a Brother among you is a fornicator, or covetous, or a servant to Idols, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a person: put away the evil from among you;* and again: *If anyone does not obey our Word, note this person by Epistle, and do not mix with him, that he may be ashamed, yet do not count him as an enemy, but correct him as a Brother,* and as the Lord says, *let him be to you as a Publican and a Pagan,* <note>original: "Publicàn & Pagàn." In the historical context of the New Testament, this meant someone outside the religious community, often translated in Dutch as "tollenaar" (tax collector) and "heyden" (heathen).</note> that is, that such a person be deprived of all help from the Church, and of its ministry, and of the fellowship of its unity.

<column-break/>

<margin>
How the Church Ban must be used.
</margin>
Now, while all men, even upon such reprimands, still do not wish to better themselves or leave off their evil ways, the Lord Jesus also teaches us how one must finally come to deal with such people, who also boldly refuse the Church—that is, those who govern and maintain the same—the obedience they owe. This consists namely of this: that one must subject them to punishment, primarily because of their disobedient rebelliousness. This is confirmed by the Apostle in this way: *For I, truly, though absent in body but present in spirit, have as if present already decided to deliver that man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit and soul may be saved in the day of the Lord;* and again in another place: *if anyone who is called a brother among you is an adulterer, or a covetous man, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a thief, you shall not even eat with such a person: put that evil one away from your midst;* and finally: *if anyone does not give ear to our word, make him known to me through a letter and meanwhile do not associate with him any longer, so that he may thereby come to reflection. Yet do not hold him as an enemy, but reprimand him as a brother.* The Lord Christ had even set this example for the Apostle: *let such a person,* he said, *be to you as a heathen and as a tax collector;* that is, let him remain excluded from all help and service of the Church and from all fellowship of its union.

General Memorial-Writ

### VII. MAIN SECTION.

| On Marriage. <note>original Occitan: "Del Mariage."</note> | Concerning Marriage. <note>original Dutch: "Vannet Houwelik."</note> |
|--------------|------------------|

<margin>In what degrees of kinship marriage can exist.</margin>
Marriage should be performed according to the degrees <note>referring to degrees of consanguinity or blood relation.</note> which God has permitted, and not according to those which He has forbidden; but it should by no means be done according to the conscience of those of the Pope <note>referring to the Roman Catholic Church's complex laws on marriage which required special permissions.</note>, even if one has given him no gold or silver to obtain a dispensation. For that which God has not forbidden can be done without him.

<margin>Whose consent is required.</margin>
The marital bond of Holy Marriage should not be made without the consent of the parents of both parties: for children belong to the Father and the Mother.

<column-break/>

Marriage must be entered into by Christians only according to the degrees of kinship that the Lord allowed, and not according to those he forbade. Meanwhile, one need not make any difficulty regarding those rules of the Pope, even if one had not given him gold or silver for his ecclesiastical letters of permission <note>The author is criticizing the practice of paying for "dispensations" to marry within degrees of kinship forbidden by Catholic canon law.</note>. For all that which is not forbidden by God, may be done very freely without the knowledge of the Pope.

The parents of both sides must always be recognized regarding permission for the bond of Holy Marriage. For children belong to their Fathers and Mothers.
