### VIII. MAIN SECTION.

| Of the Tavern. <note>original Occitan: "De la Taverna."</note> | Concerning the Tavern. <note>original Dutch: "Vande Kroeg."</note> |
|----------------|--------------|

<margin>How harmful the Tavern is.</margin>
The Tavern is a fountain of sin and a school of the Devil, where he performs his miracles in the way they suit him. In the Holy Church, God is accustomed to show His virtues or His miracles, such as giving sight to the blind, making the lame walk, the mute speak, and the deaf hear: but the Devil does in the Tavern the exact opposite. For when the glutton goes to the Tavern, he goes there upright, and when he returns he often cannot support himself, and has almost lost his sight, hearing, and speech, as well as his sense, reason, and memory. Such are the miracles that the Devil works in the Tavern. The lessons that are read in this school of the Devil are gluttony, swearing and perjury, lying, blasphemy, and the denying of God, and the saying and doing of many other sins; for in the Tavern are prepared brawls, slanders, contentions, and homicides.

<margin>The innkeepers share in the guilt.</margin>
And the innkeepers, who permit this, are partners in all the sins and the evil that—

<column-break/>

The Tavern is a well of sin and the School of the Devil, where he works fine miracles in his own fashion. For just as God is always accustomed to show His powers and perform His miracles in His Church—at which time He gives the blind their sight, makes the lame walk, the mute speak, and the deaf hear—so the Devil does the opposite in the Tavern. For when the glutton goes to the Tavern, he can still walk straight on his limbs; but when he returns, he has enough to do just to keep himself upright, and has as it were lost his sight, hearing, and speech. Behold there the opposite miracles which the Devil can do in the Tavern. Also the lessons that are recited in that schoolroom of Satan are foul gluttony, drunkenness, perjuries, lies, blaspheming and denying God, and committing many other sins against Him. For it is primarily in the Tavern that all strife, slander, quarreling, and homicides are born.

Now the Tapsters <note>or Innkeepers; those who serve alcohol.</note>, who permit that, are themselves not a little guilty of all those sins and evil—

### IX. MAIN SECTION.

### Of the Dance. ->Concerning Dancing.<-

The Dance <note>original Occitan: "Lo Bal"</note> is the procession of the Devil, and whoever enters the Dance, enters into his procession. Of the Dance, the Devil is the guide, the middle, and the end. For every step a man takes in the dance, he takes a corresponding leap into hell. In the Dance one sins in many ways: in walking, for all the steps are numbered; in touching, in ornament, in hearing, in seeing, in speaking, in songs, in lies, and in vanities. The Dance is nothing other than misery, sin, and vanity. Therefore we wish to show concerning the Dance, first by the testimony of Scripture, and thereafter by many reasons, how great an evil a thing it is to dance. The first testimony which we place here is that which is read in the Gospel, where the female player and dancer <note>Referring to Salome, the daughter of Herodias.</note> caused the head of Saint John the Baptist to be cut off. The second is in Exodus, when Moses approached the company and saw the calf, and threw the tablets from his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain; thereafter he took the sons of Levi and they slew twenty-three thousand <note>While Exodus 32:28 typically records 3,000, the author here likely cites 1 Corinthians 10:8, which mentions 23,000 in the context of idolatry.</note> of the people.

*Furthermore, the ornaments that women wear to the Dance are like crowns for the many victories that the Devil has had over the children of God through them. For the Devil...*

<column-break/>

Dancing is the procession of the Devil, and whoever gives themselves to the Dance, goes <margin>What evil lies in Dancing.</margin> into his procession. The Devil is the leader, the middle, and the end of the Dance. As many steps as a person takes in dancing, so many leaps he makes toward hell. One sins in dancing in various ways; namely in the walking (for all the steps there are counted), in the touching, in the primping, in the hearing, in the seeing, in the speaking, in the lying, in the singing, and in other vanities. So that Dancing is nothing other than misery, sin, and vanity. And for this reason, we intend here to show plainly, first with the testimonies of Holy Scripture and thereafter also with various reasons, how great an evil dancing may be. The first proof that we then cite consists of <margin>1. Scriptural proof.</margin> that which we read in the Holy Gospel, in which we find that a girl who knew well how to dance caused the Holy John the Baptist to be beheaded because of it. The second we see in the first book of Moses <note>The Book of Genesis is the first book, but "the books of Moses" refers to the Pentateuch; here the author refers to Exodus.</note>, <margin>2. Of that kind.</margin> namely, when he approached the Assembly and saw them dancing in a circle around the calf, he threw down the tablets of the Law, which he himself carried in his hands, at the foot of the mountain and broke them; and thereafter, taking the children of Levi with him, he cut down twenty-three thousand heads of the people.

But now to begin with the other reasons: the finery with which the women <margin>1. reason.</margin> adorn themselves for the Dance are nothing but so many crowns of various victories...

The fourth reason is that those who dance break the covenant <term>covenant: a formal, sacred agreement</term> which they made with God at their Baptism, when their godparents said on their behalf: "I renounce the Devil and all his pomps." The dance is the pomp and the Mass of the Devil, and whoever enters the dance enters into his pomp and his Mass. For the woman singing at the dance is the Prioress of the Devil, and those who respond are his clerks, and those who are there to watch are the parishioners; the sounds and the pipes are the bells, and the minstrels who play are the Ministers of the Devil. For just as when pigs are scattered, the swineherd makes one of them squeal so that the others gather together at the sound; in the same way, the Devil makes a woman sing at the dance, or plays the pipe, so that all his pigs—that is, the dancers—may gather together.

Furthermore, at the dance, the ten Commandments of the law of God are transgressed. Against the first: "You shall have no other God but me." At the dance, one worships the person whom they study to serve; concerning which Saint Jerome says: "That the God of each person is that which he worships and loves above all things."

Against the second Commandment one sins at the dance, when one makes an Idol of that which he loves.

Against the third: "You shall not take the name of your Lord God in vain." At the dance, one serves the vanity of the flesh.

Against the fourth: Through the dance, Sunday <note>The Day of Rest</note> is profaned by dancing.

Against the fifth: "Honor your father, etc." In the dances, the fathers are often...

<margin>4. reason.</margin> The fourth reason is this: namely, that all those who hold such Balls <note>The Dutch uses "Baletten," referring to social dances or balls.</note> break the covenant that they entered into with God in Baptism, when their Godparents solemnly testified for them that they renounced the Devil and all his pomp. Now, dances are a devilish pomp, and he who allows himself to be found at a Ball gets involved in his pomp, indeed even in his Mass. For a young lady who sings while dancing is a Priestess of the Devil; those who answer her are the Clerks or servers; the onlookers are the people from the parish or district; the flutes and the noise are the sound of bells; and finally, the musicians are the servants of the Devil. Indeed, just as a swineherd, when the herd is somewhat scattered, makes just one of them scream to pull all the others together at once; so the Devil also makes but one woman sing at the dance, or one person play the flute, to make all the other pigs—that is, those little dancers—come together all at once with a dash.

<margin>5. reason.</margin> Added to this is that at a Ball, one transgresses all the ten Commandments of the Lord. Namely, one sins in dancing against the first Commandment: *You shall have no other God but me;* because the person one seeks to please is almost as if worshiped. In which sense Saint Jerome

### D d d

*...often dishonored: for many pacts are made without their counsel.* <note>This likely refers to the "rightful honor" of parents or guardians mentioned in the previous page's discussion of the fourth and fifth commandments.</note>

*Against the sixth. You shall not kill.* <note>original Latin: "Non occides"</note> One is often killed at the Ball: for every person who studies to please others kills as many in the soul as he causes to lust.

*Against the seventh. You shall not commit adultery,* <note>original Occitan: "Non scortarès"</note> is a sin in the Ball: for the person, whether male or female, commits adultery as much as they lust. As the Lord says: *Everyone who sees a woman to lust after her, has already committed adultery with her in his heart.*

*Against the eighth. You shall not steal.* One sins at the Ball against this commandment when one person steals the heart of another from God.

*The ninth. You shall not bear false witness.* Against which one sins when they speak falsely against the truth.

*The tenth. You shall not covet, etc.* One sins against this commandment when women covet the ornaments of others: and when men covet the wife, daughters, or female servants of their neighbor.

<margin>6. Reason.</margin> *Therefore it can be shown how great an evil it is to Dance by the multitude of sins committed by those who Dance. For they sin in walking: for they do not move except by measure and number. Regarding which Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> said: The miserable one does not know that for every step he takes in the Ball, he approaches hell by just as many leaps.*

*They sin in their finery in five ways. The first; for they become proud. The second; for they inflame the hearts of the onlookers to lust. The third; for they bring shame to other people who do not have such ornaments, giving them cause to covet*

<column-break/>

...their rightful honor is not seldom deprived thereby. For many gatherings of such dances are held, without those [parents] even being asked for their consent.

One also offends in the dance against the sixth Commandment; *you shall not kill:* because many are killed at a Ball. And truly every young lady, who seeks to please another, kills as many youths, even regarding the soul, as she arouses to hot desire.

It is no better with the seventh; *you shall not commit adultery.* For everyone, whether of the male or female sex, commits as much adultery and unchastity in dancing as they desire other persons. *For all those, so state the words of our Savior, who look upon a woman to desire her, have already committed adultery with her.*

The eighth, *you shall not steal*, also does not go free. For in dancing it is violated by those who turn another's heart away from God.

One also offends against the ninth, *you shall not bear false witness*, when one commonly speaks against the truth and better knowledge during the dance.

Against the tenth, *you shall not covet*, etc. one also offends through dancing, when the womenfolk—as usually happens—covet each other's jewelry, and the men covet the wife, daughters, or maids of their neighbor. <note>original Dutch: "evenaaften," meaning one's equal or neighbor.</note>

Finally, it can yet be shown through a multitude of other sins committed by such dancers, how great an evil dancing is. Namely, they sin first with their gait, as they do not take a step that is not arranged by number and measure. Concerning which St. Augustine uses these words very aptly: "The wretched dancer does not consider that he takes as many leaps toward hell as he takes steps in dancing."

They also sin in their finery in five ways: firstly when they pride themselves therein; thereafter when they inflame the hearts of the spectators to lust thereby; thirdly, when they thus make all others ashamed who do not have such adornments; fourthly...

### CHAPTER X.

*How the people should behave toward those on the outside.* <note>original Occitan: "En qual modo lo poble se deo haver à quelli de defora." This section outlines the ethical code for interacting with the non-Waldensian world.</note>

1. *They must not love the world.*
2. *They must flee evil company.*
3. *If it is possible, they must have peace with all.*
4. *They must not contend in judgment.* <note>This refers to avoiding lawsuits or secular courts.</note>
5. *They must not avenge themselves.*
6. *They must love their enemies.*
7. *They must be willing to endure labors, slanders, threats, rejections, shame, insults, and all kinds of torments for the sake of the truth.*
8. *They must possess their souls in patience.*
9. *They must not...*

<column-break/>

How the people must live with those who are outside.

1. They must never love the world.
2. They must diligently avoid evil company.
3. They must, if it is possible, live in peace with everyone.
4. They must not plead before the Judge. <note>original Dutch: "voor den Regter niet dingen"; a directive to avoid secular litigation.</note>
5. They must not avenge themselves.

->Concerning a discussion regarding the aforementioned *Barbes*, or ancient Teach-<-

Having now spoken so extensively of the antiquity of the **Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont**, as well as of their Doctrine, Morals, and Discipline, it will undoubtedly be very fitting for us to give the reader some thoughts here regarding the excellent men whom God has used to preserve and pass down those precious jewels to us at all times; men who, as we shall subsequently see, have been understood and known of old under the name of ***Barbes***, or "Uncles." <note>The term *Barbe* comes from the local dialect for 'uncle,' a title of respect used for Waldensian pastors to distinguish them from the 'Fathers' of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>

<margin>The fiction of Reinerio regarding the order of the *Barbes* or Teachers of the Waldensians.</margin>
The often-mentioned Monk Reinerio <note>original: "Reinerio." This refers to Reinerius Saccho, a 13th-century inquisitor who wrote a famous treatise against the Waldensians after leaving their movement.</note> gives us in his book, written against the Waldensians, a truly strange description of the office and customs of these *Barbes*. He asserts particularly that there was always a supreme Teacher among them who—alongside two Assessors or Assistants, one of whom he called the "fine elder" and the other his "later-born son"—held the power and status of a Bishop; and that besides these two, there was a third among them in the capacity of a Deacon. He likewise adds that this Bishop gave the **laying on of hands** to other Teachers and, with the same power as the Pope himself, would depose them at his pleasure.

<margin>Refuted by the 1st reason.</margin>
But it is quite in vain that he has attempted to occupy the minds of men with such fictions and oddities, since it is already evident from what we have just seen in the ancient **Discipline of the Waldensians** that the calling of all their Teachers and the manner of their ministry was situated quite differently. For firstly, it is clearly stated there that those who were to be promoted to the **Teaching Office** among them were required to ask the Congregation to please accept them—if they found them suitable—and to pray to God for them, so that they might be made worthy of so great a calling.

<margin>2nd reason.</margin>
In addition, we also see that none of those Teachers were allowed to undertake anything of importance without the consent and advice of his fellow ministers.

# General Memorial

<margin>3rd argument.</margin>
Finally, we find also that they had no other sustenance or clothing than what the good people whom they taught provided for them.

All these circumstances are very far removed from that supreme power and worldly splendor that the aforementioned Reynerius <note>Reynerius Sacconi (c. 1200–1250), a former Cathar turned Dominican inquisitor who wrote extensively about "heretical" groups.</note> attributed to the poor ministers of that "little flock of Christ" <note>A common biblical reference to the faithful few, from Luke 12:32.</note> merely to make the world believe that they were somehow imitating Roman Catholic ceremonies. I am always quite certain that all the histories, all the journals, and other works they have left behind testify completely and entirely to the contrary.

<margin>What kind of people they were then.</margin>
Namely, they were godly, humble, upright, gentle, peaceful, and quiet people, who attended to their Service with diligence and poverty; they kept a watchful eye over the flocks entrusted to them and worked so faithfully in the vineyard of the Lord <note>A metaphor for the Church and its missionary work.</note> that they employed all their time and all their gifts to win souls and bring many to righteousness. They also did this with unspeakable effort, such as night-watches, fasting, and enduring much grief, all slander, insults, and imprisonments, often putting their own lives in danger. Likewise, a great number of them finally sealed the sound Doctrine—which they had proclaimed everywhere with such purity and zeal—with their own blood, after they had steadfastly endured the cruelest tortures that the rage of their enemies’ horrific inhumanity could devise. In a word, they were people who, entirely despising all manner of pride, ambition, splendor, riches, pleasures, and dignities that the world might offer them, lived as "strangers and travelers" <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:13, describing the faithful as pilgrims on earth.</note> here on earth, whose hope was not rooted in these things from below, but in the heavenly Jerusalem and in that eternal house above in the Heavens, not made with hands. Thus they have blessedly fought the good fight and finished their race to receive the crown of glory <note>original: "hooftpronk"</note> that God has prepared for those who sincerely love His appearing. But as we shall see the examples and proofs of their suffering in the following book, I will here—regarding their morals and the care they took for the conversion of those who had strayed and the further sanctification of their Congregation—only transcribe a single Letter (for the sake of brevity I shall add no more, especially as this one will sufficiently show by what spirit they were led, what doctrines they mostly followed, and how, alongside the purity of Doctrine, they insisted very strongly on holiness of life; this is also evident on almost every page of the Writings that the Reader has already seen in this work). I shall here only transcribe a single Letter, which one of those good <term>Barbes</term> <note>The traditional title for Waldensian pastors, meaning "uncle" in the local dialect, used to distinguish them from the "Fathers" of the Roman Church.</note> wrote to the Churches of Pragela <note>A valley in the Cottian Alps, historically a Waldensian stronghold.</note> as follows:

## Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

...according to [our] ability, and not to fall short of all the good principles, usages, and customs given by our ancestors, and [of which we are] unworthy. For it would profit us little to be changed by paternal urging and the light given to us by God, only to give ourselves over to worldly, diabolical, and carnal conversation <note>original: "carnal converſation"; here meaning lifestyle or conduct</note>, abandoning the principal thing, which is God and the salvation of souls, for this brief temporal life. For the Lord says in the Gospel: *What shall it profit a man if he gain the whole world, and suffer the destruction of his own soul?* <note>Matthew 16:26</note> For it would be better for us not to have known the way of justice than, having known it, to do the contrary. For at the judgment of God we shall be without excuse, and damned more profoundly: for stronger torment shall be given to the strongest and most knowledgeable. For which cause I pray you by the charity of God, that you would not diminish, but increase the charity, fear, and obedience due to God, and among yourselves, and all good customs belonging to [you], both heard and understood from God’s part and ours: and to remove and purge from among you every defect and failing that disturbs peace, love, and concord, and every cause that takes from you the liberty of the service of God and your salvation, and the administration of the truth, if you desire that God prosper you in temporal and spiritual things. For you can do nothing without Him. ...laws <note>The Dutch 'regten' here refers to the traditional rules or "usages" mentioned in the left column.</note>, left to us unworthy ones by our ancestors, to keep them in being without diminution, and, as much as is possible, to increase and love them. Indeed, the Lord Himself says somewhere in the Gospel: *what does it profit a man, if he gain the whole world and yet lose his soul?* Truly it would be much better for us that we had never known the way of truth, than that we, knowing it, should do the opposite. Namely, by that one deserves less excuse and greater damnation, because heavier punishments are prepared for those who shall have more knowledge. Therefore I pray you for the love of God, that you not only do not diminish the duty of love, peace, and obedience to the Lord and to one another, but even cause it to grow, and strive with diligent care to follow all the good instructions that you have heard and understood from us on God’s behalf: that you further also cleanse yourself and put away from your midst all evil and misunderstanding that might disturb peace, love, and unity, and furthermore everything that in any way takes away the freedom to serve God, your salvation, and the service of truth, if you otherwise desire that God be merciful to you in temporal and spiritual matters, since you cannot accomplish the least thing therein without Him. <margin>How they lived in general terms.</margin> It is true that regarding some specific circumstances of the Discipline <term>Tugt: the strict moral and ecclesiastical rules governing the Waldensian community</term>, used at that time among the Barbes <term>Barbes: the traditional Waldensian title for their pastors, from the word for "uncle"</term>, these same things are described somewhat incompletely in our writings on their Church Discipline, because several pieces were lost in so many fires <note>Refers to the destruction of historical records during persecutions and the burning of Waldensian villages</note>. The rest of their ancient writings then tells us of their established Synods <term>Synodens: formal assemblies of church leaders</term>, namely that the Barbes or Teachers came together once a year to handle their affairs in a general assembly. They also always scheduled this meeting usually in the month of September <note>original: "Herfstmaand" (Harvest-month), the traditional Dutch term for September</note>, as can be seen in a certain Italian manuscript book from the year 1587, the original of which, along with others, is kept in the University of Cambridge; and they have [continued] that custom...

### Regarding the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches ###

...already for some hundreds of years, there being once in the Valley of Pragela as many as one hundred and forty of those <term>Barbes</term> <note>The word "Barbe" (meaning "uncle" in the local dialect) was the title used for Waldensian pastors to distinguish them from Catholic "fathers."</note> gathered at such a Synod. They have always, it is further stated in that book, strictly maintained their consistories and the practice of **discipline**, whenever it was not a time of persecution. For on such occasions, the Barbes consulted in secret and held their church meetings in the winter, when the deep snow took away the courage of their enemies to go up and seek them. Likewise, at such a time, each one taught just as much in his own home, whereas in the summer they were not seldom forced to perform their worship on the highest peaks of the **Alps**. Some of these Barbes entered into the state of marriage, to show that they did not condemn marriage in clergy. Others remained unmarried—either because they had the gift of continent chastity, or because they were necessitated by occurring circumstances to change their place of residence often, as the greater service of the Church required. Always, they frequently had to make very great and difficult journeys to other believers in foreign and distant lands, most notably in the year 1180, with whom they maintained a constant and faithful friendship; and in particular with those of **Bohemia, Germany, Gascony, Provence, Dauphiné, England, Calabria, Puglia,** and all the rest of **Lombardy**; to which places those Barbes traveled by turns, as travelers and pilgrims, to visit the brothers of those regions and to proclaim the Gospel of our Lord there. 

The other Barbes, who stayed at home or within the Valleys, took care—beyond the proclamation of the Word and the administration of church discipline—that the youth were well instructed and especially those who were raised and destined for the Holy Ministry. They made them well-versed in **Grammar, Logic, Ethics, and Languages**, but above all in **Holy Theology**. Most of them also applied themselves at the same time very much to the art of **Medicine and Surgery** and were very renowned in sciences and arts, as we see in many chronicles; becoming by that means famous physicians both of the bodies and of the souls. Others again, to follow Saint Paul, who was a tentmaker, and the Lord Jesus himself—who until the time of his manifestation, as Justin Martyr mentions in a certain *Dialogue against the Jews* <note>Original: "Samenfpraak tegen de Joden." This refers to Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho*, where he describes Jesus making plows and yokes.</note>, worked and built with his supposed father Joseph—learned various trades and artistic handicrafts.

I think that it will now not be unpleasant to the reader that I here add a list of the names of the Teachers, or Barbes of the Valleys of Piedmont, of whom their writings somewhat mention and whose memory must be blessed by posterity; since from this one can know, to the honor of our great God and Savior, by what means it pleased Him to keep the torch of His Gospel always on the table in those places in such a way that it could constantly shine before the true members of the household of Faith. Behold here then a list of the names of all the Barbes, or ancient Teachers of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, who stood out above all others, especially since five or six hundred years ago, whose notes I have been able to bring together, as follows:

<margin>List of all the Barbes.</margin>

**Peter de Bruys**, after whom they were named **Petrobrusians**, was in high regard at the beginning of the eleventh century, even before the time of Saint Bernard, who first wrote against his disciples.

**Henry**, his disciple, after whom they received the name of **Henricians**, was very famous in the year 1120.

The Barbe **Arnold**, on account of whom they bore the surname of **Arnoldists**, lived in the year 1130 or 1140; and being from Flanders, according to the saying of Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and historian.</note> in his chronological work regarding the year 1163, went to Cologne...

# General Memorial Record

...traveled, where he dared to enter into a public disputation <note>original: "fintwist" (theological debate)</note> against the Teachers of Reims; he was burned there along with nine of his students, just as Caesarius of Heisterbach <note>Caesarius of Heisterbach (c. 1180–1240) was a Cistercian monk and author of historical chronicles.</note> also recounts in the 19th chapter of his 5th book.

**Barbe Esperon**, his successor, was in such a position around the year 1140 that they were nicknamed **Esperonists** after him.

**Barbe Joseph** was a contemporary of his, or perhaps lived even a bit longer than he did, likewise leaving them the name of **Josephists**.

**Peter Waldo** of Lyon also began to teach during the time of this Joseph.

**Bartholomew of Carcassonne** rebuilt the churches of **Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, Bulgaria,** etc., in a very wondrous way, just as the Lord of Saint-Aldegonde <note>Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde (1540–1598), was a prominent Dutch statesman and theologian.</note> speaks of it in the first table of the *Conflicts of Faith*; so much so that one **Matthew Paris** <note>Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259) was a celebrated English chronicler and monk of St. Albans.</note> calls him their Pope and Bishop for that reason, citing to that end a certain letter that a certain Bishop had written to the Archbishop of Rouen, when he was the Pope’s Legate in those regions, to obtain his help and assistance against them. This indeed occurred, so that they were eventually forced to hide themselves in the wilderness, according to the prophecy of **Revelation** in the 12th chapter.

**Barbe Belazinanza** of Verona and 
**Giovanni de Luglio**, who Reinerio <note>Reinerius Saccho was a 13th-century inquisitor and former member of the Waldensians who wrote extensively about them.</note> says followed courageously in the footsteps of Bartholomew, remained in the Valleys and were—as the same writer notes—both held in great high-esteem and respect around the year 1240.

**Barbe Arnaudo Ilot**, who also had no small influence then, held that famous **Disputation of Montreal**, which most French historians still mention.

**Barbe Lollard**, who was a man of great authority in the Valleys of Piedmont and wrote an excellent commentary on the **Book of Revelation**, brought the knowledge of their religion to **England**, where his students were called **Lollardists** after his name. <note>The text attributes the name "Lollard" to this specific leader, though the term's origins are historically complex and often linked to the Dutch word for "mumbling" or "chanting."</note>

### Concerning the History of the Waldensian Churches

**Giacobo Germano** from the Perouse Valley <note>The Perouse Valley (Val Perosa) is one of the three historic Waldensian valleys in the Cottian Alps of Italy.</note>.
**Benedetto Giovanni**.
**Giovanni Romagnolo** of Siena in Italy.
**Barbe** <term>Barbe: A title for Waldensian pastors, derived from the local word for 'uncle,' used to avoid the title 'Father' associated with the Catholic clergy.</term> **Franceschino** from the Freissinières Valley.
**Michaële Porta** from the Pragela Valley.
**Giacobo di Legero**.
**Daniël de Valence**.
**Giovanni de Molines** from the Queyras Valley.

These last two were sent by the other Barbes to **Bohemia** to minister to the Waldensian churches gathered in that kingdom. However, through an extreme lack of caution, they revealed so much to the enemies of those churches that it incited a great and cruel persecution against them. Because of this, the Bohemian churches wrote back to the Evangelicals of the Valleys, requesting that they never again send a teacher whose prudence and loyalty were not better known to them. This event confirms—to mention it here in passing, as we have proven more extensively elsewhere—that the Valleys were like a nursery or academy where a great number of church ministers were trained and drawn from. These men were then sent in every direction, even to the most distant places, to build and sustain the churches that had been planted there by their Barbes.

**Pietro Massone** of Burgundy and
**Georgio Morello** of Freissinières were sent out in the year 1530 to enter into discussion with the prominent teachers of **Germany**—namely **Luther**, **Oecolampadius**, **Melanchthon**, and several others—regarding certain points of doctrine and ceremonies about which they still had some doubts. During the journey, Pietro Massone was taken prisoner at Dijon.

**Stefano Negrino** and
**Ludovico Pascale** (from whom I am descended in a direct maternal line) were also dispatched in the year 1560 to **Calabria** to visit the churches of Montalto, Santo Xisto, and the other neighboring places. On this journey—which provides further evidence for what we just mentioned, namely that the Valleys were the Mother Churches of all others, having not only given them birth but also nourishing them with the milk of the Word through the ministers sent from time to time—Negrino was snatched away and dragged to Cosenza, where he was starved to death in prison. His companion, Pascale, was transported to **Rome**, where he was burned alive in the presence of **Pope Pius IV** and his Cardinals. He was so vibrant and courageous in the midst of the flames that he rebuked them and summoned them to appear before the judgment seat of the Lamb <note>original: "Rijxstoel des Lams"</note> to give an account for their cruelties and inhumanity, as well as for the heresies, superstitions, and idolatries with which they had defiled the Church.

**Giovanni de Mus** of Provence, also sent to Calabria, died on the way near the city of Lucca in Italy. This again confirms the truth stated above.

**Thomaso Bermonde** of Pragela.
**Pietro Benilaque** from the St. Martin Valley.
**Barbe Giovannetto** from the Freissinières Valley.
**Barbe Paolo Bermonde** from the Pragela Valley.

**Pietro Borello** of Villaret in the Cluson Valley was also taken into custody during his journey to Calabria at a certain Italian place called Poccapaglia, but he was completely released after the payment of a large ransom.

<margin>What the word Barbe means.</margin>
If the reader now asks me what that name *Barbe* signifies, I say that it means the same as "Uncle"; and when one addresses a Teacher by that title, it is the same as if one called him "Reverend Uncle" <note>original: "Heeroom." <meta>This page continues the discussion of Waldensian leadership, moving from a list of specific names to an explanation of the titles and social standing of these "Barbes" (pastors). ### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

Still today, as in ancient times, there is a title of great respect and value throughout all the Piedmontese and neighboring Valleys, with the distinction that in the French-controlled areas, the French word *Oncle* <note>meaning "Uncle"</note> is used. To show greater respect, the teachers are called *Oncle Jean*, *Oncle Pierre* (Uncle John, Uncle Peter), and so on, even when there is no biological kinship. In the Piedmontese valleys, the term is specifically *Barbe*, and they are called *Barba Giovanni*, *Barba Pietro*, etc. I still remember very well that even in the year 1630, the teachers were commonly given this title of honor. And truly, who does not know that of old, the first President of Paris was simply called Master John or Master Peter, and that it later progressed from Master to Mister, and finally from Mister to Excellency? 

It has gone almost the same way with the teachers. For in the aforementioned year of 1630, such a heavy plague broke out through all the Valleys that—with the exception of two venerable old men, namely Messieurs Gillio and Grosso—it swept away all the teachers at once. This forced the people to seek refuge in France, and particularly in Geneva, to obtain others in their place. They were very glad to receive ten new ministers, though these men preached only in French, whereas the people had always heard God's Word in Italian before. Consequently, these men began to be called "Sirs" <note>original: "Heeren"</note> and their wives "Ladies" <note>original: "Juffers"</note>; indeed, even the original ministers from the Valleys enjoyed this same honor, being called *Messer Gillio*, *Messer Grosso*, or Mister Gillio, and so on.

<margin>From the word *Barbe* comes the name *Barbets*, given mockingly to the Waldensians.</margin>
Now, from this word *Barbe*, which was so highly valued by the Waldensians, the Roman Catholics of Italy created the term *Barbet* (which otherwise refers to a long-haired dog or water dog). They have nicknamed the Waldensians *Barbets* at all times because they were pupils of the *Barbes*, in much the same sense that the Reformed in France are called Huguenots. So much so that even today in Piedmont, someone of our faith—no matter what nation they are from—is almost never given any other insulting name than that of *Barbet*. For if one wanted to ask a Frenchman, German, or Dutchman if he were a Calvinist or a Lutheran, etc., one would simply say there: "Is he a Barbet?"

***

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

#### On the present nature of the aforementioned church discipline and their ecclesiastical governance.

Although the Waldensians or inhabitants of the Valleys sent delegates at the time of the Reformation to enter into conversation with Bucer, Melanchthon, Oecolampadius, Zwingli, Luther, Calvin, and others regarding certain points of doctrine and church discipline, I do not find that they changed anything at all in that regard, except for the fact that they held views nearly identical to the Anabaptists <term>Anabaptists: A radical Reformation group known for, among other things, their refusal to bear arms or swear oaths.</term> regarding the use of weapons. For they believed that it belonged only to the authorities to wield the sword; but as for themselves, when they were persecuted in one place, it should be enough for them to flee to another, or at the very most to keep themselves in a state of defense without moving a foot to pursue their enemy, even if the enemy retreated of their own accord. Indeed, they were still of that same opinion in the years 1560 and 1561, when their Prince, Emmanuel Philibert <note>Duke of Savoy (1528–1580).</note>, fell upon them with that cruel war, being incited and supported therein by the Pope, Spain, and finally France itself.

### Regarding the Events of the Waldensian Churches.

<meta>catchword: there</meta>

<margin>Two notable changes. 1. Plague.</margin>
But in the aforementioned year of 1630, two great changes occurred in the Valleys. The first consisted of this: a ghastly time of plague <note>The Great Plague of Milan (1629–1631) which devastated Northern Italy</note>, just as had happened exactly a hundred years prior, mowed down three-quarters, or at least more than two-thirds of the inhabitants. Out of the fifteen pastors they had, it left only two remaining: Mr. P. Gillio <note>Pierre Gilles (1571–1633), pastor and historian</note> and Mr. V. Groſſo <note>Valerius Grosso</note>, who were both good, venerable old men, quite worn out by many years of hardship. Because of this, they had to seek comfort in France and especially in Geneva <note>the intellectual center of the Reformed tradition</note> to provide new Shepherds <note>pastors</note> for the remnant of that poor flock. Meanwhile, as we have already touched upon, it was impossible to find any who preached in Italian, as the deceased ministers had done previously. Those former ministers were indeed native to the Valleys, but they used that language because it was very easily understood by all the people, even though in most places they used their old Waldensian mother tongue <note>a dialect of Occitan</note> among themselves, as you have been able to see in their original writings regarding Doctrine and Church Discipline which we have presented here before. The Italian language was nonetheless necessary for them because all public documents must be drafted in Italian, as is commonly done. But there was no other choice: they either had to remain without pastors or manage as best they could with French ones. This was still somewhat easy for those living in the Valleys of Perosa <note>original: "Peyrouſe"</note> and San Martino, and in part of the Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note> Valley, which lies close to France alongside the others. Conversely, it was very difficult for the churches of the said Luserna Valley which bordered Turin. Consequently, Mr. Grosso, who previously had a church in the San Martino Valley, had to be moved to the church of Villar in the Luserna Valley. The good Mr. Gillio remained in his own church at Torre Pellice <note>original: "La Tour"</note>; but to provide for the church of San Giovanni <note>original: "S. Jan"</note>, my uncle Mr. Antoine Léger <note>1594–1661; a prominent Waldensian pastor and theologian</note>, court preacher to Mr. Haga <note>Cornelis Haga, the first ambassador of the Dutch Republic to the Ottoman Empire</note>—then Ambassador of the High and Mighty Lords States of the United Netherlands—had to be summoned back from Constantinople. I must also note here in passing that the Patriarch Cyrillus <note>Cyril Lucaris (1572–1638), the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople known for his Pro-Reformed views</note> personally handed him the Confession of his Faith, which corresponds with those of the Reformed Churches printed in Geneva and elsewhere. I still have the original manuscript of this in my possession, signed by the hand of the aforementioned highly venerable Patriarch. He also requested, through a magnificent letter in his own hand written shortly before he was so cruelly put to death <note>he was strangled by the Janissaries in 1638 on suspicion of treason</note>, that my aforementioned uncle would please testify openly to the whole world that he would certainly and surely die in that holy Faith.

<margin>2. The transfer of the same to the Crown of France.</margin>
The other great change that occurred in the Valleys in the aforementioned year lies in this: that the King [of France], through the efforts of Cardinal Richelieu, brought the valleys under his power to such an extent that he even captured the city of Pinerolo <note>original: "Pinerol"</note>, which is located below the Valleys, along with many other places. Thus, the Valleys then became thoroughly French for the first time, even with the promise that they would be attached to the Crown of France and that the excellent treaty would be kept inviolable—the one Mr. de Lesdiguières <note>original: "de l'Ediguieres"</note> had entered into with them in the year 1592, fully confirmed by his Lord, King Henry the Great <note>Henry IV of France</note>, and his Royal Council, as we shall speak of more broadly in the account of the Valley Persecutions hereafter.

<margin>Several things abolished by this.</margin>
Now this change of State, and especially that of the pastors, dragged many other changes along with it. For they not only left behind the aforementioned threefold sprinkling and the similar breaking of the host <note>original: "ouwel"; the communion wafer</note>, but there

### Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

But in the aforementioned year 1630, two great changes occurred in the Valleys. <margin>Two notable changes. 1. Plague.</margin> The first consisted in this: namely, that a horrific time of plague, just as there had been exactly one hundred years prior, mowed down fully three-quarters, or at least more than two-thirds, of the inhabitants. It left them with only two of the fifteen Ministers they previously had—namely, Mr. P. Gillio <note>Pierre Gilles, a prominent pastor and historian of the Waldensians</note> and Mr. V. Grosso <note>Valerius Grosso</note>—who were, moreover, two good, venerable old men, quite exhausted by many years and hardships. Because of this, they had to seek comfort in France and especially in Geneva, to provide new Shepherds for the remains of that poor flock.

Meanwhile, as we have already touched upon, it was impossible to find any among them who could preach in Italian, as the deceased Church ministers had done previously. Those former ministers were indeed born in the Valleys, but they nevertheless used that language [Italian], as it was very easily understood by all those people, even though among themselves in most places they used their old Waldensian mother tongue <note>A dialect of Occitan or Franco-Provençal native to the Alpine valleys</note> in such a manner as you have been able to see in their original documents, which we have already presented here regarding both Doctrine and Church Discipline. The Italian language was nevertheless all the more necessary for them because all public documents must be drafted in Italian, as is generally the case. But there was no other choice: they either had to remain without Ministers or make do in some measure with French. 

This was still somewhat easy for those who lived in the Valleys of Perosa <note>original: "Peyrouse"</note> and Saint Martin, and in a part of the Valley of Lucerna, which—along with the others—is situated close to France. Conversely, it was very difficult for the Churches of the aforementioned Valley of Lucerna, which bordered near Turin. Consequently, Mr. Grosso, who previously had a Church in the Valley of Saint Martin, had to be relocated to the Church of Villar in the Valley of Lucerna. The good Mr. Gillio remained in the parish <note>original: "fijne"; likely a transcription of 'vigne' or 'fin' meaning territory/end</note> of La Tour <note>Torre Pellice</note>; but to provide for those of San Giovanni <note>original: "S. Jan"</note>, my uncle Mr. Antoine Léger <note>original: "Antonius Leger"</note>—the Court Chaplain to Mr. Haga <note>Cornelis Haga, the first Dutch ambassador to the Ottoman Empire</note>, then Ambassador of the High and Mighty Lords of the States General of the United Netherlands—had to be summoned back from Constantinople. 

I must also note here in passing that on this occasion, the Patriarch Cyrillus <note>Cyril Lucaris, the Pro-Protestant Patriarch of Constantinople</note> personally handed him the Confession of his Faith, which corresponds with those of the Reformed Churches printed in Geneva and elsewhere. I still have the original manuscript of this in my possession, signed by the hand of the aforementioned highly esteemed Patriarch himself. He also requested, through a splendid letter in his own hand written shortly before he was so cruelly put to death <note>Cyril Lucaris was strangled by Janissaries in 1638 on suspicion of treason</note> (which I also still have), that my aforementioned uncle would please testify openly to all the world that he would surely and certainly die in that holy Faith.

<margin>2. The transfer of the same to the Crown of France.</margin> The other great change that occurred in the Valleys in the aforementioned year lies in this: that the King [of France], through the actions of Cardinal Richelieu, brought them under his power in such a way that he even captured the city of Pinerolo <note>original: "Pinerol"</note>, which lies below the Valleys, along with many other places. Thus, the Valleys henceforth became entirely French, even with the promise that they would be attached to the Crown of France and that the excellent agreement would be kept inviolably, which Mr. the Constable de Lesdiguières <note>original: "De L' Ediguieres"</note> had entered into with them in the year 1592, fully confirmed by his Lord, King Henry the Great, and his Council of State, as we shall relate more broadly in the account of the persecutions of the Valleys hereafter.

<margin>Various things abolished by these [changes].</margin> Now, this change of State and especially that of the Ministers brought no small number of other changes with it. For they not only left behind the aforementioned triple sprinkling <note>A traditional baptismal rite</note> and the similar breaking of the communion wafer, but there

# General Memorial-Record

following that, even the use of unleavened bread, in order to conduct the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>The Eucharist or Communion</note> entirely as it is done in Geneva and France. The most important change was that <term>Church Discipline</term> was no longer maintained as well or as strictly as before, because the newly chosen Ministers, accustomed to a softer and more relaxed rule, considered the aforementioned discipline to be too harsh and heavy. They also would by no means tolerate that the Head of the great Valley Church Assembly, accompanied by his Assistant and an Elder delegated for that purpose, should continue the custom of visiting all churches once a year. In that old custom, one of those two Ministers would always preach a sermon in each church, giving them such lessons as he judged necessary after observing their failings. He specifically took very careful note of the doctrine and conduct of the Ministers of each place, being permitted and required to hear not only the Church Council but also the Congregation on the matter, and thereafter report everything to the Assembly—that is, to the general <term>Synod</term> <note>A formal meeting of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine and administration</note> of those churches, which usually met in the <term>Harvest-month</term> <note>September</note>, as has been mentioned before. These new men, I say, no longer followed that old and good custom. Thus, that practice of Church Visitation fell into complete disuse at that time and has remained so. I will now pass over many other small changes of less importance.

<margin>The monthly Church Conversations kept in existence.</margin>
Nevertheless, despite all this, this good system has always remained intact in its entirety and has been restored to a functional state until now, even though it often fell behind during times of war. This was done to keep both Ministers and Churches to their duty and the practice of Discipline, and even to strengthen them both in it. It consists of this: that the <term>Church Conversation</term> <note>A regional meeting of ministers and elders, similar to a Classis or Presbytery</note> of the Lucerna Valley was held on the last Friday of every month, and that of Perosa and San Martino on the first Friday of every month, where all the Ministers and one or two Elders from each church appeared. Each church hosted this meeting in turn, and every Minister of the Gospel preached in it in his proper time. His sermon was subjected to judgment according to the custom of the times: until the year 1630, it was judged by the whole Congregation; shortly thereafter, by the Elders and fellow Ministers; or finally, as is still the case today, only by the Ministers. At these meetings, all disputes were handled that could not otherwise be settled before the local Church Council. Consequently, nothing can be brought before the General Assembly except by way of appeal from such a Church Conversation, or unless it is referred there by the meeting itself.

<margin>Means to prevent all litigation, used at all times by the Waldensians of the Valleys.</margin>
Furthermore, there is a general rule that is observed everywhere: provided that the Ministers and Church Councils do their work well, all those who wish to go to law before a <note>original: "Paufgefinde"</note> Catholic judge are very strictly disciplined. For the Discipline expressly forbids anyone from the Valleys, whoever they may be, under any pretext or for any cause, from ever summoning his brothers to court without first placing their dispute in the hands of the Elders of the Quarter. If the Elders cannot settle the matter, they refer it to the Church Council. Whereupon the Council obliges them to choose <term>Goodmen</term> <note>original: "goemannen"; trusted neutral arbitrators chosen from the community</note> and to make mutual promises, signed by both sides, in which the disputing parties testify that they will accept the verdict of those arbitrators as final and will always follow it peaceably, under the penalties and fines included therein. But if it should happen that even those Goodmen cannot agree, the President of the Church Assembly, if appropriate, or otherwise the Minister of that Congregation, is taken as an Umpire. It is rare to see disputes that are not settled by this means; if they are not, they proceed to the aforementioned <term>Classes</term> and finally, if necessary, to their Supreme Council.

<margin>How candidates are accepted into the church ministry.</margin>
Now concerning the Ministers, they are never accepted there before they have been very strictly tested, both regarding their doctrine and their life. But before they even reach that inquiry or examination, they must—as <term>Proponents</term> <note>From the Dutch 'Proponenten'; these were student ministers or candidates who had completed their studies but were undergoing a probationary period before ordination</note>, or practitioners of Holy Theology—having already been heard in one or two church discourses in Latin and French, or Italian, perform two more <term>Propositions</term> <note>Formal trial sermons or theological defenses</note> or church orations before the entire <term>Synod</term> <note>The governing assembly of the church</note>, one in French or Italian, and the other in Latin <note>original: "Latijn"</note>. If they are judged capable by the delegated Ministers and Elders after all these trials, the President gives them a lengthy discourse on their duties. After the required and customary promises are made, he commands them to come and kneel before him, as everyone in that land also kneels during prayer. Then, laying his hands upon their heads in that position, he prays with a fervent and magnificent prayer for an abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit over one or more of the Called, and thereafter extends to them the hand of fellowship. Afterward, they go to confirm him in the Church to which he has been appointed, in exactly the same manner as is done in France and even here in these Netherlands.

<margin>How they arrange the delegations to the Synod.</margin>
Each Minister, before he can travel to the Synod, must ask the heads of households from among the common people to remain behind at the end of a certain church lesson and subsequently inform them when the Synod will be held, so that they may delegate someone there according to their best judgment. For they do not go there by turns, as is the custom in this country; but only by the choice and election of the <term>Congregation</term> <note>The local body of believers</note>, which has the right to elect these delegates. When they are satisfied with their own Minister (who must stand outside and remain outside the Church as long as the most prominent Elder, or Commander of the Society, asks for the votes on his behalf; but afterward he is called back inside), they request by their letters of commission or authorization that the Synod be pleased to approve that election. This usually happens, unless the Synod has some particular objection or deems it necessary to send him to another Church; in which case the Synod is free to do so. The common folk also always testify in those aforementioned letters what they have to say regarding the doctrine and conduct not only of their Minister, but even of his household. But should any Church not be very well provided for with their Preacher, they simply request a change in the matter, giving their reasons and making known whom they would like to have in his place. Whereupon that Assembly proceeds in the same matter according to its ancient prudence, sometimes allowing such exchanges when it finds that they are required for the greater edification of the Church.

<margin>How they provide for the churches.</margin>
The Congregation may not fill any open vacancy by calling a Minister without the permission of the aforementioned Church Assembly; but according to custom, they must name two or three of those they have their eye on, from whom the Synod then, according to its discretion, grants them one of the group.

<margin>Of the Schools.</margin>
All Churches there are required to maintain and establish a sufficient number of schoolrooms, so well-ordered and managed that they perfectly teach the foundations of the Faith there. But while hardly any commerce is conducted in that land, very little care is taken to let the children learn to write well. For this reason, one finds very few there who, although they can read well and are highly practiced in the Holy Scriptures, can nonetheless write their own names. Indeed, there are not a few <term>Collectors of Taxes</term> <note>Public officials responsible for gathering local duties or tributes</note> who, by means of certain known symbols, keep all their accounts on a square stick, recognizing the names of the payers and the received coins by cutting into it with a knife <note>This refers to the use of 'tally sticks,' an ancient accounting method where notches represented specific amounts or names</note>. There is nevertheless one general School, maintained by all the Valleys together, to which...

# General Memorial-Script

...the most excellent minds are found, from which those are subsequently chosen who are promoted to the <term>Holy Ministry</term> <note>original: "H. Dienst"</note>. They are also brought there to study <term>Philosophy</term>, without having to attend lower schools in any college.

<margin>Of the Elders and Deacons.</margin>
No one is placed in the office of the <term>Eldership</term> <note>The office of the "Ouderling," a lay leader responsible for the spiritual oversight of the congregation</note> of the <term>Church Council</term> <note>original: "Kerkenraad"; often referred to in Reformed traditions as a Consistory</note> until they have been meticulously questioned in everything and have received the proper calls in the Church. But those who are called to it remain so for their entire lives, provided they do nothing to make themselves unworthy of it. There is no more than one <term>Almoner</term> <note>original: "Aalmoeffenier"; an official in charge of distributing charity to the poor</note> in each church, and that is always one of the esteemed Elders themselves; however, he distributes nothing without the order of the Church Council, or at least only by the command of the <term>Minister</term> <note>original: "Leeraar"</note>; which serves as a voucher for him in rendering his accounts.

<margin>How they perform a general visit and Catechism before the Holy Supper.</margin>
The <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>original: "H. Avondmaal"; the ritual of Communion or the Eucharist</note> is served only four times a year in those churches. But before the services of Christmas and Easter—or at least the latter—are held, all the Ministers together oversee all the members of their church in this manner. Every village has its Elder, and where it is somewhat large, there are even two or three. In the house of such an Elder, men, women, manservants, and maidservants must come together on the appointed day, whom the Minister has called out from the pulpit. Being gathered there, the Minister comes to question them one by one without passing anyone by who could already have the slightest knowledge. Indeed, if anyone were accidentally skipped over (as has sometimes happened to me) and not made to give an account of their faith, they would even come to complain about it, as if their Minister had seriously wronged them. There, every arising dispute is also mediated by them, of whatever nature it might be. In this way, the Ministers must visit all their districts, some even twice, others at least once a year.

<margin>Of the Reprimands of the Church Council.</margin>
There, the <term>Reprimands</term> <note>original: "Bestraffingen"; formal corrections or censures for behavior</note> of the Church Councils are also practiced. The Minister himself is obliged first to pray to his Church Council that it might please them to think of the faults he might have committed at any time, and to present them to him in love; after which, by standing outside, he grants them the opportunity and time for this. Being called back inside afterward, the most prominent Elder presents to him orally everything that has been brought against him, in which his way of life is either blamed or praised, and what they would like to see improved therein: which also happens for the sake of the oath without any turning of a blind eye or flattery. On that same basis, the reprimand then passes over all the Elders and Deacons. Meanwhile, the oath I mentioned—both to ensure everything can be said freely and that, on the one hand, no one is overlooked through favoritism, and on the other, nothing is brought forth lightly or out of unfair motives—occurs at the beginning of that whole work with the raising of everyone's hands to God: by which they all equally testify that they will work therein only according to love, etc., and keep everything so covered and secret that it can never be known who said what on the occasion of another.

<margin>How they deal with those who cause offense and what Discipline they impose on murderers, adulterers, etc.</margin>
Now, concerning the punishment for given offense, their current <term>Church Discipline</term> <note>original: "Kerktugt"</note> works in this way. A murderer, an adulterer, and similar grave sinners are first—after a long-term deprivation of the Holy Seals of Faith (I say, of the <term>Holy Sacraments</term> <note>original: "H. Sacramenten"</note>, because no one would even be allowed to stand as a <term>godparent</term> <note>original: "gevader"</note> or baptismal witness for a child as long as he was still under <term>Censure</term> <note>original: "Censure"; formal ecclesiastical punishment excluding one from the spiritual life of the community</note>, even if he himself did not yet go to the Supper; indeed, one would not even marry them or bless their marriage before they were admitted to the Supper again)—and after a long-lasting proof...

...demonstrating great signs of <term>penitence</term> <note>original: "boetvaardigheyt"; a public display of regret for sin</note> under this satisfaction, they are brought back into the peace of the Church. Namely, they must sit for three Sundays in a row during the entire sermon in a special place in front of the <term>pulpit</term> <note>original: "Preekstoel"</note> in the sight of the whole congregation. Now, after the conclusion of the service and before the speaking of the blessing, the <term>Minister</term> <note>original: "Leeraar"; literally "Teacher," the standard term for a pastor in this context</note> announces to the people that such-and-such a person, who has committed such a fault, shall be granted their public amendment. After this, the penitent falls upon his knees and listens to everything the Minister then sets before him; who, on the first Sunday, must show him the heinousness of his misdeed and the judgments of God which he has deserved. The second time following, he sets before his eyes the necessity and fruits of true repentance. Finally, for the last time—while the Penitent prays aloud to God and the Church for forgiveness, promising to edify them henceforth all the more as he had previously offended them—he announces to him, in the name and on behalf of the Lord our God, the forgiveness of his sins and his restoration to the Church. Having then given an earnest exhortation to the people—so that those who still stood might watch themselves, lest they fall—he finally exhorts the penitent very fervently and thereafter concludes the whole work with prayer.

<margin>2. For Fornicators.</margin>
Regarding simple fornication, the same manner of proceeding is used, except that instead of three Sundays, one needs to come for only two, and sometimes even only one Sunday and one weekday.

<margin>3. For Apostates.</margin>
When someone, whether through weakness or however else it might be, has renounced the Faith and attended the <term>Mass</term> <note>The Roman Catholic Eucharistic service, which the Waldensians considered an act of idolatry or "apostasy"</note>, he cannot be readmitted into the fellowship of the Church except through such a public satisfaction for at least one Sunday. All those, on the contrary, who embrace our orthodox religion after leaving the Roman Catholic faith, must make their renunciation before the entire congregation.

<margin>4. For Blasphemers.</margin>
Strict laws have also been established against swearers and blasphemers. But during the full 23 years that I was there in the <term>Holy Ministry</term> <note>original: "H. Dienst"</note>, and the full 12 of my presidency, I never had an example of it. I believe also that one might live among them for a hundred years before one would ever hear them swear by God.

<margin>5. For Sabbath-breakers.</margin>
The same Discipline likewise dictates that all those who profane the Day of Rest—such as those who bake bread in the oven on that day, or carry any loads or bundles, especially if it happens before the setting of the sun—must also be publicly rebuked.

<margin>6. For Gamblers, etc.</margin>
When someone is also convicted of having played with cards or dice (one rarely sees this happen there except among strangers, because all games of chance, as we have already said, have never had a place there), he must, according to the circumstances of time, place, and the status of the persons, perform more or less penance for it.

<margin>7. For Dancers, etc.</margin>
Finally, all dancing is not only entirely forbidden and subject to public rebuke in all cases (they must always kneel for it at the very least before the <term>Church Council</term> <note>original: "Kerkenraad"; the local governing body of elders and the minister</note>), but even those who merely go to watch the dancing of the <term>Papists</term> <note>original: "Pausgesinde"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> do not go entirely free. I know one of the most eminent Ministers of the Valleys, who is still living today, whose wife had been led by a lady from <term>Dauphiné</term> <note>A province in southeastern France bordering the Waldensian valleys</note> (her close relative) without second thought to see the planting of the <term>Maypole</term> <note>original: "Meyboom"; a traditional folk festival involving dancing</note> in the market of <term>Lucerna</term> <note>modern Luserna San Giovanni</note>, around which people were dancing. Which woman, I say, because her husband was the Minister of that church, had to ask another to preside over his Church Council for as long as it took to determine what rebuke she should endure for it, even though she had only seen those dances from afar. On the contrary, we have seen before that the men practice heavily in slinging, etc., but indeed

From this small sample, the reader will now easily be able to judge the whole work, and what form their Church Discipline must still have today, along with all its regulations regarding the other main points. I can always, by God's grace, without in any way flattering my Fatherland—as all those must grant me who, like myself, can speak of it with knowledge—assure with truth that there is nowhere a Reformed Church <term>Gereformeerde Kerk</term> <note>The Dutch term for the Protestant church following the Calvinist tradition.</note> where the Word of God is accepted with more zeal, humility, and diligence; where the people are so well or better practiced in the same and in the disputes of Faith against the Papists <note>original: "Paufgefinde"; a 17th-century term for those aligned with the Pope or the Catholic Church.</note> (for of other heretics they have never heard mention); or where the Ministers and the Holy Service are held in greater dignity and the Church Discipline <term>Kerktugt</term> <note>The system of moral oversight and correction by church elders.</note> is in stricter practice. <margin>Five things highly necessary for the restoration of the Valleys.</margin>But five things are, in my judgment, most highly necessary to bring those poor Churches to that blessed goal. That is to say, they must first, after a serious conversion to the hand of Him who has struck them, maintain a holy, upright, and constant union both among themselves and with all their Heads in everything that is according to God. For they well know that just as the motto of the Devil and his followers has always been *if you wish to reign, divide* <note>original Latin: "si vis regnare, divide"</note>, so on the contrary, through unity <term>eendragt</term> <note>Unity or concord; a core value in Dutch political and religious thought, famously part of the motto of the Dutch Republic.</note> all small things become and remain great, whereas misunderstanding hastens the downfall even of the greatest. Never will their enemies seek anything so much, as they have always done before, as to tear them entirely away from one another, so as to then be able to break one after the other without effort—something they would otherwise attempt in vain as long as they remained bound to one another like a bundle of arrows <note>A common emblem of the time representing the strength of unified provinces or groups.</note>. For this reason, then, just as a snake—filling one ear with earth and the other with its own tail so as not to hear the voice of the charmer—escapes unharmed from his hands because he then has no advantage over it; so they also must stop the ear to all deceptive flatteries of those whom they know crave only their ruin and downfall. They must be fully assured that when these people take it upon themselves to give them this or that advice (as if they loved them so much, or were so afraid to see them entangled in some mournful misfortune, or had such a feigned compassion for them and their families), they are then acting exactly like the Crocodiles, who weep over those they wish to devour. And if they, believing such people, wretchedly desert their Brothers, they can expect no other benefit from it in the end through a righteous judgment of God—as they have had experience of it a thousand and a thousand times—than that which the Cyclops <note>In Homer's Odyssey, the one-eyed giant Polyphemus.</note> once gave to Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note>, which consisted in this: that he should be eaten the very last of all.

Thereafter, it would also be necessary that His Royal Highness, ruling at present by the grace of God, should himself magnanimously take knowledge of all that concerned them, granting them free access to His Highness, listening to their petitions with patience, and after he has rescued them from the violence of a Count...

<meta>catchword: ten</meta>

Count of Bagnolo <note>The Count of Bagnolo (Banjol) was a local official in the region whose conduct often affected the Waldensian communities.</note> and the injustices of some wicked commanders, care should be taken that they be done justice by more reasonable and gentle folk; and that they themselves were also careful to conduct themselves so humbly, so prudently, and so wisely, that they might always enjoy such a precious privilege after having sighed for it for so long. At the same time, through such precise obedience and loyal steadfastness, they should overlook no crimes or criminals, so that they might continually oblige his well-regarded Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note> to fulfill and always increase the works of his benevolence, his gentleness, and his mighty protection.

Furthermore, work had to be done with great diligence, not so much in the preaching of the Holy Word as in the questioning exercises <term>Vraagoeffeningen</term> <note>A form of catechism or instructional questioning used to ensure that the congregation understood the core tenets of their faith.</note>, which their ancestors established with such diligence and fruit; so that not only the youth, but also all sorts of people, of whatever age, status, or gender they might be, might be strengthened daily more and more in the restorative knowledge of the mysteries of their salvation and the living of good morals, and be provided with a good and powerful antidote against both sins and errors.

Likewise, not only the pastors, elders, and almoners ought to hold a very strict hand to the restoration and practice of a good Church Discipline <term>Kerktugt</term>; but even the heads of communities and all people of standing, whoever they may be, must support the same with all their power, as much as is possible.

Finally, that which is everywhere very necessary for the preservation of these same churches: a means ought to be found to have a fixed and suitable state [of funds] for the maintenance of the Holy Service and educational exercises. And here they are in a difficult position, because there is so little opportunity for it. I often saw, before the mournful massacre of the year 1655 <note>Known as the "Piedmontese Easter," this was a brutal massacre of the Waldensians by the troops of the Duke of Savoy, which sparked international outrage.</note>, that in various places the schools declined because no salary could be found for the teachers due to the infertility of the harvest, the freezing of the vineyards, the dying off of the corn, and the lack of chestnuts. The poor ministers themselves were also forced, so to speak, to beg for the maintenance of themselves and their families—from one farmer a bit of corn, from another some wine, from some chestnuts, and finally from another some cheese and oil: and nonetheless, tears still rolled down their cheeks because they could not even be sufficiently satisfied with rye bread.

It was upon the knowledge that Mr. Morland <note>Samuel Morland was Oliver Cromwell’s envoy to the Valleys; he later wrote a famous history of these churches.</note> had of these matters that My Lord <margin>Cromwell provides them a fixed salary.</margin> Oliver Cromwell of blessed memory, who then bore the title of Protector of the Realm, etc. (he was dispatched with that commission to the Court of Savoy in the years 1655 and 1656 and stayed a whole year within Geneva), having received full report thereof, wished to hold back the greater part of the large and rich collection of money that had occurred there—that is, 12,000 pounds sterling and more—and place it as capital to earn interest. For he testified, at the humble request of those miserable Churches of the Valleys, just as he also spoke of it with Mr. van Ommeren, then Ambassador there from the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Netherlands, and with the Messrs. Hirzeell, De Bonstetten, Socin, and Stockar, likewise delegates of the Protestant Cantons; that he, as well as those churches, thought it good that the aforementioned funds should remain with the State in perpetuity. Indeed, he even had a magnificent document drawn up by his Council in Whitehall on the 18th of May <note>original: "Bloeymaant" (Blossom-month), a traditional Dutch name for May.</note> in the year 1658, adding by what distribution he understood and desired that—

<margin>*Their latest affliction.*</margin> And truly, all those aforementioned salaried officials of the Valleys were able to live very well upon that glorious income, until Charles II, by the grace of God, was recently restored to the Crown of Great Britain. For although since that time they continued to persist with such long and costly Embassies and with such humble and moving Petitions for that cause, they nevertheless had to forgo the same with sadness; for His Majesty of Britain could in no way agree to carry out the decrees of a Usurper and Tyrant <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, whose government Charles II considered illegitimate.</note>, or to pay his debts. See there, then, how miserable those Churches are at present, even after those renewed devastations which they endured again in the years 1663 and 1664—as the Reader shall be able to see in the following volume—without having been granted the least penny of tax relief during those three years, which they spent for the most part without sowing or harvesting, having been, on the contrary, most pitifully ruined and plundered and fallen into the heaviest poverty. See there, how they are currently stripped of the means of life for their Pastors and Tutors, etc., without being able to provide for it themselves through any conceivable means. This goes so far that, up to this very moment as I write these things, there are several among them who have fallen two or three years behind and hardly know, as they say, where to turn or what to begin.

# Concerning the Occurrences of the Waldensian Churches.

<margin>A remedy against that.</margin>
And what other help is there against that great evil, which could cause the total downfall of those <term>Mother Churches</term> <note>The "Mother Churches" refers to the original, ancient congregations in the Piedmontese valleys from which other Reformed communities felt they descended.</note>, than that He who has until now so mercifully and miraculously kept them standing, would be pleased in His compassions to move the hearts <note>original: "ingewanden," literally "innards" or "bowels," a 17th-century term for the seat of deep compassion</note> of those in distant regions? We speak of those who have not yet allowed these churches to feel the power of the **Communion of Saints** through financial aid; or even those who have already done so richly, that He might bless them so abundantly in all things that they may be able to do the same once again. Truly, both the individual members and whole churches—and even all the world powers—over whom the Giver of all good gifts pours out His temporal and spiritual blessings, should consider it an honor that they can give a few droplets of their oil to keep a lamp burning. This is a lamp lit from the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>A biblical reference to Malachi 4:2, often used to symbolize Christ or Divine Truth.</note>, which no storm, no whirlwind, and no tempest has ever been able to blow out. May the Lord grant that grace to both the givers and the receivers.

**CATHARISM/WALDENSES.** <note>original: "CATHARISME/VAUDOIS"</note> LÉGER, Jean: *Memorial regarding the occurrences of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont; otherwise known as Waldenses... Part I, all that was published.* Leiden, Jan le Carpentier, 1670. Old parchment (lightly stained) <margin>missing</margin> **20** pages, 371p., **5** pages. With engraved title page, portrait of Léger, folding map and 5 illustrations in folio. <gloss>mark</gloss> f. **2400.-** <note>This refers to 2,400 Dutch guilders, a significant sum reflecting the rarity of the book.</note>

Very rare Dutch translation, by M. OEVERING, of the <margin>L.S.</margin> <note>L.S. likely stands for "Lectori Salutem," a Latin greeting meaning "Greetings to the reader."</note> ~~most~~ authentic history of the religion of the Waldenses <gloss>contains</gloss> ~~and contains~~ all original French, Latin, and Piedmontese texts. According to Pastor Léger, who describes both the <gloss>principles</gloss> <note>original: "beginselen"</note> ~~convictions~~ as well as the organization of the Waldenses, their origin goes back to the 8th century, and this sect can be considered one of the purest forms of the Christian faith.

<summary>This page features a rare 17th-century bibliographic entry for Jean Léger’s history of the Waldenses, a proto-Protestant group. It highlights the book's value, its inclusion of multi-language primary sources, and its claim of the group's ancient, "pure" Christian lineage.</summary>
